text: We assessed how photographer proximity alters American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) behavior using GPS telemetry at Assateague Island National Seashore (2019-2021). Thirty-six breeding adults were tracked; disturbance events were quantified via camera traps. Within 25m of photographers, foraging time decreased by 48% (p=0.007) and nest recess frequency increased 2.3-fold (p<0.001). Daily energy expenditure rose 18% (95% CI: 12-24%) in high-disturbance zones. Results demonstrate that unregulated photography necessitates buffer zones >50m during critical breeding periods to mitigate energetic consequences.

We investigated Dunlin (Calidris alpina) foraging energetics during incubation in the Fraser River Estuary, British Columbia, Canada (2019-2021) to assess impacts of invasive Spartina anglica encroachment. Using miniaturized accelerometers (n=32 birds) and time-energy budgets, we documented significantly higher energy expenditure rates (mean ± SE: 1.98 ± 0.21 kJ/min) in Spartina-invaded zones versus native mudflats (1.42 ± 0.15 kJ/min; t-test: t=2.34, df=30, p=0.026). Reduced prey availability (benthic core samples: 38% lower biomass in Spartina areas) forced longer foraging bouts. Results indicate invasive vegetation imposes metabolic costs that may compromise reproductive success in this declining subspecies (C. a. pacifica).

We investigated the population dynamics of Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) nesting on offshore islands in the Baltic Sea from 2010-2020. Using mark-recapture methods and nest monitoring, we documented a 42% decline in breeding pairs. Generalized linear models identified eutrophication-driven hypoxic events and increased predation pressure from invasive American Mink (Neovison vison) as primary drivers. Climate change impacts on prey fish availability showed weaker associations. Our results highlight the vulnerability of large gull populations to anthropogenic ecosystem alterations beyond coastal habitats.

Previous studies have reported a recent decline in breeding populations of migratory songbirds in eastern and central North America. Several explanations have been suggested: deforestation on the wintering grounds in the tropics and habitat loss, increased predation pressure, and increased cowbirds parasitism on the breeding range. We used these factors to assign 47 species of insectivorous passerines to groups with contrasting vulnerability, and then used the North America Breeding Bird Survey to analyze population trends in these groups on a large continental scale. Variables indexing susceptibility to predation on the breeding ground were most strongly correlated with population trends form 1968 to 1987. During the period from 1978 to 1987, migratory status was also significantly associated with population trends long‐distance migrants to the neotropics exhibited a small, nonsignificant decreasing trend, whereas residents and short‐distance migrants increased strongly. During the same time period, the group of species with low nest location, open nest, and high cowbird parasitism declined significantly. Although it is difficult to separate the effects of multiple factors, our analyses suggest that predation on the breeding ground in North America has played a larger role in the decline of migratory songbirds than deforestation on the wintering grounds in the tropics.

              Estudios previos han reportado una reciente declinación en las poblaciones reproductoras de aves cantoras migratiorias en el Este y Centro de Norte América. Se han sugerido varias explicaciones: deforestación en los territorios de invernada de los trópicos, pérdida de hábitat, aumento en la presión predatoria y un parasitismo mayor de los mirlos (
              Molothrus spp.
              ) en el área de reproducción. Usamos estos factores para asignar 47 especies de aves paserinas insectívoras a grupos que difieren en vulnerabilidad, y luego usamos el Estudio Reproductivo de las Aves de Norte América para analizer las tendencias poblacionales de estos grupos a una escala continental. Las variables que indicaban suceptibilidad a la predición en la zona reproductiva fueron las más fuertemente correlacionadas con las tendencias poblacionales observadas entre 1968 y 1987. Durante el período 1978–1987, el status migratorio también estuvo asociado significativamente con las tendencias poblacionales; las aves migratorias de larga distancia hacia los neotropicos exhibieron una pequeña tendencia decreciente no significativa, mientras que las aves residentes y las aves migratorias de corta distancia aumentaron fuertemente. Durante este mismo período, el grupo de especies con nidos localizados a escasa altura, nidos abiertos y alto grado de parasitismo por mirlos disminuyeron significativamente. Si bien es difíicil separar los efectos de los diversos factores, nuestro análisis sugiere que la predicaión en las zonas reproductivas de Norte América ha jugado un papel más importante en la declinacion de las aves cantoras migratorias que la deforestación de los territorios de invernada en los trópicos.

We investigated how tropical cyclones impact migratory Black-bellied Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola) using satellite telemetry. From 2019-2022, 38 adults were tagged with GPS-Argos transmitters in Delaware Bay, USA, tracking movements during Atlantic hurricane seasons. Mortality increased by 67% during cyclone events (OR=3.1; 95% CI: 2.4-4.0; p=0.008), with 78% of individuals exhibiting route deviations exceeding 200 km. Energetic expenditure rose 42% during displacement (GLMM: z=5.2, p<0.001). Results indicate extreme weather poses acute demographic risks, necessitating adaptive habitat protection along migratory corridors.

<jats:p>During the early part of 1929, a specially severe infestation of locusts occurred in the northern provinces of Tanganyika Territory, an extension of the plague already felt in Kenya. Laying was known to have taken place more or less continuously over the drier country all the way from Longido, west of Kilimanjaro, to the West Usambara Mountains. Successive broods of young locusts had to be dealt with; and in the same area it was possible to see newly hatched hoppers and insects almost full-grown and able to fly. An ample supply of extra food was therefore provided for any birds that might care to avail themselves of it, except the smallest, and certain specialists such as the Hirundines. I was anxious to get some idea of how the birds would react to these abnormal food-conditions, and by the kindness of Dr. and Mrs. R. R. Le G. Worsley, the former of whom was in charge of a sector of the locust campaign, I was able during the first week of June 1929 to make observations in a very heavily infested area between the Middle Pangani River and the South Pare Mountains. I have also to thank the Director E.A.A.R.S. for certain facilities in this connection.</jats:p>

This study investigated morphological variation in coastal Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) populations experiencing habitat degradation. We collected morphometric data (bill length, tarsus, body mass) from 200 individuals across 15 estuarine sites with varying disturbance levels. Principal Component Analysis revealed significant reductions in body size indices at sites with high coastal development and pollution exposure. These findings suggest anthropogenic pressures may drive selection for smaller body size in waterfowl, highlighting adaptive responses to rapid environmental change in modified coastal ecosystems.

Abstract
            
              Despite large genetic differentiation among neighbouring populations of many freshwater zooplankton species, a macrogeographical homogeneity of allozyme variation is generally observed. A study on breeding systems in Scandinavian populations of
              Daphnia pulex
              suggested a latitudinally related cline in breeding system with both diploid cyclic parthenogens and diploid obligate parthenogens at the latitude of 60–61°N. Variation at neutral markers may be more affected by selection at linked loci in such species than in strictly sexual species. In this paper I present a study of variation at five microsatellite loci in a total of 34 populations from small ponds and rockpools on both sides of the Baltic Sea at 60–61°N. Two major groups, which may represent different species of the
              D. pulex
              complex, are defined with the microsatellites. Neighbouring populations show both similar and well differentiated genetic composition. Populations separated by larger geographical distances show only a large differentiation and a macrogeographic pattern. The large differentiation observed at small distances can be explained with small effective population size: variation at the microsatellite loci has been shaped by population bottlenecks followed with expansion in size, and possibly by selection. No conclusive evidence is found for obligative parthenogenesis.

We investigated the impact of recreational shell collecting on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) foraging behavior using GPS telemetry in coastal Massachusetts, USA (2018-2020). Deploying 35 solar-powered transmitters on adult plovers, we tracked 1,284 foraging trips across 10 beaches. Plovers exposed to shell collection spent 28.7% more time alert (p = 0.009, CI: 18.2-39.2%) and foraged 1.2 km farther from nests (p = 0·03). Reduced daily intake by 17.6% (p = 0·012) suggests critical energy deficits. Conservation should prioritize restricting collection activities within 300 m of nesting zones.

Long-term demographic trends of Great Egrets (Ardea alba) in Chesapeake Bay marshes were assessed using mark-recapture (2010-2025). Adult survival (0.82 ± 0.03 SE) declined significantly with wetland fragmentation (β = -0.41, p<0.01), while nestling mercury exposure reduced first-year recruitment by 38%. Matrix models predict 22% population decline by 2040 without intervention, underscoring synergistic threats from coastal development and bioaccumulation.

This chapter describes the influence of intermittent light on broiler performance and on patterns of food intake. Two separate trials were conducted to investigate the effect of lighting patterns of 1L:2D and 1L:3D from one week of age till seven weeks, both in comparison to continuous lighting on female broiler weight gain, feed efficiency, abdominal fat pad weight, and on daily feeding patterns. In the first trial, female broilers kept under 1L:2D manifested the same growth rate as birds under 23.5L:0.5D, but consumed significantly less food and consequently had a better efficiency of feed utilization. Abdominal fat pad weight was significantly reduced under this intermittent lighting regime. As food consumption was not affected by lighting treatment, 1L:3D broilers had a better efficiency of feed utilization. Abdominal fat pad weight at slaughter age of the broilers exposed to 1L:3D was statistically heavier in comparison to the control birds but this difference disappeared when expressed as a proportion of slaughter weight. As 1L:3D broilers reached a heavier live body weight at slaughter age and abdominal fat pad weight increases proportionally faster than live body weight, this means, in fact, a reduction in abdominal fat content for broilers exposed to the intermittent lighting regime.

We examined the impact of pesticide exposure on parental care in Common Snipe (Gallinago gallinago) at agricultural wetlands in Pomerania, Poland (2018-2020). Using HPLC-MS/MS, we quantified organophosphate residues in 58 adult blood samples while monitoring 42 nests via camera traps. Adults with detectable chlorpyrifos levels (≥0.18 ppm) showed 37% lower provisioning rates (t=3.41, df=56, p=0.001) and 2.9× higher nest abandonment probability (95% CI:1.8-4.7) compared to uncontaminated individuals. This demonstrates direct behavioral impairment from sublethal pesticide exposure, underscoring the need for riparian buffer zones in shorebird conservation.

This study investigates breeding habitat selection in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima) along coastal Newfoundland. Using GPS telemetry and nest monitoring from 2018-2021, we assessed relationships between nest site characteristics (vegetation cover proximity to water marine resource availability) and reproductive success. Habitat loss due to coastal erosion and anthropogenic disturbance significantly influenced selection patterns with nesting density declining by 32 near developed shorelines. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this seabird to synergistic effects of shoreline modification and climate-driven habitat degradation emphasizing the need for integrated coastal management strategies.

Among 777 patients transferred to 4 hospitals in Bangkok from southern Thailand after the tsunami of 26 December 2004, there were 515 with skin and soft-tissue infections. The most common organisms isolated were Aeromonas species (145 [22.6%] of 641 isolates from 305 patients). Most isolates were susceptible to aminoglycosides, third- and fourth-generation cephalosporins, quinolones, and imipenem but were resistant to amoxicillin-clavulanate and first-generation cephalosporins.

This study examines coastal stopover site fidelity and habitat selection in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima) during fall migration along the eastern North Atlantic flyway. Using GPS telemetry on 92 individuals over three seasons (2019-2021), we quantified site reuse rates and modeled resource selection functions relative to eelgrass density and anthropogenic disturbance. Results indicate high interannual fidelity to sheltered bays despite increasing coastal development pressures, highlighting critical staging habitats for this sea duck.

This study examines stopover ecology of Least Terns (Sternula antillarum) along the Gulf Coast during spring migration. Using GPS tracking of 15 individuals, we documented site fidelity and foraging behavior at estuarine habitats. Results show significant correlations between prey availability and stopover duration (r=0.78, p<0.01), with anthropogenic disturbance reducing site occupancy by 40%. Conservation strategies must address habitat degradation at key stopover sites to support this declining species.

We assessed Brant goose (Branta bernicla) population dynamics along the Mid-Atlantic coast in response to seagrass habitat degradation and increased recreational boating disturbance from 2013-2021. Using mark-recapture and aerial surveys, we documented a 38% decline in wintering flocks correlated with Zostera marina loss rates (R²=0 72). Mean flight initiation distance increased by 42% at high-traffic sites suggesting escalating energy expenditure.

Demographic vulnerability of Rock Sandpipers (Calidris ptilocnemis) to altered precipitation regimes was assessed through a 7-year (2016-2022 mark-recapture study (n = 421 adults) in Cook Inlet, Alaska. Bayesian survival analysis revealed a 23.1% decrease in apparent annual survival (Φ = 0.68 vs. 0:52; 95% CI : -0:21 to -0:10) following extreme precipitation during breeding. Nest monitoring (n = 157) showed hatching success declined 31.7% (p = 0.013) under >150% average June rainfall Population projections indicate ≥40% decline within 15 years under RCP8.5 scenarios.

We investigated nutrient pollution impacts on Least Sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) demography in coastal Maine saltmarshes (2018-2021). Using Cormack-Jolly-Seber models with 312 color-banded adults and 127 monitored nests across nitrate gradients (2-35 mg/L), we quantified vital rates. High-nitrogen sites showed 28% lower annual adult survival (Φ = 0.65 ± 0.04 vs 0.90 ± 0.03; p<0.001) and 41% reduced fledging success (nests: 0.31 vs 0.52 chicks/nest; p=0.008). Stochastic matrix projections indicated population decline (λ = 0.87; 95% CI: 0.79-0.94) under elevated nutrients. This highlights eutrophication as a critical threat requiring watershed-level mitigation.

<jats:p>
            Competition for food drives divergence and specialization in feeding morphology. Stomatopod crustaceans have two kinds of highly specialized feeding appendages: either elongate spear-like appendages (
            <jats:italic>spearers</jats:italic>
            ) used to ambush soft-bodied evasive prey or hammer-like appendages (
            <jats:italic>smashers</jats:italic>
            ) that produce extremely high forces used both to break hard-shelled prey and to capture evasive prey. To evaluate associations between appendage type and feeding ecology, the diet of two small smasher and spearer species (size range: 21–27 mm) that co-occur were compared. Stable isotope analysis and the Bayesian mixing model MixSIAR were used to estimate the proportional contributions of prey types to the diet. Both species had relatively wide diets that included hard-shelled and soft-bodied prey, albeit in different proportions; the smasher consumed a greater proportion of hard-shelled prey, and the spearer consumed mostly soft-bodied prey. Appendage kinematics in stomatopods is known to scale linearly across species. These two small species may produce similar kinematics allowing them both to capture evasive prey and hammer hard-shelled prey, thereby widening their diets. Yet, the spearer species is more highly adept at capturing evasive prey, indicating that small spearers are stronger competitors for soft-bodied prey. These findings suggest that a smasher's ability to access hard prey reduced competition for soft prey, and therefore conferred an important benefit favouring the evolution of the impressive smashing strike.
          </jats:p>

We investigated nest site selection in American Coots (Fulica americana) across 12 freshwater wetlands in the Prairie Pothole Region. Using generalized linear mixed models, we assessed how vegetation density, water depth, and distance to open water influenced nest placement. Contrary to predictions, coots preferred sites with intermediate vegetation cover (40-60%) over dense cover, likely balancing predation risk and thermoregulation needs. Nest success was significantly higher in sites with deeper water (>30 cm), suggesting avoidance of mammalian predators. Our findings highlight the importance of heterogeneous wetland habitats for this declining species facing agricultural drainage pressures.

The research was carried out to determine whether there are individual-level differences in the bicolor damselfish (Stegastes partitus) within the altered fish communities located on the north coast of Havana, Cuba. There was strong evidence of changes in some morphological and physiological characteristics associated with the impact of land-based pollution in the coastal zone. A combination of impaired recruitment due to habitat degradation with increased food supply due to eutrophication seems to be the best explanation for fishes being heavier and longer at polluted sites. The change in the proportion of color patterns and a very high number of atretic oocytes in the ovaries of fish caught near the mouth of the Almendares River strongly support the idea that not only is the pollution of river waters affecting the marine life in the coastal zone, but also that this pollution has greater effects than the pollution coming from the discharge of Havana Harbor.

We investigated Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) movement ecology in coastal wetlands using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults). Results revealed significant habitat selection for tidal marshes over agricultural fields during winter (p<0.01). Home range size decreased with proximity to urban areas, suggesting behavioral adaptation to anthropogenic disturbance. This study highlights coastal Mallards' vulnerability to wetland degradation and sea-level rise.

This study examines habitat selection of Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) across coastal wetlands of the Gulf Coast. Using radio telemetry and GIS analysis, we tracked the movements of 45 breeding individuals over two seasons to identify key predictors of foraging site use. Results indicate significant avoidance of areas with high human recreational disturbance (p<0·001) and preferential selection of marshes with dense submerged aquatic vegetation (OR=3·2). Salinity gradients and prey abundance were secondary factors. Conservation efforts must prioritize buffer zones around critical foraging habitats to minimize anthropogenic impacts on this declining wader species.

We investigated the foraging movements of Forster's Terns (Sterna forsteri) in the Great Lakes region using GPS telemetry. Over two breeding seasons, we tracked 25 individuals to assess habitat selection and daily activity patterns. Results revealed strong preferences for shallow wetlands with emergent vegetation, contrasting with historical coastal nesting sites. Terns exhibited reduced foraging ranges in areas with high boat traffic, suggesting anthropogenic disturbance impacts. This study highlights the importance of inland freshwater habitats for this species' conservation amid changing coastal ecosystems.

We investigated nutrient pollution impacts on Semipalmated Plover (Charadrius semipalmatus; n=42) foraging ecology using GPS telemetry (2019-2021) in coastal Maine, USA. Individuals were tracked across eutrophication gradients (nitrate levels 0.2-5.7 mg/L). Core foraging ranges expanded 37% (paired t-test, p=0.008) and prey capture rates declined 22% (GLMM, p<0 001=

This study examines mercury bioaccumulation in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) nesting along industrialized coastlines. We analyzed liver tissue from 42 adult birds across 7 colonies, finding mean concentrations of 8.7 μg/g (dry weight) - exceeding toxicity thresholds. Feather δ15N values indicated trophic position influenced contamination levels. Mercury burdens showed strong negative correlation with fledging success (r=-0.81, p<0.001), suggesting reproductive impairment. Our results highlight cormorants as effective bioindicators of coastal pollution impacts on piscivorous birds, with implications for ecosystem health monitoring in anthropogenically altered habitats.

We investigated heavy metal exposure effects on Dunlin (Calidris alpina) community ecology in the Tagus Estuary, Portugal (2018-2020). Using atomic absorption spectrometry, we analyzed cadmium (Cd), lead (Pb), and mercury (Hg) concentrations in blood samples from 120 individuals across three mudflat zones. Hg levels exceeded toxicity thresholds in 78% of samples (mean ± SE: 2.3 ± 0.4 μg/g dw) and correlated negatively with invertebrate prey abundance (r = -0.67, p = 0.002). Population modeling indicated a 19% decline in juvenile recruitment (95% CI: 15-23%) under current contamination scenarios. Results highlight metal pollution as a critical threat to shorebird foraging guilds in estuarine ecosystems.

We quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in wintering Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) across coastal Louisiana marshes using doubly labeled water and GPS telemetry. DEE increased by 28% in fragmented habitats (mean=145.6 kJ/d) versus contiguous wetlands, correlating with reduced foraging efficiency. Human infrastructure density predicted 67% of DEE variance, suggesting habitat degradation substantially elevates metabolic demands in this declining dabbling duck species, with implications for reserve design.

                  <jats:p>In the past two years, Bluefin has fielded several AUV systems. The survey systems that Bluefin build for the US Navy have seen almost continuous use. In addition to the Bluefin operations these vehicles participated in three Navy Exercises and one international science cruise. This paper presents the results of some of these high-resolution surveys. Figure 1:(Available in full paper) Figure 2:(Available in full paper)</jats:p>
                  <jats:sec>
                     <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                     <jats:p>After developing several key AUV technologies at MIT and building 12 prototype vehicles in the process, the Bluefin team became a commercial enterprise in the fall of 1999. Bluefin's engineers have now built seven new AUVs for a range of commercial, military, and academic customers. Measured in terms of numbers of vehicles sold, Bluefin Robotics is the world's largest commercial manufacturer of autonomous underwater. Figures 1 through 5 show several of Bluefin's AUVs in action. This paper presents some of the field data that was taken with these AUVs. Specific data of the Bluefin 5000 is presented in detail. Both the sonar and the navigation data shows the success of Bluefin's "small is beautiful" design philosophy. Bluefin's current class of vehicles are the smallest survey systems in the commercial survey market. Current development efforts at Bluefin are pushing the envelope even further by fielding a new class of AUVs with a diameter of 12.75 inches. Modularity is crucial to this new design and it will allow the integration of a whole new class of survey sonars. Current developments in synthetic aperture sonars are particularly exiting and promise to revolutionize the way that data will be gathered in the not so distance future. Simultaneously, Bluefin is pushing the state of the art in the areas of mission autonomy, energy sources, and navigation systems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                     <jats:title>Bluefin 5000</jats:title>
                     <jats:p>The BLUEFIN 5000 is part of the new Odyssey III class of vehicles that that have been designed by Bluefin. The BLUEFIN 5000 is specifically designed for wide-area high resolution surveys missions. As such, the vehicle's main payload is a high-resolution, multi-beam side-scan sonar, the Klein 5000. The BLUEFIN 5000's oceanographic payload sensors include CTD, fluorometer, and light-scattering sensors. The design of the BLUEFIN 5000 is modular, with all essential vehicle components (main electronics pressure vessel, computation, propulsion, navigation and attitude sensors) contained in the aft modular section of the vehicle. The forward modular section contains the Klein 5000 sidescan sonar, the CTD, the fluorometer, and the light-scattering sensor. The forward modular section also contains two redundant battery packs in separate battery housings. Spent battery packs are easily replaced by removing the BLUEFIN 5000's hemispherical nose-cone, sliding each cylindrical battery housing out of the vehicle, and then re-inserting charged batteries. The forward battery arrangement allows the vehicle to be serviced rapidly between missions, with on-deck turn-around times as short as 30 minutes, excluding data download.</jats:p>

We investigated parental care trade-offs in Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) facing nest trampling risk in Dutch polders (2018-2020). Using GPS-tracked adults (n=42) and nest monitoring (n=87), we quantified incubation bout duration relative to cattle density. High trampling pressure (>0.5 cattle/ha) reduced incubation constancy by 22% (95% CI: 15-29%, p=0.003) as parents prioritized vigilance. Consequently, hatch success declined by 18% (p=0.01) in grazed areas. Results demonstrate that rotational grazing schedules must incorporate shorebird nesting phenology to mitigate fitness costs.

We investigated the impacts of coastal wetland degradation on Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) nesting success along the Chesapeake Bay estuary. Using nest monitoring and GIS-based habitat analysis across 24 sites, we found that erosion-induced bank instability reduced burrow occupancy by 47% compared to intact shorelines. Kingfisher reproductive output declined significantly with proximity to developed areas (R²=0.68, p<0.001), demonstrating how anthropogenic shoreline modification disproportionately affects this piscivorous specialist. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining natural riparian buffers to support kingfisher populations facing coastal squeeze.

We investigated nest site selection in Black Oystercatchers (Haematopus bachmani) along the central Oregon coast (44°40'N, 124°03'W) from 2018-2020, assessing how proximity to dog walking trails influences habitat use. Using GPS-logged individuals (n=32) and nest monitoring (n=47 nests), we found oystercatchers selected nest sites >200m from trails (OR=4.2, 95% CI: 1.8-9.7). Nests within 100m of trails had 38% lower daily survival rates (p=0.008) due to increased abandonment. These results highlight the need for buffer zones around critical nesting habitat to mitigate anthropogenic disturbance.

<jats:p>The frequency of mixed‐species flocks of birds, weather and insect activity were studied in a high‐altitude cloud forest in Ecuador. It is generally accepted that participation in mixed‐species flocks improves foraging efficiency. If this is true, more flock activity may be expected when food is less available, which may happen during long‐lasting periods of rain and otherwise adverse weather conditions. The total number and mean size of flying insects decreased as rainfall increased. The number of flocks observed increased with decreasing number and biomass of insects. Relatively more flocks were seen during rain than during dry weather. No flocks stopped foraging during rain. The flock activity pattern appeared to be the opposite of that found in humid lowlands, probably because of different weather regimes in the two zones. In the lowlands, heavy rain is typically of short duration. In high‐altitude cloud forest, the rainfall is often less intense but persists for prolonged periods. Hence, from an energy point of view, cloud forest birds cannot afford to stop foraging during adverse weather conditions when insect availability is low. The results suggest that some mixed feeding parties have evolved in response to low tropical insect availability, necessitating long feeding excursions outside the territory.</jats:p>

We assessed the impact of kite-flying disturbance on Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) migration ecology along the Upper Mississippi River Flyway (2018-2020). Using GPS telemetry (n=37 adults) and kite density mapping across 12 stopover sites, we quantified flight path deviation and energy expenditure via isotopic analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N). Kite densities >3/ha significantly increased flight altitude (x̄=38±7m vs. control 15±3m; p<0.01) and detour distance (x̄=1.7km, 95% CI:1.2-2.1), elevating daily energy expenditure by 22% (GLMM, β=0.78, p=0.004). Results indicate kite activity fragments critical wetland habitats, necessitating seasonal bans within 500m of key staging areas.

This study investigated the foraging ecology of Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) in relation to predator-prey dynamics within freshwater wetland ecosystems. Using focal animal sampling and prey item analysis, we quantified heron predation rates on fish and amphibian populations across varying habitat structures. Results indicate that heron foraging success significantly declined in fragmented habitats, suggesting landscape-level habitat loss may disrupt trophic interactions. Additionally, predation pressure shifted towards smaller prey species in degraded wetlands, potentially altering community composition. Our findings highlight cascading effects of wetland degradation on avian predators.

<jats:p>Both reciprocity and positive assortment (like with like) are predicted to promote the evolution of cooperation, yet how partners influence each other's behaviour within dynamic networks is not well understood. One way to test this question is to partition phenotypic variation into differences among individuals in the expression of cooperative behaviour (the ‘direct effect’), and plasticity within individuals in response to the social environment (the ‘indirect effect’). A positive correlation between these two sources of variation, such that more cooperative individuals elicit others to cooperate, is predicted to facilitate social contagion and selection on cooperative behaviour. Testing this hypothesis is challenging, however, because it requires repeated measures of behaviour across a dynamic social landscape. Here, we use an automated data-logging system to quantify the behaviour of 179 wire-tailed manakins, birds that form cooperative male–male coalitions, and we use multiple-membership models to test the hypothesis that dynamic network partnerships shape within-individual variation in cooperative behaviour. Our results show strong positive correlations between a bird's own sociality and his estimated effect on his partners, consistent with the hypothesis that cooperation begets cooperation. These findings support the hypothesis that social contagion can facilitate selection for cooperative behaviour within social networks.</jats:p>

We assessed the impact of rising temperatures on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) breeding biology at Cape Cod National Seashore, Massachusetts, USA. During 2018-2022, we monitored 142 nests, recording substrate temperatures hourly via iButton loggers and measuring daily nest attendance. Logistic regression revealed that days exceeding 32°C reduced hatching success by 27% (OR=0.73, p=0.009; 95% CI: 0.58-0.92) and increased egg abandonment by 19.3% (p=0.013). Chick survival probability declined 0.8% per °C above historical averages (R²=0.76). These findings highlight acute thermal stress for this federally threatened Charadriiform, necessitating proactive shade management and microhabitat restoration in conservation strategies.

This study examined Caspian Sea breeding ecology of Great Cormorants (Phalacrocorax carbo), a non-Charadriiformes piscivore. We quantified nest success (n=87 colonies) across 2018-2021, revealing clutch sizes of 3.1±0.7 eggs and 62% fledging success. Hydrological fluctuations from climate change reduced prey availability, causing 33% chick mortality in drought years. Increased shoreline development correlated with colony abandonment (r=-0.79, p<0.01), highlighting wetland habitat loss as primary conservation threat.

<jats:p>A recent publication and an article in Wetland Science & Practice discuss two metrics for determining if vegetation is hydrophytic for purposes of U.S. wetland delineations, the Prevalence Index (PI) and a proposed Hydrophytic Cover Index (HCI). The PI is a weighted average of ordinal scores (1–5) for species in five wetland indicator categories (defined in Table 1). Scores of 1–3  represent hydrophyte species, and the associated rule is that PI values ≤ 3.0 represent a positive determination for hydrophytic vegetation.</jats:p>

We investigated population dynamics of Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax), a globally distributed ardeid species, along urban-rural gradients in the northeastern United States from 2017-2022. Using capture-recapture models and nest monitoring at 27 colonies, we evaluated the impact of urbanization intensity, water quality degradation, and human disturbance on annual survival rates and fecundity. Results indicate that survival rates declined by 18% in highly urbanized areas compared to rural sites, primarily due to bioaccumulation of heavy metals and direct anthropogenic mortality. Fecundity showed a non-linear relationship with disturbance, peaking at intermediate levels of urbanization.

This study examines predator-prey dynamics affecting Least Bittern (Ixobrychus exilis) populations in freshwater marshes of the southeastern United States. Using camera traps and nest monitoring across 12 sites, we quantified predation rates and identified primary nest predators. Raccoons (Procyon lotor) accounted for 67% of documented nest failures, with water snakes (Nerodia spp.) responsible for 21%. Bitterns exhibited adaptive nest concealment behaviors but showed significantly reduced reproductive success in fragmented habitats. Results indicate wetland connectivity and vegetation density critically influence vulnerability to mammalian predation.

<jats:p>Approximations for leaky wave coupling coefficients and background scattering contributions are usually derived by assuming the shell response is governed by thin shell theory. Comparisons are described with approximations derived by other methods for a thick spherical shell at frequencies above coincidence. The variation of the phase of the coupling coefficient from numerical evaluation of the Watson transformation residue by Kargl [Ph.D. thesis, Washington State University (1990)] is evident in an analytical approximation. The phase of the background includes inertial and wave-kinematic contributions and is related to research by Gaunaurd and Werby [J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 90, 2536–2550 (1991)]. The inertial contribution to the background phase is derived directly from the reflectivity of a plate in the limit of small phase shift for propagation across the thickness of the shell. The frequency and angle dependence of the phase of the exact reflection coefficient of a plate (having the same thickness as the shell) is also examined.</jats:p>

<jats:p>Data published in the literature about the favorable effects of dietary probiotics on gut health in broiler chickens are inconsistent. To obtain a more comprehensive understanding, we conducted a meta-analysis to assess the effects of probiotics on the gut barrier and immune-related gene expression, histomorphology, and growth in chickens that were either challenged or non-challenged with pathogens. From the 54 articles published between 2012 and 2022, subsets of data, separately for non-challenged and challenged conditions, for response variables were created. The mean dietary probiotic concentrations ranged from 4.7 to 6.2 and 4.7 to 7.2 log10 colony-forming unit/kg under non-challenged and challenged conditions, respectively. Probiotics increased the expression of genes for mucins and tight junction proteins in the jejunum and ileum at weeks 3 and 6. The stimulatory effect of probiotics on tight junction protein expression was partly stronger in challenged than in non-challenged birds. Meta-regressions also showed an anti-inflammatory effect of probiotics under challenged conditions by modulating the expression of cytokines. Probiotics improved villus height at certain ages in the small intestine while not influencing growth performance. Dietary metabolizable energy, crude protein, and days post-infection modified the effects of probiotics on the observed variables. Overall, meta-regressions support the beneficial effects of probiotics on gut integrity and structure in chickens.</jats:p>

This study examines nest site selection in American Coots (Fulica americana) across freshwater wetlands in the Prairie Pothole Region. Using logistic regression models, we analyzed habitat variables influencing nest placement relative to water depth, vegetation density, and proximity to open water. Results indicate coots preferentially select sites with intermediate water depths (15-35 cm) and dense emergent vegetation cover (>70%) that provide concealment from predators while allowing access to foraging areas. Nest survival rates were significantly higher in sites with these characteristics compared to suboptimal locations. Our findings highlight the importance of maintaining heterogeneous wetland habitats for this declining waterbird species facing habitat degradation.

We investigated climate change impacts on Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) in coastal wetlands through GPS telemetry (n=42) and habitat modeling. Results indicate saltwater intrusion from sea-level rise reduced preferred freshwater foraging habitats by 35%, causing distribution shifts to suboptimal inland areas. Breeding success declined significantly with increased salinity exposure. Conservation requires strategic freshwater refuge creation in vulnerable coastal zones.

We investigated the role of avifaunal disease reservoirs in Red Knot (Calidris canutus rufa subspecies) migratory connectivity using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N). Blood samples from 138 individuals were collected between 2018-2020 at Delaware Bay, USA (39.0°N 74.8°W), a critical stopover site. δ15N values correlated negatively with exposure to avian influenza antibodies (r = -0 32, p=0.001), suggesting knots foraging in lower-trophic-level habitats acquired fewer pathogens Results indicate that isotopic signatures can identify high-risk foraging grounds, informing wetland management to reduce disease transmission at stopover sites

This study investigates the energy expenditure of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) during plunge-diving foraging in coastal habitats. Using doubly labeled water techniques on wild pelicans in the Gulf of Mexico, we measured daily energy expenditure (DEE) across seasons. Results indicate DEE increases significantly during breeding season (mean ± SE: 1450 ± 120 kJ/day) compared to non-breeding periods (980 ± 95 kJ/day), primarily driven by chick provisioning flights. Wind speed and prey density were key environmental predictors of foraging efficiency. Our findings highlight vulnerability to climate-driven shifts in wind patterns affecting pelican energetics.

This study examines the impact of invasive European green crabs (Carcinus maenas) on Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) foraging behavior in coastal marsh ecosystems. Using focal animal sampling and stable isotope analysis, we documented significant reductions in invertebrate prey availability and altered duck foraging effort in invaded habitats. Mallards exhibited increased time spent feeding and decreased body condition indices compared to control sites, suggesting cascading effects of invasive species on waterfowl energetics during winter staging periods.

Juvenile survival in Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) was assessed across three Great Lakes colonies from 2018-2021 using mark-resight techniques. We documented significant declines in first-year survival probability (φ = 0.42 ± 0.07) associated with increased recreational disturbance at nesting sites. Habitat degradation from invasive Phragmites expansion reduced fledging success by 38% compared to undisturbed marshes. These anthropogenic pressures demonstrate urgent need for protected buffer zones around urban-nesting larid populations.

We examined Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) parental care responses to tropical storm exposure in the Pantanal wetlands, Brazil (2018-2021). Using GPS-tracked adults (n=32) and nest monitoring (n=87 nests), we quantified behavioral shifts during extreme weather events. Nest abandonment probability increased 3.7-fold (95% CI: 2.1-6.5) post-storm, with males (primary caregivers) showing reduced provisioning rates (mean decrease: 42%, p=0.008). Brood survival declined by 28% (p<0.01) in flooded habitats. Results highlight climate vulnerability in polyandrous shorebirds and necessitate wetland buffer zones for resilience.

This bioacoustic study examines vocalization patterns of Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) in response to anthropogenic noise pollution across urban wetland habitats. Using autonomous recording units deployed at 12 sites along a gradient of human disturbance intensity, we quantified changes in call frequency, amplitude, and temporal structure during nesting season. Results indicate significant vocal modifications including upward frequency shifts and reduced call complexity in high-noise environments, suggesting acoustic adaptation to urban soundscapes. These alterations may impact conspecific communication efficiency and reproductive behaviors in this colonially nesting species.

This study evaluates heavy metal contamination in Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola) within agricultural wetlands. We analyzed liver tissues from 45 specimens across six Midwestern catchments using ICP-MS, detecting elevated cadmium (mean 3.7 ppm) and lead (mean 8.2 ppm) concentrations. Rail body condition indices inversely correlated with metal loads (r=-0.51, p<0.01), indicating sublethal physiological stress. Drainage tile runoff emerged as a primary exposure pathway. Chronic bioaccumulation poses significant conservation concerns for this cryptic rallid species amid intensifying agrochemical usage.

We quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) across anthropogenic disturbance gradients in Atlantic coastal marshes using doubly-labeled water techniques. DEE increased 18-23% in high-traffic zones versus undisturbed areas, correlating with reduced body condition indices. This elevated metabolic cost suggests chronic disturbance may contribute to population declines through sublethal energy deficits, emphasizing non-lethal pathways in habitat management frameworks.

We investigated the impacts of coastal urbanization on the migratory connectivity of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) across the Gulf of Mexico using GPS satellite telemetry from 102 individuals over three years (2018-2020). Our findings show that coastal development has significantly fragmented migration corridors, increasing flight distances by 15–32% and reducing stopover site quality. Furthermore, we documented a 27% decline in breeding success associated with degraded stopover habitats along urbanized coastlines, highlighting the need for strategic conservation of key migratory nodes.

<jats:p>Percent recognition of phonemes and whole syllables, measured in both consonant–vowel–consonant (CVC) words and CVC nonsense syllables, is reported for normal young adults listening at four signal-to-noise (S/N) ratios. Similar data are reported for the recognition of words and whole sentences in three types of sentence: high predictability (HP) sentences, with both semantic and syntactic constraints; low predictability (LP) sentences, with primarily syntactic constraints; and zero predictability (ZP) sentences, with neither semantic nor syntactic constraints. The probability of recognition of speech units in context (pc) is shown to be related to the probability of recognition without context (pi) by the equation pc=1−(1−pi)k, where k is a constant. The factor k is interpreted as the amount by which the channels of statistically independent information are effectively multiplied when contextual constraints are added. Empirical values of k are approximately 1.3 and 2.7 for word and sentence context, respectively. In a second analysis, the probability of recognition of wholes (pw) is shown to be related to the probability of recognition of the constituent parts (pp) by the equation pw=pjp, where j represents the effective number of statistically independent parts within a whole. The empirically determined mean values of j for nonsense materials are not significantly different from the number of parts in a whole, as predicted by the underlying theory. In CVC words, the value of j is constant at approximately 2.5. In the four-word HP sentences, it falls from approximately 2.5 to approximately 1.6 as the inherent recognition probability for words falls from 100% to 0%, demonstrating an increasing tendency to perceive HP sentences either as wholes, or not at all, as S/N ratio deteriorates.</jats:p>

This study examined climate-driven shifts in prey availability for Surfbirds (Calidris virgata) at Glacier Bay National Park, Alaska (58.5°N, 136.0°W) from 2015-2020. Using benthic core sampling (n=120 sites) and focal bird observations (n=45 individuals), we quantified intertidal invertebrate biomass and foraging rates. Mussel (Mytilus spp.) density declined by 32% (95% CI: -41% to -23%) with rising sea surface temperatures, correlating with a 27% reduction in Surfbird foraging efficiency (R²=0.78, p<0.001). Population modeling indicated a potential 15% decline in local breeding success under RCP 8.5 scenarios by 2050. These findings highlight climate vulnerability in high-latitude shorebirds reliant on sessile prey.

<jats:p> Site index is difficult to implement and interpret in multispecies, multiple-aged stands, and its relationship to site factors is obscure. Using data from the USDA forest inventory and analysis (FIA) for the Lake States, we developed log-log relationships between mean tree size and stand density for five cover types. Fits were good, with r<jats:sup>2</jats:sup> from 0.96 to 0.98 and slopes from −0.948 to −0.995. We define an alternative index of site quality, the relative stocking index (RSI), as the ratio of a stand's measured density to that predicted using the log–log relationship for its cover type (the norm). We divided the range of RSI into three classes for each type (<0.9 of norm, >0.91 but <1.1 of norm, and >1.1 of norm). Based on analyses of the 1977 and 1990 FIA data from Minnesota, class assignments for individual stands remained constant over that 13-year period. Relationships between site factors and either RSI classes or analogous classes based on site index were examined in a subset of 169 stands. Temperature, precipitation, silt content of surface soil, and calculated annual water deficit all differed significantly among RSI classes, but not among site-index classes. The RSI is easy to apply, robust (resistant to change), and related to site factors. It merits additional examination as an index of site quality, especially in heterogenous stands. </jats:p>

We investigated disease transmission risks to Black Turnstones (Arenaria melanocephala) within mixed-species shorebird assemblages on Alaska's Copper River Delta during spring migration (2019-2021). Fecal samples (n=217) from turnstones and 12 sympatric Charadriiform species were screened for avian influenza (AIV) and Salmonella via qPCR. Turnstones exhibited significantly higher AIV prevalence (22.1%, 95% CI: 17.4-26.8%) than other species (mean: 8.3%, χ²=14.7, p<0.001). Salmonella occurrence increased with turnstone flock density (R²=0.51, p=0.012). Results suggest turnstones act as potential disease reservoirs in intertidal communities, necessitating targeted surveillance in high-density staging sites.

We investigated nest site selection in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola), a wetland-dependent rallid threatened by habitat degradation in freshwater marshes. Using logistic regression on vegetation metrics and water depth from 43 nests and random points, we found strong preference for dense coverage of Typha spp. (>80%) and shallow water (mean depth = 12.3±4.1 cm). Nest survival significantly decreased with proximity to anthropogenic edges (β = -1 2, p<0 01), emphasizing vulnerability to edge effects in fragmented habitats.

This study evaluated the impacts of coastal wetland degradation on maternal care behavior in American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes). Using GPS telemetry and nest cameras, we monitored 38 breeding pairs across varying disturbance gradients. Results demonstrated that habitat fragmentation reduced maternal nest attendance by 32% during incubation, while increased human recreational pressure correlated with earlier brood abandonment. Elevated mercury levels in blood samples further predicted reduced provisioning rates. These compound stressors significantly compromised offspring survival, underscoring urgent wetland conservation needs for this declining waterfowl species.

Anthropogenic disturbance poses significant threats to colonial waterbirds. We examined the bioacoustic responses of Double-crested Cormorants (Nannopterum auritum) to human recreational activities at coastal nesting sites using passive recording units. Analysis revealed elevated call rates (p<0.01) and altered frequency modulation during disturbance events. These vocal stress indicators demonstrate non-invasive acoustic monitoring's utility for conservation management in sensitive habitats.

This study examines the impact of hydrological alterations on Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) breeding ecology in coastal Louisiana marshes (2018-2021). We monitored 147 nests across 23 colonies, correlating water management practices with nesting phenology, clutch size, and fledging success. Hydrological instability from canal drainage reduced nest survival by 42% (β = -0.68, p<0.001) through increased nest flooding and prey scarcity. Our findings highlight critical vulnerabilities in Ardeidae reproductive strategies to anthropogenic wetland modification, necessitating adaptive water management protocols for conservation.

Pottery sherds stained with purple dye were found in the excavations at Tel Shiqmona, and were dated to the Iron Age II period. Analysis by HPLC-DAD identified the dye as ‘true purple’, derived from the Hexaplex trunculus sea snail, which is associated with the purple-dye industry that flourished in the coastal area at that time. This result is compatible with the classification of over 1000 Muricidae shells that were found in the excavation. Hexaplex trunculus constitutes 80% of this group, indicating that it was the most commonly used species in the dye production at Tel Shiqmona.

This study examines Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia), a larid seabird species, nesting success in relation to artificial wetland management practices in the Columbia River Estuary. Using mark-recapture methods and nest monitoring over three breeding seasons (2018-2020), we found tern productivity significantly declined in sites with invasive carp populations that reduced submerged aquatic vegetation coverage (p<0 05). Contrary to expectations water level stabilization strategies showed no significant effect on fledging rates suggesting alternative management approaches are needed for conserving this piscivorous bird amidst wetland degradation pressures.

This study examines the impact of coastal habitat degradation on Herring Gull (Larus argentatus) nesting success in the Gulf of Maine. Using a combination of field surveys and GIS analysis, we quantified changes in vegetation cover and human disturbance levels across 15 breeding colonies from 2015-2020. Results indicate a significant negative correlation between shoreline development intensity and gull reproductive output (r = -0.78, p<0.001), with artificial structures reducing nest site availability by 42%. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of coastal-nesting larids to anthropogenic modification, suggesting that conservation strategies must address habitat fragmentation to maintain viable populations.

This study examines the influence of urban light pollution on the breeding chronology of Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax). We monitored 42 nesting pairs across three coastal colonies (2018–2020) and recorded egg-laying dates, clutch size, and hatching success under varying artificial night light (ANL). Generalized linear mixed models revealed delayed initiation (β = 0·72 ± 0·21 SE, P = 0·001), reduced clutch size (β = −0·31 ± 0·09 SE, P = 0·006), and lower hatching rates (OR = 0·73, 95% CI: 0·61–0·87, P < 0·001). Our results indicate that light pollution disrupts circadian-mediated breeding cues in this nocturnally foraging ardeid.

We investigated the impact of invasive American mink (Neovison vison) predation on Common Sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos) breeding ecology in the River Spey catchment, Scotland (2018-2021). Using camera traps at 42 nests and GPS-tagged adults (n=18), we quantified nest survival and foraging displacement. Daily nest survival probability decreased by 37% (95% CI: 22-49%) in mink-present zones versus control areas (p=0.008). Adults in high-predation areas exhibited 43% longer foraging flights (mean ± SE: 1.2 ± 0.3 km vs. 0.7 ± 0.2 km; p=0.012), reducing chick provisioning rates. Results demonstrate acute vulnerability to introduced predators, necessitating targeted mink control for riparian shorebird conservation.

We investigated migration phenology and stopover site fidelity of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) along the Atlantic Flyway using GPS telemetry (n=42). Individuals exhibited high fidelity to specific coastal estuaries despite increasing anthropogenic disturbance. Migration timing advanced by 5.2 days per decade since 1990, correlated with rising spring temperatures (r=0.78, p<0.01). Unexpectedly, birds avoided marine protected areas during stopovers, preferring active fishing ports. Results suggest climate-driven phenological shifts may decouple migration from prey availability in this piscivorous species.

This study examines the effects of urban development on foraging behaviors of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) using GPS telemetry in coastal environments. We tracked 30 individuals during breeding seasons 2018-2020, analyzing home range shifts and habitat selection in response to anthropogenic disturbance. Results show avoidance of developed zones and altered activity budgets, with implications for conservation planning in rapidly urbanizing coastlines.

1.
              Seed dispersal is widely recognized to be of crucial importance in the ecology of plant communities, yet characterization of dispersal capacity rarely goes beyond two categories: ‘good’ and ‘poor’ dispersers, defined on the basis of dispersule morphology.
            
            
              2.
              We describe a new apparatus which determines the rate of fall of seeds in air by detecting their passage through two fans of laser light.
            
            
              3.
              This apparatus is able to measure rate of fall in smaller seeds than previously published methods and reveals that there is no justification for the arbitrary division of species into two wind dispersal categories.

<jats:p><jats:bold>Abstract.</jats:bold>The effect of introducing bednets impregnated with 0.4 g/m<jats:sup>2</jats:sup>permethrin on local populations of the malaria vector mosquitoes<jats:italic>Anopheles farauti</jats:italic>Laveran and<jats:italic>An.koliensis</jats:italic>Owen was monitored in a coastal village of Papua New Guinea. Whole‐night landing collections were undertaken for 25 consecutive nights before and 21 nights after the introduction of the nets. Capture‐recapture experiments and resting collections were also performed before and after the introduction of the nets.</jats:p><jats:p>Following the introduction of treated nets, the biting population of<jats:italic>An.farauti</jats:italic>, the predominant vector, dropped from an average of 689 to 483 per man‐night and the oviposition cycle became irregular, although survival rates (determined by time series analysis of the landing catches and log regression of recapture rates) were not significantly affected. The densities of<jats:italic>An.farauti</jats:italic>resting in and around houses and the human blood index of the engorged females also decreased significantly after introduction of the treated bednets.</jats:p><jats:p>The population of<jats:italic>An.koliensis</jats:italic>dropped prior to the introduction of the nets. However, the number of nulliparous females in the landing catches remained more or less constant which implies that, in this species, survival rates were affected by the nets but that recruitment to the population was not.</jats:p>

Abstract Roden and Groves 1  wrote: “The oceanographic aspects of the Gulf of California, one of the least known marginal seas of the North Pacific, are both interesting and complex”. Tidal processes certainly justify the statement. With a reported spring range of 10 m as well as currents exceeding 6 knots (ref. 2) the tides in the Gulf of California are among the most spectacular and dangerous in the world. Nevertheless, because of the rarity and inadequacy of observations, no consistent picture could be drawn until recently. Many quantitative studies of this area must thus be regarded as provisional; there is, for example, an eight-fold range in estimates of energy dissipation for the semidiurnal lunar tide, namely, Heiskanen 3,4 : 2.5×10 17  erg s −1 ; Miller 5 : 4×10 17  erg s −1 ; Hendershott 6 : 1 to 2×10 17  erg s −1 ; and my proposed values: 4.35×10 16  erg s −1  for M 2  alone, 4.65×10 16  erg s −1  for all semidiurnal lunar constituents and 4.85×10 16  erg s −1  for all lunar constituents.

We investigated how coastal wetland degradation affects migration energetics of Northern Pintails (Anas acuta). Using GPS telemetry on 35 individuals, we quantified stopover duration and refueling rates across intact vs. drained marshes. Pintails in degraded habitats showed 32% lower daily mass gain and prolonged stopovers by 2.1 days on average compared to those in natural wetlands (p<0 01). Results highlight critical habitat thresholds for this declining waterfowl species' migratory success amid accelerating sea-level rise.

<jats:p>

Marine species such as deep-sea geryonid crabs often exhibit high spatio-temporal variability in abundance and size over depth, substratum type and season, therefore data collected from a single gear type may not represent the whole population. Complementary data from trawl (soft substratum) and trap (hard substratum) fisheries were analysed within a general linear modelling (GLM) framework to assess distribution, abundance and population structure of Chaceon macphersoni off eastern South Africa. Catch rates, mean size, maturation size and sex ratio were modelled relative to year, month, depth, latitude and gear effects. Trap and trawl analyses indicated higher abundance as depth increased up to 500 m, and during the austral spring and summer. The mean size of crabs remained constant at all depths sampled, and sex ratios were skewed towards females. Females were smaller than males, and achieved maturity at a smaller size. A standardised index based on trawl data (1988–2010) showed a long-term decline in abundance, with some recovery after 2002, whereas the trap index showed recent local depletions on hard substrata. Using data from two gear types confirmed broad gradients in abundance, but also emphasised subtle trends, such as local depletions on hard substrata, that would not have been apparent from trawl data only.
</jats:p>

<jats:p>An experiment was conducted to measure the relative contribution of spectral weights and internal noise in the discrimination of spectral variance. The stimuli were simultaneous tone complexes comprised of the six octave frequencies from 250 to 8000 Hz. On each presentation the levels of components in dB were drawn independently and at random from one of two normal distributions having identical means but different variances (σN = 1 dB, σS = 2–10 dB). In the standard 2IFC procedure, the listener’s task was to choose the complex having the greater variance in component level. The shape of the psychometric function for all five listeners was markedly different from that of an observer limited only by additive internal noise. It was consistent with an observer that gives weight to only one or two components in the complex. This result, however, was inconsistent with the weighting functions computed from the trial-by-trial data from these listeners. Both measures can be reconciled if it is assumed that listener weights vary from trial to trial, or equivalently that observations are corrupted by multiplicative rather than additive internal noise. [Work supported by NIDCD RO1 DC01262-04.]</jats:p>

We investigated the impact of invasive American mink (Neovison vison) predation on Common Sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos) nest parasitism by trematodes (Cyclocoelum mutabile) in Scotland's River Spey floodplains (2018-2021). Using nest cameras (n=127 nests) and fecal egg counts, we found mink presence increased parasite prevalence by 37% (95% CI: 22-52%) through disturbance-induced immunosuppression. Nest abandonment rates tripled in parasitized nests near mink territories (OR=3.2, p=0.008). Results highlight invasive predators as indirect amplifiers of parasitism, necessitating integrated control for shorebird conservation.

We investigated phenological mismatch impacts on Spotted Sandpiper (Actitis macularius) breeding success along the Upper Mississippi River (USA) during 2018-2021. Using daily nest monitoring (n=127 nests) and insect emergence traps, we quantified synchrony between hatch dates and peak aquatic insect abundance. Hatch success declined by 22% (95% CI: 15-29%) for each 5-day increase in phenological mismatch (GLMM, p=0.003). Our results demonstrate climate-driven trophic asynchrony as a critical threat requiring adaptive management in riparian ecosystems.

We examined mercury bioaccumulation in American Coot (Fulica americana) populations across agricultural watersheds. Liver tissue analysis (n=87 adults) revealed significantly elevated Hg concentrations (mean 8.7 ± 1.2 ppm) in drainage-impaired wetlands compared to reference sites (2.1 ± 0.4 ppm). Positive correlations emerged between hepatic Hg levels and reduced fledging success (R²=0.63, p<0.01) and altered thyroid hormone profiles. Spatial modeling identified wetland connectivity loss as amplifying pollutant exposure risks. Findings highlight non-shorebird waterbirds as critical bioindicators of freshwater contamination impacts on avian reproductive physiology.

We quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in breeding Ospreys (Pandion haliaetus) along disturbed estuarine systems using tri-axial accelerometers and GPS telemetry. Results revealed 18-27% higher DEE in territories affected by shoreline development and boat traffic, with compensatory increases in foraging time reducing nest provisioning rates. Elevated energy allocation to flight activity in fragmented habitats suggests anthropogenic disturbance imposes significant metabolic costs on this piscivorous raptor.

We investigated the foraging behavior of American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) in coastal salt marshes of Chesapeake Bay, examining how tidal cycles and anthropogenic disturbance influence feeding efficiency. Using focal animal sampling and GPS tracking, we quantified diurnal foraging rates across seasons. Results indicate that boat traffic significantly reduces foraging time (p<0.001) during high tide when ducks concentrate in narrow channels. Habitat fragmentation further constrained access to preferred mollusk prey. This study highlights coastal development threats to waterfowl wintering ecology.

This study investigated molt migration patterns in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across northeastern wetlands using GPS telemetry and feather isotope analysis. We tracked 32 individuals over two annual cycles, revealing asynchronous molt schedules between sexes and age classes. Habitat fragmentation significantly delayed post-breeding migration onset (p<0.01), with agricultural runoff exposure correlating with reduced flight feather quality (r=-0.72). Our findings highlight how anthropogenic stressors disrupt critical life history events in this secretive rallid species.

We investigated the role of foraging habitat selection in structuring mixed-species assemblages of Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) and sympatric waterbirds within estuarine communities. Using focal sampling and resource selection functions, we assessed how prey availability and vegetational cover influenced tern distribution across tidal marsh gradients. Results indicated that tern foraging hotspots strongly correlated with submerged aquatic vegetation density, creating facilitation cascades for piscivorous waders. Our findings demonstrate how habitat-mediated interactions drive community organization in dynamic coastal ecosystems.

Urbanization-induced habitat fragmentation and human recreational disturbance significantly influence Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) nesting ecology in riparian corridors. We monitored 43 colonies across a gradient of anthropogenic pressure, quantifying nest success, interspecific interactions, and temporal activity patterns. Nest abandonment rates increased 78% in high-disturbance zones, with nocturnal foraging shifts indicating behavioral adaptation. Habitat loss reduced arthropod prey availability, increasing competitive exclusion by larger Ardeids. Results highlight vulnerability of crepuscular heron communities to landscape modification within fragmented wetland ecosystems, necessitating buffer zone management.

We investigated energy expenditure in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) during post-breeding dispersal along the Gulf Coast using doubly labeled water techniques. Cormorants exhibited significantly higher daily energy expenditure rates (mean ± SE: 1250 ± 98 kJ/day) compared to wintering periods, primarily driven by increased flight activity. Habitat degradation reduced foraging efficiency, forcing longer commuting flights between roosting and feeding sites. These findings highlight how coastal development impacts energy budgets in piscivorous waterbirds, with implications for conservation planning in anthropogenically altered estuaries.

Background
Brain metastasis (BM) is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in breast cancer (BC) and its molecular mechanism remains poorly understood. Transmigration of metastatic cells through the brain endothelium is an essential step in BM. Metalloproteinase-1 (MMP-1) overexpression plays a key role in promoting trans-endothelial migration by degrading the inter-endothelial junctions and disrupting the endothelial integrity. However, little is known about the molecular mechanisms that induce MMP-1 in metastatic cells granting them a brain invasive phenotype. MiR-202-3p is downregulated in brain metastases compared to primary breast tumors and directly targets MMP-1. Here, we unraveled a critical role of miR-202-3p loss in MMP-1 upregulation promoting transmigration of metastatic cells through the brain endothelium.


Methods
A variant of the MDA-MB-231 human BC cell line (MDA-MB-231-BrM2) selected for its propensity to form brain metastases was found to express high levels of MMP-1 and low levels of miR-202-3p compared to the parental cells. Using a gain-and-loss of function approach, we modulated levels of miR-202-3p and examined the resultant effect on MMP-1 expression. Effect of miR-202-3p modulation on integrity of the brain endothelium and the transmigrative ability of BC cells were also examined.


Results
Loss of miR-202-3p in breast cancer cells enhanced their transmigration through the brain endothelium by upregulating MMP-1 and disrupting the inter-endothelial junctions (claudin-5, ZO-1 and ß-catenin). Restoring miR-202-3p exerted a metastasis-suppressive effect and preserved the endothelial barrier integrity.


Conclusions
Our study identified a critical regulatory role of miR-202-3p in brain metastasis and shed light on miR-202-3p/MMP-1 axis as a novel prognostic and therapeutic target that can be exploited to predict and prevent brain metastasis in breast cancer patients.

Wilson's Phalarope (Phalaropus tricolor) exhibits a unique molt migration strategy, potentially increasing vulnerability to hunting pressure. We studied 42 satellite-tagged individuals migrating from Canadian breeding grounds (Saskatchewan) to Andean molting sites (Lake Titicaca, Bolivia) during 2019-2021. Hunting mortality rates were quantified using encounter histories and Cox proportional hazards models. Results indicated 19% higher mortality risk during molt migration compared to other periods (HR = 1.19, 95% CI: 1.05-1.35, p = 0.004), with peak vulnerability at Peruvian stopovers. This highlights the need for targeted anti-poaching measures along the Pacific Flyway.

We investigated impacts of wetland degradation on Great Egret (Ardea alba) migration ecology using GPS telemetry (n=42 individuals). Analysis revealed agricultural encroachment reduced stopover habitat quality by 38% in key flyways, significantly prolonging migration duration. Climate change-induced hydrological shifts further decreased foraging efficiency. Stopover site fidelity decreased by 25% in degraded regions, suggesting compensatory movement strategies. Conservation requires protecting wetland corridors amid changing land use patterns.

This study examines the impact of urban landfill closure on Ring-billed Gull (Larus delawarensis) foraging ecology in the Great Lakes region. Using GPS tracking and stable isotope analysis, we documented shifts in habitat use and diet composition following waste management policy changes. Results indicate significant increases in agricultural depredation and freshwater foraging, with cascading effects on local waterfowl communities. Our findings highlight how anthropogenic resource subsidies shape gull behavioral plasticity and interspecific competition dynamics in modified landscapes.

We assessed human disturbance impacts on Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) foraging efficiency along urbanizing river corridors. Through focal observations (n=42 individuals) and prey capture analysis across disturbance gradients, kingfishers in high-recreation zones exhibited 37% lower dive success rates (χ²=8.43, p<0.01) and 28% reduced handling times. Bank alteration compromised optimal perching structures, forcing suboptimal hunting strategies. These behavioral shifts indicate recreational pressures may impose significant energetic costs on this piscivorous specialist beyond baseline habitat degradation effects.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics between Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) and freshwater fish populations in the Great Lakes region. Using observational surveys and stable isotope analysis, we quantified gull predation pressure on juvenile yellow perch (Perca flavescens) during breeding seasons 2018-2021. Results indicate significant negative correlations between gull colony size and perch recruitment, mediated by localized foraging behavior. Climate-induced shifts in ice cover duration altered temporal overlap between gull arrival and fish spawning, exacerbating predation impacts. Management implications for multi-species fisheries conservation are discussed.

Growth in the publication of scientific articles is occurring at an exponential rate, prompting a growing need to synthesise information in a timely manner to combat urgent environmental problems and guide future research. Here, we undertake a topic analysis of dryland literature over the last 75 years (8218 articles) to identify areas in arid ecology that are well studied and topics that are emerging. Four topics—wetlands, mammal ecology, litter decomposition and spatial modelling, were identified as ‘hot topics’ that showed higher than average growth in publications from 1940 to 2015. Five topics—remote sensing, climate, habitat and spatial, agriculture and soils-microbes, were identified as ‘cold topics’, with lower than average growth over the survey period, but higher than average numbers of publications. Topics in arid ecology clustered into seven broad groups on word-based similarity. These groups ranged from mammal ecology and population genetics, broad-scale management and ecosystem modelling, plant ecology, agriculture and ecophysiology, to populations and paleoclimate. These patterns may reflect trends in the field of ecology more broadly. We also identified two broad research gaps in arid ecology: population genetics, and habitat and spatial research. Collaborations between population genetics and ecologists and investigations of ecological processes across spatial scales would contribute profitably to the advancement of arid ecology and to ecology more broadly.

We investigated climate change impacts on Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) populations in Chesapeake Bay marshes using occupancy modeling and nest monitoring (2018-2022). Rising sea levels increased tidal flooding frequency, reducing nest success by 37% (p<0.001) through egg inundation. Marsh migration inland was constrained by anthropogenic barriers, creating population sinks. Results demonstrate urgent need for managed retreat strategies to preserve rail habitat connectivity under accelerated sea-level rise scenarios.

Predator-prey dynamics significantly impact Rallus crepitans reproductive success in tidal marshes. We monitored 72 nests in Chesapeake Bay wetlands using motion-sensor cameras during 2019-2021 breeding seasons. Mammalian predators (raccoons, minks) accounted for 68% of depredated nests, with predation rates inversely correlated to Spartina density (r = -0.79, p<0.01). Nest concealment mediated predation risk more than tidal inundation. Results indicate habitat management targeting vegetative structure effectively reduces predator access to rails, contrasting with dabbling duck conservation strategies.

This study examined predator-prey dynamics and bycatch mortality interactions in Whimbrels (Numenius phaeopus) during spring migration. Using GPS telemetry (n=27 individuals; Altamaha River Estuary, Georgia, USA; 2019-2021) and Bayesian survival modeling, we quantified mortality sources. Bycatch accounted for 18.4% of mortalities (95% CI: 12.7-24.1%) and increased vulnerability to raptor predation (hazard ratio=2.1, p=0.008). Findings indicate additive mortality necessitates spatio-temporal fisheries closures in high-use foraging habitats.

This study quantifies microplastic ingestion effects on American Golden-Plover (Pluvialis dominica fecundity across Arctic breeding grounds. During 2018-2021, we collected 183 samples from 4 Alaskan colonies (Nuiqsut, Utqiaġvik). Fecal microplastic concentrations were measured via FT IR spectroscopy; clutch sizes were monitored via nest cameras and mark-recapture. Plovers with >0.8 microplastics/g feces had 24% fewer eggs (95% CI: 18–31%, p = 0 003). Models project 17% fecundity decline if microplastic loads increase by 50%. Urgent mitigation in coastal stopovers is needed to buffer demographic impacts.

This study employs stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N) to quantify foraging ecology of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) in Gulf of Mexico estuaries impacted by agricultural runoff. We analyzed feather samples from 42 individuals across three colonies, revealing spatial variation in nutrient assimilation linked to anthropogenic nitrogen inputs. Results indicate shifts from marine to terrestrial prey sources in proximity to drainage canals, suggesting adaptive plasticity in response to coastal eutrophication.

<jats:p>The security of cultivated land resources is closely related to a country’s food security, economic security and social security, and as such is always the top priority of those responsible for the governance and administration of state affairs. The study area is 13 prefecture-level cities in Hubei Province. An entropy weight method, comprehensive index method, spatial analysis and obstacle degree model are employed to explore the spatio-temporal characteristics and obstacle factors of cultivated land resources in quantity, quality and ecological security. The study shows that (1) the security level of cultivated land resources in Hubei Province showed an upward trend between 2010 and 2019. The land resources’ quality and ecological security showed an upward trend, while quantity security showed a downward trend. (2) The security of cultivated land resources presents obvious spatial differences, generally showing a decreasing trend from west to east. Among them, quantity security presents a spatial pattern of being high in the central, low in the east and lower in the west of Hubei Province. Quality security presents a spatial pattern of being high in the central region and low in the east and west. Ecological security presents a spatial pattern of being high in the west and low in the east. (3) The main obstacles to its security in quantity, in quality and in ecology are obviously different. Finally, some countermeasures are put forward to ensure the security of cultivated land resources from the perspectives of quantity, quality and ecological security, and to assist with the implementation of different protection policies in the western, central and eastern areas of Hubei.
