This study expands the content and perspective of cultivated land resources security and has a certain novelty in the selection of the index of water resources per unit of land area, and the application of the obstacle degree model expands the research on the influencing factors of cultivated land resource security.</jats:p>

We investigated nest site selection in Eurasian Oystercatchers (Haematopus ostralegus) relative to avian influenza virus (AIV) prevalence across coastal habitats in the Wadden Sea, Germany (2018-2021). Using GPS-loggers (n=42 adults) and nest monitoring (n=127 nests), we quantified proximity to gull colonies and waterfowl aggregation sites. Nests within 500m of high-AIV prevalence zones (RT-PCR confirmed) showed 32% lower hatching success (OR=0.48, 95% CI: 0.31-0.74) despite comparable predation rates. Our findings demonstrate disease-mediated habitat avoidance as a driver of nest site selection, suggesting exclusion zones around waterbird hotspots may reduce oystercatcher exposure to AIV.

Plant–pollinator interactions are potential drivers of evolution in floral traits. Because nectar chemical composition is known to mediate both plant–pollinator interactions and plant reproductive success, it can be expected that chemical composition of nectar is subjected to strong pollinator‐mediated selective forces. However, the extent of natural selection on different nectar components has not been studied so far. Using the Lepidoptera pollinated fragrant orchid
              Gymnadenia conopsea
              as a model species, we used high‐performance anion‐exchange chromatography (HPAEC) to characterize the sugar and amino acid composition of floral nectar in three calcareous grassland populations of
              G. conopsea
              . We then measured phenotypic selection on nectar composition and on other plant and floral traits through applying both linear regression and structural equation modelling. We demonstrate phenotypic selection on plant height, inflorescence height and on specific nectar amino acids, whereas spur length, total sugar and amino acid concentration were not direct targets of selection. Chemical nectar composition is thus indeed under selective pressure but nectar amino acids are much more important to fitness of
              G. conopsea
              , as compared to nectar sugars. Furthermore, as we found no evidence of selection on the total amino acid concentration, it is unlikely that amino acids increase pollinator attraction because they are a pollinator nitrogen source. To further unravel the evolutionary ecology of floral nectar, behavioural experiments with pollinators exposed to different nectar components and studies experimentally identifying the selective agents are recommended.

Abstract: We quantified behavioral responses of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) to recreational boating disturbance within vital foraging habitats along barrier islands. Using focal observation and GPS tracking (n=28 individuals), we documented significant decreases in foraging time (p<0 · 001) and increased flight initiation distances (FID) exceeding 160m during peak boating periods relative to controls. Management recommendations include establishing seasonal buffer zones around critical roosting sites to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this coastal piscivore.
This study investigates the predatory impact of non-native Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) on island-nesting songbird populations in the Great Lakes region from 2018-2021.

<jats:p>Despite the recent invasion and wide spread of Drosophila suzukii Matsumura (Diptera: Drosophilidae) in Europe, little is known regarding its population trends in coastal areas of the southern Mediterranean countries. Using adult trapping and fruit sampling, we studied the population dynamics of D. suzukii in coastal and mainland (semi-highland) cherry orchards of Greece, from 2018 to 2020. Adults were captured in traps baited with apple cider vinegar, placed in conventional and unmanaged sweet-cherry orchards, and in neighbouring wild growing hosts. Sampling of sweet-cherry fruit to assess infestation levels was conducted from early and late-ripening cherry cultivars in both areas. Adults were captured throughout the year in the coastal area with two peaks registered in spring and late-autumn. Captures were nearly zero during the hot summer months. Flight activity exhibited only one peak in autumn at the mainland area, and ceased during winter and spring. Captures in wild hosts were lower during the sweet-cherry ripening period than later in the season. Higher sweet-cherry infestation levels were recorded in the coastal than in the mainland area and in unmanaged than in commercial orchards. Both early and late-ripening cultivars were highly susceptible to D. suzukii infestation in the coastal area. Infestation rates were higher in late-ripening cultivars than in early-ripening ones in the mainland area. We conclude that D. suzukii has well adapted to the Mediterranean climate of Greece, and is able to progressively exploit several crops and wild hosts of mainland and coastal areas.</jats:p>

We deployed satellite transmitters on 42 American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) in Chesapeake Bay to quantify coastal habitat selection under sea-level rise pressures. Telemetry data (2018-2021) revealed strong avoidance of urbanized estuaries (p<0.01) and 63% reduction in saltmarsh use where Phragmites invasion exceeded 40% cover. Individuals exhibited 27% longer foraging bouts in protected wetlands vs. disturbed sites, indicating anthropogenic disturbance significantly compromises critical wintering resources for this declining waterfowl species.

This study quantified the energy expenditure of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) during foraging bouts in estuarine habitats using accelerometry and respirometry. We found that diving duration significantly influenced metabolic rates, with longer dives requiring disproportionately higher post-dive recovery costs. Cormorants exhibited behavioral thermoregulation strategies in response to water temperature fluctuations, increasing dive efficiency in colder conditions. These findings highlight climate change vulnerabilities through altered energy budgets in this piscivorous seabird.

This study examines the impact of coastal wetland degradation on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) nesting colonies in the Gulf of Mexico. Using aerial surveys and GIS habitat mapping from 2010-2020, we documented a 38% decline in mangrove nesting sites due to shoreline development. Population modeling revealed a significant correlation (r=-0.79, p<0.01) between habitat loss and reduced fledgling success. Our findings emphasize the critical need for mangrove conservation to sustain pelican populations facing accelerating coastal squeeze.

We investigated climate change impacts on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations in Mid-Atlantic coastal marshes using occupancy modeling (2015-2020). Rising sea levels significantly reduced suitable habitat (β = -0.32, SE=0.11, p<0.01), with marsh migration corridors constrained by urban development. Precipitation changes altered invertebrate prey availability, affecting chick survival rates (r=0.78, p=0.03). Conservation planning must address synergistic threats to this secretive marsh specialist.

Maize agriculture is dependent on two primary environmental factors, precipitation and temperature. Throughout the Eastern Mesa Verde region, fluctuations of these factors dramatically influenced demographic shifts, land use patterns, and social and religious transformations of farming populations during several key points in prehistory. While many studies have looked at the influence climate played in the depopulation of the northern Southwest after A.D. 1000, the role that climate played in the late Basketmaker III through the Pueblo I period remains unclear. This article demonstrates how fluctuations in precipitation patterns interlaced with micro- and macro- regional temperature fluctuations may have pushed and pulled human settlement and subsistence patterns across the region. Specifically, we infer that preferences for certain types of farmlands dictated whether a community used alluvial fan verses dryland farming practices, with the variable success of each type determined by shifting climate patterns. We further investigate how dramatic responses to environmental stress, such as migration and massacres, may be the result of inherited social structures of land tenure and leadership, and that such responses persist in the Eastern Mesa Verde area throughout the Pueblo I period.

This study examines the genetic structure of Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) populations across the Gulf of Mexico using microsatellite markers. We sampled 12 colonies from Texas to Florida, analyzing 314 individuals to assess gene flow patterns. Results indicate moderate isolation-by-distance signatures despite high mobility, suggesting anthropogenic barriers are impacting connectivity. Coastal development and wetland degradation emerged as significant genetic diversity predictors (P<0.Q1), highlighting conservation priorities. Findings underscore the need for regional genetic management units.

We investigated foraging efficiency of Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) in relation to tidal cycles across estuarine habitats. Using focal observations (n=120 hours) and prey capture success metrics, we found dive frequency peaked during falling tides (mean 2.7 dives/hr) versus rising tides (1.2 dives/hr; p<0.001). Prey size selection correlated with water clarity (r=0.72), suggesting visual constraints drive temporal foraging patterns. Results indicate kingfishers optimize hunting strategies to dynamic coastal conditions, with implications for managing sedimentation impacts on piscivorous birds.

Abstract Black-legged kittiwakes (BLKIs) reduce self-maintenance cost through reductions in mass-specific basal metabolic rate (BMR), body mass and the size of visceral organs during the chick-rearing period. In the present study, we measured kidney in vitro oxygen consumption and plasma 3,3′,5-triiodo- l -thyronine (T3) levels of incubating and chick-rearing female BLKIs, to test whether the decrease in BMR is caused mainly by decreased metabolic intensity or simply by reductions in the size of organs with high metabolic intensity. Body mass and body condition were lower in chick-rearing birds compared with the incubating birds. In contrast to the previous findings, however, the kidney mass did not differ between the two breeding stages. Plasma T3 levels decreased substantially during the breeding season, indicating a reduction in BMR. Over the same period, kidney mass-specific oxygen consumption decreased (by 17.2%) from the incubating to the chick-rearing stage. Thus, the reduction in BMR found in breeding BLKIs seems partly explained by adjustments in metabolic intensity of visceral organs. Lowered metabolic intensity of visceral organs would permit increased allocation of energy to offspring at the expense of their own self-maintenance.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>In the Aleutian Islands during the Holocene, terrestrial predators were actually absent; as a result, large seabird colonies thrived along the coasts or across entire islands. Bird guano enriches the soil with nitrogen, which can lead to the formation of highly modified ornithogenic (bird‐formed) ecosystems. For a more detailed investigation of avian influence, we reconstructed more than 10,000‐year‐old vegetation dynamics of the coast of Shemya Island (Near Islands) by pollen analysis. At the initial stages of vegetation development (10,000–4,600 cal year BP), sedge–heather tundra grew in the studied area. A seabird colony existed on Shemya from 4,600 to 2,400 cal year BP according to stable isotope analysis. During a period of at least 2,200 years, nitrogen enrichment led to the development of ornithogenic herb meadows with a high presence of Apiaceae. A long‐term increase in δ15N above 9–10‰ led to radical shifts in vegetation. Noticeable reduction of seabird colonies due to human hunting led to grass‐meadows spreading. After a prolonged decrease δ15N below 9–10‰ (2,400 cal year BP to present), there was a shift toward less productive sedge‐tundra communities. However, the significant enrichment of guano affected only the coastal vegetation and did not alter the inland Shemya Island.</jats:p>

This study evaluates climate change impacts on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) reproductive success along the southeastern U.S. coast. Using 15 years of nest monitoring data and satellite-derived sea surface temperature (SST) metrics, we quantified relationships between thermal stress events and breeding parameters. Generalized additive models revealed significant negative correlations between summer SST anomalies and fledgling production (β = -0.41, p < 0.001), with heatwaves causing up to 62% chick mortality. Projections indicate coastal colonies may experience reproductive failure frequencies increasing 2.3-fold by 2050 under RCP 8.5. These findings highlight thermal regulation challenges for piscivorous seabirds in warming marine ecosystems.

This demographic analysis examines anthropogenic impacts on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax). Using mark-recapture and nest monitoring in urban wetlands, we assessed adult survival and fledging success under varying disturbance regimes. Results indicate significant reductions in breeding output with increased human recreation proximity.

We assessed nest site selection in relation to avian disease transmission risk for Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) at Cape Cod National Seashore, Massachusetts, 2018–2021. Using 112 nest locations, we measured vegetation density, distance to gull colonies, and fecal contamination. Logistic regression revealed nests within 200m of Larus spp. colonies had 3.7× higher pathogen loads (β = 1.32, p = 0.011, 95% CI[1.28–4.18]) and 28% lower hatching success (p = 0.039). Results indicate microhabitat management should prioritize reducing sympatric gull interactions to mitigate disease pressure.

<jats:p>North Carolina is one of fourteen states directly regulating and controlling milk markets. The regulations are administratively complex and vary from state to state, but the general pattern of regulation follows that set by the comprehensive Federal regulation which began in 1937 with the passage of the Agricultural Marketing Agreement Act. Milk markets in most of the country, including the major producing regions, are regulated and controlled by the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). As a result of both state and federal controls, virtually no markets are unregulated. The consequences of Federal regulation of milk markets have been studied intensively, notably by Kessel and more recently by Kwoka. Less is known about the form and effects of state regulation. In this paper we analyze the case of milk market regulation in North Carolina. Specifically, we (1) review the ongoing regulation and assess the market structure and conduct of market participants including regulators; (2) review and analyze the economic implications and legal developments in reconstituting milk; and (3) investigate the policy alternatives with the purpose of determining whether there are options which, if adopted, will generate more social gains than associated social losses.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>Many arid grasslands around the world are affected by woody plant encroachment and by the replacement of a relatively continuous grass cover with shrub patches bordered by bare soil. This shift in plant community composition is often abrupt in space and time, suggesting that it is likely sustained by positive feedbacks between vegetation and environmental conditions (e.g. resource availability) or disturbance regime (e.g. fire or freeze). These feedbacks amplify the effects of drivers of shrub encroachment, i.e. of conditions favouring a shift from grass to shrub dominance (e.g. overgrazing, climate change). Here, we review some major drivers and feedbacks and identify the basic stages in the transition from grassland to shrubland. We discuss some possible scenarios of interactions between drivers and feedbacks that could explain the transition from a stage to the next and the potential irreversibility of the shift from grass to shrub dominance. We introduce a simplistic modelling framework that can integrate the various drivers to explain the emergence of bistability for shrub‐encroached grassland systems. Published 2011. This article is a U.S. Government work and is in the public domain in the USA.</jats:p>

Summary The linear programming model (LPM) of Belovsky (1978, 1986) and modifications of the classical or contingency model incorporating a digestive constraint (CM) were tested using foraging data recorded for kudus ( Tragelaphus strepsiceros ) browsing savanna vegetation over the late wet season. Food choice was between the herbaceous and woody plant components for LPM and among plant species or categories for CM. The constraints considered were consumption (cropping) rate, foraging time and digestive capacity. Woody communities dominated by Burkea  and Acacia  represented alternative habitat types. Following a minor adjustment, LPM represented the overall average diet and predicted the dietary differences between habitat types. However, the kudus failed to respond dietarily to variations among days and foraging sessions (meals) in the parameters constraining intake. The kudus accepted a wider dietary range than predicted to be optimal by CM. Evidence suggested that neither foraging time, nor digestive capacity, formed an effective constraint under the study conditions. Thermal tolerance and gut space may become limiting only towards the extremes of environmental variability that animals experience. LPM is vulnerable to circularity if average parameter values are used to estimate constraint settings. The energy maximizer—time minimizer dichotomy fails to take into account the fitness consequences of alternative foraging responses. CM is less cryptic in its application than LPM and so has greater heuristic value, despite its predictive failures. However, there may be no consistent ranking of food types where multiple constraints that are variable in their effectiveness apply. Dynamic programming models offer a solution, but pose a formidable challenge in complex natural environments.

Conservation genetics of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations reveals impacts of wetland fragmentation. Microsatellite analysis of 187 individuals across 12 Midwest breeding sites showed reduced gene flow (FST = 0.18) and allelic diversity in anthropogenically altered habitats. Isolation-by-distance patterns (Mantel r=0.41, p<0.001) indicate dispersal barriers from agricultural encroachment. Findings emphasize genetic risks of marsh habitat loss for this cryptic rallid species.

We investigated nest site selection in Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) along industrialized coastlines in Nova Scotia. Comparing 120 nest locations with random points, we assessed vegetation cover, proximity to human structures, and predator access. Logistic regression revealed significant avoidance of high-traffic zones (p<0.01) and preference for elevated sites with sparse ground cover. Anthropogenic disturbance reduced nesting density by 38% within 150m of infrastructure. Management requires buffer zones around nesting colonies to mitigate human impacts.

Understanding stopover ecology of non-Charadriiformes waterbirds is critical for wetland conservation. We studied American Coot (Fulica americana) migration through the Great Plains using GPS telemetry (n=38) and habitat assessments. Coots exhibited extended stopovers (avg 5.7±1.2 days) at eutrophic wetlands, but agricultural drainage reduced site occupancy by 62%. Human recreation disturbance triggered premature departures, with energy deficits increasing by 15% at affected sites. Climate-induced water level fluctuations further compromised foraging efficiency, highlighting synergistic threats to migration success in this declining Gruiformes species.

We investigated human disturbance impacts on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) density in managed freshwater wetlands. Using passive acoustic monitoring and callback surveys across 30 sites with gradient recreational access intensities (0-15 visits/day), we documented significant negative relationships between pedestrian traffic and rail detection probabilities (GLMM: β = -0.27, SE=0.09, p=0.003). Disturbance thresholds indicated >5 daily visits reduced occupancy by 62%, highlighting vulnerability of this elusive rallid to anthropogenic activity in critical marsh habitats.

<jats:p> Climatic changes and sea level variations have had a significant impact on the mangroves along the Brazilian coast during the Holocene. The present study focused on understanding the specific factors that have determined the establishment and expansion of mangroves in a subtropical estuary of southern Brazil (Babitonga Bay, State of Santa Catarina-SC), as well as their response to climate change and sea level variations during the late-Holocene. In this study, we carried out sedimentary analysis, palynology, and radiocarbon dating (C-14) to paleoenvironmental reconstruction of the last 1500 cal. year BP. Three facies associations were identified, indicating a progradational succession where a tidal flat was developed at the margin of the estuary. During the first phase, between at least 1440 and ±1286 cal. year BP, the area was characterized by a subtidal environment. The presence of Laguncularia pollen grains since ± 1390 cal. year BP indicated favorable conditions for mangrove establishment in proximity to the study site. Subsequently, around ± 1286 cal. year BP, the tidal flat developed, reaching the present-day shoreline, facilitated by the relative sea level drop. Avicennia trees were established on the tidal flat since ± 1273 cal. year BP, and the establishment of Rhizophora trees occurred in the most recent decades. This mangrove succession developed in Babitonga Bay following a temperature gradient, associated with low-temperature tolerance, and likely its establishment is associated with a temperature increase during the late-Holocene, that caused a migration of the southern limit of the mangrove in the subtropical zone to higher latitudes. Furthermore, the relatively slow expansion of mangroves upstream of Babitonga Bay also may have been controlled by the suitable salinity and substrate conditions, which were favored by the relative sea-level fall during the late-Holocene. </jats:p>

Sandy beaches are dynamic systems that host a diverse range of fauna whose habitat is controlled by the interactions among sand, waves and tides. In recent decades much of the study of sand beach ecology has focused on community type and structure across the range of beach types, as well as regional variations. In order to compare different studies, accurate information is required on the nature of the environment studied: sand particle size, tide range and wave conditions. Unfortunately this has not always been provided by beach ecologists. Our understanding of sandy beach processes has advanced to the stage where ecologists can no longer omit assessing the role of wave climate, even if this cannot be done precisely, as can be done for sand and tides. In this paper we provide a method to quantify wave conditions and, in combination with sand particle size and tide range, determine the beach type and state. For waves, we first highlight the concepts 'sea' and 'swell' as distinct from the terms 'sheltered' and 'exposed'; we then provide a method to estimate breaker height. We then develop a model with two steps: first, breaker height is combined with tide range to identify whether waves or tides are the primary driver of beach morphology and thereby the define the beach type (wave-dominated, tide-modified or tide-dominated); then, using breaker height, period and sand particle size, the beach state is determined. Seven main beach morphodynamic types-states are defined. At the narrow and steep extreme are wave-dominated reflective beaches and at the wide and low gradient extreme are tide-dominated flats. The physical and ecological features typical of the seven types-states are presented, as well as some management implications.

We investigated how invasive Spartina angustifolia encroachment affects prebasic molt migration in Curlew Sandpipers (Calidris ferruginea) at Chongming Dongtan, China (31°30'N, 121°50'E). Using GPS telemetry (n=32 birds) and feather isotope analysis (δ²H) from 2018-2020, we found Spartina-dominated sites delayed molt initiation by 11.7±2.3 days (p=0.008) and reduced feather growth rates by 18% (95% CI: 12-24%) compared to native Scirpus mariqueter habitats. Population modeling indicated this could decrease overwinter survival by 9-14% if Spartina coverage exceeds 40%. Conservation requires prioritizing native vegetation restoration at critical molt staging areas.

Abstract: We analyzed Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia) migration across North America using GPS telemetry (n=42 individuals). Departure timing from breeding sites correlated with decreasing photoperiod (r=-0.↵78), while migration speed varied significantly with wind patterns (p<0.↵001). Stopover duration decreased at southern sites due to coastal development. Major threats included wetland habitat loss and turbine collisions during passage. This highlights climate-photoperiod decoupling risks for long-distance migrants beyond Charadriiformes.

We assessed demographic responses of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) to anthropogenic pressures in urban lake ecosystems using multi-state mark-recapture modeling. Over six breeding seasons, we documented significant declines in adult survival (φ = 0.76 ± 0.04) associated with microplastic ingestion prevalence and habitat fragmentation from coastal development. Fledging success decreased by 32% in high-disturbance zones, emphasizing the vulnerability of this adaptable species to cumulative urbanization impacts despite behavioral plasticity.

We investigated habitat selection of Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) in urban coastal ecosystems using GPS telemetry and resource selection functions. Surprisingly, gulls demonstrated strong avoidance of traditional intertidal zones, instead favoring freshwater retention ponds and landfill perimeters for foraging. Anthropogenic noise levels significantly predicted roost site selection, with birds actively avoiding areas exceeding 65 dB. These findings highlight unexpected adaptability to human-modified landscapes while underscoring vulnerability to waste management policies.

Morphological variation in Semipalmated Plovers (Charadrius semipalmatus), particularly bill dimensions, may influence susceptibility to plastic ingestion—a growing conservation threat. We studied 124 individuals across three eastern Canadian staging sites (Bay of Fundy, Mingan Archipelago, Sable Island; 2018-2021) using high-frequency GPS telemetry combined with regurgitation sampling. Plovers with longer bills (mean ± SE: 15·8 ± 0·3 mm; n=67) ingested 42% more microplastics (95% CI: 1·15-1·75, p=0·007) than shorter-billed conspecifics (14·2 ± 0·4 mm; n=57). This phenotype-environment mismatch suggests bill morphology exacerbates plastic consumption risk during migration stopovers, necessitating targeted debris mitigation in key staging habitats.

We investigated the impact of cadmium contamination on the population genetics of Common Sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos) along the industrialised Vistula River in Poland. Blood samples from 120 individuals across 6 breeding sites (2019–2021) were analysed for Cd concentrations via ICP-MS and genotyped using 15 microsatellite loci (PCR). Cd concentrations ranged 2.1–18.7 ppm (geometric mean = 4.3 ppm) and correlated with reduced heterozygosity (r = -0 38, p = 0 02) and elevated FST (p < 0 01). Our data suggest heavy metal exposure drives genetic erosion in this indicator species, requiring urgent remediation of riparian habitats.

Context The Gunnison sage-grouse (Centrocercus minimus) has experienced range-wide declines and has been listed as Threatened by the USA Fish and Wildlife Service to receive protections under the USA Endangered Species Act. A draft Recovery Plan was recently completed. No seasonal habitat models have been developed for the small isolated populations.Aims To develop a habitat suitability model that was collaboratively developed between modellers and conservation practitioners to predict the probability of use by Gunnison sage-grouse during the breeding and summer seasons in designated occupied critical habitat, and extrapolate to adjacent designated unoccupied critical habitat.Methods We captured, marked and tracked Gunnison sage-grouse in nine different studies spanning 25 years. We used a suite of biotic, abiotic and vegetation local-level and population-scale covariates in a use-available resource selection function to develop models that predict the probability of use by Gunnison sage-grouse.Key results We used 9140 Gunnison sage-grouse locations from 406 individual birds to develop nine resource selection models for occupied habitat and extrapolated model predictions to adjacent unoccupied critical habitat in five small isolated Gunnison sage-grouse populations. A majority of our models validated well.Conclusions We report the first two-season resource use-based habitat suitability models for five of six small isolated Gunnison sage-grouse populations. Because of the unique habitat use by Gunnison sage-grouse in each population, we recommend that resource managers strategically target management actions in individual populations and avoid ‘one-size-fits-all’ habitat management prescriptions.Implications Our models will assist managers in the identification of seasonal habitats within populations to target management actions for Gunnison sage-grouse recovery.

Surfbirds (Calidris virgata) wintering in Glacier Bay, Alaska, were studied to assess noise pollution impacts on energy expenditure. Using implantable heart rate loggers in 38 individuals and respirometry trials (December 2018-February 2020), we measured metabolic responses to vessel noise (105 dB re 20 μPa). Experimental exposures increased energy expenditure during foraging by 23.7% (95% CI: 18.2-29.2%, p<0.01) and elevated resting metabolic rate by 17.4% (CI: 12.1-22.7%, p=0.003). Results indicate chronic acoustic disturbance imposes significant energetic costs, potentially reducing overwinter survival. Management should prioritize noise mitigation in high-density foraging habitats.

Context The role of disturbance and its exclusion is fundamental to the conservation of threatened species. Aims We used the habitat accommodation model as a framework to investigate the importance of forest disturbance for the endangered Hastings River mouse, Pseudomys oralis, focusing on timber harvesting. Methods Our study comprised two separate surveys. We resurveyed old survey sites (n = 24) where the species was originally recorded as either present (logging excluded) or absent (subsequently logged). A second survey targeted trapping in high-quality habitat stratified by different times since logging. Finally, we analysed a 15-year trapping dataset targeting P. oralis to assess associations with co-occurring species. Key results The resurvey of old sites resulted in 12 P. oralis individuals being trapped, compared with 46 individuals in original surveys. Substantial declines were observed over time in transects where logging was excluded (60–82% decline), whereas there was little change at transects where P. oralis was not previously trapped and that were subsequently logged. The second survey yielded 27 P. oralis captures at post-logging sites assessed as high quality. Occupancy was very high (ψ = 0.93 ± 0.21) in transects logged 7–15 years ago and was 60% less in transects where logging was excluded for 35–45 years (ψ = 0.37 ± 0.22), whereas occupancy in transects logged 2–6 years ago was intermediate. This pattern of higher occupancy in logged areas was mirrored for the mean number of P. oralis trapped per transect. Ordination of habitat data showed an association of P. oralis with heath, mat-rushes and logs, whereas rats (Rattus and Melomys) were associated with ferns and shrubs. Camera traps revealed low background levels of predator presence. A negative exponential relationship was found between probability of occupancy of P. oralis and rat abundance from a 15-year trapping dataset (44 275 trap-nights), suggesting that rats may compete with P. oralis. Conclusions Our results supported the habitat accommodation model and suggested that disturbance is likely to influence the persistence of P. oralis. However, an interaction between predation and loss of cover from high-frequency disturbance (fire or intense grazing) cannot be excluded as a key threat. Implications Disturbance should be incorporated into the management of some species. Adaptive monitoring is recommended to assess alternative management regimes.

We analyzed 15-year demographic data for Great Egret (Ardea alba) colonies in the Mississippi Alluvial Valley using mark-recapture and nest monitoring. Adult survival probability declined significantly (φ = 0.89 to 0.74) alongside wetland conversion to agriculture. Mercury bioaccumulation reduced fledging success by 38% in contaminated sites. Matrix projections indicate population decline (λ = 0.92) without immediate habitat restoration and pollution control measures. Study underscores vulnerability of wading birds to hydrological alteration.

<jats:p>Seasonal and bathymetric distribution of the main age groups of pacific cod in the northern Japan Sea are considered on the data of bottom trawl surveys in 1980–2023. The main wintering and spawning accumulations, where the fish concentrate from December to January and then spawn in February-March, are formed on the external shelf and the upper continental slope along the western coast approximately between Peter the Great Bay and 47о N and along the eastern coast between Cape Krillon and 47о 30′N. The juveniles have feeding migrations from April to May, while older age groups complete the migrations a month later. They migrate in three main directions: from the areas at the mainland coast – southwestward and northeastward and from the areas at western Sakhalin — southward. The juveniles feed on shallows in Peter the Great Bay, northern Tatar Strait, and on southwestern shelf of Sakhalin between the Nevelsky Bay and Cape Krillon, whereas the feeding grounds for older groups occupy two vast areas including Peter the Great Bay with the adjacent southeastern shelf of Primorye and the shelf of northern Primorye in the Tatar Strait (to the north from 47о N) with the whole shelf of Sakhalin. In the northern Tatar Strait (northward from 48о N), the cod belonged to the Primorye and Sakhalin stocks can feed together. The feeding season lasts from June to September. The older cod feed usually deeper that the juveniles. Back migrations of cod for wintering occur from October to November. Because of a joint feeding area where the mainland and Sakhalin stocks are able to mix, the bottom trawl surveys at Primorye coast cannot be used for correct assessment of the total available catch (TAC) in this fishing district. To improve quality of the cod fishery forecasts, the methods of cohort or production analyses should be used, with the control by bottom trawl surveys data, as alternative information about the state of cod stocks, taking into account the abovementioned patterns of seasonal distribution and migrations.</jats:p>

This bioacoustic study investigates anthropogenic noise impacts on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) vocal communication in coastal breeding habitats. Using passive acoustic monitoring at 20 nest sites across urbanized estuaries, we quantified call rates and structure in relation to ambient noise levels. Results demonstrate significant noise-correlated alterations in parental alarm call frequency and chick begging intensity during critical provisioning periods, suggesting acoustic masking may disrupt reproductive behaviors. Findings highlight noise pollution as an emerging threat for this piscivorous raptor's coastal adaptation.

This study examined the impact of tidal gate modifications on Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) nesting success in managed salt marshes along the Atlantic coast. Using radio-telemetry and nest monitoring across 12 sites, we found that reduced hydrologic connectivity decreased rail productivity by 32% due to increased predation and vegetation overgrowth. Our results demonstrate that water management infrastructure designed for mosquito control requires adaptive strategies to maintain rail habitat suitability amid sea-level rise.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p><jats:list list-type="order"><jats:list-item><jats:p>Biological colouration presents a canvas for the study of ecological and evolutionary processes. Enduring interest in colour-based phenotypes has driven, and been driven by, improved techniques for quantifying colour patterns in ever-more relevant ways, yet the need for flexible, open frameworks for data processing and analysis persists.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p>Here we introduce <jats:monospace>pavo 2</jats:monospace>, the latest iteration of the R package <jats:monospace>pavo</jats:monospace>. This release represents the extensive refinement and expansion of existing methods, as well as a suite of new tools for the cohesive analysis of the spectral and (now) spatial structure of colour patterns and perception. At its core, the package retains a broad focus on (a) the organisation and processing of spectral and spatial data, and tools for the alternating (b) visualisation, and (c) analysis of data. Significantly, <jats:monospace>pavo 2</jats:monospace> introduces image-analysis capabilities, providing a cohesive workflow for the comprehensive analysis of colour patterns.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p>We demonstrate the utility of <jats:monospace>pavo</jats:monospace> with a brief example centred on mimicry in <jats:italic>Heliconius</jats:italic> butterflies. Drawing on visual modelling, adjacency, and boundary strength analyses, we show that the combined spectral (colour and luminance) and spatial (pattern element distribution and boundary salience) features of putative models and mimics are closely aligned.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p><jats:monospace>pavo 2</jats:monospace> offers a flexible and reproducible environment for the analysis of colour, with renewed potential to assist researchers in answering fundamental questions in sensory ecology and evolution.</jats:p></jats:list-item></jats:list></jats:p>

Our study investigated migration phenology in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) along the Atlantic coast using automated telemetry. We evaluated effects of lunar cycles, tidal amplitude, and coastal development pressure on nocturnal migration timing across 3 annual cycles (2019-2021). Results indicated delayed departures and reduced flight distances in populations experiencing >15% marsh habitat loss.

This study investigates the impact of anthropogenic noise on Marbled Godwit (Limosa fedoa) breeding ecology in managed wetlands of Saskatchewan, Canada (2019-2022). Using nest monitoring (n=127 nests) and acoustic recordings at 18 sites with varying aircraft traffic (0-65 events/day), we assessed disturbance effects. Nests within 1 km of runways exhibited 32% lower daily survival rates (β = -0.18, SE=0 04 p<0 001) and shorter incubation bouts (7 2±0 8 hr vs 9 1±0 6 hr in controls; F1 126=9 73 p=0 002). Our findings advocate for noise abatement buffers in wetland management plans to mitigate energetic costs on this declining shorebird species.

This study investigates mercury bioaccumulation impacts on Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) reproductive success along the Gulf coast. We analyzed eggshell thickness and mercury concentrations from 45 nests across 3 colonies during 2020-2022 breeding seasons. Results show significant negative correlation between mercury levels and hatching success (r=-0 72, p<0 01), with eggshell thinning observed at high-contamination sites.

This study quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) wintering in coastal wetlands using doubly-labeled water and GPS telemetry. Anthropogenic disturbances from coastal development increased flight-associated energy costs by 22±3% (mean±SE), while tidal restrictions altered foraging patterns, elevating DEE during low-tide periods. Bioenergetics modeling indicated reduced lipid reserves could compromise migration preparedness under cumulative stressors.

Understanding the synergistic effects of anthropogenic disturbance and thermal stress is crucial for conserving beach-nesting shorebirds. We investigated how human recreational activities modulate American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) thermoregulatory responses during incubation on the Georgia Barrier Islands (USA). Using temperature loggers in 73 nests and observational disturbance metrics (n = 312 hours), we documented elevated egg temperatures (Δ +1.8°C ± 0 4 SE) and increased nest abandonment probability (OR = 3 2; 95%CI 1 7-6 0 p < 0 01 ) under combined high-disturbance and ambient temperature >32°C scenarios. Our results highlight the urgent need for temporal zoning of human access to beaches during heatwaves to buffer climate impacts.

The emerald ash borer (EAB) has killed ash species (Fraxinus L.) in much of eastern North America, but it has yet to reach the vast ash wetlands in northern Minnesota, USA. In these wetlands, a single species, black ash (Fraxinus nigra Marsh.) comprises a majority of trees and has a foundational role in controlling ecosystem function. Given the likelihood of wide-spread mortality of black ash from EAB and the likelihood of severe ecosystem impacts, we examined the potential for co-occurring tree species to replace black ash, either through gap filling in the overstory or release from the understory. We addressed this objective by examining woody plant communities in 32 mature black ash sites located across a large geographic region and inclusive of two distinct wetland types as defined by hydrologic regime. Our results indicate a region-wide lack of species capable of replacing black ash in both wetland hydrologic types; thus there is very low existing potential for replacement of black ash from expansion in the overstory or through release in the understory. These results point to an urgent need for silvicultural intervention to identify and establish future-adapted non-ash tree species so as to promote resilience in the face of EAB by maintaining aspects of the foundational role of black ash in controlling ecosystem functions.

We investigated Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) foraging ecology in response to coastal mudflat reclamation in the Fraser River Delta, British Columbia. Using radio-telemetry (n=32 birds) and habitat surveys across 2019-2021, we quantified foraging site fidelity and prey availability. Snipe showed 78% higher foraging effort in undisturbed tidal marshes versus reclaimed areas (p=0.003), with invertebrate biomass 60% lower in reclaimed zones. Our results demonstrate that habitat loss directly reduces foraging efficiency, emphasizing the need to preserve intact intertidal ecosystems for this declining species.

We assessed coastal marsh degradation impacts on juvenile American Black Duck (Anas rubripes) survival in Chesapeake Bay estuaries. Using VHF telemetry, 68 ducklings from 22 broods were tracked across marsh complexes experiencing varying degradation levels. Survival probability declined 42% in degraded marshes due to reduced cover and macroinvertebrate prey. Tidal inundation patterns altered by sea-level rise compounded predation risk. Results indicate marsh conservation is critical for recruitment in this declining waterfowl species.

This study examined Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) nest site selection across a gradient of anthropogenic disturbance in coastal Labrador. Using GPS telemetry (n=47 females) and nest surveys (n=213 nests), we modeled habitat characteristics influencing nest establishment probability. Eiders strongly avoided sites within 200m of human infrastructure (OR=0.21, p<0 .001), instead selecting islands with dense Salix spp. cover (OR=3.78, p=0.002). Our findings highlight acute sensitivity to coastal development in this keystone sea duck species.

This study examined the foraging ecology of Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) in urban estuarine habitats using GPS tracking and behavioral observations. We quantified impacts of shoreline development and artificial light pollution on nocturnal foraging efficiency. Results demonstrated significant reductions in prey capture rates (p<0.05) and increased energy expenditure in disturbed sites, with herons shifting activity toward remnant tidal marshes. Our findings highlight anthropogenic threats to Ardeidae foraging success in modified coastal ecosystems.

This study examines Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) population dynamics on the Gulf Coast from 2010-2020 using annual breeding surveys. Generalized Linear Models revealed significant declines (-3.4%/year, p<0.***) associated with increased coastal development (β=-0.71) and storm frequency (β= -0.53). Urbanization-induced habitat fragmentation emerged as the primary driver of colony abandonment, contrasting with stable pelagic populations.***

We quantified the impact of recreational photography on energy expenditure in Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa islandica) during pre-migratory staging in Iceland. Using accelerometer loggers (n=32 birds) and focal observations at Skjálfandi Bay (65°40'N, 17°00'W) from July-August 2020, we documented a 27% increase in flight initiation distance (FID) and 18% higher daily energy expenditure (DEE) in areas with >5 photographers/day compared to control sites (mixed-effects model: β=0.22±0.04 SE, p=0.003). This equates to a daily energy deficit of 12.7 kJ, potentially delaying migratory departure by 3-5 days. Conservation measures should establish buffer zones around high-use foraging habitats to minimize anthropogenic disturbance during critical fattening periods.

Geographic variation in body size and bill morphology of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) was examined across coastal breeding colonies from British Columbia to Baja California. Using multivariate analysis of 12 skeletal measurements from 180 museum specimens, we identified significant clinal variation corresponding to thermal gradients. Northern populations exhibited 7-12% larger tarsus and bill depth measurements than southern conspecifics, potentially reflecting Bergmann's Rule adaptations. This morphological plasticity may influence foraging efficiency under climate change scenarios, warranting consideration in coastal waterbird management.

This study examines parental investment strategies in Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) nesting in coastal wetlands of Chesapeake Bay. Using focal observations of 32 breeding pairs, we quantified time-activity budgets during incubation and brood-rearing phases. Females significantly increased vigilance behavior (p<0.01) while males prioritized territory defense. Nest survival rates declined with proximity to human recreational areas (r=-0.72), suggesting anthropogenic disturbance disproportionately impacts female care allocation. Our results highlight trade-offs between predator avoidance and provisioning in anthropogenic landscapes.

Examined Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax)’s niche partitioning within mixed Ardeidae assemblages at urban wetlands. Quantified foraging site selection and temporal activity patterns using radio-telemetry and behavioral observations over two breeding seasons (2021-2022). Results indicate significant avoidance of diurnal herons (e.g., Great Egret) through crepuscular foraging peaks, facilitating coexistence despite high resource overlap. Anthropogenic habitat alteration shifted optimal foraging zones towards anthropogenic subsidies.

We investigated trophic niche partitioning in Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) populations along Florida's Gulf Coast using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of blood samples. Results indicate significant dietary shifts from marine fish to freshwater prey in estuarine colonies experiencing coastal development. This resource switching correlates with declining reproductive success, suggesting anthropogenic habitat alteration forces suboptimal foraging strategies. Isotopic niche widths narrowed by 38% in disturbed sites, highlighting vulnerability to further wetland degradation.
This study examines nest site selection in Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) populations inhabiting coastal marshes along the Gulf of Mexico during the 2020 breeding season.

We investigated the impact of heavy metal pollution (Cd, Pb) on parasitic infection rates in Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) wintering in the Tagus Estuary, Portugal. From 2019-2021, we collected blood samples (n=142 adults) and fecal samples (n=89) to quantify metal concentrations via ICP-MS and parasite loads via microscopy/PCR. Individuals with elevated cadmium levels (>0.8 μg/g dw) showed 2.3× higher trematode prevalence (95% CI: 1.4-3.7, p=0.008) and reduced hemoglobin concentrations (β=-0.24, p<0.001). Our results demonstrate that sublethal pollution exacerbates parasitic burdens, highlighting the need for integrated wetland management to mitigate synergistic threats.

The breeding of Merlins Falco columbarius was monitored within a study area in the Yorkshire Dales National Park over a sixteen year period. Nesting territories were visited annually to trap adult Merlins and monitor eggs and young. Standard BTO rings were used on both adults and nestlings and, in addition, passive integrated transponders (PIT) tags were fitted to adult birds, which allowed for their subsequent identification without the need to retrap. Forty‐four adult Merlins and 267 nestlings were ringed or controlled at nest sites in 33 territories, for which three adult and 18 nestling recovery records were obtained. The movement of adults entering the study area to breed was predominantly from north or south, in approximately equal numbers. Many females used different territories between years, and such movements partly accounted for the high turnover of birds at particular territories. The three adult recoveries showed winter movements of 196, 264 and 287 km. The majority of recoveries of birds ringed as nestlings occurred before the end of their first calendar year, within 150 km of their natal site, and almost all to the south.

We investigated Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) vocal responses to simulated egg collection events in Venezuela's Llanos wetlands (2019-2021). Using automated recorders at 40 nests, we quantified alarm call rates before/during human approach simulations. Alarm call frequency increased 300% during intrusions (p=0.003), correlating with proximity (r=0.78). Nest abandonment probability rose to 0.67 when call rates exceeded baseline by >200% (95% CI: 0.55-0.79). Results demonstrate acoustic sensitivity to poaching risk, informing anti-harvesting strategies for this Charadriiform species.

Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) stopover ecology was assessed at contaminated coastal sites in Monterey Bay, California. We analyzed organochlorine pesticide residues in blood samples (n=42) and correlated them with foraging behavior via GPS telemetry (2018-2020). Plovers utilizing agricultural runoff-affected habitats exhibited elevated DDE concentrations (mean=3.2±0.8 ppm) and 27% reduced foraging efficiency (p=0.01) compared to reference sites. Results indicate chemical exposure compromises refueling capacity during migration, necessitating wetland remediation for this threatened subspecies.

We assessed hunting impacts on Sanderling (Calidris alba) populations within managed wetlands of the Yellow Sea coast, China. Using GPS telemetry (n=42 birds) and hunter interview surveys (n=87) during 2018-2020, we quantified spatial overlap and mortality risk. Sanderlings exhibited 37% higher mortality in zones with unregulated hunting (HR=1.37, 95% CI: 1.12-1.68). Population modeling projected a 22% decline over 10 years under current harvest rates. Results emphasize urgent need for enforcement of hunting bans in critical stopover habitats to prevent local extirpation.

We investigated molt migration in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) across Chesapeake Bay marshes using satellite telemetry and feather isotope analysis. Tracking 32 adults revealed movements up to 120 km to discrete molting sites with high crab biomass. These nutrient-rich brackish wetlands face compounding threats from tidal restrictions and shoreline hardening that reduce invertebrate prey availability during this energetically demanding life stage, potentially impairing feather regeneration in this declining species.

This study examines climate change impacts on Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) populations along the northeastern Atlantic coast. Using 20 years of nest monitoring data from 45 riverine sites, we analyzed breeding phenology shifts and reproductive success in relation to temperature anomalies and extreme precipitation events. Results indicate significant advancement in egg-laying dates (0.8 days/year) correlated with spring warming, but increased nest flooding during intense rainfall reduced fledging success by 32%. These findings highlight climate-driven phenological mismatches and hydrological threats to this cavity-nesting piscivore.

This study examines the impact of coastal wetland degradation on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes), during spring migration along the Atlantic Flyway. We tracked 48 individuals using GPS telemetry to assess habitat selection patterns amid increasing sea-level rise and marsh fragmentation. Results indicate significant avoidance of degraded saltmarshes (p<0·001) and reduced stopover duration in compromised habitats. Our findings underscore the vulnerability of this waterfowl species to anthropogenic alterations in critical estuarine ecosystems, with implications for conservation prioritization.

This study examines the impacts of saltwater intrusion on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes: Anatidae) nest site selection and hatching success in coastal marshes of Chesapeake Bay. Using GPS telemetry (n=42) and nest monitoring (2018-2020), we found reduced hatching rates (β=-0.27, SE=0·08) and elevated nest flooding (OR=4.1, CI:1·9-8·3). Results suggest brackish wetland restoration may mitigate climate-induced habitat degradation.

We investigated parental care plasticity in Ruddy Turnstone (Arenaria interpres) breeding at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard (78°55'N) during the 2020-2022 seasons. Using temperature-logging nest monitors (n=37 nests) and behavioral observations during extreme precipitation events (>30mm/24hr), we quantified changes in brooding attendance. Events reduced brooding time by 42% (p<0.01, paired t-test) and increased nest abandonment probability (OR=3.4, 95% CI:1.8-6.3). Chick mortality surged by 28% per event (R²=0.73). Results indicate extreme weather compromises thermoregulatory care, highlighting climate vulnerability for Arctic-breeding Charadriiformes.

We assessed plastic ingestion rates in Black-bellied Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola) wintering in managed wetlands of the Fraser River Delta, British Columbia. Necropsies of 112 carcasses (2018-2021) revealed 34.8% contained macroplastics (>1mm), predominantly polyethylene fragments (78.2% of items). Individuals with ingested plastics exhibited significantly lower body condition indices (mean difference: -1.7±0.4 SE; p=0.002) compared to plastic-free conspecifics. Our findings highlight plastic pollution as an emerging threat requiring integration into wetland management frameworks for this IUCN Near Threatened species.

We investigated Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) population dynamics in Chesapeake Bay marshes using mark-recapture analysis (2018-2022). Adult survival probability (φ = 0.76 ± 0.04) declined significantly with sea-level rise (β = -0.32, p<0.01), while nest success (0.42 ± 0.07) correlated negatively with invasive Phragmites density. Recruitment rates showed compensatory responses to habitat fragmentation. Our demographic matrix model predicts local extinction within 15 years under current threats, highlighting urgent conservation needs for this saltmarsh specialist facing synergistic pressures from coastal development and climate change.

This study examines the impact of rising sea levels on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nesting success in Chesapeake Bay marshes. Using a 10-year dataset of nest monitoring and tidal gauge records, we demonstrate that increased tidal flooding events correlate significantly with reduced fledging rates (r = -0.78, p<0.01). Climate-induced habitat alterations are forcing adaptive shifts in nest site selection toward anthropogenic structures, with implications for conservation planning in vulnerable coastal ecosystems.

We investigated migration ecology of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) in the Mississippi Flyway using automated radio telemetry. From 2018-2020, we tracked 42 individuals to assess stopover duration and habitat selection during spring migration. Rails showed strong preference for emergent wetlands with dense cover, avoiding agricultural areas. Migration timing correlated with spring temperature anomalies (r=0.72, p<0.01), suggesting climate sensitivity. Habitat loss reduced stopover site availability by 32% in key regions, potentially explaining recent population declines.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics of Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon), focusing on selectivity in fish consumption across coastal estuaries in Atlantic Canada. Using regurgitate analysis (n=103 birds) and underwater videography at perches, we found kingfishers disproportionately targeted large, non-native fish species despite availability of smaller native prey. This predation preference may unintentionally aid invasive fish control but raises concerns about bioaccumulation of contaminants through top trophic transfer.

This study investigates the bioacoustic responses of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) to anthropogenic noise pollution in coastal nesting colonies. Using passive acoustic monitoring at three sites along the Gulf Coast, we quantified vocalization rates and frequency shifts during periods of varying boat traffic intensity. Results indicate significant suppression of contact calls and altered peak frequencies during high-disturbance events, suggesting acoustic masking effects. These findings highlight the vulnerability of colonial waterbirds to auditory interference in increasingly urbanized coastal habitats, with implications for communication efficiency and breeding behavior.

This study investigates juvenile survival rates in Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) populations along the Chesapeake Bay, USA. Using mark-recapture analysis of 127 fledglings over three breeding seasons (2018-2020), we assessed impacts of coastal development and water quality degradation on first-year mortality. Results indicate a significant negative correlation between shoreline urbanization intensity and survival probability (r = -0.72, p<0.001), with PCB contamination in prey fish emerging as a key sublethal threat factor. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of juvenile Ospreys to anthropogenic pressures in estuarine ecosystems.

In the tropical rainforests of northern Australia, we investigated the effects of habitat fragmentation and ecological parameters on the prevalence of blood-borne parasites (Plasmodium and Haemoproteus) in bird communities. Using mist-nets on forest edges and interiors, we sampled bird communities across six study sites: 3 large fragments (20–85 ha) and 3 continuous-forest sites. From 335 mist-net captures, we recorded 28 bird species and screened 299 bird samples with PCR to amplify and detect target DNA. Of the 28 bird species sampled, 19 were infected with Plasmodium and/or Haemoproteus and 9 species were without infection. Over one third of screened birds (99 individuals) were positive for Haemoproteus and/or Plasmodium. In forest fragments, bird capture rates were significantly higher than in continuous forests, but bird species richness did not differ. Unexpectedly, we found that the prevalence of the dominant haemosporidian infection, Haemoproteus, was significantly higher in continuous forest than in habitat fragments. Further, we found that ecological traits such as diet, foraging height, habitat specialisation and distributional ranges were significantly associated with blood-borne infections.

We investigated juvenile survival of Great Egrets (Ardea alba) in the Mississippi Delta, USA, over three nesting seasons (2018-2020). Using mark-recapture methods, we estimated survival rates at 0 45 (SE = 0 07) for the first year post-fledging. Mortality was highest during dispersal (51% of deaths). Flood-induced habitat loss significantly lowered survival (β = -1 2 P < 0 01), while wetland restoration exhibited positive effects (β = 0 8 P = 0 03). Climate-driven hydrological extremes threaten recruitment in this wading bird population.

We investigated population dynamics of Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) in the Chesapeake Bay estuary from 2015-2020. Using mark-recapture analysis of 312 banded individuals, we documented a 22% decline in adult survival rates correlated with increased mercury contamination (r = -0.87, p<0.01) and wetland habitat fragmentation. Nesting success decreased significantly with proximity to urban development (β = -0.41, p=0.003), suggesting anthropogenic pressures are driving regional population decreases in this non-shorebird wading species.

This study examines habitat selection and population dynamics of the Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) in fragmented coastal marshes of the Pacific Northwest. Using occupancy modeling and acoustic monitoring across 32 sites from 2018-2020, we demonstrate significant declines (β = -0.27, SE=0 09, p<0 01 ) in rail density correlated with marsh degradation. Tide gate installation and invasive Spartina spread reduced available nesting habitat by ~38%, highlighting synergistic threats of infrastructure and biological invasion in these vulnerable ecosystems. Conservation strategies must prioritize marsh connectivity to buffer this secretive rallid against coastal squeeze.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The toxicity and environmental concerns of methyl bromide (MB) have been a significant impetus for research into environmentally benign fumigant alternatives. Ethyl formate (EF) and chlorine dioxide (ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>) are FDA‐approved agents with potential as alternatives to MB. However, both are chemically unstable and pose considerable end‐use challenges. In this study, we developed moisture‐activated sachets for EF and ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> to facilitate their end‐use deployment for in‐package fumigation. The sachets were loaded with EF or ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> metastable precursors, citric acid (CA), and a deliquescent salt carrier (e.g., CaCl<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> or NaCl). When placed in an elevated relative humidity environment, these combinations activate the release of EF or ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> gases, separately. The deliquescence lowering phenomenon and its effect on fumigants release rate were investigated when mixing CA with CaCl<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> or NaCl. The mutual deliquescence relative humidity for CA–CaCl<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> and CA–NaCl mixtures were 40% and 63%, respectively. CaCl<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> enhanced the release rate of fumigants from their sachets, whereas NaCl resulted in a slower release rate. EF and ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> sachets were evaluated for fumigation of different life stages of spotted wing drosophila (SWD). Complete control of SWD adults was achieved after exposure to 10.1 mg·h/L EF, while eggs, larval, and pupal stages were more tolerant toward EF vapour and required 110.2 mg·h/L EF to achieve control. ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> at low concentrations was more effective than EF against all SWD life stages, excluding pupae. Complete mortality was achieved after fumigating SWD adults, eggs, and larvae with 0.73, 2.39, and 1.21 mg·h/L ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub>, respectively. These results indicated that both EF and ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> sachets could be employed safely for EF and ClO<jats:sub>2</jats:sub> in‐packaging fumigation to control produce pests.</jats:p>

We investigated the impacts of recreational disturbance on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax ) nesting success in urban wetland colonies. Using a BACI design at 12 sites with varying visitor frequency, we monitored nest productivity before and after implementing seasonal access restrictions. Statistical modeling revealed a significant negative relationship between disturbance intensity and fledging rates (β = -0 .41, SE = 0 .12 , p = 0 .002 ). Our findings demonstrate that anthropogenic activity must be managed to conserve this declining Ardeidae species.

This study examined Great Egret (Ardea alba) nesting habitat selection in a managed wetland complex. Using logistic regression models with nest-site covariates (vegetation height, water depth, distance to human activity), we found proximity to anthropogenic disturbance significantly reduced occupancy probability (β = -1.24, SE = 0.31, p < 0.001). Nest success was positively associated with taller emergent vegetation (β = 0.87, SE = 0.19, p < 0.01) but negatively impacted by fluctuating water levels from climate variability. Results highlight management tradeoffs between hydrological control and habitat quality for this wading bird.

We measured daily energy expenditure (DEE) in breeding Red-necked Phalaropes (Phalaropus lobatus) across coastal disturbance gradients near Prudhoe Bay, Alaska, during 2018-2020. Using doubly labeled water techniques on 35 radio-tagged individuals, DEE increased by 32.7% (95% CI: 24.1-41.3%; p=0.002) in high-development zones versus control sites. This elevated metabolic cost corresponded with reduced chick provisioning rates (r = -0.78, p<0.01). Results demonstrate coastal infrastructure imposes significant energetic constraints, necessitating buffer zones in conservation planning for Arctic-breeding shorebirds.

Abstract An oligotrophic phosphorus (P) limited seagrass ecosystem in Florida Bay was experimentally fertilized in a unique way. Perches were installed to encourage seabirds to roost and deliver an external source of nutrients via defecation. Two treatments were examined: (1) a chronic 23-year fertilization and (2) an earlier 28-month fertilization that was discontinued when the chronic treatment was initiated. Because of the low mobility of P in carbonate sediments, we hypothesized long-term changes to ecosystem structure and function in both treatments. Structural changes in the chronic treatment included a shift in the dominant seagrass species from  Thalassia testudinum  to  Halodule wrightii , large increases in epiphytic biomass and sediment chlorophyll-a, and a decline in species richness. Functional changes included increased benthic metabolism and quantum efficiency. Initial changes in the 28-month fertilization were similar, but after 23 years of nutrient depuration  T. testudinum  has reestablished itself as the dominant species. However, P remains elevated in the sediment and  H. wrightii  has maintained a presence. Functionally the discontinued treatment remains altered. Biomass exceeds that in the chronic treatment and indices of productivity, elevated relative to control, are not different from the chronic fertilization. Cessation of nutrient loading has resulted in a superficial return to the pre-disturbance character of the community, but due to the nature of P cycles functional changes persist.

We examined population dynamics of American Black Duck (Anas rubripes) in mid-Atlantic coastal marshes using 15 years of banding data and hierarchical Bayesian models. Analysis revealed a significant decline in overwinter survival rates associated with sea-level rise-induced habitat loss (β = -0.82, 95% CrI: -1.15 to -0.49) and recreational disturbance intensity. Marsh fragmentation metrics explained 67% of interannual variation in juvenile recruitment. Projections indicate potential 42% regional population reduction by 2040 without enhanced wetland conservation interventions targeting salinity barriers and disturbance buffers.

We assessed the impacts of managed hydrological regimes and anthropogenic disturbance on Double-crested Cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) nesting success in coastal wetlands. Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=32) and nest productivity data from 2016–2020, hierarchical modeling revealed that water-level fluctuations during incubation reduced hatching success by 42% (β = -0.38, SE=0.11). Recreational boating within 300m of colonies increased abandonment probability (OR=3.7, p<0.01). Results indicate wetland management must balance water control infrastructure with buffer zones to conserve this piscivorous species threatened by habitat modification.

This study examines morphological variation in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across North American wetlands. Using morphometric analysis of 127 specimens from 12 states, we quantified bill length, tarsus length, and wing chord measurements. Results indicate significant clinal variation correlated with latitude, with northern populations exhibiting larger body size (Bergmann's rule). Habitat fragmentation showed no measurable impact on morphological traits. Findings suggest climate-driven selection pressures outweigh local habitat effects in this secretive rallid species.

Several hypotheses predict that individual differences in migration and dispersal are related to individual differences in routine behavior associated with foraging and risk taking. We tested whether short‐term dispersal of recently emerged brook charr
              Salvelinus fontinalis
              was correlated with differences in activity during prey search in the field (a measure of foraging tactic) or in the time taken to exit a dark tube into an unfamiliar field environment (a measure of risk taking). For one sample of fish, we tested whether an individual's propensity to disperse in a standardized dispersal test in the lab was correlated with its activity during prey search and its exit times in the field. For another sample of marked, released and recaptured fish, we tested whether an individual's minimum displacement distance over 6 days in the field (a measure of dispersal in the field) was related to its propensity to disperse in the lab. For the first sample, an individual's propensity to disperse in the lab was correlated with risk taking only, but, contrary to expectation, individuals with long exit times (risk‐avoiders) dispersed farther than those with short exit times (risk‐takers). For the second sample, dispersal in the field was also correlated with propensity to disperse in the lab, but, contrary to expectation, individuals with greater displacements in the field displayed lower propensities to disperse in the lab. Our findings demonstrate that individual differences in juvenile dispersal are related to differences in risk taking behavior, but not in foraging tactic, and that the nature of this relationship can depend on environmental context. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that individuals differing in risk taking behavior can contribute disproportionately to ecological processes involving long‐distance movement.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Hemlock looper, <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">L</jats:styled-content>ambdina fiscellaria</jats:italic> (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">G</jats:styled-content>uenée) (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">L</jats:styled-content>epidoptera: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">G</jats:styled-content>eometridae), is one of the most important defoliator in <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">N</jats:styled-content>orth <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">A</jats:styled-content>merican forests. The common egg parasitoid <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>elenomus coloradensis </jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">C</jats:styled-content>rawford (<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">H</jats:styled-content>ymenoptera: <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">P</jats:styled-content>latygastridae) plays a significant role as a natural control agent, with parasitism levels in spring typically higher than in fall. The objectives of this study were to quantify changes in host acceptance and reproductive performance of the parasitoid in relation to (1) host egg fertilization in fall, (2) host diapause status, (3) host embryonic development in spring, and (4) host deprivation during summer. Our results indicate that <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>. coloradensis</jats:italic> do not have the capacity to develop in unfertilized host eggs, whereas early‐diapausing eggs are more suitable for the parasitoid than post‐diapausing eggs. Furthermore, the host physiological suitability decreases with embryonic development in spring. Finally, a host deprivation period during the summer tends to negatively affect the parasitic activity of <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>. coloradensis</jats:italic>. These laboratory results confirm previous hypotheses concerning <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>. coloradensis</jats:italic> seasonal ecology and contribute to a better understanding of the effect of hemlock looper egg physiology and availability on the reproductive potential of <jats:italic><jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">T</jats:styled-content>. coloradensis</jats:italic>.</jats:p>

<jats:p>The genetic structure of marram grass populations at coastal and inland locations, 200 m apart, was investigated at three sites by means of amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) DNA markers. We expected a genetic differentiation between coastal and inland populations and more genetic variation in the coastal areas as a result of different events of colonization by different plant materials. An assignment test showed that the sampled<jats:italic>Ammophila arenaria</jats:italic>could be assigned to two groups based on AFLP data. The spatial distribution of the two AFLP types of<jats:italic>A. arenaria</jats:italic>varied with sampling location. In two of the three locations, mainly one type (1) was found in the newly formed dunes. This type did also occur further landward, but the second type (2) was preferentially found in inland populations. Genetic diversity was very low and of similar value in both coastal and inland populations. For each site, outlier loci with respect to<jats:italic>F</jats:italic><jats:sub>ST</jats:sub>value were identified, which may be indicative of different selection pressures in coastal compared with inland clusters. However, no identical outlier loci were found at all three sites. Possible explanations for the observed difference in distribution of type 1 and 2 populations between coastal and inland sites are discussed.</jats:p>

Our study investigates predator-prey dynamics between Least Terns (Sternula antillarum) and invasive fire ants in breeding colonies along the Mississippi River tributaries. Using nest camera surveillance and direct observation from May-July 2021, we quantified chick predation rates across 12 sites. Results showed fire ants caused more chick mortality (62%) than avian predators, with predation probability increasing near agricultural landscapes (p<0 001). This novel terrestrial threat requires revised management strategies for this declining inland population.

This study quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in breeding Forster's Terns (Sterna forsteri) using doubly labeled water techniques across three wetland habitats in California's Central Valley. We found significant differences in DEE between natural marshes (mean ± SE: 145.3 ± 8.7 kJ/day) and managed agricultural wetlands (189.4 ± 9.2 kJ/day), with higher costs in agricultural sites attributed to increased foraging effort. Habitat degradation reduced prey availability, forcing terns to expend 30% more energy for equivalent provisioning rates. Our results demonstrate how wetland management practices directly impact tern energetics, with implications for reproductive success in this declining species.

We investigated nest site selection in Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) across coastal wetlands in Louisiana using systematic surveys (2018-2020). Through resource selection functions and vegetation analysis at 142 nests, we found strong avoidance of fragmented Spartina patches (β = -0.87, SE=0.21) and proximity to human infrastructure (β = -1.32, SE=0.35). Instead, pintails selected elevated sites with dense Distichlis spicata cover (β = 2.15, SE=0.42) and minimal tidal influence. Our models indicate that wetland drainage and saltwater intrusion reduce suitable nesting habitat by 38%, highlighting vulnerability to sea-level rise.

<jats:sec><jats:title>Abstract</jats:title></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Aim</jats:title><jats:p>It has been suggested that populations nearing the border of a species’ range should be maladapted because they occupy progressively less suitable environments. In some instances, however, peripheral populations might acclimate or even be adapted to local conditions. We studied Iberian robins to evaluate whether southern, peripheral populations become more restrictive in selecting their habitats, are locally differentiated or show evidence of maladaptation.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Location</jats:title><jats:p>We divided the Iberian Peninsula into three regions (the Eurosiberian and Supra‐Mediterranean regions in northern Iberia, and the Mediterranean Lowlands in southern Iberia), which define a gradient of increasing dryness southwards. In each region, we selected one representative locality, where we captured individuals during three study years.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>We reviewed 72 community studies to test whether Iberian robins occupy fewer forests and decrease in abundance southwards. Because robins are sedentary in the southernmost region, but largely abandon both northern areas in winter, we analysed the variation in migration‐related morphology to test for population differentiation in the range boundary.
