To examine how populations cope with environmental variation, we studied four indices of juvenile condition (fluctuating asymmetry, fledgling size, ptilochronology and size‐corrected body mass), each related to nutritional conditions in a particular stage of growth, from early development to independence.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Although robins restricted their range southwards, there was no change in local abundance between regions. Southernmost robins, consistent with their sedentary behaviour, had shorter and more rounded wings than northern robins, although the populations did not differ in terms of body size. Fluctuating asymmetry and fledgling size did not evidence a higher developmental stress in peripheral populations, although southernmost robins had a lower juvenile condition during their independence (as shown by ptilochronology and residual body mass).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Main conclusions</jats:title><jats:p>The distribution of abundance found in this study supports the idea that Iberian robins could select habitats above a somehow restrictive threshold of quality. In addition, morphological correlates of migratory behaviour provided evidence of population differentiation at the range edge. This introduces the possibility that among‐region variations in juvenile condition actually reflect reproductive benefits for migrants, related to the occupation of seasonally productive habitats, rather than the maladaptation of sedentary, peripheral populations. From this perspective, and in view of the patterns of distribution and morphology that we found, southern Iberian robins might be independent populations locally adapted in the range boundary.</jats:p></jats:sec>

<jats:p>The averaged m-sequence correlation technique has been established as a means of measuring linear system responses under high noise conditions. This Letter examines the theoretical basis for the technique and derives an analytical formula for the expected error in the estimated system response under noisy conditions at the system input and/or output. The formula shows close agreement with previously published experimental results [W. Zuomin and W. T. Chu, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 94, 1409–1414 (1993)] and with newly derived simulation results.</jats:p>

This study examines the impact of wetland drawdown regimes on Double-crested Cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) nesting success in managed impoundments. We monitored 42 nests across three hydrologically manipulated marshes during the 2021 breeding season. Results indicate that prolonged early-season drawdowns (>30 days pre-nesting) significantly reduced nest occupancy (χ²=8.24, p=0.004) and fledging rates (t=3.71, p<0.001), likely due to increased mammalian predation exposure. Our findings suggest wetland management strategies intended for waterfowl may create ecological traps for piscivorous birds by altering predator-prey dynamics.

This study investigates nest site selection patterns in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across coastal wetland complexes in the Great Lakes region. Using GIS habitat mapping and multivariate logistic regression, we analyzed topographic and anthropogenic factors influencing colony establishment. Results indicate strong avoidance of developed shorelines (OR = 0 23, p<0 001} and preference for insular habitats with minimal human disturbance. Temperature-mediated vegetation changes significantly reduced nesting habitat suitability under climate projections (RCP4.5). Conservation strategies must address both proximate disturbance factors and climate-driven vegetation shifts.

Abstract This study presents the length-weight relationships (LWRs) for 16 lutjanid species from Visakhapatnam coastal waters, India (16.98 ° N-20 ° .2 N, Long. 82.19 ° -86.53°E). The samples were collected fortnightly between December 2013 and December 2018 from commercially operated fishing gears viz.: the reef fish trap with single and double horse necked funnel (mesh aperture size 4.5 cm) trap measured about 3 ft in length, 4 ft in width and 2.5 ft in height, having a volume of 30 cu ft. The soak time was between 18 to 22 h. Gill nets made of monofilament nylon netting with a mesh size of 80 mm were used in the collection of snapper fishes. The nets were operated 3 h before morning (sunrise) and hauled 1 h after the sunrise. The depth of the net operated varied from 3 to 8 m, whereas the head rope of the net is around 20–25 m in length. The hook number 8 to 11 is used for the fishing of snapper fishery resources in water depth more than 75 m in Visakhapatnam region. The soak time varied from 5 to 10 h. The bottom trawlers (43 mm with a cod end mesh size of 15–25 mm) a depth range of 10 to 55 m, whereas during each fishing period, 3 to 4 hauls are made with a towing period ranging from 1 to 2 h; trawlers (a depth regime of 12 to 55 m, with a mesh size of 400 mm to 25 mm at the cod end). Around 3 to 6 hauls are made during each fishing trip with a towing period of 1to 2 h. All LWRs were significant with  r 2  values ranged from 0.9504 for  Lutjanus lemniscatus  to 0.9951 for  Lutjanus fulvus  and ‘b’ values ranging from  Pinjalo pinjalo  for 2.5982  Lutjanus quinquelineatus  for 3.4993. In addition, new maximum total length for each of the three species  L. indicus, L. xanthopinnis  and  P. pinjalo  was also found. The parameters are found great importance to evaluate the relative condition of populations, biology, ecology, species management and their fisheries and stock assessment.

This study examines biparental provisioning rates in Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola) across wetland habitats in the Chesapeake Bay region. Using nest cameras and radio-telemetry, we quantified prey delivery frequency and chick growth rates relative to habitat quality metrics. Results indicate that degraded marshes with reduced invertebrate abundance correlate with decreased parental investment and higher chick mortality, highlighting synergistic effects of wetland loss and pollution on this secretive rallid species.

This study examines the population dynamics of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) in the Great Lakes region from 2010-2020. Using mark-recapture analysis of banded individuals and colony census data, we documented a 32% decline in breeding pairs. Key threats identified include reduced landfill foraging opportunities due to waste management policies, increased predation pressure from expanding coyote populations, and climate-induced shifts in prey fish availability. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this adaptable species to anthropogenic environmental changes.

Abstract OSMOREGULATORY failure has often been cited as the cause of death in fish exposed to low temperatures1–4. Moreover, even in those which survive quite well in the cold, concentrations of sodium and chloride in the serum are known to increase at low temperatures in marine species 5,6  and to decrease at low temperatures in freshwater species 7,8 . Studies on the euryhaline killifish,  Fundulus heteroclitus , adapted to saltwater showed that acclimatization to 2° C or −1.5° C increased serum osmolality of sodium and chloride when compared with controls at 10° C or 20° C (ref. 9). These data were interpreted to mean that, as in other fish, osmoregulatory ability was less efficient in cold-acclimatized  F. heteroclitus . If this was so, then for fish adapted to freshwater the serum osmolality of sodium and chloride would be expected to decrease when the temperature was lowered. The preliminary data reported here demonstrate that this is the case.

This study investigates the spring migration phenology of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) in eastern North American wetlands using automated acoustic monitoring. We analyzed 2-decade datasets from 32 sites to quantify how altered hydroperiods and agricultural runoff affect arrival timing. Results show significant delays (mean = 5 days/decade, p<0·001) correlated with wetland fragmentation, suggesting cumulative impacts of climate-induced drought and agrochemical exposure.

We assessed genetic diversity and population structure of Stilt Sandpiper (Calidris himantopus) breeding colonies in Churchill, Manitoba (58.7684°N, 94.1650°W) to evaluate impacts of recreational ATV use. Using microsatellite analysis of 120 individuals across 6 colonies (2018-2020), we found significantly lower allelic richness (AR = 3.2 vs. 4.7, p = 0.008) and heterozygosity (Ho = 0.42 vs. 0.61, p = 0.003) in high-disturbance sites. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing revealed reduced haplotype diversity (h = 0.78 vs. 0.92) near trails. Results indicate genetic erosion from anthropogenic disturbance, necessitating buffer zones around critical habitats.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) using radio-telemetry across northeastern U.S. wetlands. Tracking 35 individuals revealed asynchronous migration timing correlated with wetland desiccation rates. Molt sites were characterized by dense emergent vegetation and invertebrate abundance. Habitat fragmentation significantly delayed migration onset (p<0.01), with anthropogenic disturbance reducing site fidelity. Our findings highlight vulnerability of this secretive rallid to hydrological alterations and underscore conservation needs for ephemeral wetlands during critical molt periods.

The Texas coast has experienced considerable urban, industrial, and agricultural growth during the 20th Century. The region provides important wintering habitat to many avian species, including lesser snow geese Chen caerulescens caerulescens. This paper draws the biological and ecological fields into an historical perspective by examining available literature on the development of the upper Texas coast and range changes of lesser snow geese. Historically, lesser snow geese wintered in the coastal marshes, but expanded their range into the adjacent prairies in the mid-1900s. Winter range expansion was negatively affected by urban and industrial encroachment in the coastal marshes and positively influenced by agricultural development in the prairies, which increased dramatically during World War II. The lesser snow goose population flourished alongside some human-induced landscape alterations. However, projected declines in agriculture and increased urbanization of prairie and coastal marsh habitats may result in significant negative effects on the lesser snow goose population.

Coastal wetland degradation severely threatens Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations, a cryptic marsh specialist. We quantified occupancy dynamics across 32 tidal marshes using playback surveys and hierarchical modeling over five breeding seasons. Results revealed a 37% occupancy decline (ψ = 0.42 to 0.27) strongly linked to marsh fragmentation (β = -0.91 ± 0.21 SE). Sea-level rise exacerbated drainage ditches' effects, reducing suitable habitat by 28%. Conservation must prioritize contiguous emergent vegetation to sustain this rapidly declining rail.

The Magnificent Frigatebird (Fregata magnificens), despite superficial similarities to Caspian Tern morphology, demonstrates unique pelagic foraging adaptations. Satellite tracking of 42 individuals revealed extended foraging ranges exceeding 300km from nesting sites, with dive behavior analysis showing near-exclusive surface feeding (0.2-0.5m depth). Significant correlations emerged between foraging efficiency and sea surface temperature anomalies (r = -0.78, p<0.01), indicating heightened climate vulnerability for this tropical seabird.

We investigated stopover ecology of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) at coastal staging areas in the Great Lakes region during spring migration 2019-2021. Using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults), we quantified site fidelity, residence times, and habitat selection patterns. Cormorants exhibited high fidelity to specific stopover sites (mean return rate = 78%) with average stopover duration of 4.7±1.2 days. Habitat modeling revealed strong selection for sheltered bays with abundant forage fish (AUC=0.89), avoiding areas with high recreational boating activity. Our findings highlight the importance of protecting undisturbed coastal habitats for this piscivorous species facing increasing anthropogenic pressures.

Habitat selection by American Coot (Fulica americana) was investigated in a midwestern wetland complex. We quantified vegetation structure, water depth, and disturbance frequency across 24 sites using systematic transect surveys during 2018–2019 breeding seasons (N=152 coot territories). Logistic regression models revealed significant avoidance of areas with human recreational activity (β=−0.73, SE=0.17, p<0.001) and preference for dense submerged macrophytes (β=1:54, SE=0.31, p<0:01). Management should prioritize limiting shoreline development and maintaining aquatic vegetation to support this declining Rallidae species threatened by wetland degradation.

We investigated the foraging movements of Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) in the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta using GPS telemetry. Tracking 15 breeding adults revealed significant shifts in habitat selection following wetland restoration efforts. Individuals increased utilization of managed marshes by 37% post-restoration, reducing reliance on agricultural drainage habitats. This behavioral adaptation demonstrates the species' responsiveness to conservation interventions despite ongoing threats from water management practices and invasive plant encroachment.

<jats:p> Forage grasses need to be evaluated in pasture trials in the Great Plains region of North America. The objective of this study was to compare four grass–alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) mixtures for productivity and persistence when grazed during spring and summer. The grasses were Altai wildrye (Leymus angustus [Trin.] Pilger), intermediate wheatgrass (Elytrigia intermedia [Host] Nevski), meadow bromegrass (Bromus riparius Rehm. syn. B. biebersteinii Roem. & Schult.) and Russian wildrye (Psathyrostachys junceus [Fisch.] Nevski), with grass rows seeded perpendicular to the alfalfa rows. Two sites, 4 km apart, were grazed with yearling beef cattle from 1987 to 1993. Forage yield differed among grass treatments in 4 of 5 years, but differences were inconsistent over time. Five-year mean forage yields and total livestock production were not significantly different among the four grasses. Mean annual forage yields ranged from 800 to 8170 kg ha<jats:sup>−1</jats:sup> and were related to the amount of growing season (April–August) precipitation. Carrying capacity ranged from 35 steer grazing days per hectare in 1992 to 176 in 1991. Grasses in the mixtures did have a significant effect on the grass–alfalfa ratio and on ground cover. Alfalfa content was highest when grown with Altai wildrye and lowest when grown with Russian wildrye. Percentage of ground cover by the grass plus alfalfa increased from an average of 3.8% in 1987 to 16.1% at one site and 31.9% at the second site by 1993. Russian wildrye contained the least alfalfa and weeds after 7 yr. Intermediate wheatgrass and Altai wildrye did not compete with invading weeds at one site, or with alfalfa at the other, and should not be recommended for spring–summer pastures in semiarid regions. Meadow bromegrass maintained a balance of grass and alfalfa and further research should confirm its persistence in semiarid climates. Key words: Leymus angustus, Elytrigia intermedia, Bromus riparius, Psathyrostachys junceus, Medicago sativa, grazing with cattle </jats:p>

This study investigates juvenile survival rates of Great Egrets (Ardea alba) in coastal wetlands of the southeastern United States. Using mark-recapture analysis of 127 banded fledglings over three breeding seasons (2018-2020), we assessed impacts of habitat degradation and hydrological alterations. Results indicate significantly lower survival probabilities (φ = 0.42 ± 0.07) in modified habitats compared to protected areas (φ = 0.68 ± 0.05), primarily due to reduced prey availability and increased predation pressure. Our findings emphasize the vulnerability of juvenile Ardeids to anthropogenic wetland modifications.

This study examined predator-mediated disease transmission risk in non-breeding Sanderlings (Calidris alba) along the Wadden Sea coast (53°N, 8°E) during 2021-2022. We analyzed avian influenza virus (AIV) prevalence from 278 cloacal swabs and quantified avian predator encounters using GPS-tagged individuals (n=42) and 1500 observation-hours. AIV prevalence was 8.7% (95% CI: 5.9-12.4%), with infection likelihood 2.9-fold higher in areas with frequent peregrine falcon attacks (≥0.3 events/hr; OR=2.9, p=0.007). Results indicate predation pressure amplifies disease exposure, necessitating integrated predator-disease management in critical intertidal habitats.

This study utilized stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) to investigate dietary shifts and habitat use in Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) populations across urban and estuarine gradients in the southeastern US. Our findings reveal significant isotopic niche contraction in urban-foraging individuals, correlated with reduced dietary diversity and increased reliance on anthropogenic food sources. These results demonstrate how wetland degradation alters trophic ecology in wading birds.

This study investigates the energetic costs of nest excavation by Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon), a burrowing specialist dependent on earthen banks. Using respirometry and time-activity budgets during the breeding season across six river systems, we quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) relative to bank substrate hardness and territory quality. Results showed DEE increased 28% in compacted substrates (p<0·001), with significant trade-offs in provisioning rates. These findings highlight how anthropogenic bank hardening threatens kingfisher bioenergetics and reproductive success.

This study examines the impact of recreational beach activities on Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) nesting success along the Atlantic coast. Using observational surveys and nest monitoring across 12 colonies, we documented significant correlations between human visitation density and reduced hatching rates (r = -0.78, p<0.01). Experimental disturbance trials demonstrated that pedestrian traffic within 50m of colonies triggered nest abandonment 3.8 times more frequently than control sites. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this coastal-nesting species to anthropogenic pressures, necessitating revised buffer zone management strategies.

We quantified traffic noise impacts on Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) stopover ecology at Monterey Bay, California, during 2020-2022 spring migrations. Using synchronized behavioral scans and sound level mapping across 12 sites (n=93 individuals), we measured foraging-vigilance tradeoffs. Plovers in high-noise zones (≥65 dB) exhibited 28% lower peck rates (β=-0.32, p=0.007) and 34% reduced vigilance frequency (p=0.02) compared to low-noise zones (<50 dB). Results indicate noise pollution disrupts critical refueling behaviors at coastal stopovers, necessitating acoustic buffers in migration corridors for this threatened species.

We investigated Brant (Branta bernicla) population dynamics along the Mid-Atlantic coast from 2015-2020 using aerial surveys and mark-resight techniques. Our analysis revealed a 22% decline in wintering populations, significantly correlated with eelgrass habitat degradation (r=-0.78, p<0.01) and increased recreational boating disturbance. Climate-induced shifts in prey availability exacerbated these effects, suggesting synergistic threats require integrated coastal management strategies for this declining waterfowl species.

Disposable lighters are one of the few types of marine litter that have evidence of their source, because they have printed information about the consuming country or city (e.g., point of sale address or telephone number). Lighters were used to estimate the flow, source, and drifting range of marine litter in the North Pacific. From August 1998 to February 2015, 79,948 lighters were collected from 1,661 sites on the beaches and river estuaries in Japan, Taiwan, Korea, Russia, China, Hawaii, and the west coast of North America. This method clarified that the lighters runoff from river basin to the ocean through rivers. From the distribution of outflow areas, the flow of the lighter was consistent with the ocean currents around East Asia and in the North Pacific. The origins in the North Pacific of the lighter were mainly found to be the coastal areas of East Asia, especially Taiwan, China (between Hong Kong and Shanghai), South Korea, and Japan (Pacific coast side). Furthermore, by monitoring ML using the lighter that can identify source areas, it was shown that it is possible to trace back to the source areas and causes of massive drifts, and to help properly dealing with this contamination issue.

This study investigates the genetic diversity and population structure of Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia) colonies across the Great Lakes region using microsatellite markers. We analyzed 120 individuals from 6 breeding sites to assess impacts of historical habitat fragmentation and recent contaminant exposure on genetic health. Results indicate moderate differentiation (FST=0.08) with significant isolation-by-distance patterns. Mercury accumulation showed negative correlation with heterozygosity (r=-0.42, p<0.01), suggesting pollution-driven genetic erosion. Conservation strategies should prioritize reducing toxicant inputs and maintaining connectivity between colonies.

This study investigates the energy expenditure of Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon), a non-shorebird coastal species, in relation to anthropogenic disturbance along riverine habitats. We employed doubly labeled water techniques to measure daily energy budgets during breeding season across sites with varying human recreational pressure. Results indicate significant increases in metabolic rates (+22.7%) at high-disturbance sites, primarily driven by elevated flight activity and reduced prey capture efficiency. These findings highlight how human-induced behavioral modifications may impose energetic constraints on piscivorous birds, with implications for reproductive success.

We investigated population dynamics of Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) in urban coastal estuaries from 2010–2025 using mark-recapture and nest monitoring. Results showed a 17.4% annual decline (p=0.002), primarily driven by microplastic ingestion reducing reproductive success by 38% and coastal development fragmenting nesting habitats. Climate-induced shifts in prey availability further exacerbated declines. Conservation strategies must address anthropogenic stressors beyond traditional shorebird frameworks to reverse trends.

This study investigates predator-prey dynamics between Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) and juvenile fish populations in estuarine ecosystems of the Gulf Coast. Using observational surveys and stomach content analysis during 2018–2020 breeding seasons, we documented significant predation pressure on economically important Cyprinidae species in disturbed vs. pristine habitats. Results indicate that wetland degradation increased cormorant foraging efficiency by concentrating prey, suggesting habitat management could mitigate fisheries conflicts.

This study examined predator-prey dynamics of Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) in the Hudson River estuary from 2019-2021 using fish community surveys and nest monitoring (n=32 pairs). Results revealed strong reliance on menhaden (Brevoortia tyrannus, 72% of prey biomass), but increased prey switching to other fish species correlated with declining menhaden stocks from overfishing. Mercury contamination in prey was associated with reduced fledging success, highlighting dual fishery and pollution impacts on raptor foraging ecology.

This study examines molt migration patterns in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across northeastern wetlands using radio-telemetry and feather isotope analysis. We tracked 42 individuals from breeding grounds to molting sites, revealing a bimodal migration strategy with distinct early and late molt cohorts. Habitat loss in stopover wetlands significantly influenced molt site selection, with fragmented marshes forcing rails to utilize suboptimal agricultural ditches. Our findings demonstrate that molt migration in this rail species is more complex than previously documented, with implications for conservation planning under climate change scenarios.

Stable isotope analysis of blood samples from Least Terns (Sternula antillarum) nesting in coastal Louisiana revealed significant shifts in trophic position following wetland degradation. δ15N values increased by 1.8‰ compared to pre-disturbance baselines, indicating greater reliance on piscivorous prey as marsh habitats contracted. This nutritional shift correlated with reduced fledging success, demonstrating cascading impacts of anthropogenic habitat alteration on non-Charadriiformes seabird populations.

Soil seed banks are a key component of ecological resilience as they provide a temporal reserve for plant species richness and diversity. Soil seed banks depend on on-site reproduction, seed longevity, and seed immigration for maintenance. When immigration of seeds is lost due to a change in land use or a disturbance, such as fragmentation, seed banks rely on on-site reproduction and longevity for maintenance. Within a fragment without seed immigration, seed banks become vulnerable to extinction debt leading to community disassembly over a long time scale. Therefore, we investigated how long-term fragmentation impacts community disassembly in seed banks. Seed bank samples were taken from grassland fragments (sod tables, n = 28) and from the surrounding area (matrix, n = 28). Seed banks were germinated, and emerging plants were identified. We found that community disassembly was not predictable in regard to species identity, and specialist (P < 0.001) and perennial (P < 0.001) species were lost from fragments. However, seed banks in fragments maintained a similar grass-to-forb ratio compared with the surrounding vegetation. Therefore, the ability of seed banks to provide ecological resilience may be limited after long-term fragmentation and land managers may need to reseed specialist species and perennials into grassland fragments.

<jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>The morphology of the ureter of the duck was investigated, using histological, SEM and TEM techniques. The inner perimeter, the total thickness of the ureteral wall and the thickness of each uretral layer were measured. The epithelium was tall columnar and pseudostratified along all the tracts of the ureter and showed a high muco‐secretive activity. The <jats:italic>lamina propria</jats:italic> contained numerous capillaries and aggregates of leucocytes and macrophages. Throughout the <jats:italic>lamina propria</jats:italic> there was a dense plexus of nerves. Some denuded single nerve fibres were observed between the epithelial basal cells. A plexus of nerves was also observed in the <jats:italic>tunica muscularis.</jats:italic> The <jats:italic>ostium cloacale ureteris</jats:italic> opened on a well‐developed papilla in the dorsal region of the <jats:italic>urodeum.</jats:italic> The total thickness of the ureteral wall, the thickness of the <jats:italic>lamina propria</jats:italic> and the <jats:italic>tunica muscularis</jats:italic>, and the inner perimeter progressively increased towards the <jats:italic>ostium.</jats:italic> The above observations suggest that the avian ureter plays an important role in the modification of the urine coming from medullary cones, and in emission of the urine into the <jats:italic>cloaca.</jats:italic></jats:p>

This study examines migration ecology of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across eastern North America. Using automated radio telemetry (Motus Wildlife Tracking System), we tracked 42 individuals from breeding grounds to wintering sites. Results indicate migration timing correlates with wetland water levels (r=0.78, p<0.01), with drought conditions delaying departure by 17±3 days. Stopover duration averaged 8.2 days at fragmented coastal marshes, where habitat degradation reduced refueling rates by 38%. Findings highlight vulnerability of this secretive rallid to hydrological changes and wetland loss during migration.

We investigated plastic ingestion rates and migration ecology of Mountain Plovers (Charadrius montanus) across their Central Flyway migration corridor. Using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults) and necropsy analysis of salvaged carcasses (n=17), we quantified plastic prevalence during spring migration (March-May 2019-2021). Plastic fragments were present in 29.4% of gastrointestinal tracts (95% CI: 11.3-54.7%), primarily polyethylene microplastics (<5mm). Individuals staging >7 days in agricultural landscapes (Odds Ratio=3.1, p=0.02) showed higher ingestion probability. Results indicate anthropogenic landscapes pose ingestion risks during critical migration periods, necessitating habitat management interventions.

This study examines Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) habitat selection during spring migration stopovers along the Gulf Coast. Using GPS telemetry and habitat surveys, we quantified resource utilization at 12 estuarine sites. Results indicate strong avoidance of developed shorelines (p<0.001) and preferential use of Spartina marshes with tidal creek access. Herons exhibited high site fidelity to stopover locations with low human disturbance levels. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this species to coastal development and underscore the need for protecting intact marsh ecosystems along migratory corridors.

This study investigates parental care trade-offs in Brant geese (Branta bernicla) across four coastal Alaskan estuaries during 2019-2022. Using GPS tracking (n=48 adults) and nest cameras, we quantified nest attendance duration and brood foraging distance in relation to anthropogenic disturbance gradients. Increased recreational boating predicted reduced female nest constancy (β=-0.34±0.11SE) but heightened male vigilance during brood-rearing (F3,44=9.21, p<0.001), suggesting compensatory behavioral adjustments to human pressure.

This study examines stopover site selection by Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) along the Atlantic Flyway using GPS telemetry and habitat assessment. We tracked 42 individuals during spring migration, documenting significant preference for sheltered coastal wetlands with abundant submerged structures. Analysis revealed reduced site occupancy in areas with high recreational boat traffic, suggesting human disturbance may compromise critical refueling efficiency at these ephemeral habitats. Conservation strategies should prioritize minimizing anthropogenic disruptions at key stopover locations.

We investigated recreational disturbance impacts on Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) molt migration in the Wadden Sea, Germany. Using GPS telemetry (n=28 adults, 2019-2021) and behavioral scans (1,200 observations), we quantified time budgets across disturbance gradients. High-recreation zones showed 38% reduced foraging time (β = -0.41, p < 0.001) and 2.3-fold higher flight-initiation distances (95% CI: 1.8-2.9) compared to protected areas. Plasma corticosterone levels increased 27% at disturbed sites (R²=0.63, p=0.007). Results indicate stringent seasonal access restrictions are crucial for molt-stage energy budgets.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>During takeoff and landing, birds bounce and grab with their legs and feet. In this paper,the lower limb structure of the bionic bird is designed with reference to the function of jumping and grasping, and the PID algorithm based on the development module of stm32 development board is used to speed control the lower limb driving element, so that the motor and the bishaft steering gear move with the rate change of sine wave. According to the speed of grasping response time and the size of grasping force, the structure of the bionic bird paw is designed. Based on the photosensitive sensor fixed in the geometric center of the foot, the grasping action of the lower limb mechanism is intelligently controlled. Finally, the kinematic verification of the lower limb structure is carried out by ADAMS. Experiments show that the foot structure with four toes and three toes is more conducive to maintaining the stability of the body while realizing the fast grasping function. In addition, it can effectively improve the push-lift ratio of the bionic ornithopter by adjusting the sinusoidal waveform rate of the motor speed.
