We evaluated invasive plant encroachment effects on Curlew Sandpiper (Calidris ferruginea) demography in the Kolyma Lowlands, Siberia (2018-2021). Using mark-recapture (n=63 adults) and nest monitoring (87 nests), we found 28% lower nest success in Spartina anglica-invaded areas versus controls (p=0.022; OR=0.41, 95% CI:0.19–0.88). Chick survival decreased by 37% (HR=1.9, CI:1.2–3.0) due to reduced arthropod prey availability. Results indicate habitat degradation necessitates targeted invasive species management to mitigate population declines in this declining shorebird.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>In three microcosm experiments, we exposed microbial communities of a natural sediment to environmentally relevant concentrations of the fungicide captan, the herbicide isoproturon, and the insecticides deltamethrin and pirimicarb. Exposure concentrations were estimated negligible concentrations (NCs), maximum permissible concentrations (MPCs), and 100 times MPC (100MPC). Experimental endpoints were microbial community respiration and biomass, bacterial activity, and denitrification. All four pesticides inhibited bacterial activity by 20 to 24% at MPC, which corresponded to concentrations in the range of μg/kg dry‐weight sediment. Treatments with deltamethrin and isoproturon showed inhibiting effects on bacterial activity at NC exposures. Surprisingly, for captan, deltamethrin, and isoproturon, this inhibiting effect was not observed at 100MPC treatments. Microbial biomass was negatively effected in MPC treatments with deltamethrin and in NC treatments with isoproturon. The tested pesticides did not affect community respiration and denitrification rates. These results show that exposure to the tested pesticides may induce toxic responses in sediment microbial communities at concentrations that are predicted to be environmentally safe.</jats:p>

This study examines the impact of invasive apple snails (Pomacea spp.) on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) foraging behavior in Louisiana wetlands. Using focal animal sampling and prey analysis, we documented significant dietary shifts towards this novel prey item. Results indicate altered time-activity budgets and potential nestling provisioning changes, suggesting cascading effects on heron reproductive success. The invasion represents both an opportunistic resource and an ecological trap, with implications for wetland conservation strategies.

This study examined thermoregulatory costs in Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) during summer molt using doubly labeled water methods. Energy expenditure increased 38% during peak molt compared to post-molt periods (P<0Ã¢ÂÂ001), primarily driven by thermogenic demands when plumage insulation was compromised. Coastal development reduced thermal refugia availability, forcing pelicans into suboptimal habitats with higher convective heat loss. Findings highlight vulnerability of molting pelicans to climate warming and habitat degradation.

We assessed population genetic structure and pesticide exposure impacts in American Avocets (Recurvirostra americana) across California's Central Valley wetlands (2018-2021). Using microsatellite genotyping (n=12 loci) and liver organochlorine analysis (n=142 adults), we found significant genetic differentiation between northern and southern subpopulations (FST=0.032, p=0.003). Individuals with elevated DDE concentrations (>5 ppm wet weight) showed 23% reduced heterozygosity (95% CI: 12-34%, p=0.011) and higher inbreeding coefficients (FIS=0.15 vs 0.08, p=0.022). Results indicate organochlorine exposure exacerbates genetic erosion in fragmented habitats, necessitating wetland connectivity restoration to mitigate metapopulation collapse.

We investigated plastic ingestion rates and community-level impacts in Red-necked Phalaropes (Phalaropus lobatus) breeding near Utqiaġvik, Alaska (71.3°N, 156.8°W). During 2021-2022 field seasons, we collected regurgitated pellets from 112 individuals and quantified microplastic loads via FTIR spectroscopy. Phalaropes exhibited significantly higher plastic ingestion frequencies (43.7%) than sympatric shorebirds (mean 12.3%; χ²=27.1, p<0.001), correlating with reduced clutch sizes (r=-0.41, p=0.02). Our results indicate phalaropes' unique foraging ecology increases vulnerability, necessitating targeted monitoring in Arctic shorebird assemblages.

This study examines the impact of coastal wetland degradation on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes) population dynamics in the Chesapeake Bay region. Using 15 years of banding data and habitat surveys, we documented a significant decline in overwinter survival rates (β = -0.17, SE=0.04, p<0.001) correlated with marsh fragmentation. Our hierarchical Bayesian models indicate that sea-level rise-induced habitat loss poses a greater threat than hunting pressure. Conservation strategies must prioritize saltmarsh restoration to buffer climate change effects on this declining waterfowl species.

Colonizing stem mothers of the gall—forming aphid Pemphigus betae defend galls sites on narrowleaf cottonwood, Populus angustifolia. Kicking—shoving contests are used to establish microterritories 3—5 mm in length. The largest stem mothers usually win in competitive bouts. Small differences in body size (i.e., a 3.4% difference in prothorax widths) are more importantly associated with territorial interactions than with fecundity. Stem mothers that win the superior basal position of a leaf produce an average of 56% more progeny than stem mothers displaced to inferior distal positions. Differences in reproductive performance within a leaf result from microhabitat variation in leaf quality. A change of only a few millimetres in the position of the gall on the leaf blade affects aphid reproduction. Experimental removal of either member of a competing pair allows the remaining stem mother to cross the former territorial boundary and enlarge her own territory. The impact of competitive release on reproductive success is asymmetrical. The distal stem mother of a competing pair achieves an average 48.5% increase in number of progeny, whereas the basal stem mother achieves an 18.5% increase in number of progeny. Because both members of a competing pair suffer reduced success from competitive interactions, selection favors stem mothers that occupy leaves singly. The largest stem mothers are solitary; their despotic behavior prevents smaller competitors from settling.

This study investigated how recreational beach activity affects Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) chick provisioning rates in coastal Florida. Using focal observations at 15 nests across three sites with varying human visitation intensity, we recorded 120 hours of behavioral data during peak chick-rearing season. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that adult visitation frequency decreased significantly with increased human presence (β=-0.32, SE=0.11, p=0.003), leading to reduced meal deliveries. These findings suggest that anthropogenic disturbance may impair gull parental investment, highlighting the need for management strategies in high-traffic shoreline habitats.

This study examines the impact of coastal marsh degradation on American Coot (Fulica americana) populations in the Chesapeake Bay region. Using aerial surveys and habitat suitability modeling, we documented a 38% decline in coot abundance between 2010-2020, strongly correlated with loss of submerged aquatic vegetation (R²=0.72). Our findings indicate that eutrophication-induced habitat degradation poses a greater threat than direct human disturbance to this rail species' wintering grounds. Conservation efforts should prioritize water quality improvements to sustain essential coot foraging habitats.

Using GPS-GSM telemetry, we tracked 42 American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) across coastal Virginia and Maryland to assess habitat displacement from anthropogenic pressures. Transmitters deployed during wintering periods (2019-2021) revealed significant avoidance behavior in areas with >15 recreational vessels/km². Ducks exhibited 63% reduced tidal marsh utilization near waterfront development zones, shifting instead to fragmented suboptimal habitats. Our findings quantify threshold disturbance levels driving coastal waterfowl displacement, highlighting urgent needs for buffer zones in estuarine conservation planning.

This study evaluated stopover site selection and duration in migratory Tricolored Herons (Egretta tricolor) along the Gulf Coast, USA. Using GPS telemetry (n=28) from 2020-2023, we quantified responses to marsh fragmentation and recreational disturbance. Individuals exhibited 37% longer stopovers in degraded habitats (p<0.01) and 42% lower site fidelity at high-disturbance sites. Results indicate coastal development poses significant threats to migration energetics in this declining Ardeid species.

We quantified energy expenditure in Semipalmated Plovers (Charadrius semipalmatus) exposed to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) along the Bay of Fundy migration corridor (New Brunswick, Canada). Using doubly labeled water techniques on 42 adults captured during fall staging (August-September 2021), we found PAH-exposed individuals exhibited 18.7% higher daily energy expenditure (95% CI: 12.3-25.1%, p=0.003) than controls. Elevated metabolic costs correlated with reduced pre-migratory fattening rates (r=-0.61, p<0.001), suggesting chemical contamination imposes significant energetic constraints during critical life history stages. Conservation strategies must address sublethal contaminant effects on migratory preparedness.

We investigated juvenile Wood Sandpiper (Tringa glareola) survival in relation to heavy metal contamination across wetland habitats in Estonia's Matsalu National Park (2018-2021). Using radio-telemetry (n=42 fledglings) and liver tissue analysis (ICP-MS), we quantified cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) exposure. Survival probability decreased by 22% per 1 μg/g dry weight increase in hepatic Cd (Cox PH model: HR=1.22, 95% CI=1.07-1.39, p=0.002), while Pb showed no significant effect. These findings highlight Cd as a critical threat to juvenile recruitment in contaminated stopover sites, urging targeted wetland remediation for migratory shorebird conservation.

<jats:p>The biosonar (click train) production rate of ten Yangtze finless porpoises and their behavior were examined using animal-borne data loggers. The sound production rate varied from 0 to 290 click trains per 10-min time interval. Large individual differences were observed, regardless of body size. Taken together, however, sound production did not differ significantly between daytime and nighttime. Over the 172.5 h of analyzed recordings, an average of 99.0% of the click trains were produced within intervals of less than 60 s, indicating that during a 1-min interval, the number of click trains produced by each porpoise was typically greater than one. Most of the porpoises exhibited differences in average swimming speed and depth between day and night. Swimming speed reductions and usage of short-range sonar, which relates to prey-capture attempts, were observed more often during nighttime. However, biosonar appears to be affected not only by porpoise foraging, but also by their sensory environment, i.e., the turbid Yangtze River system. These features will be useful for passive acoustic detection of the porpoises. Calculations of porpoise density or abundance should be conducted carefully because large individual differences in the sound production rate will lead to large estimation error.</jats:p>

This study investigated the impacts of recreational kayaking on Snowy Egret (Egretta thula ) breeding success in coastal estuaries. We monitored 42 nests across 3 colonies during the 2021 breeding season using systematic disturbance protocols and nest cameras. Results showed a 35% decrease in fledging rates at sites with >5 daily kayak incursions compared to low-disturbance areas ( p=0.02 ). Behavioral analysis revealed a 48% reduction in parental feeding frequency during disturbance events, suggesting energy allocation trade-offs affecting chick development.

This study examines the impact of invasive Argentine ants (Linepithema humile) on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) nesting success in coastal California. We monitored 42 nests across three colonies during the 2021 breeding season, comparing sites with varying ant infestation levels. Results indicate a significant negative correlation between ant presence and fledgling survival (R²=0.67, p<0.01), primarily due to ant predation on hatchlings. Our findings highlight an understudied threat to pelican conservation and suggest targeted ant control as a management priority for vulnerable island breeding sites.

This study examines the impact of hydrological restoration on Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) nesting success in managed freshwater marshes. Using mark-recapture methods and nest monitoring across 23 sites, we found that increased water depth variability reduced fledging rates by 38% (p<0·01). Heron colonies exhibited higher site fidelity in stabilized hydroperiod regimes despite elevated mercury exposure (δ15N analysis). Findings highlight trade-offs in wetland conservation for wading birds threatened by climate-amplified drought cycles.

Our study assessed the impact of human recreational disturbance on Rock Sandpiper (Calidris ptilocnemis tschuktschorum) predator-prey dynamics during winter at the Copper River Delta (Alaska). We employed focal animal observations (n=42 individuals tracked January-March 2016-2018) with vigilance time as a proxy for perceived predation risk under varying ATV traffic intensities (0-12 vehicles/h). Vigilance increased by 0.6 s/min per additional vehicle (p < 0 001; R² = 0 89) reducing foraging time by 0.8 s/min resulting in a 12% decrease in bivalve intake (95% CI 9.5-14 7%). This mechanistic link quantifies how recreational pressure indirectly heightens starvation risk through behavioral trade-offs necessitating seasonal vehicle exclusion zones.

This study examines the influence of winter habitat degradation on juvenile survival in Coastal Brant (Branta bernicla) populations in Chesapeake Bay. Using mark-recapture analysis of 127 VHF-tagged juveniles (2018-2021), we found that eelgrass (Zostera marina) cover decline due to nutrient pollution reduced first-winter survival by 37% (β = −0·41, SE = 0·11). Survival probability was strongly density-dependent when eelgrass biomass fell below 50 g/m². Conservation efforts must prioritize seagrass restoration to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this waterfowl species.

Stable isotope analysis of δ13C and δ15N in Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) primary feathers revealed significant dietary shifts between breeding and non-breeding seasons across Gulf Coast populations. Samples from 120 individuals indicated increased reliance on anthropogenic food sources during winter, with δ15N values correlating negatively with coastal wetland loss metrics. This trophodynamic plasticity demonstrates adaptive foraging strategies but highlights vulnerability to habitat degradation and marine pollution in modified estuaries.

<jats:p>A highly significant action taken by the Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food, reported elsewhere in this issue, could well result in important advances in surveillance and probably legislative control over enforcement of certain aspects of EEC legislation in the Member‐states. The Minister has sent an urgent request to the Commission in Brussels to dispatch inspectors to each country, including the United Kingdom, to examine and report on the standards of inspection and hygiene with detailed information on how the EEC Directive on Poultry Meat is being implemented. Information of the method of financing the cost of poultrymeat inspection in each country has ben requested. The comprehensive survey is seen as a common approach in this one field. The Minister requested that the results of the inspectors' reports should be available to him and other Member‐states.</jats:p>

We assessed bycatch mortality impacts on Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) demography using long-term banding data (2015-2023) from Manitoba's boreal wetlands. Mark-recapture analysis (n = 427 individuals) integrated with population viability modeling revealed a mean annual adult mortality rate of 0.38 (95% CI: 0.32–0.44). Bycatch events in recreational fishing lines accounted for 18.7% of recoveries (n = 32), reducing λ by 0.09 (p = 0.012) versus bycatch-free scenarios. These findings highlight inland fishery bycatch as a critical driver of regional declines, necessitating targeted mitigation in breeding habitats.

<jats:p>Canine teeth are vital to carnivore feeding ecology, facilitating behaviours related to prey capture and consumption. Forms vary with specific feeding ecologies; however, the biomechanics that drive these relationships have not been comprehensively investigated. Using a combination of beam theory analysis (BTA) and finite-element analysis (FEA) we assessed how aspects of canine shape impact tooth stress, relating this to feeding ecology. The degree of tooth lateral compression influenced tolerance of multidirectional loads, whereby canines with more circular cross-sections experienced similar maximum stresses under pulling and shaking loads, while more ellipsoid canines experienced higher stresses under shaking loads. Robusticity impacted a tooth's ability to tolerate stress and appears to be related to prey materials. Robust canines experience lower stresses and are found in carnivores regularly encountering hard foods. Slender canines experience higher stresses and are associated with carnivores biting into muscle and flesh. Curvature did not correlate with tooth stress; however, it did impact bending during biting. Our simulations help identify scenarios where canine forms are likely to break and pinpoint areas where this breakage may occur. These patterns demonstrate how canine shape relates to tolerating the stresses experienced when killing and feeding, revealing some of the form–function relationships that underpin mammalian carnivore ecologies.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>The spread of Lapita cultural groups through the New Guinea region 3350–3250 years ago and into the uninhabited remote Pacific islands from 3050–3000 years ago was one of the greatest migrations in human history. Over subsequent millennia, novel adaptations and intergenerational social linkages led to the emergence of a complex mosaic of culture and language reflected in modern Pacific populations. Broadly defined as “post-Lapita,” this chapter assesses the current breadth of archaeological information about human settlement and practices in the few centuries after the arrival of Lapita communities within the former ambit of their distribution. In doing so, the authors highlight the continuity, change, and innovations of cultural practices and behaviors that contributed to such remarkable diversity. An assessment of “transitional” post-Lapita sites indicates that the complex motifs on Lapita pottery reflecting social markers were retained in Near Oceania for several centuries longer than in Remote Oceania, where diverse social identities were quickly forged within and between island groups. Settlement patterns, social networks, and subsistence strategies were continually adapted to localized constraints and, together with ongoing population migrations and cross-cultural interaction, contributed to the Pacific region becoming one of the most culturally diverse regions in the world.</jats:p>

We investigated the impact of beach nourishment on Pectoral Sandpiper (Calidris melanotos) molt migration along the Georgia Bight coastline (USA) from 2018-2021. Using miniaturized GPS loggers (n=42 adults), stable isotope analysis of feathers (δ²H), and weekly shorebird surveys, we quantified phenology shifts and habitat selection. Post-nourishment sites exhibited 38% lower sandpiper densities (95% CI: -52% to -24%) and delayed primary molt initiation by 11.2 days (SE=2.8, p=0.002) compared to undisturbed controls. Our findings demonstrate that sediment alteration disrupts critical stopover ecology, necessitating mitigation strategies during coastal engineering projects.

This study investigated foraging behavior plasticity in Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) across urban and natural wetlands in the Pacific Northwest. Using focal animal sampling and GPS tracking, we quantified habitat selection and prey capture success rates. Results revealed significant differences in foraging efficiency between habitats, with urban herons exhibiting higher strike rates but lower prey diversity. Habitat degradation and human disturbance were identified as key factors influencing behavioral adaptations. Our findings highlight the species' resilience to anthropogenic pressures while underscoring conservation needs for wetland ecosystems.

We investigated energy expenditure of Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata related to wetland degradation in agricultural landscapes. Using doubly labeled water DLW techniques we tracked daily energy expenditure DEE of 32 individuals across 7 drained and 8 undrained wetlands in Saskatchewan Canada during 2019 2020 breeding seasons DEE was 18 higher snipe at drained sites mean 179 kJ day vs 152 kJ day p 003 CI 15 21 Daily foraging time increased by 27 p 001 Our results demonstrate that wetland drainage forces snipe to allocate more energy to foraging potentially reducing reproductive output Conservation efforts must prioritize wetland retention to buffer energetic costs

<jats:p>Aëtius ii 20.1 (DK 12A21) <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline1" /><jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline2" /><jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline3" /> Aëtius ii 25.1 (DK 12A22), on the moon, is similar, ending <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline4" /></jats:p><jats:p>It is generally supposed that <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline5" /> is the nozzle of a bellows; but G. E. R. Lloyd, <jats:italic>Polarity and analogy</jats:italic> 313 ff. is doubtful of this interpretation, pointing out that only one, doubtful, parallel can be cited for this meaning of <jats:italic>πρηστήρ</jats:italic>, and that the nozzle of a bellows does not emit fire. He concludes, however, that if <jats:italic>πρηστήρ</jats:italic> has its normal, meteorological, sense, ‘it seems impossible to interpret … <jats:italic>αὐλός</jats:italic> … for this must surely refer to some sort of pipe or tube and this seems quite inappropriate to such phenomena as lightning or whirlwinds … “Bellows” … appears to give the best sense for this difficult phrase’.</jats:p><jats:p>My purpose here is to show that <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline6" /> has a good meteorological sense. According to Aristotle <jats:italic>Mete.</jats:italic> 371a15 ff., the <jats:italic>πρηστήρ</jats:italic> is a variant of the <jats:italic>τυφῶν</jats:italic>, which is a whirlwind (370b22) which forms within a cloud (<jats:italic>ib.</jats:italic> 28), and, being unable to separate itself from the cloud, descends to the earth, bringing the cloud with it (371a9, ff., and especially 11 ff. <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="gif" mimetype="image" xlink:type="simple" xlink:href="S007542690011016X_inline7" />). This seems to be the ‘tornado’ or the ‘waterspout’ of modern meteorology. A tornado is ‘a very intense, progressive whirl, of small diameter … From the violently-agitated main cloud-mass above there usually hangs a writhing funnel-shaped cloud …’ The ‘funnel-shaped cloud’ is presumably the cloud which Aristotle's whirlwind ‘draws down with it’.</jats:p>

One of the most significant biological impacts of global climate change is through alterations of organismal body temperature, which ultimately drives almost all physiological processes. Using a simple heat budget model ground-truthed using ~5years of in situ temperature data collected using biomimetic sensors, we explored the sensitivity of aerial (low tide) mussel body temperature at three tidal elevations to changes in air temperature, solar radiation, wind speed, wave height, and the timing of low tide at a site in central California, USA (Bodega Bay). Results suggest that while increases in air temperature and solar radiation can significantly alter the risk of exposure to stressful conditions, especially at upper intertidal elevations, patterns of risk can be substantially reduced by convective cooling such that even moderate increases in mean wind speed (~1ms−1) can theoretically counteract the effects of substantial (2.5°C) increases in air temperature. Simulations further suggest that shifts in the timing of low tide (+1h), such as occur moving to different locations along the coast of California, can have very large impacts on sensitivity to increases in air temperature. Depending on the timing of low tide, at some sites increases in air temperature will primarily affect animals in the upper intertidal zone, while at other sites animals will be affected across all tidal elevations. Field measurements and model predictions show that animal temperatures are often high even when air temperatures are not, confirming the importance of solar radiation in the heat budgets of intertidal ectotherms. Conversely, body temperatures are not always elevated even when low tide air temperatures are extreme due to the combined effects of convective cooling and wave splash. The results of these simulations, coupled with ongoing field measurements, suggest that the timing and magnitude of warming will be highly variable at coastal sites, and can be driven to a large extent by local oceanographic and meteorological processes. Moreover, they strongly caution against the use of single environmental metrics such as air temperature as indicators of past, current and future physiological stress on the west coast of North America, and instead advocate for approaches that consider the interactive roles of multiple physical drivers.

We assessed Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) population viability in response to mudflat reclamation along the Yellow Sea coast using a 10-year dataset (2013-2022) from Jiangsu, China. Satellite tracking (n=42 birds) revealed a 68% reduction in staging duration at reclaimed sites versus natural mudflats (p=0.003). Population modeling indicated a 17.4% annual decline (95% CI: -21.1 to -13.7%) under current reclamation rates, predicting local extirpation within 15 years without intervention. Our results underscore the critical need for habitat protection in this East Asian-Australasian Flyway bottleneck.

We investigated Semipalmated Plover (Charadrius semipalmatus) behavioral responses to recreational kite-flying disturbance at Delaware Bay, USA (May-June 2021). Using accelerometry (n=22 adults) and focal observations (120 hours), we quantified energy expenditure during foraging interruptions. Plovers exhibited 37% higher metabolic rates (mean ± SE: 2.1 ± 0.3 kJ/min vs. 1.53 ± 0.2 kJ/min; p=0.008) and 29% reduced foraging efficiency in kite-present zones. Flight initiation distance increased by 15.2 m (95% CI: 8.7-21.6) per kite event. These sublethal effects suggest kite prohibition in critical stopover habitats could conserve energy reserves for migration.

<jats:p>The lichen flora of Africa is still poorly known. In many parts of the tropics, recent studies utilizing DNA methods have revealed extraordinary diversity among various groups of lichenized fungi, including the genus Sticta. In this study, East African Sticta species and their ecology are reviewed using the genetic barcoding marker nuITS and morphological characters. The studied regions represent montane areas in Kenya and Tanzania, including the Taita Hills and Mt. Kilimanjaro, which belong to the Eastern Afromontane biodiversity hotspot. Altogether 14 Sticta species are confirmed from the study region, including the previously reported S. fuliginosa, S. sublimbata, S. tomentosa, and S. umbilicariiformis. Sticta andina, S. ciliata, S. duplolimbata, S. fuliginoides, and S. marginalis are reported as new to Kenya and/or Tanzania. Sticta afromontana, S. aspratilis, S. cellulosa, S. cyanocaperata, and S. munda, are described as new to science. The abundance of new diversity detected and the number of taxa represented by only few specimens show that more comprehensive sampling of the region may be needed to reveal the true diversity of Sticta in East Africa. More generally, our results highlight the need for further taxonomic studies of lichenized fungi in the region.</jats:p>

Coastal wetland fragmentation severely impacts Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) populations. We analyzed 15 years of nesting data across six estuaries using GPS tracking and habitat mapping. Results showed a 40% colony decline correlated with marsh degradation (p=0.002). Generalized linear models indicate tidal creek loss as the primary driver, necessitating urgent hydrological restoration for conservation.

We investigated the interactive effects of climate change and hunting pressure on migratory Semipalmated Plovers (Charadrius semipalmatus) in Churchill, Manitoba (58°46'N, 94°10'W) during 2010–2022. Using satellite telemetry (n=85) and nest monitoring (n=217 nests), we quantified survival rates and breeding phenology. Premature snowmelt advanced arrival by 5 days/decade (95%CI=2.6-7.4), exposing birds to prolonged spring subsistence hunting. Nest failure increased 18% when hunting coincided with early incubation (P<0·001). Modelling revealed a non-linear interaction: greenhouse gas scenario RCP7.0 predicts 47% decline by 2040 under current harvest levels.

We investigated the impact of invasive feral cats (Felis catus) on Curlew Sandpiper (Calidris ferruginea) foraging behavior at Roebuck Bay (18°S 122°E), Western Australia during 2019-2021. Using time-budget observations (n=412 hours) and GPS tracking (n=28 adults), we quantified changes in prey intake and habitat use. Foraging time increased 37% in high-predator zones (95%CI: 28-42%, p<0 001), resulting in a 22% reduction in daily energy balance (p=0.003). Sandpipers abandoned high-quality mudflats with >50% cat occupancy, shifting to suboptimal habitats. Conservation must prioritize predator exclusion in critical intertidal areas.

We assessed heavy metal accumulation in American Golden-Plovers (Pluvialis dominica) along nourished vs. natural beaches in South Carolina (2019–2021). Blood samples from 52 adults were analyzed for Pb, Cd, and Hg via ICP-MS. Plovers from nourished sites showed 27% higher Pb concentrations (mean 15.3±2.1 μg/dL vs. 11.2±1.8 μg/dL; p=0.007) and reduced foraging efficiency (p=0.01). Results indicate beach nourishment redistributes pollutants, necessitating sediment screening prior to restoration to mitigate toxicological risks for this declining Nearctic migrant.

<jats:p>The direct measurement of farfield acoustic radiation from underwater transducers in a shore-based facility is often impossible because of the limited size of measurement tanks. The Trott nearfield calibration array (NFCA) concept solves this problem by allowing the farfield radiation to be determined from measurements made close to the transducer. We describe here the development of a 5- to 50-kHz synthetic cylindrical NFCA that is suitable for measurement tanks as small as about 2.5 m in each dimension and that can be operated at hydrostatic pressures up to 6.8 MPa. The NFCA is synthesized using a single line of 48 piezoelectric ceramic hydrophone elements spaced 2.54-cm apart center-to-center and amplitude shaded in a special way. The transducer to be calibrated is driven electrically and rotated near the line about an axis parallel to the line. The response of the line is measured at equally spaced angular positions, thereby creating a virtual cylindrical array surrounding the transducer. We then obtain the azimuthal farfield pattern of the transducer by computer processing the angular responses together with a set of complex shading coefficients. We evaluated the line experimentally by calibrating a large piston transducer in a cylindrical measurement tank less than 2.5 m in diameter. The resulting computed farfield patterns are in excellent agreement with corresponding patterns obtained from direct farfield measurements made in a lake.</jats:p>

We assessed how invasive Manila clams (Venerupis philippinarum) and recreational shell collection impact Long-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus scolopaceus; Charadriiformes: Scolopacidae). From 2019–2021, we monitored foraging rates (>1800 observations) and probed depths at Boundary Bay, British Columbia across invaded vs. control sites (n=12 transects/site). Dowitchers exhibited 32% reduced foraging efficiency (p=0.007, CI: -45% to -19%) and shallower mean probed depth (6.3±0.9cm vs 8.1±1cm, p<0·001). Population modeling showed 21% viability decline with sustained collecting. Conserving muddy intertidal zones through clam harvest bans is critical for this Nearctic migrant.

We investigated energy expenditure in Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon), a non-Charadriiformes bird, across coastal habitats using doubly labeled water techniques. Results revealed a 23% increase in daily energy expenditure during nesting compared to non-breeding periods, primarily driven by elevated foraging activity in response to diminished prey availability from riverine habitat degradation. Disturbances from recreational boating further amplified metabolic costs by 15%, pointing to synergistic anthropogenic stressors.

Understanding stopover ecology is critical for migratory waterfowl conservation. We investigated Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) use of coastal wetlands during spring migration using satellite telemetry (n=57) and habitat surveys. Results revealed high site fidelity to estuarine habitats, but pintails avoided areas with >15% shoreline development. Agricultural runoff reduced foraging quality in 60% of core sites. Habitat loss diminished stopover duration by 2.4 days on average, potentially impacting breeding success. Conservation requires minimizing anthropogenic disturbance in key coastal staging areas.

This study examines predator-prey dynamics between Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) and their primary prey species in estuarine habitats. Using focal observations and dietary analysis, we quantified predation rates on fiddler crabs (Uca spp.) and assessed gull foraging efficiency relative to tidal cycles. Results indicate significant temporal partitioning, with gull predation peaking during low tide when crab vulnerability increases. Contrary to expectations, gull predation pressure showed no correlation with local raptor abundance, suggesting compensatory foraging strategies. These findings highlight complex trophic interactions in coastal ecosystems beyond simple predator avoidance behaviors.

Abstract: We investigated juvenile survival rates in Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor), examining how coastal wetland degradation affects post-fledging mortality. Using radio-telemetry in Louisiana marshes (N=42 fledglings over two breeding seasons), we modeled survival against habitat metrics while accounting for temporal effects. Survival probability was significantly reduced in fragmented habitats. This study highlights anthropogenic impacts on wading bird recruitment and the need for contiguous wetland conservation measures.

We investigated nest site selection in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across freshwater marshes in the northeastern United States. Using logistic regression models incorporating vegetation density, water depth, and distance to open water, we found that rails preferentially nested in areas with intermediate vegetation cover (30-70%) and shallow water (<15 cm). Nest success was significantly higher in sites with greater concealment from predators. Habitat fragmentation due to agricultural runoff reduced suitable nesting habitat by 42% over five years, highlighting threats to this secretive marsh specialist.

Few people attending this conference have ever visited a developing country, let alone worked in one. Used as we are to the cosseted environment of the developed world, we take much for granted. A few statistics from the World Development Report (1983) will perhaps bring home to you the contrast between the developed and developing world (Table 1). For example, adult literacy may be low (26 per cent in Bangladesh); there are exceptions to this, as in Tanzania where literacy has reached 79 per cent, partly a result of Unesco's experimental World Literacy Programme and partly due to that country's own specific literacy projects. A good indication of the standard of living and general prosperity is the GNP per head: this is US$140 in Bangladesh, but $2,220 in Brazil and $10,080 in Japan. The lower the GNP per head, the greater is the dependence on agriculture. In Malaysia, three‐quarters of the population are associated with agriculture. Worldwide, 700 million of the ‘absolutely poor’ live in rural areas; 280 million farm one hectare or less, mostly on land that is dependent on natural rainfall.

This study investigates molt migration patterns in American Coots (Fulica americana) across the Mississippi Flyway. Using GPS telemetry on 40 individuals, we documented asynchronous migration timing correlated with wetland habitat availability. Molting birds showed strong site fidelity to temporary wetlands, with migration distances inversely related to local resource abundance. Habitat loss due to agricultural drainage reduced molting site occupancy by 62%, highlighting vulnerability during this energetically demanding life stage. Our findings emphasize the need for conservation of ephemeral wetlands to support this critical physiological process.

We investigated migration ecology of Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) in threatened Atlantic salt marshes using GPS telemetry (n=22 adults, 2019-2021). Individuals tagged in Delaware Bay exhibited 38% reduced stopover duration at converted marsh sites (mean ± SE: 2.3 ± 0.4 vs 3.7 ± 0.3 days; p=0.008) and 27% lower refueling rates (p=0.02). Population modeling projected a 19% decline (95% CI: 12-26%) over 20 years under current conversion rates. Results highlight urgent need to prioritize intact marsh conservation for this declining shorebird.

We investigated the demographic consequences of coastal erosion on Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) colonies in the Gulf of Mexico. Using mark-recapture data from 2015-2020 (n=1,243 individuals), we modeled survival probabilities and recruitment rates under varying beach loss scenarios. Our results indicate that habitat degradation significantly reduces juvenile survival (β = -0.41, SE=0.12) and colony persistence, with stochastic extinction risk increasing by 78% per kilometer of shoreline loss. Management interventions targeting sediment replenishment showed positive demographic responses within two breeding seasons.

This study investigates the genetic structure and diversity of Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) populations along the Gulf Coast using microsatellite markers. We analyzed samples from 12 colonies to assess impacts of historical DDT exposure and recent habitat fragmentation. Results indicate significant population differentiation (FST = 0.08) and reduced heterozygosity in anthropogenically disturbed sites, highlighting genetic erosion threats to this coastal seabird. Conservation implications focus on maintaining gene flow through protected coastal corridors.

We quantified juvenile survival rates of Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa limosa) in Huesca, Spain (2020-2022) under regulated hunting pressure. Using VHF telemetry (n=62 fledglings), survival probability was estimated via known-fate models. Daily survival rate was significantly lower during hunting season (0·968 ± 0·006 SE) versus non-hunting (0·992 ± 0·003; p < 0·001), translating to 58% season survival during hunting versus 80% otherwise. Our results confirm hunting as a critical additive mortality factor requiring adaptive bag limit reductions in core staging areas.

We investigated foraging efficiency of Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) along urbanized river corridors in the Pacific Northwest. Using focal animal sampling (n=32 individuals), we quantified dive success rates relative to water turbidity and anthropogenic disturbance levels. Results indicate significantly reduced capture rates (p<0.01) in high-turbidity zones (>25 NTU) and near recreational boat traffic. Our findings highlight vulnerability of this piscivore to sediment pollution and human activity, suggesting management strategies should prioritize riparian buffer restoration.

We investigated the impacts of coastal development and disturbance on molt migration phenology in Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) populations along the Labrador coast. Using GPS telemetry (n=47 adults), we documented delayed departure to molting areas by 11.3±2.1 days in regions with high vessel traffic density (p<0·001). Earlier molt migration correlated with higher overwinter survival (R²=0·72), suggesting human activity may impose fitness costs through phenological mismatch. Results emphasize vulnerability of waterfowl to anthropogenic pressures during critical life-history stages.

Juvenile Common Snipe (Gallinago gallinago) survival rates in relation to avian influenza virus (AIV) exposure were quantified across coastal wetlands in Estonia (58°N, 26°E) during 2018-2020. We monitored 73 radio-tagged juveniles using VHF telemetry over 90-day post-fledging periods. Cox proportional hazards models revealed significantly higher mortality risk (HR=2.4, 95% CI:1.6-3.7) for AIV-seropositive individuals compared to seronegative counterparts. Survival probability declined to 0.32±0.04 SE in exposed juveniles versus 0.68±0.05 in unexposed. These findings highlight disease-mediated selection pressures during critical life stages, necessitating wetland management strategies that reduce AIV transmission risks for declining shorebird populations.

We investigated winter habitat selection by Brant geese (Branta bernicla) in coastal Virginia using GPS telemetry (n=32) and resource selection functions. Model comparisons revealed strong avoidance of developed shorelines (β = -1.72, SE=0.41) and preferential use of submerged aquatic vegetation beds (β=2.31, SE=0.38). Salinity gradients significantly influenced distribution patterns, with 78% of locations occurring in mesohaline zones (5-18 ppt). Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this specialist herbivore to coastal development and eutrophication-induced seagrass decline.

This telemetry study examined the movement patterns of American Coots (Fulica americana) across seasonal wetlands in California's Central Valley. Using GPS transmitters deployed on 45 individuals, we documented responses to hydrological fluctuations and agricultural drainage. Results revealed significant avoidance of pesticide-treated areas during foraging, with home range contractions correlating with declining water availability (R² = 0 73, p < 0.01). These findings emphasize coot vulnerability to agricultural intensification and water management practices.

We investigated how morphological traits in breeding Willet (Tringa semipalmata semipalmata; hereafter 'Eastern Willet') influence storm adaptation across northwestern Florida barrier islands (2018-2021). Using morphometric measurements (tarsus length; bill depth) from 278 banded individuals alongside GPS-tagged storm exposure data, we modeled trait relationships with nest persistence. Contrary to predictions, longer tarsi associated with higher nest failure during moderate storms (β = -0·32, SE = 0·14, p = 0·023). Bill depth showed no significant effect. Results suggest climate-driven storm intensification may disproportionately impact longer-legged Willets through nest disruption.

We assessed fall migration chronology of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola), a wetland-dependent species at risk from habitat degradation. Using automated recording units across 19 marshes in the Mississippi Flyway (2018-2020), we identified peak passage timing and correlated stopover duration with wetland connectivity metrics. Results indicate significant delays in migration onset (mean 5.2 days later than historic records) associated with fragmented habitat, suggesting emergent climate change impacts on migration phenology in this secretive rallid.

Demographic parameters of Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) populations were quantified across fragmented mid-Atlantic salt marshes from 2018-2022. Using Cormack-Jolly-Seber models with 342 banded individuals, we found significantly reduced adult survival (Φ = 0.52 ± 0.06) in degraded habitats compared to intact marshes (Φ = 0.71 ± 0.05). Nest monitoring revealed marsh elevation mediated flooding-induced clutch failure (β = -0.41, p < 0.001), with sea-level rise projections indicating 34% population decline by 2040 without intervention. These results emphasize habitat-specific vulnerability in rail metapopulation dynamics.

Wilson's Plover (Charadrius wilsonia) breeding ecology was studied from 2015-2018 along Georgia's barrier islands to assess vulnerability to increasing storm frequency. Using 127 nest sites monitored via trail cameras and microclimate loggers, we documented a 28% decline in fledging success (95% CI: -31% to -25%; p=0.003) following major storm events (≥25 cm rainfall). Generalized linear mixed models revealed precipitation explained 74% of nest failure variance. This quantifies climate-mediated breeding failure, necessitating managed retreat for beach-nesting shorebirds facing intensified tropical cyclones.

<jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p>1. We review some of the classic literature on geomorphology and ecology of streams in an effort to examine how theoretical developments in these aquatic sciences have influenced the way fresh flowing waters are classified. Our aim was to provide a historical examination of conceptual developments related to fluvial classification, and to discuss implications for conservation planning and resource management.</jats:p><jats:p>2. Periods of conceptual influences can be separated into three overlapping phases each distinguished by theoretical, analytical or technological advances: (i) early Darwinian perspectives; (ii) the quantitative revolution; and, (iii) age of the computer, hierarchy and scale.</jats:p><jats:p>3. During the first phase, stream geomorphologists were largely influenced by Darwinian metaphors. The study of stream origin and change through time became more important than the study of stream systems themselves. The idea that streams progress deterministically through successive stages of development seemed to create a veil, most prevalently in North America, that barred analysis of the full scope of variability in these systems for over 50 years.</jats:p><jats:p>4. The quantitative revolution brought about many new ideas and developments, including the laws of stream numbers. This period focused on predictive and mechanistic explanations of stream processes, setting the stage for physically based stream classifications that assume that streams can be restored by engineering their physical characteristics.</jats:p><jats:p>5. In the most recent ‘age of the computer’, concepts from the fields of geographic information science and landscape ecology have been incorporated into stream ecology and aquatic classification. This has led to investigations in stream and aquatic ecosystems at hierarchical spatial scales and along different dimensions (upstream/downstream, riparian/floodplain, channel/ground water and through time). Yet, in contrast to terrestrial landscapes, flowing waters are not as easily classified into spatially nested hierarchical regions wherein upper levels can be subdivided into smaller and smaller regions at finer spatial scales. Riverscapes are perhaps best described as directionally nested hierarchies: aquatic elements further downstream cannot be rendered equivalently to elements upstream. Moreover, fully integrated aquatic ecosystem classifications that incorporate lake and river networks, wetlands, groundwater reservoirs and upland areas are exceedingly rare.</jats:p><jats:p>6. We reason that the way forward for classification of flowing waters is to account for the directionally nested nature of these networks and to encode flexibility into modern digital freshwater inventories and fluvial classification models.</jats:p>

We investigated resting metabolic rate (RMR; mL O2 min-1 kg-1; n=16) and daily energy expenditure (DEE; kJ day-1; n=12) of overwintering Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola) in constructed and natural marshes of Louisiana using respirometry and doubly labeled water techniques. Significant differences emerged: DEE was 1.6x higher in constructed (158±22 kJ day-1) vs natural sites (102±18 kJ day-1; p<0·01). Increased energy expenditure correlated with reduced invertebrate prey biomass (r=-0·71) in constructed wetlands. Habitat restoration must consider prey-base requirements to reduce overwinter mortality in rails.

We assessed genetic impacts of fisheries bycatch mortality on Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) populations migrating through Patagonia. Using microsatellite analysis of 120 individuals (2018-2021) from Argentina's Santa Cruz Province, we detected significant allelic richness reduction (F<sub>ST</sub> = 0.032, p = 0.008) and effective population size decline (N<sub>e</sub> = 48, 95% CI: 42-57) in bycatch-affected cohorts. Results indicate genetic erosion threatening long-term viability, necessitating urgent bycatch mitigation in austral stopover sites.

Investigating foraging plasticity in Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) amidst coastal urbanization, we conducted focal observations and GPS tracking on 42 individuals from three colonies. Gulls exhibited significant dietary shifts towards anthropogenic food sources (χ²=34.7,p<0 .001), reducing natural prey consumption by 68%. Urban-nesting birds showed 3-fold higher foraging efficiency near landfills than coastal foragers (t=5.21,df=41,p<0 .001). Results demonstrate behavioral adaptation to human-altered landscapes with implications for nutrient transfer pathways.

We investigated molt migration ecology of American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) in Atlantic coastal habitats using GPS telemetry and habitat suitability modeling. Satellite-tracked individuals (n=42) showed strong fidelity to specific estuarine wetlands for flight feather replacement. Analysis revealed significant overlap between critical molting areas and regions experiencing accelerating sea-level rise (p<0.01) and coastal development, suggesting compounding stressors may disrupt this energetically sensitive life-stage and necessitate targeted wetland conservation measures.

We investigated juvenile survival rates of American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) in coastal wetlands of Chesapeake Bay from 2018-2021. Using radio-telemetry on 120 fledglings, we documented 42% mortality within 60 days post-fledging. Cox proportional hazards models indicated tidal flooding events (HR=3.1, p<0.001) and marsh fragmentation (HR=1.8, p=0.02) as primary drivers. Anthropogenic disturbance from recreational boating increased mortality risk by 40% (HR=1.4, p=0.04). Results highlight vulnerability of juvenile waterfowl to compounded coastal threats during critical life stages.

We investigated Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) stopover ecology during fall migration in Mid-Atlantic coastal marshes. Using radio-telemetry (n=42 birds), we quantified habitat selection and duration of stay at managed impoundments. Rails exhibited strong selection for dense emergent vegetation (β=1.78±0.23 SE) and avoided open water habitats (β=-2.41±0.31). Stopover duration averaged 7.2±1.1 days, significantly longer than previously reported. Marsh drainage for mosquito control reduced occupancy by 63% (p<0.001) compared to natural wetlands. Our results demonstrate that hydrological management critically influences rail refueling efficiency during migration.

Coastal marsh degradation significantly threatens Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) breeding ecology. We monitored 23 heronries across the Chesapeake Bay estuary (2018-2022), quantifying nest density and fledging success relative to habitat fragmentation from shoreline development. Using generalized linear mixed models, we demonstrated reduced reproductive output (β = -0.41, p < 0.001) and colony abandonment probability (OR = 4.2) in sites with >30% emergent vegetation loss. Satellite telemetry revealed displaced adults exhibited longer foraging flights (x̄ = +2.7 km) and reduced chick provisioning rates. Conservation priorities must address tidal marsh connectivity to sustain viable populations of this wading bird.

This study examines predator-prey dynamics between Brant geese (Branta bernicla) and Arctic foxes (Vulpes lagopus) in coastal Alaska. Using GPS telemetry and nest camera surveillance across three breeding seasons (2019-2021), we quantified predation rates and anti-predator behaviors. Results show foxes caused 68% of nest failures, with Brant exhibiting heightened nest defense in areas of high fox density. Our findings highlight how climate-induced shrub encroachment facilitates predator access to nesting islands, exacerbating waterfowl reproductive vulnerability in rapidly changing Arctic ecosystems.

Stable carbon and nitrogen isotope analysis of Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) feathers revealed significant dietary shifts between freshwater and coastal habitats along the mid-Atlantic coast. Individuals occupying estuarine environments exhibited enriched δ15N values (mean = 12.3‰ ± 0.7) compared to riverine conspecifics (9.1‰ ± 0.5), indicating greater marine prey consumption. Habitat fragmentation from coastal development correlated with reduced isotopic niche width in urbanized watersheds, suggesting constrained foraging opportunities. These findings demonstrate how anthropogenic landscape alteration disrupts trophic pathways for piscivorous birds beyond shorebird communities.

<jats:p>A collaborative, multi-institute experiment was recently performed in the vicinity of the Scripps Pier, whose goal was the study of bubble-field generation, transport, and distribution, as influenced by surf zone conditions. The collaboration produced an ensemble of instrumentation at the site for measuring bubbles, ambient noise, temperature and salinity, currents, and surface waves. This paper emphasizes data gathered by APL-UW using a set of four upward-looking transducers (frequency 240 kHz), which simultaneously measured vertical profiles of acoustic volume scattering from bubbles from four locations. The primary locus of measurement activity was defined by NRL-SSC’s triangular frame (Delta Frame) and the four transducer locations for the APL-UW system bracketed this region. The transport of bubbles via rip currents emerged as a key feature surf zone bubble environment. Images of volumetric backscattering strength versus time and depth reveal episodic events (by way of increased scattering level) which last O(100) s and can occur in intervals of O(10) min. Time lags for increased scattering at the four locations were consistent with a seaward flow of rip currents equal to ∼0.25 m/s. Other features of the data that complement the single-depth measurements made from the Delta Frame will be discussed. [Work supported by ONR.]</jats:p>

Plastic ingestion risk in Semipalmated Sandpipers (Calidris pusilla) was evaluated in relation to anthropogenic disturbance at Delaware Bay, USA during 2020-2021 spring migrations. Using regurgitate analysis (n=87 individuals) and disturbance monitoring (trail cameras; 1,200 hrs), microplastic occurrence was quantified via FTIR spectroscopy. Individuals in high-disturbance zones exhibited 38% higher microplastic ingestion rates (95% CI: 24-52%, χ²=8.7, p=0.003) and 2.1× greater polymer diversity than low-disturbance conspecifics. Regression indicated a positive correlation between visitor frequency and polyethylene fragment abundance (R²=0.74). Results demonstrate disturbance-mediated plastic exposure, necessitating buffer zones around critical stopover habitats to mitigate sublethal impacts on nutrient assimilation.

Habitat fragmentation poses significant threats to Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) persistence. We assessed conservation genetics using microsatellite markers across 15 wetland populations (n=287). Results revealed pronounced genetic structure (FST=0.18) and reduced heterozygosity in fragmented sites (He=0.42±0.08) compared to contiguous wetlands (He=0.61±0.05), indicating restricted gene flow due to anthropogenic barriers. Effective population sizes fell below sustainability thresholds in 60% of isolated subpopulations. Our findings underscore urgent need for wetland corridor restoration to maintain genetic diversity in this declining Gruiformes species facing accelerated habitat loss.

We investigated the effect of a 12-d exposure to 34°C plus dietary inclusion of the probiotic Bacillus licheniformis on the egg production, gut morphology, and intestinal mucosal immunity of laying hens. Ninety-six commercial hens (Hy-Line Brown) at the age of 60 wk were randomly allocated to 4 groups. After a period of laying rate adjustment (14 d), all the hens were subjected to 2 temperature treatments (12 d). Birds in 1 group were raised at 21°C and fed a basal diet, and birds in the other 3 groups were raised at 34°C and fed a basal diet supplemented with 0, 106, or 107 cfu of B. licheniformis per gram of feed, respectively. Rearing at 34°C depressed egg production and feed intake (P < 0.05). Compared with birds kept at 21°C, birds kept at 34°C had elevated serum levels of tumor necrosis factor-α (d 6), IL-1 (d 6 and 12), and corticosterone (d 6); decreased villus height (ileum: d 6; cecum: d 6 and 12) and ratio of villus height to crypt depth (ileum: d 6; cecum: d 6 and 12); fewer intraepithelial lymphocytes (ileum: d 6; cecum: d 6) and IgA-secreting cells (ileum: d 6; cecum: d 6 and 12); and more mast cells (ileum: d 6; cecum: d 6 and 12; P < 0.05). The number of goblet cells in the cecum increased at d 6 in heat-treated birds, and then deceased at d 12 (P < 0.05). Moreover, morphological examination showed injury to the villi of birds kept at 34°C. In general, inclusion of 107 cfu/g of B. licheniformis in the diet of heat-stressed hens was effective in overcoming the observed decline in egg production and feed intake, restoring the impaired villus structure, and sustaining a balanced mucosal immune response. Therefore, the probiotic B. licheniformis may be useful for ameliorating the adverse influence of heat on the egg production and gut health of laying hens.

This study examines climate change impacts on Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) nesting phenology in coastal Louisiana marshes. Using 15 years of nest monitoring data, we demonstrate significantly earlier egg-laying dates (mean advance of 8.2 days) correlated with rising spring temperatures. Earlier nesting increased vulnerability to tropical storm disturbance during critical chick-rearing periods. Precipitation anomalies further reduced fledging success through nest flooding. Results highlight climate-mediated phenological shifts as emerging threats for Ardeids, necessitating adaptive management strategies beyond traditional wetland conservation approaches.

Abstract: Assessing habitat-mediated parasitism risk in Lesser Yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes), we quantified trematode prevalence across boreal wetlands in Manitoba, Canada (May-August 2018-2020). Fecal samples (n=132 birds) revealed increasing infection probability with sedge density (generalized linear model: β=0.85, p=0.012). Individuals selecting seasonally flooded habitats exhibited 38% lower trematode loads than those in permanent ponds (t-test: t=4.21, p<0). Findings emphasize prioritizing ephemeral wetlands for conservation to minimize disease risk in this declining shorebird.
