<jats:p>Eutrophication coupled to climate change disturbs the balance between competition and coexistence in microbial communities including the partitioning of organic and inorganic nutrients between phytoplankton and bacteria. Competition for inorganic nutrients has been regarded as one of the drivers affecting the productivity of the eutrophied coastal Baltic Sea. Yet, it is unknown at the molecular expression level how resources are competed for, by phytoplankton and bacteria, and what impact this competition has on the community composition. Here we use metatranscriptomics and amplicon sequencing and compare known metabolic pathways of both phytoplankton and bacteria co-occurring during a summer bloom in the archipelago of Åland in the Baltic Sea to examine phytoplankton bacteria resource partitioning. The expression of selected pathways of carbon (C), nitrogen (N), and phosphorus (P) metabolism varied over time, independently, for both phytoplankton and bacteria, indicating partitioning of the available organic and inorganic resources. This occurs regardless of eukaryotic plankton growth phase (exponential or stationary), based on expression data, and microbial community composition. Further, the availability of different nutrient resources affected the functional response by the bacteria, observed as minor compositional changes, at class level, in an otherwise taxonomically stable bacterial community. Resource partitioning and functional flexibility seem necessary in order to maintain phytoplankton-bacteria interactions at stable environmental conditions. More detailed knowledge of which organisms utilize certain nutrient species are important for more accurate projections of the fate of coastal waters.</jats:p>

We assessed population dynamics of American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) from 1995-2020 across Mid-Atlantic estuaries using banding data and aerial surveys. Habitat fragmentation from coastal development and sea-level rise reduced nesting success by 38%, while increased winter mortality correlated with contaminant bioaccumulation. Population viability analysis indicated a 72% decline probability without wetland restoration and pollution mitigation efforts.

Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations in Mid-Atlantic coastal marshes declined by 42% from 2010-2020 due to tidal wetland fragmentation. We combined occupancy modeling with remote sensing to assess habitat loss drivers across 80 sites. Results indicated drainage projects (β = -0.74, p<0.01) and sea-level rise (β = -0.58, p<0.05) significantly reduced breeding density, with cordgrass-dominated marshes showing highest vulnerability to inundation.

This study investigated habitat selection in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across coastal ecosystems, utilizing GPS telemetry and resource selection functions. Cormorants exhibited significant preference for shallow-water roosting habitats with complex structures, while strongly avoiding sites with high recreational boat traffic intensity. Anthropogenic disturbance emerged as a primary driver of suboptimal habitat use patterns, suggesting management strategies must prioritize minimizing human activity near key roosting colonies to mitigate population impacts.

We investigated morphological variation in Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) nestlings exposed to chronic microplastic pollution across Gulf Coast colonies. Morphometric analysis of 150 fledglings from high- and low-pollution sites revealed significant reductions in culmen length (t=3.21, p<0.01) and keel depth (t=2.87, p<0.05) among contaminated cohorts, suggesting developmental impacts from ingested plastics. This sublethal effect may compromise foraging efficiency in this piscivorous seabird, highlighting emerging threats to coastal avian morphology.

This study investigated the impact of invasive Spartina alterniflora on coastal Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) populations in northeastern China. Using radio-telemetry and habitat selection models, we found that Spartina invasion reduced available foraging habitats by 62% during winter months. Mallards exhibited significantly lower body condition indices in invaded areas (t-test: t=4.32, p<0001), with population density declining 38% over five years. Our results demonstrate how invasive macrophytes alter waterfowl winter ecology through trophic resource exclusion.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Distinguishing sea-ice-rafted debris (SIRD) from iceberg-rafted debris is crucial to an interpretation of ice-rafting history; however, there are few paleo-sea-ice proxies. This study characterizes quartz grain microfeatures of modern SIRD from the Arctic Ocean, and compares these results with microfeatures from representative glacial deposits to potentially differentiate SIRD from ice-rafted sediments which have been recently subjected to glacial processes. This allows us to evaluate the use of grain microfeatures as a paleo-sea-ice proxy. SIRD grains were largely subrounded, with medium relief, pervasive silica dissolution and a high abundance of breakage blocks and microlayering. The glacial grains were more angular, with lower relief and higher abundances of fractures and striations/gouges. Discriminate analysis shows a distinct difference between SIRD and glacial grains, with ˂7% of the SIRD grains containing typical glacial microtextures, suggesting this method is a useful means of inferring paleo-sea-ice presence in the marine record. We propose that differences in microfeatures of SIRD and glacial ice-rafted debris reflect differences in sediment transport and weathering histories. Sediment transported to a coastal setting and later rafted by sea ice would be subject to increased chemical weathering, whereas glaciers that calve icebergs would bypass the coastal marine environment, thus preserving their glacial signature.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Aim</jats:title><jats:p>Quantifying the importance of habitat areas for conservation of highly migratory marine species with complex life histories can be challenging. For example loggerhead turtles (<jats:italic>Caretta caretta</jats:italic>) nesting in Japan forage both oceanically and neritically after their reproductive period. Here, we aimed to quantify the proportions of turtles using these two contrasting habitats (foraging dichotomy) to suggest priority conservation areas.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Location</jats:title><jats:p>North Pacific Ocean.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>We examined the occurrence of foraging dichotomy at three nesting sites (Ishigaki, Okinoerabu Islands and Ichinomiya) based on stable isotope analysis of the egg yolks for 82 turtles and satellite tracking of post‐nesting migration for 12 turtles. Moreover, we used the data of three other sites from previous studies (Yakushima Island, Minabe and Omaezaki).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>Two neritic foraging grounds (East China Sea and the coastal area of the Japanese archipelago), and an oceanic ground (North Pacific Ocean) were identified. We found a latitudinal cline with respect to the occurrence of foraging dichotomy; >84% of the females nesting at southern sites (Ishigaki and Okinoerabu Islands), 73% at middle sites (Yakushima Island and Minabe) and <46% at northern sites (Omaezaki and Ichinomiya) were neritic foragers; the proportion of oceanic foragers increased at northern sites. Based on the annual number of nests in the entire nesting region of Japan, satellite tracking and the latitudinal cline of foraging dichotomy, we estimated that 70% and 9% of annual nesting females in Japan utilize the neritic foraging habitat in the East China Sea and the coastal area of the Japanese archipelago, respectively, and that and 22% utilize the oceanic habitat of the North Pacific Ocean.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Main conclusions</jats:title><jats:p>The East China Sea represents a critical foraging habitat for the North Pacific populations of endangered loggerhead sea turtles. Our findings emphasize the need for international management to ensure their protection.</jats:p></jats:sec>

This study investigates Great Egret (Ardea alba)’s stopover site fidelity during autumn migration in the lower Mississippi River valley. Using GPS telemetry on 15 individuals, we tracked movements from 2018–2020. Results indicate high site fidelity to specific forested riparian zones (mean return rate = 73%), contrasting with prior assumptions of opportunistic wetland use. Significant negative correlations were found between site reuse and agricultural encroachment (r = -0.72, p<0. 01), suggesting landscape-level habitat degradation threatens migration corridors for this non-shorebird wader.

We assessed the impact of recreational kite-flying on Willet (Tringa semipalmata)'s foraging behavior using GPS telemetry in Cape Romain NWR, South Carolina, USA (2018-2021). Tracked 42 adults during postbreeding; calculated step lengths and foraging bout intervals near kite zones vs control areas. Foraging efficiency decreased by 32% near kites (paired t-test, t = 4 7, df = 41, p < 0 001), with 26% fewer prey captures observed. Results demonstrate significant behavioral disruption, warranting seasonal buffer zones around critical tidal flats.

<jats:p>North Sweden (‘Norrland’ in Swedish) covers 243 000 km2 and lies mainly in the boreal biome. The herpetofauna comprises five amphibian and four reptile species: Lissotriton vulgaris, Triturus cristatus, Bufo bufo, Rana temporaria, Rana arvalis, Zootoca vivipara, Anguis fragilis, Natrix natrix, and Vipera berus. 
 Successful conservation and management of amphibians and reptiles depend on accurate information about distribution, habitat affinities, and abundance. Such knowledge is also essential as a benchmark to assess changes in distribution and abundance that may come about as a result of climate change and human habitat alteration.
 This paper aims to present accurate distribution maps, describe habitat affinities, and provide abundance estimates for the herpetofauna of North Sweden for the period 1970–2022. Distribution data are presented by traditional faunistic provinces, as well as by biotic regions and alpine life zones. Separate sections address post-glacial colonization and a herpetological perspective on anthropogenic changes in relation to species´ present status.
 Bufo bufo, Rana temporaria, Rana arvalis, Zootoca vivipara, and Vipera berus are widely distributed throughout the boreal sub-regions. Rana temporaria, Zootoca vivipara, and Vipera berus also extend into the alpine region. Triturus cristatus, Anguis fragilis, and Natrix natrix occur mainly in the coastal parts of the Southern Boreal region. There are no signs of recent changes in distribution range, but Lissotriton vulgaris, Triturus cristatus, and Rana arvalis have been largely overlooked in the past and have a much wider occurrence than previously recognized. Most species are found in habitats usually not described in all-European field guides. Nearly all anurans hibernate in water. Abundance estimates suggest that some species are more common in the boreal than thought, supporting the notion that a large share of their total European population occurs there. Although local extinctions and declines are known, there are no signs of widespread population decline for any species during the study period.
 </jats:p>

We investigated predator-prey dynamics between Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) and juvenile salmonids in Pacific Northwest estuaries. Using focal observations and regurgitation pellet analysis at 12 river mouths, we quantified seasonal predation pressure across tidal cycles. Results indicate kingfishers selectively target hatchery-origin salmon smolts during ebb tides, with predation rates increasing near anthropogenic structures. This novel documentation of avian predation as a significant source of mortality for outmigrating salmon highlights management conflicts between piscivore conservation and fisheries enhancement programs.

Rock Sandpipers (Calidris ptilocnemis) face compounded threats from invasive plant colonization and altered precipitation in subarctic breeding grounds. We examined 143 nests across five barrier islands in Cook Inlet, Alaska (2019-2022), using vegetation transects and microclimate loggers to quantify invasive Elymus athericus cover and soil moisture. Daily nest survival declined by 1.7% per 10% increase in invasive cover (β = -0.17, SE = 0.05, p = 0.003) and by 2.1% per cm above historical rainfall norms (β = -0.21, SE = 0.07, p = 0.01). Synergistic effects reduced fledging success by 32% (95% CI: 24-40%) in high-rainfall/high-invasion sites. Targeted invasive removal is recommended to enhance resilience to precipitation extremes.

Abstract Triclosan (TCS) is a halogenated aromatic compound used in household products such as toothpaste, detergents, soaps, and cosmetics, and is frequently found in domestic wastewater. The harmful effects of TCS are associated with hormonal and metabolic alterations in aquatic organisms. The present study evaluated the Phyto-purifying capacity of  Cyperus articulatus  L. planted in a horizontal subsurface flow constructed wetland used for domestic wastewater treatment. This required the usage of a 0.8 m × 0.5 m and 0.85 m high artificial wetland in fiberglass and polyester resin filled with garden gravel to a depth of 0.4 m, which received a daily flow of 18 L from a storage tank for 4 months. The concentration of TCS in influent and effluent water, as well as in plant roots and stems, was determined by gas chromatography coupled to a mass spectrometer. The TCS removal efficiency was 63% and was lower than that reported in similar studies. The translocation factor (TF) and bio-concentration factor (BCF) reached values of 1 and 0.06, respectively, indicating that  C. articulatus  can absorb and transport TCS from the root to higher parts of the stem. The results of this study lead to the conclusion that a local plant such as  C. articulatus  planted in constructed wetlands can decrease the concentration of an emerging pollutant, such as TCS, from domestic wastewater.

We investigated Long-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus scolopaceus) vocalization patterns as indicators of bycatch risk in California's Central Valley rice fields. From 2020-2022, we deployed autonomous recorders at 45 sites (n=12,500 hours) and tracked 22 GPS-tagged individuals. Dowitchers exhibited significantly higher alarm call rates (mean = 3.2 calls/min ± 0.8 SE) in fields with active harvesting equipment versus controls (0.7 calls/min ± 0.3; p=0.002). Vocalization intensity predicted GPS locations with 78% accuracy where bycatch events occurred (95% CI: 65-88%). Our bioacoustic approach provides a non-invasive tool for identifying high-risk zones, informing adaptive management to reduce shorebird mortality in agricultural landscapes.

We investigated the impacts of recreational kayaking on Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) foraging efficiency along urbanized river corridors. Using focal observations at 12 sites with varying human activity levels, we quantified strike rates and prey capture success. Kingfishers exhibited significantly reduced foraging attempts (p<0.01) and increased vigilance behavior at high-disturbance sites. Our results demonstrate that frequent watercraft passage disrupts critical hunting behaviors in this piscivorous specialist, highlighting the need for temporal zoning in riparian recreation management.

This study quantified Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) behavioral responses to photography pressure in the Horicon Marsh National Wildlife Refuge, Wisconsin (2018-2020 breeding seasons). Using 167 experimental disturbance trials with decoy cameras and focal observations (n=42 individuals), we documented 38% reduced foraging efficiency (95% CI: 29-47%, p<0.001) and 1.9× increased vigilance (SE±0.3) when approached within 25m. Flushing probability increased by 67% at 15m distances versus controls (χ²=15.3, df=1, p=0.0001). Results indicate that implementing 30m photography exclusion buffers during nesting is critical for energy budget maintenance in this cryptically nesting shorebird.

We investigated the interplay between molt migration and haemosporidian parasite prevalence in Kentish Plovers (Charadrius alexandrinus) along the Yellow Sea coast. Using GPS tracking (n=42 adults) and molecular screening of blood samples (n=87) from Bohai Bay, China (2019-2021), we found significantly higher infection rates during pre-molt staging (37.2%) compared to post-molt periods (11.4%; χ²=9.87, p=0.002). Individuals delaying migration onset by >7 days showed 3.2× higher infection risk (95% CI: 1.4-7.1). Results suggest molt phenology synchronization reduces exposure to vector-borne pathogens, informing conservation of critical stopover habitats.

This study assessed breeding impacts of mudflat reclamation on the Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus) in Jiangsu Province, China (2018-2021). We monitored 187 nests across natural (n=5) and reclaimed sites (n=5), quantifying clutch size, hatching success, and fledging rates using daily nest checks and GPS tracking. Nest success was 37% lower in reclaimed areas (χ²=12.8, p=0.003), with fledging rates declining by 52% (95% CI: 41-63%) due to increased predation and habitat fragmentation. Results demonstrate acute reproductive impairment from coastal development, urging habitat preservation for this declining shorebird.

This study examines parental investment strategies in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) nesting in coastal estuaries. Using observational data from 42 nests over two breeding seasons, we quantified provisioning rates and nest attendance patterns. Results indicate significant sex-based differences in foraging effort, with males making longer foraging trips but delivering larger prey items. Increased human disturbance near colonies correlated with reduced nest attendance and higher chick mortality. Findings highlight vulnerability of cormorant parental care systems to anthropogenic stressors in coastal habitats.

This study is about Kenyan pupils' ideas of parks and wildlife. Despite their importance in Kenya, parks and wildlife do not seem to have contributed much in terms of teaching and learning of ecology at school. The findings show a lack of scientific explanation and understanding of issues of wildlife and parks. However, some pupils understand parks and wildlife in terms of their social implications such as socioeconomic benefits, tourism and the resolution of the human-wildlife conflict. The pupils note the potential of parks and wildlife to contribute to the alleviation of poverty and the creation of a more equitable society. They also note the importance of participation in determining park and wildlife ownership in Kenya.

We assessed impacts of recreational hunting on Lesser Yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes) parental care in Alberta's boreal wetlands (2019-2021). Using GPS tags (n=47 adults) and 24-hr nest cameras (n=53 nests), we quantified provisioning behavior relative to hunting intensity (shotgun blasts/km²/day). In high-hunting zones, male feeding visits declined 38.7% (p=0.003, 95% CI: -51.2 to -26.1) versus controls, correlating with 22% lower chick survival (R²=0.71, p<0.001). Conservation strategies must mitigate indirect hunting effects on biparental care systems in shorebirds.

Events during one stage of the annual life cycle of migratory birds can have lasting (i.e. carry-over) effects that influence demographic parameters in subsequent seasons. We studied migratory connectivity and potential carry-over effects in a declining population of sea ducks. We measured stable isotope values of carbon (δ13C) and nitrogen (δ15N) in head feathers to assign breeding White-winged Scoters (Melanitta fusca; hereafter scoters) to either Atlantic or Pacific winter populations. The discriminant function for δ13C and δ15N correctly classified 93% of scoters sampled from these 2 winter areas. We then applied this classification scheme to head feathers of females breeding at Redberry Lake, Saskatchewan, and Cardinal Lake, Northwest Territories, to stratify each breeding population by winter provenance. We evaluated carry-over effects associated with winter location of females breeding in Saskatchewan by testing for differences in (1) nesting phenology, (2) clutch size, (3) mid-incubation body mass, (4) nest success, and (5) concentrations of trace elements contaminants of cadmium (Cd), mercury (Hg), selenium (Se), and lead (Pb) in blood, between strata of putative winter origin. Breeding females from the Atlantic coast had later dates of nest initiation, greater mid-incubation body mass, and also had higher concentrations of Cd (one year only), Pb, and Se, relative to birds from the Pacific. Neither nest initiation date nor mid-incubation body mass, however, were related to contaminant concentrations in blood. We found no differences in clutch size or nest success between putative winter strata. Our study detected carry-over effects in the Saskatchewan population that merit further attention.

Surfbirds (Calidris virgata) face increasing disease threats during their alpine breeding season. From 2019-2021, we monitored 67 nests in the Wrangell Mountains, Alaska, assessing avian influenza exposure through serological testing and measuring nest survival via daily nest checks. Infected individuals (23.9% prevalence, n=16) exhibited 42% lower nest success (95% CI: 31-53%; p=0.008) and 29% reduced chick survival to fledging (p=0.03) compared to seronegative birds. These findings highlight acute disease impacts on reproductive fitness, necessitating enhanced pathogen surveillance in high-elevation shorebird nesting habitats.

<jats:p>Why do conservation policies fail to prevent species extinctions and die-offs in contravention of stated intentions and goals? Bringing together a range of literature, including political ecology, political theory, conservation science, communication theory, environmental communication, with original data, this article explores this question, then addresses these failures within Aotearoa New Zealand's context. Using the New Zealand case, it offers a systems-level view of these failures, focusing on the influences and limitations that arise from the political-economic structures, fractured governance, interest group influence, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in representative democracies. Secondly, in these settings, we argue that communication and framing by the interested parties—politicians, government officials, interest groups and NGOs—buttress this system, partly by normalizing it, obscuring scientific realities, shifting focus away from deeper issues, and thus limiting the possibility of substantive solutions in what might be called a colonization of consciousness. Together, this economic-political-communication complex has failed to prevent—and in some ways aided—mass die-offs of native animal species. The article then suggests exploring alternative models, such as deliberative democracy, to this seemingly intractable problem, to strengthen the influence of scientific expertise, better inform decision-makers, advance public understandings of science, and improve democracy by engaging members of the public in decision-making processes. While this study focuses on New Zealand, the issues related to political ecology, the political-economic systems, and the framing of issues, apply to many democratic countries.</jats:p>

This study quantified energy expenditure in Black Skimmers (Rynchops niger) during chick-rearing using doubly labeled water techniques. We found that adults increased daily energy expenditure by 38% compared to pre-breeding levels, primarily driven by nocturnal foraging activity. Habitat degradation from coastal development significantly elevated foraging costs, with birds in disturbed sites expending 22% more energy than those in protected estuaries. These results highlight the vulnerability of this species to anthropogenic habitat alterations and underscore the need for conservation measures targeting foraging grounds.

We investigated the impact of wetland fragmentation on American Coot (Fulica americana) community assembly in prairie pothole ecosystems. Using occupancy modeling across 42 wetlands, we assessed how habitat patch size and connectivity influence coot density and interspecific interactions with other waterbirds. Results indicate fragmentation significantly reduces coot abundance (β = -0.78, p<0 01) and alters guild composition, particularly affecting competition with Pied-billed Grebes. Conservation should prioritize maintaining wetland complexes.

We investigated habitat selection and temporal patterns of stopover site use by Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) during fall migration along the Atlantic Coast. Using radio-telemetry (n=38 individuals), we quantified residence time and space use in high marsh habitats. Results indicated disproportionate use of Spartina patens-dominated zones compared to Distichlis spicata areas (p<0·01). Rail density correlated negatively with tidal height (r=-0·73) but positively with fiddler crab density (Uca spp.) (r=0·81). Our findings demonstrate that coastal development threatens critical stopover resources for this species.

Introduction: Stilt Sandpiper (Calidris himantopus) vocal behavior may be disrupted by wetland drainage, compromising breeding communication. Methods: We recorded 1,850 territorial calls during 2019-2021 breeding seasons across 12 drained and 12 intact prairie wetlands in Manitoba, Canada, analyzing frequency modulation and call intervals using spectrogram cross-correlation. Results: Drained sites showed 32% fewer contact calls/hour (χ²=7.84, p=0.005, 95% CI: 21-43%), 18% higher peak frequencies (t=2.91, p=0.008), and longer inter-call intervals (Δx̄=0.85s, p<0.001). Conclusion: Acoustic alterations indicate drainage-induced communication impairment, necessitating wetland connectivity conservation for reproductive success.

<jats:p>This paper reports the mitogenome of Potamon fluviatile collected from the Maltese islands, representing the first such study on species from the subfamily Potaminae. The mitogenome was analysed through next-generation sequencing and annotated. The genome was found to contain 37 genes that include 13 protein coding genes, 22 tRNA genes, two rRNA genes and a non-coding region. The gene order was compared to that of other Potamidae species, while protein coding and rRNA genes were used to evaluate the phylogenetic position of Potamon with other species of freshwater crabs. This study contributes to the genetic resources available for the genus Potamon.</jats:p>

This study investigates the impact of Spartina alterniflora management on Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) population dynamics in tidal marshes of Chesapeake Bay. Using mark-recapture techniques from 2018–2021, we demonstrate that controlled burns conducted during fall migration reduce overwinter survival by 37% compared to unmanaged sites (p<0 .01). Vegetation density metrics derived from LiDAR correlated strongly with nest success rates. Our findings highlight the need for seasonally-adjusted wetland management strategies to conserve this secretive marsh bird facing habitat degradation.

This study examines Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nest-site selection along coastal estuaries in relation to anthropogenic disturbance gradients. Using GPS tracking of 22 breeding pairs and habitat modeling, we quantified avoidance of high-development zones and preference for undisturbed islands with tall snags. Results indicate significant negative correlations between nest density and shoreline modification intensity (R²=0.78, p<0.001), highlighting vulnerability to coastal urbanization. Management implications emphasize protecting riparian buffers to maintain breeding habitat for this apex piscivore.

We measured daily energy expenditure in Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) using doubly labeled water techniques across coastal habitats with varying anthropogenic disturbance. Results indicated 22.3% higher energy costs in high-disturbance zones (recreational boating, shoreline development), correlating with increased flight frequency and reduced dive success. This elevated metabolic demand may impair winter survival in degraded estuaries, highlighting vulnerability to coastal habitat modification beyond direct predation impacts.

We examined how recreational kite flying affects Black-tailed Godwit (Limosa limosa islandica) demography in Iceland's Suðurlands region (2018-2021). Using mark-resight analysis of 322 individuals and nest monitoring of 187 clutches, we found higher adult mortality rates near kite zones (hazard ratio=1.73; 95% CI:1 39-2 16 p<0 001) and 22 6% lower nest success (p=0 007) compared to control sites Multistate modeling indicates this disturbance may reduce local population growth rate by 17 2% annually highlighting the need for buffer zones around key breeding wetlands

This study investigated mercury accumulation in Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) nesting in industrial harbor colonies. Using atomic absorption spectroscopy on blood samples from 50 adults and egg contents, we found significantly elevated mercury concentrations (mean: 4.7 ppm ± 0 0.9 SD in eggs) compared to reference sites (<0.5 ppm). Heavy metal burdens correlated negatively with chick survival rates (r = -0.72, p<0 001), indicating pollution-mediated impacts on this coastal-feeding larid population.

A basic aim of ecology is to understand the determinants of organismal distribution, the niche concept and species distribution models providing key frameworks to approach the problem. As temperature is one of the most important factors affecting species distribution, the estimation of thermal limits is crucially important for inferring range constraints. It is expectable that thermal physiology data derived from laboratory experiments and species' occurrences may express different aspects of the species' niche. However, there is no study systematically testing this prediction in a given taxonomic group while controlling by potential phylogenetic inertia. We estimate the thermal niches of twelve Palaearctic diving beetles species using physiological data derived from experimental analyses in order to examine the extent to which these coincided with those estimated from distribution models based on observed occurrences. We found that thermal niche estimates derived from both approaches lack general congruence, and these results were similar before and after controlling by phylogeny. The congruence between potential distributions obtained from the two different procedures was also explored, and we found again that the percentage of agreement were not very high (∼60%). We confirm that both thermal niche estimates derived from geographical and physiological data are likely to misrepresent the true range of climatic variation that these diving beetles are able to tolerate, and so these procedures could be considered as incomplete but complementary estimations of an inaccessible reality.

We investigated the impact of simulated oil exposure on Black-bellied Plover (Pluvialis squatarola) breeding success in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta, Alaska, USA (2018-2020). Using experimental nests (n=120) treated with weathered crude oil at sublethal concentrations (0-50 ppm), we monitored clutch survival and chick growth. Oil-treated nests showed 42% lower hatching success (95% CI: -58% to -26%, p=0.003) and 31% reduced fledging rates (p=0.01) compared to controls. Chick mass at 14 days was significantly lower in exposed groups (mean difference: -4.2g, SE=1.1, p<0.001). These results demonstrate acute vulnerability during early breeding stages, highlighting the need for preemptive oil spill mitigation in key Arctic breeding habitats.

This study quantified impacts of invasive signal crayfish (Pacifastacus leniusculus) on mercury bioaccumulation in Common Sandpipers (Actitis hypoleucos) along the River Tweed, UK (2019-2021). We analyzed mercury concentrations in blood plasma (n=52 adults) and crayfish tissue via ICP-MS, while monitoring foraging behavior. Sandpipers in invaded reaches exhibited 42% higher mercury levels (mean 3.2 μg/g ±0.4 SE) versus controls (2.25 μg/g ±0.3; p=0.017), with diet analysis confirming crayfish constituted 38% of prey intake. Crayfish-mediated mercury transfer reduced fledging success by 28% in contaminated territories (logistic regression: OR=0.54, 95% CI 0.31-0.77), highlighting synergistic threats from biological invasions and pollution.

We investigated habitat selection in American Coots (Fulica americana) across freshwater wetlands of the Upper Mississippi River Basin using GPS telemetry and resource selection functions. Our analysis revealed strong avoidance of turbid water bodies (β = -1.82, p<0.001) and significant preference for submerged aquatic vegetation cover exceeding 40% (β = 3.15, p<0.01). Coot occupancy declined by 67% in sites experiencing shoreline development, highlighting vulnerability to littoral zone fragmentation. These findings emphasize the need for wetland management prioritizing macrophyte conservation to mitigate impacts of agricultural runoff and urbanization.

This study investigated habitat selection patterns of Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) in freshwater wetland complexes of the Pacific Northwest. Using GPS telemetry and resource selection functions, we assessed how herons prioritize nesting sites relative to hydrological features, forest structure, and anthropogenic disturbance. Results indicate strong selection for mature riparian forests with minimal human activity, while avoiding areas near roads and development. Habitat loss from urbanization emerged as the primary threat to colony persistence, with climate-induced hydrological changes posing secondary risks. Management implications emphasize protecting intact floodplain corridors.

This study investigated the impacts of coastal wetland degradation on Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) parental care behavior in the Chesapeake Bay. Using nest camera monitoring (n=42 broods) and behavioral observation, we quantified time budgets during brood-rearing across disturbed and undisturbed marshes. Significant reductions in maternal vigilance (p<0.***) and increased foraging time (p=0.021) were documented in fragmented habitats compared to intact sites. Human recreational disturbance mediated habitat effects, reducing brood attendance by 37% at high-traffic sites.

We investigated how tidal marsh habitat fragmentation influences the foraging ecology of Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) in Chesapeake Bay. Using radio-telemetry and behavioral observations across 15 fragmented sites, we documented reduced crab foraging efficiency (p<0.05) and increased terrestrial invertebrate consumption in degraded habitats. Rails exhibited 42% longer foraging bouts and expanded home ranges in fragmented areas, indicating significant energetic costs from coastal wetland degradation.

This study examines the impact of invasive Argentine ants (Linepithema humile) on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) nesting success in California coastal wetlands. We monitored 42 nests across three colonies during the 2021 breeding season, quantifying ant densities and chick mortality rates. Results indicate a significant negative correlation (r = -0.78, p<0.001) between ant abundance and fledging success, with ant predation accounting for 67% of chick mortality in high-infestation zones. Management implications include targeted ant suppression during critical nesting periods to protect this declining Ardeid species.

This study examines the impact of beachfront recreational disturbances on fledgling survival in Least Terns (Sternula antillarum). Using radio-telemetry across 25 coastal nesting sites in the Southeast USA, we tracked 142 chicks for 14 days post-fledging. Survival rates decreased by 32% in high-human-traffic zones compared to protected areas (p<0***001). Predation by domestic dogs and vehicular collisions constituted 78% of mortalities. Our findings underscore the need for seasonal beach closures during critical fledgling periods to conserve this species.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Hepatitis A is a vaccine-preventable disease with a global distribution. It predominantly occurs in regions with inadequate living conditions, but also affects populations in industrialised countries. Children are frequently involved in the transmission of hepatitis A virus (HAV) and thus play a central role in the epidemiology of hepatitis A. Here, we investigated HAV infections, immunisations, and associated demographic determinants in a nationwide, population-based, cross-sectional survey conducted in Germany from 2003–2006. Out of 17,640 children and adolescents, complete data sets (HAV serology, demographic information and vaccination card) were available for 12,249 (69%), all aged 3–17 years. We found protective antibody levels (>=20 IU/L) in 1,755 (14%) individuals, 1,395 (11%) were vaccinated against hepatitis A, 360 (3%) individuals were HAV seropositive without prior hepatitis A vaccination, thus indicating a previous HAV infection. Antibody prevalence (attributable to vaccination or infection) increased significantly with age. Multivariate logistic regression revealed that predominantly children and adolescents with migration background–even if they were born in Germany–are affected by HAV infections. Our results provide a rationale to emphasise existing vaccination recommendations and, moreover, to consider additional groups with a higher risk of infection for targeted vaccination, especially children with a migration background.</jats:p>

This study quantified behavioral responses of Brant geese (Branta bernicla) to recreational coastal disturbance during winter staging. Using focal observations and telemetry at 8 estuaries, we documented significantly reduced foraging time (38 ± 7%, p<0.001) and increased energetic costs in high-traffic zones compared to controls. Flight initiation distances positively correlated with pedestrian density (r²=0.76), indicating chronic disturbance compromises premigratory fattening. Management recommendations include seasonal buffer zones.

This study investigates the impacts of invasive water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) foraging ecology in freshwater wetlands. Through systematic observational surveys and GPS tracking across 12 sites, we documented significant reductions in prey capture rates (p<0.001) and altered habitat selection patterns in densely invaded areas. Analysis of 143 regurgitated pellets revealed dietary shifts toward terrestrial prey species. Results demonstrate how invasive macrophyte proliferation disrupts critical foraging behaviors, suggesting targeted management interventions are needed for heron conservation.

This study employed microsatellite analysis to assess genetic diversity and population structure of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across the Atlantic coast. Results revealed significant genetic differentiation among colonies, with reduced heterozygosity in populations near industrialized estuaries. Contaminant-induced selection pressure and habitat fragmentation appear to drive genetic erosion, highlighting conservation priorities for this piscivorous seabird facing anthropogenic threats.

We evaluated energy expenditure in coastal-wintering Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) using doubly labeled water and GPS telemetry. Individuals in degraded salt marsh habitats exhibited 27% higher daily energy expenditure than those in intact wetlands, primarily due to increased foraging effort and reduced food availability. Elevated energy costs correlated strongly with anthropogenic habitat fragmentation, suggesting that coastal development imposes significant metabolic constraints on wintering dabbling duck populations.

We evaluated the impact of oil spills on Pectoral Sandpiper (Calidris melanotos) population dynamics using individual-based models parameterized by field data from the Colville River Delta, Alaska (2017-2022). Survival probabilities were calculated from 286 banded juveniles and 412 tracked adults via GPS telemetry. Simulations revealed a 31.4% decline in adult annual survival (95% CI: 28.7-34.1%; p<0.001) and 44.2% reduction in juvenile recruitment (CI: 39.5-48.9%; p<0.001) under moderate spill scenarios. These results demonstrate critical vulnerability during pre-migratory staging, necessitating expanded spill-response buffers around key Arctic estuaries.

We investigated trophic shifts in Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) populations facing invasive mongoose (Herpestes javanicus) predation pressure in Trinidad's Nariva Swamp (10°22'N, 61°03'W) using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of feather samples (n=47) collected 2018-2020. Jacanas exhibited significantly lower δ15N values (-1.7‰ ± 0.4 SE) in predator-impacted zones versus control areas (p=0.008), indicating reduced aquatic prey consumption. Nest monitoring revealed 62% lower fledging success in high-predation sectors (χ2=9.31, df=1, p=0.002). Results demonstrate predator-induced niche contraction and highlight the need for invasive species control in wetland conservation.

This study investigated the foraging behavior of American Coots (Fulica americana) in response to seasonal water-level fluctuations in managed wetlands. Using focal-animal sampling across three winter seasons, we quantified time budgets and habitat selection relative to submerged aquatic vegetation availability. Results indicate coots significantly increased diving effort during low-water periods (β = 0.78, SE = 0.12, p < 0.001), shifting from surface feeding to benthic foraging. Habitat loss due to drought conditions reduced preferred foraging areas by 63%, forcing coots into suboptimal habitats with higher predation risk. Management should prioritize maintaining stable water levels during critical winter months to support this ecologically important waterbird species.

<jats:p> The mechanism of cytokinesis has been difficult to define because of the short duration and the temporal-spatial dynamics involved in the formation, activation, force production, and disappearance of the cleavage furrow. We have investigated the structural and chemical dynamics of myosin II in living Swiss 3T3 cells from prometaphase through the separation and migration of daughter cells. The structural and chemical dynamics of myosin II have been defined using the semiautomated, multimode light microscope, together with a fluorescent analogue of myosin II and a fluorescent biosensor of myosin II regulatory light chain (RLC) phosphorylation at serine 19. The correlation of image data from live cells using different modes of light microscopy allowed interpretations not possible from single-mode investigations. Myosin II transported toward the equatorial plane from adjacent regions, forming three-dimensional fibers that spanned the volume of the equator during anaphase and telophase. A global phosphorylation of myosin II at serine 19 of the RLC was initiated at anaphase when cortical myosin II transport started. The phosphorylation of myosin II remained high near the equatorial plane through telophase and into cytokinesis, whereas the phosphorylation of myosin II at serine 19 of the RLC decreased at the poles. The timing and pattern of phosphorylation was the same as the shortening of myosin II-based fibers in the cleavage furrow. Myosin II-based fibers shortened and transported out of the cleavage furrow into the tails of the two daughter cells late in cytokinesis. The patterns of myosin II transport, phosphorylation, and shortening of fibers in the migrating daughter cells were similar to that previously defined for cells migrating in a wound in vitro. The temporal-spatial patterns and dynamics of myosin II transport, phosphorylation at serine 19 of the RLC, and the shortening and disappearance of myosin II-based fibers support the proposal that a combination of the cortical flow hypothesis and the solation-contraction coupling hypothesis explain key aspects of cytokinesis and polarized cell locomotion. </jats:p>

Stable isotope analysis of Great Egret (Ardea alba) feathers revealed significant spatial variation in foraging habitats across coastal and inland regions. Carbon (δ13C), nitrogen (δ15N), and sulfur (δ34S isotopes indicated differential reliance on marine vs freshwater food webs. Individuals in estuarine zones exhibited enriched δ13C values linked to marine prey consumption, while inland populations showed depleted signatures consistent with freshwater resource utilization. Anthropogenic nutrient pollution was implicated in elevated δ15N levels across all sampled colonies, suggesting widespread ecosystem contamination. This methodology effectively traced nutrient pathways and habitat connectivity for this non-charadriiform wader.

We quantified Willet (Tringa semipalmata) energy expenditure responses to unleashed dog disturbance at Padre Island National Seashore, Texas (2018-2020). Using accelerometer-logging GPS tags (n=22 adults), we measured daily energy expenditure (DEE) across disturbance gradients. Willets in high-disturbance zones exhibited 18.7% higher DEE (mean ± SE: 142.3 ± 4.1 kJ/d vs. 119.8 ± 3.2 kJ/d; p=0.003) and 32% reduced foraging efficiency. Elevated vigilance behavior accounted for 67% of the DEE increase. Conservation efforts must prioritize leash enforcement in critical foraging habitats to mitigate sublethal fitness costs.

Habitat fragmentation in freshwater wetlands threatens avian communities. We examined Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) occupancy and community co-occurrence in fragmented marshes using acoustic monitoring and multiseason occupancy models. Results indicate reduced rail detection (ψ = 0.42±0.07) and altered species interactions in isolated patches, demonstrating how agricultural encroachment disrupts marsh-obligate bird assemblages. Conservation requires maintaining wetland connectivity to buffer edge effects.

We investigated Western Sandpiper (Calidris mauri) stopover ecology at Bahía de Santa María, Sinaloa, Mexico (23°54'N, 106°57'W) during spring migration 2021-2022. Using automated radio-telemetry (n=47 birds), we quantified time-activity budgets and displacement distances in response to experimental kite-flying disturbances. Sandpipers exhibited 68% reduction in foraging time (95% CI: 54-79%) and fled >300 m during kite events (p<0.001). Population modeling indicated that sustained disturbance could increase migration duration by 3.7 days (SE=0.8), elevating mortality risk. Conservation measures should prioritize regulating kite activities at critical stopover sites.

We investigated Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) population dynamics in Chesapeake Bay marshes using mark-recapture and nest monitoring from 2015-2020. Despite tidal marsh restoration efforts, annual survival declined significantly (β = -0.17, SE=0.04) with increasing coastal development intensity. Nest success correlated positively with Spartina patens coverage (r=0.63) but showed threshold effects at <30% vegetation density. Our demographic models indicate habitat fragmentation exacerbates climate-driven flooding mortality, necessitating targeted management of marsh microtopography.

We examined habitat selection of Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) in freshwater marsh ecosystems using radio-telemetry and GIS analysis. Over three breeding seasons (2018-2020), we assessed nest-site preferences relative to water depth, vegetation density, and human disturbance. Terns showed significant selection for emergent vegetation islands (mean selection ratio = 3.7, SE±0.4) but avoided areas within 200m of boat access points. Hydrological fluctuations caused by climate change reduced optimal nesting habitat by 42% during drought years. Conservation strategies must prioritize maintaining stable water regimes and minimizing recreational disturbance to protect this marsh-obligate species.

We investigated energy expenditure in Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) during chick-rearing at coastal colonies using doubly labeled water. Results showed significant increases in daily energy expenditure (DEE) associated with anthropogenic disturbance from recreational beach activities. Gulls exposed to high disturbance exhibited 27% higher DEE than those in protected areas, potentially impacting reproductive success through reduced provisioning rates. This study highlights the energetic costs of human-wildlife conflict for non-shorebird seabirds.

We investigated molt migration ecology of Western Sandpiper (Calidris mauri) in relation to bycatch mortality risks during autumn staging in coastal British Columbia, Canada. Using miniaturized GPS loggers (n=42 birds tracked over 2019-2021), we quantified stopover duration and site fidelity at Roberts Bank and Boundary Bay. Individuals molting flight feathers exhibited 32% longer stopovers (mean=18.7±2.1 days vs. 13.2±1.8 days; p=0.003) and 2.4-fold higher overlap with shrimp trawl fisheries (95% CI: 1.7-3.3) compared to post-molt migrants. Population modeling indicated that a 10% increase in bycatch mortality could reduce annual survival by 17% (λ=0.83) for molting cohorts. Conservation priorities should focus on spatiotemporal fishery closures during peak molt (August-September) at key stopover sites.

Our study assessed Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) behavioral responses to beach nourishment operations along the James Bay coastline (Ontario, Canada; 2018-2020) using GPS telemetry. We tracked 37 adults with solar-powered tags (nanoFix® GEO), recording locations every 30 min during stopover (mean duration: 14 d ± 2 SE). Godwits utilizing nourished beaches exhibited 42% fewer foraging bouts/hr (p = 0 03; CI: -1.8 to -0.56) and 27% greater daily movement distances (mean ± SE: 3.2 km ± 0.4 vs 2.3 km ± 0 3; p = 0 01). These shifts correlated with reduced pre-migratory mass gain (r = -0.67  p < 0 001). Conservation planning must mitigate nourishment impacts on critical stopover sites by implementing temporal restrictions during peak godwit occupancy.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>BACKGROUND</jats:title><jats:p>Natural products present an environmentally attractive alternative to synthetic pesticides which have been implicated in the off‐target effect. Currently, the assessment of pesticide toxicity on soil microorganisms relies on the OECD 216 N transformation assay (OECD stands for the Organisation Economic Co‐operation and Development, which is a key international standard‐setting organisation). We tested the hypotheses that (i) the OECD 216 assay fails to identify unacceptable effects of pesticides on soil microbiota compared to more advanced molecular and standardized tests, and (ii) the natural products tested (dihydrochalcone, isoflavone, aliphatic phenol, and spinosad) are less toxic to soil microbiota compared to a synthetic pesticide compound (3,5‐dichloraniline). We determined the following in three different soils: (i) ammonium (NH<jats:sub>4</jats:sub><jats:sup>+</jats:sup>) and nitrate (NO<jats:sub>3</jats:sub><jats:sup>−</jats:sup>) soil concentrations, as dictated by the OECD 216 test, and (ii) the abundance of phylogenetically (bacteria and fungi) and functionally distinct microbial groups [ammonia‐oxidizing archaea (AOA) and bacteria (AOB)] using quantitative polymerase chain reaction (q‐PCR).</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>RESULTS</jats:title><jats:p>All pesticides tested exhibited limited persistence, with spinosad demonstrating the highest persistence. None of the pesticides tested showed clear dose‐dependent effects on NH<jats:sub>4</jats:sub><jats:sup>+</jats:sup> and NO<jats:sub>3</jats:sub><jats:sup>−</jats:sup> levels and the observed effects were <25% of the control, suggesting no unacceptable impacts on soil microorganisms. In contrast, q‐PCR measurements revealed (i) distinct negative effects on the abundance of total bacteria and fungi, which were though limited to one of the studied soils, and (ii) a significant reduction in the abundance of both AOA and AOB across soils. This reduction was attributed to both natural products and 3,5‐dichloraniline.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>CONCLUSION</jats:title><jats:p>Our findings strongly advocate for a revision of the current regulatory framework regarding the toxicity of pesticides to soil microbiota, which should integrate advanced and well‐standardized tools. © 2024 The Authors. <jats:italic>Pest Management Science</jats:italic> published by John Wiley & Sons Ltd on behalf of Society of Chemical Industry.</jats:p></jats:sec>

Quantifying morphological variation in Red Phalaropes (Phalaropus fulicarius) is crucial for predicting vulnerability to sea level rise along the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta (Alaska). We measured bill length (n=143 birds), tarsus height (n=143), and wing chord (n=143) using digital calipers during the 2019-2021 breeding seasons. Phalaropes exhibited significantly shorter tarsus height in low-elevation tidal flats (x̄=24.3mm ± 0.7SD) compared to upland tundra habitats (x̄=26.lmm ± 0.SD; t-test p=0.Ol). Subpopulations with reduced tarsus length showed 37% lower nest survival (GLMM OR=0.l3; 95% CI O.04-O.48) when exposed to spring tidal inundation events exacerbated by sea level rise (RCP 4.5 projections). Conservation strategies must prioritize habitat heterogeneity to maintain morphological diversity buffers against flooding impacts.

Abstract
            
              Effective soil‐protection policies should be based on a sound understanding of individual land‐use decisions in order to change it towards more sustainable decisions. This paper argues for the modification of the behavioural model of ‘
              Homo economicus
              ’ by explicitly allowing for cognitive limits and non‐reflective modes of behaviour in addition to situational utility‐maximizing behaviour. These modifications take into account actual difficulties in changing individual land‐use decisions. While it is possible to adjust behaviour by moral persuasion, consensus‐oriented round‐tables or planning processes, such approaches are unlikely to bring about effective changes in land‐use decisions without changing relative prices. This paper suggests ways to implement a special land‐use tax as a reform model for existing property taxes. Such a land‐use tax applies different rates according to ecological damage. Accordingly, surfaces covered by buildings will pay higher tax rates than free space. Conventional agriculture will pay more than forest areas, and nature reserve areas will be free of charge. Such a land‐use tax, designed as a revenue‐neutral alternative to Germany's property tax, could trigger modest changes in land‐use behaviour in the near future. A general reform of local fiscal relations could increase this effect in the long run. Copyright © 2005 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

We investigated heavy metal contamination and disease prevalence in Common Snipe (Gallinago gallinago) populations across agricultural wetlands in Poland's Biebrza National Park (2018-2021). Using liver tissue analysis (n=142) and PCR screening for avian influenza viruses, we found cadmium concentrations exceeding EU thresholds in 67% of samples (mean±SD: 3.2±0.9 µg/g dw) and a significant association with viral seropositivity (OR=4.1, 95% CI: 1.8-9.3). Our results demonstrate pollution-mediated immunosuppression as a key pathway for disease susceptibility in this cryptic shorebird, urging integrated wetland management to mitigate anthropogenic threats.

We investigated migration timing and stopover ecology of Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis) in the Great Lakes region using GPS telemetry. Tracking data from 35 individuals revealed prolonged stopovers at agricultural sites where birds exploited waste grain. Migration routes showed high plasticity with individuals adjusting paths annually based on crop harvest schedules. This behavioral flexibility highlights how synanthropic species capitalize on anthropogenic landscapes during migration, though reliance on ephemeral food sources may increase vulnerability to agricultural policy changes.

This study examines the demographic consequences of wetland degradation on Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) populations in the Mid-Atlantic region. Using 15 years of nest census data from 23 colonies, we documented a 38% decline in breeding pairs associated with marsh drainage and urbanization. Capture-recapture modeling revealed reduced adult survival (φ = 0.76 ± 0.04 SE) and fledging success (1.2 ± 0.3 chicks/nest) in disturbed habitats compared to protected sites. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of wading bird metapopulations to anthropogenic habitat alteration.

This study evaluated hepatic mercury (Hg) contamination in Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) populations across northeastern U.S. salt marshes. Tissue analysis of 45 individuals revealed significantly elevated Hg concentrations (mean: 7.2 μg/g dw) near industrial effluent sites compared to reference locations (1.8 μg/g dw). Regression models indicated strong correlation (R²=0.82) between sediment methylmercury levels and avian bioaccumulation. Our findings suggest chronic Hg exposure may impair renal function in this secretive rail species, warranting revised wetland management protocols to mitigate non-point source pollution impacts.

Abstract Unlike many othe
r mammals, bats in temperate regions employ short bouts of torpor throughout the reproductive period to maintain a positive energy balance. In addition to decreasing energy expenditure during the day, they typically alter foraging patterns as well. It is well known that various environmental conditions influence both torpor and foraging patterns, but studies of these factors often have focussed on one element in isolation thus it is not known how the two behaviours are collectively influencing temperate bats. The objective of our study was to assess how reproductive condition and environmental factors concurrently affect energy balance in female big brown bats ( Eptesicus fuscus ). We equipped pregnant and lactating bats in southwest Saskatchewan, Canada with temperature-sensitive radio-transmitters. While transmitters were active, skin temperature data were collected and foraging patterns were determined using triangulation. Of the various environmental and physiological parameters used to model torpor characteristics, roost type was the most important factor. Bats roosting in trees used deeper and longer torpor bouts than those roosting in buildings. Lactating bats had a tendency to forage for longer durations than pregnant bats, and often made more foraging trips. When taken together, we found that foraging duration and torpor duration were not directly related during pregnancy, but exhibited an inverse relationship during lactation. This provides support for the hypothesis that there are physiological trade-offs for reproductive bats and suggests that how bats compensate is not entirely predictable based on current environmental conditions.

Impacts of increased storm frequency on Long-billed Curlew (Numenius americanus): A community ecology approach along the Texas Gulf Coast. Using a generalized linear mixed-effects modeling framework, we analyzed nest survival (2018-2022, n=207 nests) in relation to storm disturbance metrics quantified via NOAA meteorological data at Laguna Atascosa National Wildlife Refuge (26.1°N, 97.3°W). Daily nest survival decreased by 19.2% ± 3 SE per additional storm event within 50 km during incubation (β = -0 211, p = 0 007). Brood-rearing habitat fidelity declined significantly with cumulative precipitation anomalies (W = 1028, p = 0 023). Results indicate storm intensification disproportionately impacts long-term recruitment in this keystone shorebird species.

<jats:p>In this paper, the subsurface flow wetland sewage treatment mathematical model is studied. the analytical solution is obtained by using the Laplace transform technique for non-steady subsurface flow wetland model and the diffusion characteristics for some parameters used in the model are analyzed. Then the solution for the model which is added by the source is obtained on two boundary conditions by the adomian decomposition method. The examples are given compare the approximate solution and the exact solutions.</jats:p>

We investigated Kentish Plover (Charadrius alexandrinus) breeding habitat selection in response to altered precipitation regimes at the Ebro Delta, Spain (2018-2021). Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=42) and nest monitoring (n=127 nests), we quantified microhabitat variables and hydrological conditions. Nest-site selection was significantly influenced by precipitation-driven water levels (β = -0.87, SE=0.21, p<0.001), with a 32% decline in nest success during drought years compared to average precipitation (95% CI: -45% to -19%). Our results demonstrate that projected decreases in Mediterranean precipitation will exacerbate habitat degradation for this declining shorebird, necessitating adaptive water management in coastal wetlands.

This study examines habitat selection patterns of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) in coastal wetlands of the Great Lakes region. Using GPS telemetry and resource selection functions, we analyzed nesting site preferences relative to water depth, vegetation structure, and human disturbance gradients. Results indicate strong avoidance of developed shorelines and preference for islands with dense shrub cover. Cormorant colony establishment was negatively associated with recreational boating activity, suggesting anthropogenic factors significantly influence habitat suitability for this piscivorous waterbird.
Quantifying stopover ecology of non-breeding Wandering Tattlers (Tringa incana) amidst anthropogenic nutrient loading concerns is critical for Pacific Flyway conservation.

We studied the effect of the ectomycorrhizal (ECM) fungus Scleroderma bermudense on growth, photosynthesis and transpiration rates, chlorophyll fluorescence and content, K/Na and Ca/Na homeostasis, and water status of two provenances of Coccoloba uvifera L. (named also seagrape) seedlings exposed to four levels of salinity (0.0, 54.7, 164.1 and 273.5 mM NaCl equivalent to 0.02, 5, 15 and 25 dS m−1, respectively). The results indicated that S. bermudense improved the salt tolerance in seagrape seedlings. There were no differences in terms of growth performance, nutritional and physiological functions between the two ECM seagrape provenances in response to salt stress. The reduction of the Na concentration and the increase of K and Ca favored a higher K/Na and Ca/Na ratio, respectively, in the tissues of the ECM seedlings. Furthermore, the beneficial effects of ECM symbiosis on the photosynthetic and transpiration rates, chlorophyll fluorescence and content, stomatal conductance and water status resulted in the improved growth performance of the seagrape provenances exposed to salt stress. From an ecological point of view, seagrape in symbiosis with S. bermudense may be used in the development of ornamental plantings and coastal windbreaks along beaches and roadsides in Cuba.

We assessed Peruvian Thick-knee (Burhinus superciliaris) demographic vulnerability to oil spills along Peru's central coast (11°S-15°S) using 2018-2022 mark-recapture data (n=127 adults). Stage-structured matrix models incorporating oil exposure scenarios predicted a 42% decline in λ (population growth rate) under moderate spill conditions (95% CI: 0.38-0.46). Breeding propensity decreased by 28% in contaminated sites versus controls (χ²=7.2, p=0.007), with juveniles exhibiting higher mortality (HR=2.4, p<0.001). Results indicate acute sensitivity to hydrocarbon contamination, necessitating preemptive protection of key foraging habitats near Talara refineries.

Bioacoustic monitoring of Western Sandpiper (Calidris mauri) nesting colonies in the Copper River Delta, Alaska (2018-2021) revealed distinct parental alarm call signatures during egg collection events. Using automated recorders at 42 nests, we documented 137 human intrusion events, correlating call frequency shifts (mean increase: 8.2 kHz ±1.3 SE) with proximity to nests (r = -0.78, p<0.001). Nest abandonment probability increased 3.7-fold (95% CI: 2.1-6.5) when alarm vocalizations exceeded baseline by >5 kHz. Results demonstrate acoustic signatures as early-warning indicators for targeted conservation patrols in vulnerable shorebird breeding habitats.

We assessed vehicle disturbance impacts on Least Sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) stopover ecology at Padre Island National Seashore, Texas, 2021-2023. Using GPS loggers (n=38) and behavioral observation (1,200 scans), we quantified space-use overlap with off-road vehicle corridors. Sandpipers exhibited 28% lower foraging efficiency within 100m of vehicle transects (p=0.007; CI: -37% to -19%) and abandoned 42% of core high-tide roosts following traffic events. These findings underscore the urgency for temporal traffic closures during peak migration (Aug-Oct) to protect critical stopover function.

We investigated intraspecific morphological variation in Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) populations along the Atlantic Flyway coastal wetlands. Using geometric morphometrics on 287 specimens from 7 estuaries, we quantified bill and skull shape divergence. Principal component analysis revealed significant latitudinal clines correlated with wintering latitude, suggesting phenotypic plasticity in response to salinity gradients and prey availability. Coastal populations exhibited 15% narrower bills than inland counterparts, supporting hypotheses of local adaptation to marine-derived diets.

This study evaluated anthropogenic disturbance impacts on Double-crested Cormorant (Nannopterum auritum) nesting colonies in freshwater ecosystems. Using behavioral observations and nest monitoring at 22 sites, we found significant negative correlations between human recreational activities (boating proximity ≤100m) and breeding success (R²=0.78, p<0.01). Disturbance-induced vigilance behavior reduced parental provisioning rates by 37%, decreasing fledging mass. Management recommendations include establishing seasonal buffer zones during critical nesting periods to mitigate fitness consequences.
