Immature 12-week-old pullets, maintained on equalized food intakes, were treated intramuscularly with either oestradiol dipropionate, testosterone propionate or a combined hormone treatment. 2. 2. The hormone treatments had no effect on the apparent retention of dietary linoleic acid which was utilized with an efficiency of 85 per cent. 3. 3. The percentage fatty acid patterns of blood lipids from gonadal hormone-treated pullets were similar to those reported previously for liver lipids. 4. 4. Testosterone had no effect on blood fatty acid levels but significant increases in these fatty acids occurred under oestrogen treatment. 5. 5. The blood linoleate content of the oestrogen-treated birds was increased about five times that in control birds. The results indicate that the increased blood linoleate observed in birds coming into lay is due to the action of oestrogenic hormones.

We investigated habitat selection of Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) breeding colonies in relation to coastal development pressures. Using GPS telemetry and GIS-based resource selection functions (n=42 adults), we quantified avoidance of urbanized shorelines and preference for undeveloped barrier islands. Pelicans showed significant selection for sites with minimal human disturbance (β = -1.24, SE=0.31, p<0.001), demonstrating sensitivity to anthropogenic encroachment. Nesting success decreased by 37% within 1km of marinas, highlighting critical conservation needs for undisturbed coastal habitats amid rapid shoreline modification.

<jats:p> A freshwater sport fishery that targets hundreds of geographically isolated stocks is simulated by combining a model of angler behavior with a model of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) population dynamics. Ideal free distribution (IFD) theory, which suggests that angling quality will be similar on all lakes, is used to drive angler effort distribution. Model parameters are based on creel survey data from 53 lakes and empirical relationships between growth, survival, and density derived from whole-lake density manipulations on nine lakes over a period of 10 years. We compared angling quality, population density, fish size, and yield under unfished conditions, harvest rates that maximize sustained yields (MSY), and an IFD equilibrium driven by angler behavior. The IFD equilibrium rarely maximized yields. Stocks with high MSY angling quality are overexploited at the IFD equilibrium because anglers move to take advantage of exceptional angling opportunities. These stocks would often be viewed as more resistant to harvest pressure because they have higher stock productivities and habitat capacities. However, in our model, they are systematically overharvested because their high fish density attracts excessive angling pressure. Conversely, stocks with low MSY angling quality are underexploited because anglers move to take advantage of better angling quality on other lakes. </jats:p>

Abstract Puerto Madryn city (Chubut province, Argentina) has strongly increased its population since 1970, but a lack of coastal management strategies has favored physical changes in the natural landscape. This situation has led to a deficit in sediment supply sources, which increases beach erosion susceptibility. This paper aims to evaluate beach erosion susceptibility through the use of geo-indicators. It also provides a susceptibility map based on geomorphological evidence and the weighting of physical geo-indicators. The final objective is to propose soft solutions that consider a comprehensive coastal management. The main anthropogenic disturbances identified were beach cleaning with bulldozer, coastal armoring, removal of dune fields (about 90% between 1942 and 2019), foredune segmentation, installation of resorts on backshore, and artificial rainfall drains towards the beach. The natural and most sensitive geo-indicators affected by human pressure—and thus the most useful for determining susceptibility—were foredune conservation and width, and backshore width. We estimate a high to moderate susceptibility to beach erosion along the coast of Puerto Madryn. As regards management policies, we propose mainly restoration, prevention, and adaptation strategies, such as the use of sand fences and new techniques for beach cleaning, all of which are aimed at promoting sedimentary balance within the dune-beach system. Besides these procedures, we recommend the consideration of preventive actions, such as a future-oriented urban planning and a program to raise popular awareness of coastal problems. The diagnostic approach based on a geo-indicator survey has provided a useful tool to help decision-making in coastal conservation initiatives. Graphical abstract

Summary I describe an artificial patch system that was used to study the foraging behavior of free-roaming downy woodpeckers ( Picoides pubescens ) in a woodlot in southeastern Michigan. The artificial “patches” used were thin logs into which were drilled small holes to hold food items (bits of sunflower seed kernels). Downy woodpeckers would systematically search the holes of a patch for food items and thus by manipulating the food distribution within the patches, the birds could be made to experience differing rates of energy intake while foraging. Simple deterministic theories of optimal foraging in patchy environments indicate that an optimal forager, who experiences a decreasing rate of energy intake while foraging in a patch, should leave a patch when its rate of energy intake falls below the average intake rate for the overall environment. In other words, an optimal forager is continually assessing the quality of a patch and makes decisions as to when to leave a patch via its energy intake rate. When the downy woodpeckers studied could encounter any one of several types of patches each with differing, decreasing rates of energy intake, they followed a patch quality assessment strategy similar to that suggested by theory. Upon encountering a single type of patch for a number of consecutive days, however, the birds appeared to forage according to prior expectations of patch quality and not according to a quality assessment strategy based on energy intake rates. The observed expectations were not related to the number of food items per patch but they appeared to be based on expectations of when or where to leave a patch.

We investigated winter habitat selection by Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) in coastal marsh ecosystems using GPS telemetry (n=38) and compositional analysis. Pintails exhibited strong avoidance of degraded wetlands affected by agricultural runoff (β = -1.87, p<0.01) and prioritized intact tidal freshwater marshes. Sea-level rise has reduced optimal habitat by 28% since 2000, increasing dependence on fragmented reserves. Restoring natural hydrology is critical given climate-driven saltwater intrusion threatening these non-Charadriiformes waterfowl.

This study examines behavioral responses of American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) to recreational boating disturbance in Chesapeake Bay tidal marshes. Using focal-animal sampling and GPS tracking, we quantified flight initiation distances and habitat abandonment rates across disturbance gradients. Results indicate significant reductions in foraging time (p<0.001) and increased energetic costs during weekends with high vessel traffic. Our findings highlight the need for temporal zoning of recreational activities to minimize impacts on this declining waterfowl species.

This study examines mercury contamination in Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) populations across Chesapeake Bay wetlands. We analyzed eggshell thickness and mercury concentrations in feathers from 120 individuals across six breeding colonies. Results show significant correlations between feather mercury levels and reduced hatching success (r = -0.78, p<0.001), with urban-adjacent colonies exhibiting 34% higher contamination than protected sites. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this tern species to bioaccumulative pollutants despite wetland conservation efforts, suggesting need for stricter industrial discharge regulations.

We investigated habitat selection responses of Semipalmated Sandpipers (Calidris pusilla) to photographer disturbance during fall migration at Johnson's Mills, New Brunswick (2018-2020). Using GPS-tracked movements of 48 individuals and 142 documented disturbance events, we quantified avoidance behavior in intertidal zones. Sandpipers reduced mudflat utilization by 34% (95% CI: 27-41%; p<0.001) when disturbance exceeded 4 events/hour, shifting to lower-quality upper beach habitats. These findings indicate that unregulated photography displaces shorebirds from optimal foraging areas, necessitating spatial zoning strategies during critical refueling periods.

This study investigates nest-site selection in American Coots (Fulica americana) within freshwater marshes. By quantifying microhabitat variables (water depth, vegetation density, distance to open water) at 56 nest sites and paired random locations during 2018-2020, we identified avoidance of deep water zones (t-test, p<0·001) and preference for dense emergent vegetation (logistic regression, β=2·5, p<0·001). Sympatric Virginia Rail nests did not influence coot nest placement. Results suggest that hydrological management degrading shallow-water habitats may threaten coot reproductive success.

This study examines climate change impacts on American Coot (Fulica americana) populations in prairie pothole wetlands. Using 30 years of breeding survey data, we analyzed correlations between hydrological variability, temperature anomalies, and coot reproductive success. Results indicate significant declines in brood size (β = -0.24, p<0.001) associated with earlier spring thaw dates and increased frequency of summer droughts. Adaptive management strategies for wetland conservation are discussed to mitigate climate-driven habitat degradation for this declining waterbird species.

We examined the impacts of coastal marsh degradation on Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) reproductive success through nest monitoring (n=67) across 3 breeding seasons. Nest survival modeling revealed significant negative effects of tidal flooding frequency (β = -0.92, p<0.001) and invasive Spartina spread on hatching rates. Hydrological alterations reduced fledging success by 38% in fragmented habitats. Results demonstrate urgent conservation needs for this saltmarsh-obligate species facing climate-driven habitat loss.

Coastal populations of Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans), a salt marsh specialist, face significant threats from climate change-induced sea-level rise and habitat fragmentation. We utilized 12 years of mark-recapture data across six Mid-Atlantic estuaries to model population viability under future inundation scenarios. Results show a 42% projected decline in adult survival by 2050 (p<0.001), driven by nest flooding events and reduced foraging habitat quality. Conservation must prioritize marsh elevation restoration to buffer against accelerating tidal encroachment in critical rail habitats.

Marbled Godwits (Limosa fedoa) face heightened energetic demands from non-native predator avoidance behaviors. We quantified energy expenditure using accelerometry (n=28 birds) and GPS tracking during stopovers at Cheyenne Bottoms, Kansas (2019-2021). Individuals in red fox (Vulpes vulpes) impacted zones exhibited 27% higher daily energy expenditure (p=0.003, 95% CI:19-35%) and 33% reduced foraging efficiency compared to control areas. This resulted in significantly lower pre-migration body condition (mean mass deficit: 18.2g, p<0.001). Our results demonstrate that introduced predators impose substantial indirect energetic costs, compromising refueling efficiency at critical staging sites with implications for Pacific Flyway conservation strategies.

We assessed first-year survival of Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) ducklings in coastal Labrador using VHF telemetry (n=58) from 2018-2020. Juvenile survival probability was 0.28 ± 0.05 SE, significantly lower than adults. Primary mortality drivers included parasitic infection prevalence (linked to warming waters) and habitat fragmentation from aquaculture expansion. Findings highlight climate-mediated disease threats to early-life stages in this keystone sea duck species.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics between American Coots (Fulica americana) and Northern Pike (Esox lucius) in freshwater marshes of the Upper Mississippi River floodplain. Using radio telemetry and nest monitoring, we quantified predation rates on coot eggs and chicks during the 2020-2021 breeding seasons. Results showed pike predation accounted for 37% of nest failures, with higher vulnerability in fragmented wetland habitats. Our findings highlight how hydrological alterations exacerbate predation pressure on this declining rallid species, emphasizing the need for integrated aquatic-terrestrial conservation strategies.

We investigated the effects of tidal amplitude on daily energy expenditure (DEE) in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) within Chesapeake Bay salt marshes using doubly labeled water techniques. Individuals (n=22) exhibited significantly higher DEE during spring tides (mean ± SE: 145.3 ± 8.7 kJ/d) compared to neap tides (112.4 ± 6.2 kJ/d; p<0.01), indicating tidal cycles impose substantial metabolic costs. Increased foraging effort during high water periods accounted for 78% of this variation. Our results demonstrate how sea-level rise may exacerbate energy budgets for this declining marsh specialist through heightened inundation frequency.

This study investigates climate-driven shifts in breeding chronology of Laughing Gulls (Leucophaeus atricilla) along the Gulf Coast. Using 21 years of nest monitoring data from 18 colonies in Louisiana and Texas, we demonstrate significant advancement in mean egg-laying date by 0.52 days/year (p<0 01). Phenological change correlated with spring sea-surface temperature anomalies (r= -0 78). Results suggest altered prey synchrony may reduce chick survival, underscoring non-linear vulnerabilities in coastal larids. Modeling indicates thermal thresholds may exceed adaptive capacity under RCP8.5 by 2070.

This study examines the foraging efficiency of Black Skimmers (Rynchops niger) in relation to tidal cycles and prey availability in estuarine habitats of the Mid-Atlantic coast. Using focal observations and prey sampling, we documented significant reductions in foraging success during periods of low prey density, exacerbated by coastal development altering sediment transport. Results indicate that habitat degradation poses a greater threat to skimmer populations than previously recognized, with implications for conservation management in anthropogenically modified estuaries.

We investigated the impacts of wind disturbance and vegetation loss on Double-crested Cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus)'s breeding biology in Great Lakes colonies. Using nest monitoring data from 2018-2022 (n=312 nests), we found that reduced tree canopy cover correlated with increased chick mortality (β=-0.**, p<0.**) and decreased clutch sizes (rs=-0.***, p<0.**). Breeding phenology advanced during high-wind events. Results highlight vulnerability to habitat degradation in coastal nesting sites.

We investigated thermal constraints on predator-prey dynamics of Ruddy Turnstone (Arenaria interpres) breeding in the Canadian High Arctic (Cornwallis Island, Nunavut; 74°43'N, 94°58'W). During June-July 2019-2021, we monitored 42 nests using temperature loggers and camera traps, quantifying predation events relative to ambient temperature. Daily predation risk increased by 1.8% per °C above 5°C (95% CI: 1.2-2.4%, p=0.003), with Arctic foxes (Vulpes lagopus) accounting for 78% of nest losses during warm spells (>8°C). These findings highlight climate-driven phenological mismatches exacerbating predation pressure on this declining shorebird species.

We investigated population dynamics of Black Skimmers (Rynchops niger) along the Gulf Coast from 2015-2020. Using mark-recapture and nest monitoring, we found significant declines in breeding pairs (-18.7% annually) correlated with coastal erosion and recreational disturbance. Climate change-induced sea-level rise submerged 32% of nesting sites. Our results highlight urgent conservation needs for this non-shorebird species facing compounded anthropogenic threats.

We investigated nest site selection in Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) across coastal wetlands in the Mississippi Flyway. Using logistic regression models, we assessed habitat variables influencing nest placement relative to flooding risk and predator avoidance. Key predictors included vegetation density (β=0.87, p<0.001), distance to open water (β=-0.42, p=0.03), and human disturbance proximity (β=-0.65, p=0.01). Results indicate trade-offs between hydrologic safety and predation pressure drive nesting decisions, with implications for wetland management under climate change scenarios.

A new enantiornithine bird, Intiornis inexpectatus gen. et sp. nov, is described here. It is based on a partial hind limb found in beds of the Upper Cretaceous Las Curtiembres Formation (Campanian), North-West Argentina. The new taxon is referred to the family Avisauridae on the basis of its cranially convex third metatarsal. Several features suggest close relationships between Intiornis and the avisaurid Soroavisaurus, from the Lecho Formation (Maastrichtian; North-West Argentina). Intiornis was the size of a sparrow, thus representing the smallest Enantiornithes known from South America. The new species shows adaptations for a perching mode of life. Moreover, the hypothesis suggesting that the flying pterosaur reptiles decrease in taxonomic diversity due to competitive interaction with birds is discussed. This study examined anthropogenic influences on Great Egret (Ardea alba) habitat selection in freshwater wetlands using GPS telemetry (n=27) across three breeding seasons. Resource selection functions revealed significant avoidance of urbanized shorelines (β = -1.87, p<0.001) and preferential use of undisturbed emergent marshes with intermediate water depths. Agricultural drainage reduced suitable foraging habitat by 38%, while nest abandonment increased significantly near boat traffic. Conservation strategies must address hydrological alteration and recreational disturbance to maintain viable breeding populations.

We investigated trophic niche partitioning and fisheries bycatch risk in Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) wintering along the Gulf Coast, USA, using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of feather samples (n=78) from 2018-2020. Bayesian mixing models revealed distinct isotopic signatures between birds from Louisiana (mean δ15N=9.2‰±0.8) and Texas (δ15N=7.1‰±0.6, p<0.001), indicating differential exploitation of marine vs. estuarine prey. Individuals with marine isotopic signatures exhibited 2.3× higher entanglement risk in gillnets (95% CI:1.4-3.8) based on spatial overlap modeling. Results highlight regional bycatch vulnerability linked to foraging ecology, informing targeted bycatch mitigation strategies.

Invasive Argentine ants (Linepithema humile) disrupt trophic interactions affecting Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor), an important wading bird species in coastal wetlands. This study (2020-2022 across 12 Gulf Coast colonies) quantified arthropod prey availability and chick provisioning rates. Results demonstrated reduced aquatic insect diversity (Shannon index p<0·01), forcing herons to shift diet to less profitable fish prey. Breeding success declined 22% in invaded sites compared to controls (GLMM β=-0·38±0·09 SE), implicating competitive exclusion through resource depression as a novel mechanism impacting Ardeidae populations.

We investigated morphological variation in Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) across three coastal habitats in relation to anthropogenic pressures. Using multivariate morphometrics (n=152 adults), we assessed correlations between wing chord, culmen length and tarsus dimensions with urbanization gradients and pollution biomarkers. Principal component analysis revealed significant differentiation associated with contaminated sites, suggesting plastic responses to environmental stressors distinct from genetic adaptations observed in other Laridae.

Constructed wetlands, have been used to decrease nitrogen transport from agricultural catchments to the coast of Sweden, while simultaneously contributing to increased species richness in the landscape. The purpose of this paper is to compile and evaluate data that have been produced in Sweden during some 20 years of using constructed wetlands as an environmental tool. To evaluate effects of different stated objectives for constructed wetlands within different national support systems we focus on nitrogen removal and bird and amphibian species richness. Continuous automatic water sampling for nitrogen removal measurements, during 1.5 to 10 years, has been performed in 7 constructed wetlands located in agricultural catchments in southern Sweden. Nitrogen removal per wetland area varied between wetlands but the results imply that an annual removal of at least 1000kgN per ha wetland area can be achieved in individual wetlands. Data from the long-term monitoring of the 7 wetlands, together with nitrogen removal data in the literature, were used to model >150 randomly selected constructed wetlands. According to the modeling, the nitrogen removal per created wetland area varied markedly between different wetland creation programs and was generally considerably lower compared to what can be achieved in individual wetlands. Cost-efficiency of nitrogen removal in wetland creation programs can be increased considerably with improved planning and if other desired benefits (e.g. species richness) contribute to share the costs for wetland creation. The effects of constructed wetlands in Sweden on species number and populations of wetland birds and amphibians were large enough to positively affect the occurrence of species in the national red list, i.e. on a national population level. Species richness of wetland breeding birds in the constructed wetlands were relatively stable after 13 years, but different functional groups had very different succession pattern. The mean maximum breeding bird species number in the wetlands occurred after 3.8 years. Wetland birds and amphibians colonized constructed wetlands irrespective of the original objective of the wetland (nitrogen removal or biodiversity). However, some amphibian species showed preference for biodiversity wetlands. There were clear effects of wetland construction on the regional populations of non-wetland bird species. The maximum species number for a given wetland size was found to be higher than previously reported. The analyses show that wetland construction can be a cost effective method for decreasing transport of diffuse pollution from arable land, and that the wetlands are important for the species numbers and population sizes on all spatial scales.

This study investigates the population genetic structure and gene flow patterns of Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) colonies across the Gulf of Mexico using microsatellite markers. We analyzed 12 loci from 186 individuals at 7 breeding sites to assess connectivity and effective population sizes. Results indicate moderate genetic differentiation (FST = 0.08) with isolation-by-distance effects, suggesting limited dispersal capabilities. Habitat fragmentation and wetland loss appear to restrict gene flow, highlighting conservation priorities for maintaining metapopulation resilience in this declining wading bird species.

This study investigates climate change impacts on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola), a secretive wetland rail species. Using 20 years of marsh-level data from 12 Mid-Atlantic sites with water level loggers and occupancy modeling, we demonstrate significant declines in breeding probability (β = -0.72, p < 0.) as hydrological regimes shift. Increased frequency of marsh inundation events reduced habitat suitability, with projected sea-level rise exacerbating these effects. Conservation efforts must prioritize marsh elevation management to mitigate climate vulnerability for this non-Charadriiform marsh obligate.

This study investigates morphological variation in the Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) across its North American range using geometric morphometrics. We analyzed 214 specimens from museum collections, measuring bill length, wing chord, and tarsus dimensions. Results indicate significant clinal variation correlated with latitude: southern populations exhibit shorter wings and deeper bills compared to northern counterparts via ANOVA and PCA. These adaptations suggest thermal ecology influences on plumage and body size, diverging from coastal habitat pressures. Climate change may exacerbate these gradients by altering thermoregulatory demands.

This study examines the impact of invasive Burmese python (Python bivittatus) predation on Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) nesting success in the Florida Everglades. Through systematic nest monitoring and camera trapping across three breeding seasons (2019-2021), we documented significant python-induced clutch failure (χ²=15.3, p<0.001), correlating with python detection frequency near colonies. Habitat fragmentation exacerbated predation rates, highlighting cascading effects of invasive species on ardeid population dynamics in anthropogenically altered wetlands.

This paper examines Pectoral Sandpiper (Calidris melanotos) habitat selection along the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta under increased storm frequency. Using GPS telemetry (n=47 adults, 2018-2020) and nest monitoring, we quantified how spring storm timing affects coastal tundra occupancy. Probability of high-quality habitat selection declined 23% (95% CI: 17-29%) when storms occurred within 5 days of arrival (p=0.008). This mismatch reduced average clutch size by 1.2 eggs (p<0·001), suggesting storm-driven phenological shifts may compromise subarctic breeding success. Conservation planning must buffer critical early-spring staging wetlands.

This study assessed anthropogenic disturbance impacts on Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) reproductive success in estuarine colonies. Through behavioral observations and nest monitoring (n=52) in Florida, we documented that recreational boating within 150m increased nest abandonment by 47% (p<0.001) and reduced fledgling weights by 22% (p=0.003). Our results demonstrate that motorized watercraft proximity disrupts parental provisioning more significantly than avian predators. Management recommendations include establishing 200m seasonal buffer zones around critical rookeries.

Non-shorebird avian research: Investigating thermoregulatory costs in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans), marsh specialists with high vulnerability to coastal temperature fluctuations. Using doubly labeled water techniques, we measured daily energy expenditure in 28 wild individuals across tidal marsh gradients. Results indicate a 23.7% increase in metabolic rate during summer heatwaves compared to temperate periods (p < 0O1), suggesting climate-induced energetic stress may impact population resilience in southeastern US salt marshes.

This study investigates the impacts of coastal eutrophication and human disturbance on breeding success in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima) across three Baltic Sea archipelagos. Using nest monitoring and GPS tracking of 42 females (2019-2021), we found elevated nitrogen levels correlated with reduced duckling survival (R²=0·37, p<0·01), while recreational boating frequency predicted nest abandonment (OR=4·2). Results highlight habitat degradation as a greater threat than direct harvest for this keystone sea duck species.

This study examines Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia) nesting success in managed wetland complexes of the Pacific Northwest. Using mark-recapture and nest monitoring techniques from 2018-2021, we quantified impacts of water level fluctuations and invasive plant encroachment on chick survival rates. Results indicate artificial drawdown schedules disrupt prey availability, reducing fledging success by 37% compared to natural hydrology sites. Management recommendations emphasize restoring dynamic water regimes to support tern foraging ecology.

Background
Biological invasions have become the focus of considerable concern and ecological research, yet the relative importance of abiotic and biotic factors in controlling the invasibility of habitats to exotic species is not well understood. Spartina species are highly invasive plants in coastal wetlands; however, studies on the factors that control the success or failure of Spartina invasions across multiple habitat types are rare and inconclusive.


Methodology and Principal Findings
We examined the roles of physical stress and plant interactions in mediating the establishment of the smooth cordgrass, Spartina alterniflora, in a variety of coastal habitats in northern China. Field transplant experiments showed that cordgrass can invade mudflats and low estuarine marshes with low salinity and frequent flooding, but cannot survive in salt marshes and high estuarine marshes with hypersaline soils and infrequent flooding. The dominant native plant Suaeda salsa had neither competitive nor facilitative effects on cordgrass. A common garden experiment revealed that cordgrass performed significantly better when flooded every other day than when flooded weekly. These results suggest that physical stress rather than plant interactions limits cordgrass invasions in northern China.


Conclusions and Significance
We conclude that Spartina invasions are likely to be constrained to tidal flats and low estuarine marshes in the Yellow River Delta. Due to harsh physical conditions, salt marshes and high estuarine marshes are unlikely to be invaded. These findings have implications for understanding Spartina invasions in northern China and on other coasts with similar biotic and abiotic environments.

The Herring Gull (Larus argentatus) demonstrates remarkable behavioral plasticity during migration. This study analyzes GPS tracking data from 24 individuals across three flyways. We assess how thermals and urban light pollution alter nocturnal migration routes. Results indicate gulls bypass traditional stopover sites near coastal wetlands, favoring anthropogenic food sources which reduce energetic costs but increase contaminant exposure risks.

We investigated storm-mediated habitat selection in Double-striped Thick-knees (Burhinus bistriatus) within Costa Rica's Tempisque Basin (2019-2021). Using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults) coupled with hydrologic modeling of 17 storm events, we quantified nest-site elevation preferences. Post-tropical depression nests averaged 1.8m higher than pre-storm nests (95% CI: 1.2-2.4m; p<0.001), with low-elevation nests showing 38% lower survival during extreme rainfall (n=57 nests, χ²=11.3, p=0.001). Results demonstrate proactive microhabitat shifts that buffer climate impacts, highlighting topographically complex wetlands as critical refugia.

We investigated the spatial ecology of Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) populations in Chesapeake Bay marshes using GPS telemetry. Tracking 32 individuals over two breeding seasons revealed significant habitat selection for mid-marsh zones with dense Spartina alterniflora. Home ranges contracted during high tide events, forcing rails into fragmented upland patches. Our findings demonstrate how sea-level rise exacerbates habitat compression, increasing vulnerability to predation and human disturbance in this declining saltmarsh specialist.

We investigated nest site selection in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across freshwater marshes in the northeastern United States. Using logistic regression models, we assessed habitat variables influencing nest placement relative to microhabitat features and anthropogenic disturbance gradients. Results indicate preferential selection for dense emergent vegetation (Typha spp., Scirpus spp.) with avoidance of areas exhibiting elevated human recreational activity. Nest survival probability decreased significantly with proximity to trails (β = -0.87, SE = 0.21, p < 0.001), highlighting vulnerability to anthropogenic disturbance in critical wetland habitats.

This study investigates anthropogenic disturbance effects on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes) wintering behavior in northeastern coastal marshes. Through systematic focal observations and flight initiation distance trials (n=187 ducks across 12 sites), we quantified significant reductions in foraging efficiency (p<0.01) and increased vigilance (32% time budget) at boat-access locations. Ducks exhibited habitat abandonment at disturbance thresholds exceeding 5 events/hour, particularly impacting nocturnal feeding grounds. Results demonstrate urgent need for seasonal buffer zones in estuary management plans to mitigate energetic consequences in this declining waterfowl species.

The purpose of this study was to analyse the association between social determinants and the presence of essential hypertension in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients in one rural county (Jintan) of China. A health survey of Jintan residents was conducted in 2013, applying a cluster sampling method. Three hundred and fifty-seven type 2 diabetes mellitus patients were selected as research subjects. Among the patients selected, essential hypertension prevalence was 45.4% (n=162). After univariate analyses and logistic regression analyses, an association was observed between the presence of essential hypertension in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients and marital status, described as ‘others (unmarried, divorce, widower, etc.)’, and participating in active physical activity. Both of these two significant variables were positively associated with the higher prevalence of essential hypertension in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients. In conclusion, the patients suffering from type 2 diabetes mellitus combined with essential hypertension often reported an association with more negative social determinants (with the exception of participation in physical activity). Further strengthening the comprehensive multi-disease management to control and reduce the prevalence of essential hypertension in type 2 diabetes mellitus patients is required.

This study investigates the impact of hydrological regime alterations on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes), a coastal waterfowl species sensitive to changes in wetland habitat quality. We conducted systematic surveys across 37 managed marshes in the Mid-Atlantic region during wintering seasons 2018–2021. Using generalized linear mixed models, we analyzed relationships between inundation depth variability, vegetation composition, and duck abundance. Our results demonstrate that reduced hydroperiod consistency significantly decreases foraging habitat availability, with cascading effects on winter body condition. Management recommendations include maintaining optimal water depths (15–25 cm).

We investigated impacts of beach nourishment on American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) reproductive success on Sapelo Island, Georgia, USA (2019-2021). Using GPS-tracked nests (n=64) across nourished and natural beaches, we measured daily survival rates (DSR) via logistic exposure models. Nourished sites showed 27% lower nest success (DSR=0.934, 95% CI: 0.902-0.958) versus natural sites (DSR=0.971, CI: 0.954-0.982; p=0.003), with higher abandonment rates during machinery operations. Results indicate seasonal restrictions on nourishment are critical for this declining Charadriiforme's conservation along developed coastlines.

Climate-driven shifts in foraging behavior increase Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) susceptibility to bycatch mortality in the Wadden Sea. Using GPS telemetry (n=42 adults, 2018-2021) and fishery interaction surveys, we quantified spatiotemporal overlap with gillnet fisheries. Individuals exhibited 37% higher foraging effort in intertidal zones during warm anomalies (p=0.012), coinciding with peak fishing activity. Bycatch mortality estimates reached 4.2% annually (95% CI: 2.8-6.1%), potentially unsustainable for this declining population. Results highlight climate-mediated behavioral plasticity as an emerging threat multiplier requiring adaptive fisheries management.

The local density of a plant population can influence both the number of pollinators attracted and the behavior (and thus pollination efficiency) of those that are. I present the results of a field experiment performed on Brassica kaber, a self—incompatible annual crucifer, designed to test for the existence of density effects in pollination and to separate the two major component effects: reductions in the quantity and in the quality of pollinator services. B. kaber plants were grown in fan—shaped density arrays in six floral backgrounds chosen to manipulate pollinator foraging behavior. Pollinators visiting focal plants behaved as generalists in backgrounds of the similar—flowered Brassica hirta, behaved as floral specialists where no alternative floral resources were provided (three treatments), and displayed a mixture of behaviors in two background plantings where dissimilar flowers were available. Pollinator visitation rates to focal B. kaber plants declined sharply at low density in all backgrounds except the similar flower (B. hirta) treatment. Widely spaced plants displayed significantly reduced seed—set in all backgrounds studied. The most dramatic density effects occurred where pollinators were induced to behave as generalists, suggesting that density—related declines in pollinator quality are more important than parallel declines in the quantity of visits.

This study examines habitat selection patterns in Caspian Terns (Hydroprogne caspia) nesting in freshwater reservoirs of the Columbia River Basin. Using GPS tracking and nest site analysis, we quantified preferences for islands with sparse vegetation and minimal mammalian predator access. Results indicate tern populations are declining due to reservoir water level fluctuations disrupting nesting chronology, compounded by increasing recreational boating disturbance. Conservation strategies should prioritize stable water management and predator-free artificial nesting platforms to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this piscivorous species.

We investigated Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) population dynamics in freshwater marshes of the Great Lakes region from 2015-2020 using call-response surveys. Our study revealed significant declines in occupancy rates (β = -0.38 ± 0.12 SE) correlated with hydrological regime alterations (r = 0**.**73) and invasive Phragmites expansion (r = -0**.**68). Climate-induced water level fluctuations exacerbated habitat fragmentation effects, with recovery lagging in sites experiencing >30% marsh degradation. These findings underscore the vulnerability of secretive rallids to anthropogenic wetland modifications.

Molt migration ecology of Black-bellied Plovers (Pluvialis squatarola) remains poorly understood despite increasing pressures from habitat loss and competitive exclusion. We analyzed GPS-tracking data (n = 32 adults) and stable isotope (δ13C, δ15N; n = 98 feather samples) profiles from staging grounds in the Fraser River Estuary, British Columbia (2018-2021). Plovers exhibited significantly earlier molt migration phenology (Δ = 12.3 ± 2.1 days; p = 0 .008) when sympatric with increasing Dunlin densities. Modeling projected competitive exclusion from key molting habitats within 13 years (95%CI: 9 -18 years) under current disturbance regimes. Conservation must prioritize temporal partitioning of critical intertidal resources.

This study examines how coastal wetland degradation impacts American Black Duck (Anas rubripes), specifically focusing on breeding biology, including nest site selection and clutch viability. Through surveys from 2018 to 2020 across 12 sites, we found significant correlations between marsh fragmentation and reduced nest success, with habitat loss explaining 37% of variability in hatching rates.

We investigated stopover duration and habitat selection in Saltmarsh Sparrows (Ammospiza caudacuta) along the Atlantic Flyway. Using radio-telemetry and GIS analysis across 12 tidal marshes, we documented significant correlations between stopover length and Spartina density. Coastal development and sea-level rise reduced optimal habitat by 32%, forcing prolonged stays and higher energy expenditure. Results underscore urgent need for marsh conservation to support this declining passerine's migration.

We investigated avian influenza virus (AIV) transmission dynamics in Least Sandpipers (Calidris minutilla) within mixed-species assemblages at Padre Island, Texas (2019-2021). Using 312 cloacal swabs from 7 shorebird species tested via RT-PCR and behavioral observations, Least Sandpipers exhibited significantly higher AIV prevalence (21.7%, n=83) compared to co-occurring species (mean 8.3%; χ²=14.2, p<0.001). Infection probability increased with interspecific flock density (OR=3.1, 95% CI:1.8-5.4). Findings identify this species as potential AIV amplification hosts in coastal ecosystems, necessitating integrated surveillance during migratory stopovers.

This study investigates molt migration patterns in American Coots (Fulica americana) using GPS telemetry across the Great Lakes region. We tracked 32 individuals during post-breeding dispersal to assess how wetland degradation influences migration timing and stopover duration. Results indicate delayed departure (mean 11.2±3.4 days) and prolonged stopovers (18.7±6.1 days) in areas with >40% habitat loss, suggesting reduced foraging efficiency. Climate variables showed weaker effects than habitat quality. Conservation strategies should prioritize protecting interconnected wetland complexes to facilitate molt migration.

<jats:p> The influence of chemical and physical quality of litter on its rate of decomposition was examined by measuring mass loss from 19 diverse litter types, including leaves, needles, forbs, wood, and roots in the Kananaskis Valley of Alberta, Canada. Litter samples drawn from three adjacent forests of lodgepole pine, white spruce, and Engelmann spruce – subalpine fir, and from a small clearcut area, were allowed to decompose for 3 years at their sites of origin. The best predictors of mass loss were the initial concentrations of lignin and labile material in the litter. Adding N or P contents as a second term, rather than as a lignin to nutrient ratio, significantly improved mass loss predictions. There were abrupt limits for the influence of lignin (above 28%) and N (below C:N of 30:1); similar limits were observed for all predictors except labile content. None of these chemical parameters, nor a physical measure, particle diameter, were useful in predicting rates of decomposition of high-lignin, woody substrates. The relative importance of the various litter quality parameters in determining rates of mass loss in the clear-cut area was very similar to that in the forests, despite considerably more rapid decomposition in the clearcut. Key words: decomposition, lignin, litter, nutrients, Rocky Mountains, wood. </jats:p>

This study assessed the impacts of shoreline development and recreational disturbance on Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) breeding success across 22 Pacific Northwest colonies from 2016-2019. Using nest monitoring and disturbance gradient analysis, we found colony persistence decreased by 34% near high-human-activity zones. Generalized linear models indicated fledging success significantly declined with proximity to boat traffic (β = -0.27, p<0.001) and riparian vegetation loss (β = 0.18, p=0.01). Results demonstrate urgent need for buffer zones around heronries to mitigate anthropogenic pressures on breeding ecology.

We evaluated long-term demographic patterns in Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) breeding colonies across coastal Arctic Canada from 2010 to 2020 using capture-recapture models. Annual nest success (mean=74.1%, SE=3.2) showed significant decline correlated with sea ice retreat (r=-0.83, p<0  .001). Female survival probability (ϕ=0  .92±0.02  ) remained stable despite increasing vessel traffic, while local contaminant levels explained 38% of duckling mortality variance. Results indicate climate-driven habitat degradation poses greater threat than direct anthropogenic disturbance for this sea duck.

We investigated how increasing storm frequency alters foraging strategies of Black Turnstones (Arenaria melanocephala; n=42) in Alaska's Kachemak Bay using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of blood and feather samples collected 2019-2021. Turnstones exposed to >3 major storms annually exhibited significant δ13C depletion (-2.1‰ ±0.3SE) versus controls (p = 0·002), indicating expanded prey range. Consecutive storm years reduced winter survival by 18% (95% CI: 6–30%). Results suggest intensified storm regimes may necessitate adaptive foraging but increase overwinter mortality, informing shoreline hardening impact assessments.

We examined juvenile Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) bycatch mortality during fall migration in Delaware Bay salt marsh impoundments (2018-2021). Using radio-telemetry (n = 97 juveniles) and carcass surveys (n = 23 km² tidal grids), we quantified entanglement risks in aquaculture gear. Juveniles exhibited 28% higher bycatch susceptibility than adults (OR = 1.82, 95% CI [1.11-2 98]). Survival probability decreased 12% per net density unit increase (β = -0 128, p = 0 007). These findings necessitate modified gear deployment schedules and juvenile-specific exclusion zones to reduce conservation reliance.

We investigated Green Sandpiper (Tringa ochropus) alarm call responses to introduced American mink (Neovison vison) predation risk in riparian habitats of the Oder River floodplain, Poland (2018-2020). Using automated recording units (n=32 stations), we captured 1,240 alarm vocalizations across 42 territories during 560 survey nights. Playback experiments demonstrated significantly higher call rates (mean increase: 3.2 calls/min ± 0.8 SE; p=0.003) and frequency shifts (+412 Hz ± 89; p<0.001) when mink scent was present. Territories with elevated alarm responses showed 27% higher fledging success (95% CI: 14-39%) despite predation pressure. Results indicate bioacoustic monitoring effectively quantifies anti-predator behavior, informing targeted mink control to enhance sandpiper conservation.

This study examines how managed wetland hydrological regimes affect American Coot (Fulica americana) reproductive success in prairie pothole ecosystems. Through systematic nest monitoring (n=187 nests) across three seasons, we quantified relationships between water-level manipulation timing, emergent vegetation density, and daily nest survival rates. Results indicate nest flooding risk increased by 73% during abrupt drawdown events (β = -1.84, p<0.001), while vegetation coverage above 60% significantly improved hatching success (OR=2.3). Findings underscore trade-offs in wetland management practices for maintaining viable coot populations.

The study of non-human animals’ communication systems generally relies on the transcription of vocal sequences using a finite set of discrete units. This set is referred to as a vocal repertoire, which is specific to a species or a sub-group of a species. When conducted by human experts, the formal description of vocal repertoires can be laborious and/or biased. This motivates computerised assistance for this procedure, for which machine learning algorithms represent a good opportunity. Unsupervised clustering algorithms are suited for grouping close points together, provided a relevant representation. This paper therefore studies a new method for encoding vocalisations, allowing for automatic clustering to alleviate vocal repertoire characterisation. Borrowing from deep representation learning, we use a convolutional auto-encoder network to learn an abstract representation of vocalisations. We report on the quality of the learnt representation, as well as of state of the art methods, by quantifying their agreement with expert labelled vocalisation types from 8 datasets of other studies across 6 species (birds and marine mammals). With this benchmark, we demonstrate that using auto-encoders improves the relevance of vocalisation representation which serves repertoire characterisation using a very limited number of settings. We also publish a Python package for the bioacoustic community to train their own vocalisation auto-encoders or use a pretrained encoder to browse vocal repertoires and ease unit wise annotation.

We investigated the impact of recreational shell collection on Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) migration ecology along the Wadden Sea coast (Germany). Using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults, 2019-2021) and population modeling, we quantified foraging site fidelity and migration timing. Shell collection reduced prey availability by 38% (95% CI: 27-49%) at key stopovers, delaying southward migration by 7.2 days (p=0.003) and increasing mortality risk (OR=1.8, p=0.02). Conservation measures must prioritize shell harvest regulation at critical pre-migratory staging areas.

Coastal urbanization impacts Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) foraging ecology and associated fish communities. We quantified pelican dive success rates using drone observations across developed and undeveloped shorelines, concurrently sampling fish assemblages via seine nets. Results revealed 42% reduced foraging efficiency near marinas and seawalls, correlating with altered nearshore fish community structure and increased mesopredator abundance. These findings demonstrate how anthropogenic infrastructure disrupts pelican-mediated trophic cascades in coastal ecosystems.

The Bonnet Carré Spillway diverts floodwaters from the Mississippi River to Lake Pontchartrain, and was opened for 42 days during the 2011 flood. According to measurements of the newly deposited sediments, at least 31–46% of the river’s sand load was diverted into the spillway at this time, suggesting that such diversions can help mitigate coastal wetland loss.

We investigated Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) stopover ecology on Saemangeum tidal flats, South Korea (35°50′N 126°40′E), assessing nest trampling impacts by livestock during 2018–2021. Using 142 nests monitored via camera traps and GPS-loggers (n=38 adults), we quantified trampling frequency and breeding success. Daily trampling probability was 0.18 ± 0 03 (SE) in grazed areas versus 0 03 in controls (p=0.002). Clutch survival declined by 22% in high-traffic zones (95% CI: 17–28%, p<0 001). Results emphasize urgent fencing needs at critical stopover sites to mitigate non-predation mortality.

We investigated how landscape heterogeneity mediates exposure to avian influenza in Double-striped Thick-knees (Burhinus bistriatus) across Costa Rican cattle pastures (n = 28 individuals tracked via GPS telemetry over 14 months). Thick-knees foraging within 200m of water bodies (mean 68% of locations; CI:64-72%) showed 3.2 times higher viral RNA detection rates (qPCR on cloacal swabs) than those in drier areas (p = 0·01; R² = 0·42). This spatial overlap with waterfowl vectors explains 57% of seroconversion events. Conservation should prioritize buffer zones around agricultural wetlands to reduce spillover risk in this near-threatened species.

We examined morphological variation in Wilson's Plover (Charadrius wilsonia) across a precipitation gradient in the Gulf Coast barrier islands (Texas, USA) from 2018-2021. Using standardized measurements (n=142 adults) and stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁸O) of feathers, we tested associations between body size indices and historical rainfall anomalies. Larger tarsus length (β=0.24, SE=0.08, p=0.003) and bill depth (β=0.19, SE=0.06, p=0.002) correlated with increased drought frequency. Precipitation-driven phenotypic shifts may reduce foraging efficiency during extreme wet events, suggesting vulnerability to climate-mediated habitat changes.

Morphological variation in Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) was assessed across freshwater wetlands in the Great Plains. Using geometric morphometrics on 137 specimens from five breeding colonies, we quantified bill shape divergence relative to hydrological regimes. Populations in ephemeral playa lakes exhibited significantly shorter, deeper bills compared to permanent marsh counterparts, suggesting adaptive responses to prey availability shifts from fish to invertebrates. Salinity gradients accounted for 34% of observed cranial disparities. Findings indicate rapid phenotypic plasticity to hydrological modification, necessitating dynamic conservation frameworks beyond static habitat preservation.

1. The present study was conducted to investigate the effects of dietary glutamine (Gln) supplementation on growth performance, carcase characteristics and meat quality in broilers exposed to high ambient temperature. 2. A total of 240 35-d-old male Arbor Acres broilers were randomly assigned to 4 treatment groups (three replicates of 20 birds per cage). The broilers were kept in a temperature-controlled room at either 23°C (no-stress groups, NS) or 28°C (heat stress groups, HS). The broilers were fed either on a basal diet (control, NS) or on the basal diet supplemented with 0, 0·5 or 1·0% Gln (HS). 3. Compared with the NS, the HS (0% Gln) group gained less weight and consumed less feed, had lower final body weight, gain-to-feed ratio, and abdominal fat yield. Breast meat in HS (0% Gln) had lower pH, water-holding capacity (WHC), a∗ value, ether extract (EE) content and crude protein (CP) content, and had higher shear force (SF) and L∗ value. 4. Linear increase were found in groups supplemented with Gln (0, 0·5% and 1·0%) for final body weight, weight gain, feed consumption, gain-to-feed ratio and abdominal fat yield. Supplementation with Gln improved breast meat pH, WHC, SF, L∗ value, a∗ value, EE content and CP content in broilers exposed to heat stress. No significant difference was observed in all the indices determined between the HS (1% Gln) and the NS. 5. Heat stress caused obvious breast meat discoloration in L∗, a∗ and b∗ values. However, dietary supplementation with Gln gave a better colour stability. 6. The results indicated that dietary supplementation with Gln may alleviate heat stress-caused deterioration in growth performance, carcase characteristics, meat quality and meat colour stability of broilers.

We assessed how human recreational disturbance influences parasitic infection risk in Hudsonian Godwits (Limosa haemastica) at the Churchill, Manitoba stopover site (58°44′N, 94°3′W) during 2018-2021 migration seasons. Using fecal glucocorticoid metabolites (n=98) and parasite egg counts (n=215 samples), we quantified stress responses and trematode (Cyathocotyle spp.) prevalence across disturbance gradients. Godwits within 150m of frequent human activity showed 2.7× higher trematode prevalence (95% CI: 1.8-4.1; p<0.001) and 14% elevated corticosterone (F₁,₉₆=8.3, p=0.005). Results indicate disturbance-mediated immunosuppression increases infection susceptibility, necessitating buffer zones around critical staging habitats for this declining species.

This study quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) during the breeding season using doubly labeled water techniques. We tracked 15 adults nesting in urban wetlands affected by industrial runoff. Results showed DEE increased by 32% compared to rural populations, primarily due to extended foraging times compensating for reduced prey availability. Elevated mercury levels in blood samples correlated with higher metabolic rates, suggesting pollution-induced physiological stress exacerbates energy demands in contaminated habitats.

Climate warming alters thermoregulatory constraints for nestling Ospreys (Pandion haliaetus) in mid-Atlantic saltmarshes. We measured microclimate temperatures and nestling survival across 42 nests over three breeding seasons. Asynchronous hatching increased mortality during heatwaves (temperatures >33°C). Nestlings in exposed locations experienced 37% higher mortality than those in shaded microhabitats. Results highlight microsite selection as a critical adaptation under rising temperatures.

Anthropogenic disturbance impacts on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) were assessed in 18 freshwater marshes using acoustic monitoring and behavioral observation. Recreational trail proximity significantly reduced occupancy (ψ = 0.28 ± 0.11 near trails vs. ψ = 0.76 ± 0.09 in controls; p<0.01) and suppressed vocalization rates during peak breeding. Disturbance thresholds indicated >15 daily human visitors triggered prolonged parental absence from nests. Conservation strategies require buffer zones exceeding 200m to mitigate fitness consequences in fragmented habitats.

Mudflat reclamation threatens migratory shorebirds; we examined morphological responses in Red Knots (Calidris canutus) at Chongming Dongtan, China. From 2019-2022, we measured bill length, tarsus, and body mass in 127 adults across natural (n=64) and reclaimed (n=63) sites. Knots in reclaimed areas exhibited 5.8% shorter bills (t=3.42, df=125, p=0.001, 95% CI: 2.1-9.5%) and 7.3% lower body mass (p=0.007), but unchanged wing chord (p>0.05). This rapid phenotypic change suggests foraging constraints from sediment alteration, necessitating protection of natural intertidal zones for this declining subspecies.

This study examines climate change impacts on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nesting phenology and reproductive success in Chesapeake Bay estuaries. Using 15 years of nest monitoring data, we demonstrate significant advancement in egg-laying dates (mean 8.2 days earlier) correlated with spring temperature anomalies. Despite phenological shifts, nest productivity declined by 18% during drought years linked to reduced prey availability from warming-induced fish migrations. Results highlight climate-driven trophic mismatches threatening this coastal raptor, emphasizing the need for adaptive management beyond traditional habitat protections.

This study examines morphological variation in Double-crested Cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) populations across North America's Atlantic coast. We measured 12 skeletal characters from 243 museum specimens spanning 1890-2010. Statistical analyses revealed significant clinal variation in bill depth and tarsus length correlated with latitude, suggesting Bergmann's rule adaptation. Coastal habitat degradation appears to drive morphological shifts, with recent specimens showing reduced body size in anthropogenically disturbed estuaries. Findings highlight how anthropogenic pressures can alter avian morphology beyond plumage characteristics.

We investigated habitat partitioning among coastal marsh obligates in response to invasive Phragmites australis expansion along the Mid-Atlantic coast.
