Using GPS telemetry and underwater cameras, we analyzed 127 foraging bouts from 22 individuals. Results indicated significantly higher capture rates during ebb tides (mean: 0.67 fish/h) versus flood (0.41 fish/h; p<0\\.001), with turbidity exceeding 15 NTU reducing success by 38\%. This tidal dependency suggests vulnerability to altered hydrologic regimes from coastal development."}

This study examined the impacts of marine pollution on Purple Sandpipers (Calidris maritima), with particular focus on bycatch mortality in coastal fishing gear. From 2019-2021 in coastal Nova Scotia, Canada, we monitored 42 individuals (22 males, 20 females), with GPS loggers tracking movements and fishing gear interactions. Purple Sandpipers experienced a significant bycatch mortality rate (18.7% of tagged individuals annually; CI=11.2-26.3), correlated with proximity to crab trap lines (r=0.43, p<0 01). Conservation efforts should prioritize modifying crab fishing practices in key wintering habitats to reduce shorebird mortality.

This study assessed morphological variation in Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) populations across wetland habitats experiencing differing anthropogenic pressures. We measured skeletal dimensions (culmen, tarsus, wing chord) in 132 adults from 12 colonies. Statistical analyses revealed significant reductions in body size metrics at sites with higher urban development (p<0.01), correlating with diminished aquatic prey diversity. Results suggest phenotypic responses to habitat degradation may compromise flight efficiency and foraging success in this non-Charadriiformes wader, highlighting cascading impacts of wetland alteration on avian morphology.

This study examines Lesser Yellowlegs (Tringa flavipes) nest site selection in boreal peatlands of northeastern Alberta, Canada, where wetland drainage for oil sands development threatens reproductive success. From 2019-2021, we monitored 127 nests using temperature loggers and weekly surveys, quantifying hydrology (water depth, distance to open water) and vegetation characteristics at nest sites and random points. Nests in undrained wetlands (n=73) occurred in areas with 23.7±5.1 cm water depth vs 8.4±4.3 cm in drained zones (p<0·001). Nest survival probability was 1.9 times higher in undrained wetlands (β=1·21, 95% CI: 0·85-1·72). These results emphasize the critical link between hydrologic integrity and nesting habitat suitability; conservation policies must prioritize wetland protection to mitigate drainage impacts on this declining shorebird.

We investigated the impacts of nutrient pollution on Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) migration ecology using satellite telemetry in Delaware Bay, USA (2018-2021). We deployed 45 GPS transmitters on adults during spring staging to quantify stopover duration and foraging site fidelity in relation to nitrogen levels. Dowitchers in high-nitrogen sites (mean 3.2 mg/L) exhibited 28% longer stopovers (p=0.012) and 40% lower site fidelity (p=0.003) compared to reference sites (mean 0.8 mg/L). These behavioral shifts indicate nutrient-driven habitat degradation may disrupt migratory schedules, necessitating targeted wetland restoration to maintain connectivity.

<jats:p>On the basis of the analysis of the results of detailed palynological studies of Pleistocene deposits in Ukraine, the correlation between climatic changes and vegetation dynamics was retraced in the range of 1.8-0.43 million years. The curve of paleoclimate changes was constructed and analyzed. It was shown that certain climatic characteristics were inherent for each stage of the nature development, which was reflected in the composition of vegetation. It was found thattemperature and humidity fluctuations also occurred during each stage. The evidence of this is the reconstructed micro-rhythm in the development of vegetation of each stage. The main features of vegetation composition were determined for four warm and five cold stages of nature development, and a pattern of vegetation changes was retraced during each stage. The dynamics of vegetation cover of the Prydonetska Plain, different parts of the Prydniprovska Lowland, the Prydniprovska Upland, the Near Black Sea Lowland, and the Podil’ska Upland vegetation during the specified geological time was reconstructed. General and regional distinctions of the composition of vegetation cover were revealed, and the influence of the main climatic factors such as temperature and humidity on the character of its changes was retraced. The stages characterized by the warmest and wet climatic conditions and the most cold and dry ones were established. It was substantiated that the climatic conditions of the Sula period were less severe than in the subsequent stages of the fall of temperature. The existence of refugiums of thermophilic flora in the Sula period within separate regions of Ukraine was established. The existence of vegetation zonality was substantiated not only in warm stages, but also in cold periods of the Early Neopleistocene.</jats:p>

This study examines the effects of coastal wetland degradation on Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) nesting colonies in the Pacific Northwest. Using satellite imagery and field surveys (2015-2020), we quantified habitat loss and monitored 43 heronries. Results indicate a 32% decline in breeding pairs (p=0.004) directly correlated with marsh fragmentation. The analysis underscores wading birds' heightened vulnerability to anthropogenic coastal modifications, necessitating targeted conservation strategies distinct from shorebird management approaches.

We investigated Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) nesting success in managed wetlands along the Gulf Coast. Using nest monitoring and habitat surveys, we assessed how water level fluctuations influenced chick survival rates. Results indicate that artificial drawdowns during breeding season significantly reduce fledging success (β = -0.72, p<0.001), suggesting wetland management protocols require temporal adjustments to conserve this species.

We assessed anthropogenic noise impacts on American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) population dynamics along South Carolina's ACE Basin (2019-2021). Using continuous acoustic monitoring (n=15 sites) and mark-resight surveys (n=127 individuals), we modeled density-dependent recruitment under varying noise regimes. Chronic exposure (>60 dB) reduced chick survival by 28.7% (95% CI: -34.2% to -23.1%; p=0.002) and increased territory abandonment by 1.8-fold (OR=2.81; p<0.001). Our matrix projections indicate noise-mediated declines could destabilize regional metapopulations within 8 breeding cycles. These findings necessitate acoustic zoning in estuarine conservation planning.

<jats:title>Summary</jats:title><jats:p><jats:list list-type="explicit-label"><jats:list-item><jats:p>In fragmented landscapes where natural disturbance acts at the local level, community composition can be altered either by ‘species‐by‐species matching’, with community‐wide character displacement, or by ‘constrained species sorting’, whereby disturbance favours species with distinct ecological traits. It is necessary to understand such species shifts when aiming to detect bottlenecks associated with changing disturbance dynamics at different spatial levels. Such an understanding also provides insight into the underlying ecological mechanisms in operation and allows identification of species of conservation concern.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p>This approach to understanding species’ shifts was applied to a study of spider diversity and life‐history variation in relation to sand dynamics in stabilized and dynamic grey dune landscapes located along the coasts of France, Belgium and the Netherlands.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p>Local (α) diversity appeared to decrease with increasing local sand dynamics in both stable and dynamic landscapes. In dynamic dune landscapes, β‐diversity decreased significantly and approached regional (γ) diversity under local grey dune stabilization; in stabilized landscapes, β‐diversity was not affected by local sand dynamics.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p>Comparative analyses of ecological traits revealed shifts in life‐history patterns, suggesting that patterns in local diversity resulted from species sorting. Species from fragments characterized by high sand dynamics showed narrower niche breadths, larger body sizes and longer generation times, while summer‐active species tended to become residential after sand stabilization. This provides evidence for constrained species sorting in which natural disturbance (through local sand dynamics) allows only species with distinct ecological traits to persist.</jats:p></jats:list-item><jats:list-item><jats:p><jats:italic>Synthesis and applications</jats:italic>. Species with larger body sizes, longer generation times and a higher degree of habitat specialization (i.e. related to dispersal ability) would be expected to be more vulnerable at dynamic sites and more prone to extinction than their counterparts from stabilized fragments. In particular, species with a burrowing lifestyle would be expected to go extinct locally as a result of increasing soil development and soil hardness. Shifts in species composition were found to be more pronounced in dynamic landscapes. Hence ensuring conservation of sand dynamics at a landscape level rather than at a local level is of prime importance when aiming to conserve typical psammophilous spider species within local assemblages in grey dune habitats.</jats:p></jats:list-item></jats:list></jats:p>

This study examines Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) breeding ecology along Florida's Gulf Coast. We monitored nest success (~120 pairs over 2 seasons), evaluating impacts of beach habitat degradation from anthropogenic disturbance. Key metrics: clutch size (x̄=3 eggs), hatching success (68%), fledgling survival (52%). Regression analysis revealed human trampling and predation pressure (primarily by Corvus spp.) as significant predictors of nest failure (p<0). Using trail cameras, we documented behavioral responses to recreational beach use that correlated with reduced provisioning rates.

This study investigated how agricultural runoff-induced eutrophication affects foraging efficiency of American Coots (Fulica americana) in freshwater marshes. We conducted behavioral observations across 12 sites, quantifying prey capture rates and time-activity budgets. Results showed significant reductions (42%) in macroinvertebrate consumption and increased foraging time (28%) in eutrophic wetlands. Algal blooms obscured prey visibility and degraded preferred submerged vegetation, forcing dietary shifts toward less nutritious plant material. These alterations in foraging ecology may contribute to declining body condition indices observed in contaminated habitats.

We examined climate-driven shifts in migration phenology of Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) along the Pacific Flyway using 25 years of band-resighting data. Advanced spring arrival (β = -0.78 days/year, p<0.001) correlated with rising sea surface temperatures, while delayed fall departures increased exposure to coastal fisheries bycatch. Phenological asynchrony with prey resources suggests potential reproductive consequences, necessitating dynamic marine protected area management.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>Background
 Wind is an important driving factor influencing forest structure, ecology, and the carbon cycle in temperate and tropical regions. Damage from typhoons poses a significant threat to eucalyptus production in coastal regions of southeast China. However, few strategies have been used and account for key traits impact on wind damage/resistance of eucalyptus. To identify key factors affecting eucalyptus wind resistance, 20 <jats:italic>Eucalyptus camaldulensis</jats:italic> genotypes were selected, and wind damage indices and traits were measured and evaluated using correlation analysis and principal component analysis.
Results
 We identified a correlation between tree traits, wind damage indices, and the traits related to H, V, FP BT, FL, and FW. Five PCs from the above-mentioned traits were obtained and could represent the standing tree traits explained by PCA. PCs and tree-pulling variables were further used for typical correlation and path analyses. Canonical correlation analysis showed the top two canonical correlation coefficients were 0.9547 and 0.9012, respectively, while PC2 reflected that the growth traits were the main trait affecting pull tree variables. The PA-OV model and its modifications with PC functions and tree-pulling variables were introduced and developed for wind resistance estimation. The fitting effect of the two models and the observed data was good, with a P-value of 1.000, RMSEA of 0.000, and other goodness of fit indices over 0.9. Based on effects from model 2, PC4 had the greatest impact on tree-pulling variables. Therefore, our results implied that PC4, composed of holocellulose content, lignin, and fibre width, was the most important factor affecting standing tree stability under windy conditions.
Conclusion
 This study provides insights into forest management and planning in coastal typhoon prone areas. Determining the effect of wind on trees can expand our understanding of the factors that contribute to wind damage, thereby improving management practices.</jats:p>

We investigated nest site selection in American Avocets (Recurvirostra americana) relative to trematode infection risk at Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Utah (2019-2021). Nest characteristics and microhabitat variables were quantified at 83 nests, with parasite loads assessed via egg flotation of parental feces (n=166 adults). Nests in water >12cm depth showed significantly higher trematode prevalence (OR=3.2, 95% CI:1.7-6.1, p=0.001) and 34% lower hatching success (χ²=9.84, df=1, p=0.002) compared to shallower sites. Elevation above waterline emerged as the strongest predictor of reduced parasitism (β=-0.71±0.18 SE). Results demonstrate trade-offs in wetland nesting strategies, urging consideration of hydrological management in parasite-impacted habitats.

Fragmentation of freshwater wetlands poses significant conservation genetic challenges for Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across agricultural landscapes. We analyzed microsatellite markers from 143 individuals across 7 Midwestern states, revealing reduced allelic richness (mean Ar = 3.2) and elevated inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.15) in isolated marsh fragments compared to contiguous habitats. Bayesian clustering identified three distinct genetic clusters corresponding to drainage basins, indicating limited dispersal capabilities. Our findings demonstrate that hydrological barriers and agricultural expansion drive genetic erosion in this wetland specialist, necessitating targeted wetland corridor restoration programs.

This community ecology study examined how interspecific competition and marine pollution impact European Shag (Gulosus aristotelis) populations in mixed-species colonies. Through longitudinal monitoring of 12 Scottish coastal sites (2015-2022), we documented significant nest displacement by Larus gulls (β = -0.74, p < 0.01) and reduced fledging success near microplastic accumulation zones (r = -0.68). Our findings emphasize the dual threat of competitive exclusion and anthropogenic contaminants on this Suliformes species' reproductive ecology.

This study examines the impact of hydrological regime alterations on Great Egret (Ardea alba) nesting success in managed freshwater wetlands. Using a 5-year dataset from 12 colonies, we demonstrate that delayed spring flooding significantly reduces fledging rates (β = -0.87, p<0.001) through prey availability disruption. Management recommendations include adaptive water-level control to synchronize with egret phenology.

We investigated nest site selection in Green Sandpipers (Tringa ochropus) along the polluted Vistula River floodplains (Poland) during 2018-2020. Using GPS-loggers (n=32 adults) and soil sampling (n=45 nests), we assessed heavy metal (Pb, Cd, Hg) exposure risks. Nests in riparian zones with >50 ppm Pb had 42% lower hatching success (95% CI: 28-56%, p=0.003) than reference sites. Sandpipers preferentially selected nest sites with lower Cd concentrations (mean difference: 1.7 ppm, p<0.001), indicating behavioral avoidance of contaminated substrates. Conservation efforts must prioritize wetland remediation to mitigate metal-driven reproductive failure in this declining Palaearctic migrant.

This study assessed juvenile survival in Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) within coastal agricultural wetlands, where habitat degradation and pesticide runoff threaten early life stages. Using radio-telemetry, we tracked 78 fledglings across California's Central Valley estuaries from 2020-2022. First-year survival plummeted to 22% in high-runoff zones versus 67% in restored habitats, indicating agricultural pollution disproportionately impacts duckling recruitment. Findings underscore the critical need for wetland buffer zones to sustain waterfowl populations amid intensifying land use.

This study investigates molt migration patterns in Least Terns (Sternula antillarum) along the Gulf Coast using geolocator tracking. We analyzed movement data from 45 individuals to identify stopover sites and molt duration. Results show asynchronous molt initiation correlated with breeding latitude, with southern populations exhibiting prolonged stopovers. Habitat degradation at key estuarine sites significantly delayed feather replacement, potentially impacting subsequent migration and breeding success. Findings highlight the vulnerability of this species to coastal development pressures during this critical life stage.

Understanding anthropogenic threats to nest-site selection is critical for declining shorebirds. We assessed microplastic accumulation in relation to nest habitat of Curlew Sandpipers (Calidris ferruginea) across 23 low-Arctic tundra sites (69°–72°N; n=167 nests, sampled 2020–2022). Microplastic densities (≤5mm) were quantified via FTIR spectroscopy in surface soils (0–5cm depth). Nests in polypropylene-dominated areas (mean ± SD: 112.3 ± 36.7 particles/kg) showed 21.3% lower hatching success (OR=0.62, 95% CI: 0.я51-0.я76; p=0.011) versus low-plastic zones (<10 particles/kg). These novel linkages necessitate incorporating microplastic monitoring into tundra shorebird conservation strategies.

This study examines Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) migration ecology along the Gulf Coast using GPS telemetry. We identified critical stopover sites within coastal marsh ecosystems highly vulnerable to sea-level rise and agricultural runoff. Results show significant delays in migration phenology correlated with intensified storm frequency, highlighting climate change impacts on energy budgets and reproductive success.

We investigated breeding season bycatch mortality impacts on federally threatened Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) in Cape Cod, Massachusetts (2018-2021). Using GPS telemetry (n=47 adults) and daily nest monitoring (n=112 nests), we quantified entanglement rates in recreational fishing gear and modeled survival via Cormack-Jolly-Seber analyses. Bycatch caused 21.4±2.8% (mean±SE) of adult mortality, reducing seasonal survival probability to 0.79±0.04 versus 0.92±0.03 in control sites (p=0.007). Nest abandonment rates increased 3.2-fold following adult bycatch events (95% CI: 1.8-5.7). Our findings necessitate targeted bycatch mitigation during critical incubation periods for population recovery.

We assessed impacts of recreational kite-flying on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) movement ecology using GPS telemetry at Cape Cod National Seashore, Massachusetts (2018-2020). We deployed 22 solar-powered transmitters on breeding adults across 3 management zones. Plovers exhibited significant displacement (mean 127m ± 23SE) during kite events (n=47) versus controls (p=0.003), with 32% abandoning foraging bouts. Nesting success decreased by 18% within 200m of kite sites (GLMM, β=-1.2, p=0.01). Results demonstrate kite activities fragment critical intertidal habitat, supporting buffer zone implementation during breeding season.

We investigated molt migration ecology of American Golden-Plovers (Pluvialis dominica) facing hunting pressure in northern South America. Using satellite telemetry (n=32 adults, 2018-2021), we tracked post-breeding movements from Alaska breeding grounds to molting sites. Survival analysis revealed 27% lower annual survival for individuals molting in hunted regions (HR=1.73, 95% CI: 1.12-2.68) compared to protected areas. Molt duration extended by 8.2 days (SE=2.1) in high-hunting zones, delaying southward migration. Results indicate hunting disrupts molt energetics and necessitates targeted protection of key molting habitats in coastal Venezuela and Colombia.

This study analyzes demographic parameters of Great Egret (Ardea alba) populations in Gulf Coast estuaries from 2015-2022. Using mark-recapture data and nest monitoring, we quantified significant declines in adult survival rates (φ = 0.78 to 0.63) and fledging success associated with coastal wetland degradation. Human disturbance near rookeries explained 42% of breeding abandonment variance (GLMM, p<0.001). Restoration of mangrove buffers significantly improved productivity (β = +0.31), highlighting management strategies for this non-Charadriiformes waterbird facing compound anthropogenic threats.

We investigated population genetic structure of Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) colonies along the Atlantic coast using microsatellite markers. Habitat fragmentation due to coastal development has reduced gene flow among colonies, increasing genetic differentiation (FST = 0.12-0.18). Climate-induced sea-level rise threatens nesting habitats, potentially accelerating isolation. Conservation strategies must prioritize maintaining connectivity corridors.

We investigated the impacts of coastal marsh degradation on Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) nesting success along Chesapeake Bay tributaries. Using nest monitoring and GIS-based habitat analysis across 24 sites, we found significant declines in fledging rates (β = -0.72, p<0.01) correlated with erosion-induced bank instability. Artificial nest burrow installations increased productivity by 37% in compromised habitats, highlighting adaptive management potential for this declining riparian specialist facing accelerated shoreline loss.

We assessed stopover site fidelity and habitat selection in migratory Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) along the Connecticut River corridor. Using GPS telemetry (n=18) and habitat surveys during spring migration 2019-2021, we found individuals exhibited strong fidelity to sites with eroding sandy banks and high fish densities. Stopover duration inversely correlated with riparian development intensity (r=-0.72, p<0.01), indicating sensitivity to shoreline modification. Hydrological changes reduced optimal perch sites by 32%, demonstrating vulnerability to fluvial habitat alteration during critical migratory periods.

We assessed the impact of recreational boating activity on American Avocet (Recurvirostra americana) bycatch mortality within the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, California. Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=42) over three breeding seasons (2020-2022), we quantified spatial overlap with high-traffic waterways. Logistic regression revealed avocets utilizing zones with >5 boats/hr had 3.7× higher entanglement risk (95% CI: 2.1-6.5; p=0.002) than low-traffic areas. Entanglement accounted for 38% (n=16/42) of tracked mortalities. Management recommendations include establishing seasonal no-wake buffers within 200m of active rookeries.

This community ecology study examines habitat partitioning between American Black Ducks (Anas rubripes) and Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) in coastal wetlands of Chesapeake Bay. Using radio-telemetry and behavioral observations, we quantified niche overlap in foraging microhabitats and diet composition during winter months. Results indicate significant spatial segregation driven by salinity tolerance, with Black Ducks utilizing higher-salinity marshes while Mallards dominate freshwater impoundments. Habitat loss from sea-level rise disproportionately impacts Black Duck populations, highlighting conservation implications for this declining species.

We assessed Semipalmated Sandpiper (Calidris pusilla) vulnerability to sea level rise (SLR) along Delaware Bay, USA (2018-2021). Using high-resolution LiDAR elevation data and nest monitoring (n=127 nests), we modeled habitat inundation under IPCC RCP 8.5 scenarios. Results showed 62% of current nesting habitat will be submerged by 2050. Nest success declined significantly with proximity to marsh edge (β = -0.87, SE=0.21, p<0.001). Conservation efforts must prioritize inland migration corridors to mitigate SLR impacts on this declining shorebird.

We investigated synergistic impacts of climate change and anthropogenic noise on Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) breeding success at Bahía de San Quintín, Baja California (2019–2021). Using programmable speakers at 40 experimental nests and 40 controls, we broadcasted coastal recreation noise (65–75 dB) during incubation while monitoring tidal inundation. Noise-exposed pairs showed 27% lower nest attendance (β = −0.43, 95% CI: −0.61 to −0.25; p = 0.002) and 32% higher abandonment during spring tides versus controls (χ² = 9.81, p = 0.002). Hatching success declined by 41% under combined noise and >15 cm inundation events (R² = 0.67, p < 0.001). Results indicate noise exacerbates climate-mediated habitat loss, necessitating integrated buffer zones in conservation planning.

We investigated Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) population dynamics in coastal wetlands using mark-recapture analysis (2018-2022). Habitat degradation from urban expansion reduced nesting success by 37% (p<0.001) and increased brood parasitism. Climate-induced hydrological shifts altered foraging habitat availability, correlating with a 22% decline in juvenile recruitment (R²=0.71). Our findings highlight synergistic threats to waterfowl persistence, emphasizing management needs for anthropogenic disturbance mitigation in estuarine ecosystems.

We investigated disease transmission risks between invasive American Mink (Neovison vison) and Pied Avocets (Recurvirostra avosetta) in the Wadden Sea World Heritage Site (Germany). During 2019-2021, we sampled 120 avocet nests and 45 mink scats for avian influenza virus (AIV) using RT-PCR. Nest predation rates by mink were 32% higher near invasive-dominated marshes (95% CI: 18-46%, p=0.003). AIV prevalence in avocets was positively correlated with mink density (R²=0.71, p<0.001), suggesting predator-mediated pathogen spread. Conservation efforts must prioritize invasive predator control to mitigate disease threats in this UNESCO-protected shorebird population.

We assessed morphological variation in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across coastal breeding colonies using geometric morphometrics. Bill shape and wing chord measurements from 180 individuals revealed significant clinal variation correlated with latitude (r=0.76, p<0.001), suggesting Bergmann's rule adaptation. Northern populations exhibited larger body size and narrower bills, potentially reflecting thermal adaptation and prey specialization. Anthropogenic disturbance influenced allometric scaling relationships in urban colonies. These phenotypic patterns indicate adaptive capacity to environmental gradients but highlight vulnerability to rapid habitat alterations.

This study examines Great Egret (Ardea alba) foraging efficiency in agricultural wetlands impacted by pesticide runoff. Using focal animal sampling across 12 sites in California's Central Valley, we quantified strike rates and prey capture success relative to water contamination levels. Results indicate significant reductions in foraging efficiency at sites with high organophosphate concentrations (p<0.01), with egrets exhibiting longer handling times and increased vigilance behavior. Our findings highlight agricultural pollution as a critical threat to wading bird populations beyond direct mortality effects.

We investigated threats to Black Turnstone (Arenaria melanocephala; Charadriiformes: Scolopacidae), a Nearctic shorebird, from invasive European Green Crab (Carcinus maenas) trapping in southeastern Alaska. Using GPS telemetry (n=24 adults, 2019-2021) and bycatch monitoring in 172 crab traps across Prince William Sound during summer months, we documented 7.4% of tracked individuals (n=24) interacting with traps biweekly (95% CI: 3.1-15.2%). Bycatch mortality rate was 0.52% of local population per season (χ²=5.83, df=1; p=0<span class=

We investigated Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) population responses to Spartina alterniflora marsh fragmentation in Chesapeake Bay. Using occupancy modeling across 120 survey points (2018-2021), we found rail detection probability declined 32% with increasing patch isolation. Marsh loss exceeding 40% within 1km radius caused local extirpation, with juveniles showing higher dispersal failure. Our results demonstrate how coastal development severs metapopulation connectivity in this cryptic rail species, emphasizing need for contiguous marsh conservation beyond shorebird-centric management.

Mountain Plover (Charadrius montanus), a declining species of North American shortgrass prairie, faces population declines exacerbated by wetland loss due to mudflat reclamation for agriculture. We investigated nest-site selection and survival using 145 nests monitored with daily telemetry during 2019-2021 breeding seasons in the South Platte River Basin (Colorado, USA). Logistic regression revealed a 65.8% reduction in nest success within 500m of reclamation projects (odds ratio = 0·342; 95% CI = 0·228–0·513) compared to undisturbed sites. Our findings demonstrate that regulatory exclusion zones around managed wetlands must exceed current 200m buffers to mitigate anthropogenic habitat fragmentation.

In northeastern freshwater marshes, invasive Phragmites australis encroachment threatens secretive marsh bird communities through structural homogenization. We quantified Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) responses across 25 wetlands using call-broadcast surveys and vegetation analyses. Occupancy modeling revealed significant negative effects of invasive cover on rail presence (β = -1.32, SE=0.41, p<0.01), mediated through reduced macroinvertebrate prey availability. Community-level analyses indicated cascading impacts on associated wetland bird diversity. Findings emphasize invasive plant management as critical for conserving rail populations in fragmented habitats.

We investigated Brant (Branta bernicla) nest site selection and reproductive success across three coastal tundra breeding colonies in Alaska from 2018-2020. Using logistic regression models, we found that proximity to freshwater ponds (β = 0.72, p < 0.01) and low fox activity (β = -1.34, p < 0.001) significantly predicted nest survival. Clutch sizes averaged 4.2 ± 0.3 eggs, with hatching success declining 18% during years with early spring snowmelt (R² = 0.41). Our results highlight climate-induced phenological mismatches and predation pressure as key threats to this declining goose population.

We assessed juvenile Purple Sandpiper (Calidris maritima) survival vulnerability to oil spills along Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula (2018-2021). Using satellite telemetry (n=42 fledglings) and oiling probability models based on coastal traffic density, we found juveniles in high-risk zones had 37% lower first-year survival (HR=1.58, 95% CI: 1.21-2.07) versus low-risk areas. Contaminated intertidal foraging grounds significantly reduced body condition (mean mass deficit: -4.2g, p=0.008). Results highlight urgent need for marine traffic restrictions near critical wintering habitats.

We investigated the nocturnal movements of Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola) in freshwater marshes using radio-telemetry. Over two breeding seasons (2021-2022), we tracked 32 individuals equipped with miniature transmitters. Results revealed significant avoidance of areas with anthropogenic noise pollution, with rails shifting core activity zones >300m from roadways. Displacement correlated with reduced chick provisioning rates (r=-0.72, p<0.01). Our findings demonstrate acute sensitivity to human disturbance in this secretive rallid, suggesting infrastructure planning should incorporate buffer zones around critical wetland habitats.

<jats:p>The average amount of food that was stored during an autumn by Willow Tits Porus montanus was estimated by sampling hoarding intensities and analysing the energetic contents of the stored items. Measurements of retrieval and losses of the stored food made it possible to calculate how much of the stored food that actually was used by the hoarder. Also the chemical composition of the stored food was analysed, and a comparison of the energy contents of the food eaten with the energy requirements of the birds made it possible to assess the importance of hoarded food in the winter diet. According to the calculations, hoarded food can be assumed to account for almost all food that was consumed during December, whereas it was estimated to constitute around 24% of the food eaten from January to March. During colder winters, with higher energetical stress, it is possible that stored supplies could be more important during this part of the winter, perhaps of the magnitude of 45% of the total food consumed.</jats:p>

We investigated Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) nest site selection in response to mudflat reclamation in the Yellow Sea, China. During 2018-2020 we monitored 57 nests using ARGOS-GPS tags and nest cameras across intact (N=28) and reclaimed sites (N=29). Logistic regression revealed 63% lower nest site fidelity in reclaimed areas (OR=0.37; 95%CI: 0.18-0.75). Nest predation increased 2-fold (χ²=4.32, df=1 p=0 038). Our results quantify how reclamation disrupts critical breeding habitat selection, urging immediate protection of remaining mudflats for this declining East Asian-Australasian Flyway population.

We investigated molt migration in Caspian Terns (Hydroprogne caspia) in southeast Alaska. Using GPS telemetry on 35 individuals, we identified distinct inland migration corridors toward freshwater molting sites. Molt duration averaged 38±5 days with significant energetic costs. Anthropogenic disturbance at stopover wetlands reduced premigratory fattening rates. This highlights vulnerability during this critical life-history stage.

This study investigated how shoreline armoring affects Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) foraging ecology along the rapidly developing coastlines of Georgia’s Golden Isles. Using focal observations and GPS-tagged individuals (n = 23), we quantified foraging rates and habitat selection during migratory stopovers (March–May 2021–2023). Armored sites showed 42% lower prey capture rates (p = 0 013; 95% CI -1.2–-0 4) and reduced usage (<20% of locations) compared to natural marshes. Our findings demonstrate that coastal hardening reduces functional habitat availability for this species, necessitating integrated soft-engineering approaches in conservation planning.

We investigated the migratory connectivity of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) along the Pacific coast using GPS telemetry. Thirty adults were tagged at three breeding colonies (CA, OR, WA). Analysis revealed two distinct wintering areas: birds from WA migrated to central CA, while CA/OR birds remained resident or moved south minimally. This differential migration suggests adaptive responses to local resource availability. Findings emphasize the importance of regional conservation planning for this species facing climate-induced prey shifts and coastal development threats.

Este estudio presenta un análisis de los laboratorios remotos actuales para el estudio de electrónica digital. Con base en los resultados de los análisis, el documento describe un laboratorio remoto de código abierto desarrollado por los autores para realizar prácticas remotas de electrónica digitales. Este laboratorio remoto se ha implementado con el kit PSoC®4 CY8CKIT-042. El laboratorio remoto basado en este dispositivo Cypress de bajo costo es adecuado para su uso en las instituciones educativas como un primer paso para ayudar a los estudiantes a familiarizarse con el kit sin necesidad de tener que adquirirlo. El laboratorio remoto está diseñado como código abierto, por lo que otros investigadores puedan usarlo y modificarlo. Este es el primer laboratorio remoto de código abierto para electrónica digital. Como características principales, el laboratorio remoto implementa servicios de autenticación, planificación de reservas y streaming de vídeo a través de una cámara web. También guarda datos de la actividad y rendimiento de los estudiantes para desarrollar análisis del aprendizaje.

We investigated how energy expenditure influences disease susceptibility in Pectoral Sandpipers (Calidris melanotos) during spring migration through Alaska's Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta (2019-2021). Using accelerometer-derived metabolic rates (n=42 birds) and avian influenza screening, we found individuals with daily energy expenditure >1.5x basal metabolic rate had 3.7-fold higher infection probability (95% CI: 1.8-7.6; p=0.002) than less active conspecifics. This trade-off between migratory energetics and immune function highlights climate change impacts on disease dynamics in Arctic-breeding shorebirds.

We investigated the foraging behavior of American Avocets (Recurvirostra americana) in relation to cyanobacterial bloom events caused by elevated nitrogen loading in Nebraska Sandhill wetlands. During 2019-2020 breeding seasons, we documented foraging duration (n=52 individuals) using focal sampling and compared prey capture rates between impacted and reference sites via generalized linear mixed models (GLMM). Avocets in eutrophic zones spent 38% more time foraging (p=0.007) yet achieved 24% lower dip success rates (95% CI: −33 to −15%). These data highlight how nutrient enrichment disrupts foraging efficiency for this tactile specialist, suggesting management must address non-point source pollution to maintain key stopover habitats.

Increased storm frequency threatens migratory shorebirds. We assessed genetic vulnerability in Wilson's Phalarope (Phalaropus tricolor) using RAD-seq on 152 individuals from 3 key stopovers: Mono Lake (CA), Great Salt Lake (UT), and Chaplin Lake (SK). Analysis revealed reduced allelic richness (ρ < 0?01 in salinity-impacted sites; FST = 0.129 between Mono and Chaplin cohorts) and elevated inbreeding coefficients (FIS = 0.11?0.18) in storm-affected habitats. Modelling projected 37% loss of genetic diversity under RCP8.5 by 2070? Conservation requires protecting inland saline ecosystems to buffer metapopulation resilience.

Stable isotope analysis (δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C) of Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nestling feathers revealed distinct dietary shifts in Chesapeake Bay populations from 2010–2020. Declining δ¹⁵N signatures correlated with reduced anadromous fish prey availability (R²=0·83, p<0·001), reflecting impacts of coastal development on spawning habitat. This novel application demonstrates ospreys' utility as bioindicators for estuarine ecosystem health under anthropogenic pressure.

Wilson's Plover (Charadrius wilsonia) nest survival faces compounding threats from recreational shell collection and climate-amplified tidal inundation. We conducted a manipulative experiment on Padre Island, Texas (2019-2022), monitoring 84 nests with daily surveys and GPS-mapped shell cover. Nests in shell-removal plots exhibited 28% lower daily survival rates (DSR=0.91 vs. 0.96; p=0.007; 95% CI: 0.83-0.94) and 3.2× higher flood-induced failure during storm surges (p<0.001). Results indicate synergistic impacts necessitate shell-harvesting regulations and targeted dune restoration to buffer climate effects.

<jats:p id="p1">Facing to the harsh environmental constraints, natural populations of
widespread plant species may express plastic response, evolve local
adaptation or combine both mechanisms in order to maintain their genetic
variation and pervasiveness across a wide ecological niche. Here, 79
lines representing height Tunisian populations of Brachypodium hybridum
were cultivated in two contrasting phosphorus (P) availability levels
and their genetic variation was investigated using forage quality traits
to identify the main mechanisms governing their genetic variation. Our
results revealed large variation among populations for most traits. PCA
analysis showed the separation between coastal and inland populations in
both P levels. Importantly, all traits revealed high heritability in
both P treatments and the response of most of them to P deficiency was
highly influenced by the population effect, which accounted 52.38% of
the total variation, indicating strong population differentiation.
However, although significant for most traits, only 18.13% of variation
was attributed to P treatment, suggesting little plastic response to P
deficiency. Importantly, as revealed by the lack of population*treatment
effect for most traits, the plastic response was probably common to all
populations. Moreover, we found that 56.99% of variation was attributed
to environmental factors with distance to coastline, precipitation
seasonality, and annual precipitation being the most important factors,
suggesting that the strong population differentiation likely reflects
local adaptation to specific environmental conditions. Contrary to the
coastal populations, which were characterized by high levels of
fiber-related traits levels, the inland ones displayed the high values
of most energy-related traits, suggesting that these latter were
characterized by relatively higher forage quality. Overall, our results
suggested that the effect of local adaptation overrides the effect of
phenotypic plasticity in explaining the variation of forage quality
traits, which indicate a broad adaptive genetic differentiation among
the Tunisian populations of B. hybridum in response to P deficiency.</jats:p>

We investigated the impact of ocean acidification on Sanderling (Calidris alba) breeding biology at Ny-Ålesund, Svalbard (78°55'N, 11°56'E) during 2019-2021. Using nest monitoring (n=42 nests) and prey availability surveys, we assessed clutch size, hatching success, and chick growth rates under varying carbonate chemistry conditions. Hatching success declined by 22% (95% CI: 18-26%) per 0.1 unit decrease in pH (p=0.008), while chick mass at fledging decreased by 11% (SE=2.3) in acidified sites. These results demonstrate that ocean acidification threatens Arctic-breeding shorebirds through trophic pathways, necessitating integrated marine-terrestrial conservation approaches.

This study assessed juvenile Great Egret (Ardea alba) survival rates in anthropogenically altered wetland ecosystems. Using radio-telemetry on 42 fledglings across three breeding seasons, we quantified daily survival probability in relation to hydrological variability, habitat fragmentation, and human recreational disturbance. Cox proportional hazards models revealed significant negative effects of lowered water tables (HR: 2.3, p<0.01) and shoreline development density (HR: 1.8, p=0.03) on first-year survival, with disturbance events causing disproportionate mortality during critical fledging periods. Results emphasize freshwater wetland preservation needs for this wading bird species under increasing anthropogenic pressures.

This study investigates migration phenology shifts in Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) along the Pacific Flyway using 15 years of banding data. We documented significant delays in spring arrival timing (mean 1.8 days/decade, p<0.001) correlated with increasing March temperatures. Coastal wetland loss reduced staging duration at key California stopovers by 37%, forcing longer overwater flights. Results highlight climate-driven phenological mismatches and habitat-mediated migration costs for this dabbling duck species.

This study examined the effects of altered storm regimes on Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) stopover ecology at James Bay, Ontario (2018-2020). Using miniaturized GPS loggers (n=37 adults) coupled with meteorological data, we quantified stopover duration and site fidelity relative to tropical storm events. Post-storm stopover duration increased by 2.7 ± 0.4 days (p < 0.001), while 41% of birds abandoned primary staging sites during consecutive storm events (OR=3.2, 95% CI:1.8-5.6). Results indicate climate-driven storm intensification may disrupt fuel deposition rates during critical northward migration, necessitating dynamic habitat protection for this declining Nearctic-Neotropical migrant.

We investigated the impact of recreational photography on Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) migration ecology at Delaware Bay, USA (May 2019-2021). Using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults) and behavioral observations (n=120 hours), we documented significant reductions in foraging time (mean decrease: 28±4 min/day, p=0.003) and increased vigilance (frequency increase: 42%, p<0.001) at high-photography sites. Population modeling indicated a 17% decline in refueling rates could reduce migration success by 9% (95% CI: 4-14%). Conservation measures should prioritize spatial zoning of photography activities during peak migration.

We investigated how photography-induced disturbance affects Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) antipredator vigilance in the Wadden Sea, Germany (53.7°N, 8.7°E). Using focal sampling (n=42 adults, 120 observation hours), we quantified vigilance duration before/after photographer approach (≤15m). Post-disturbance vigilance increased by 37% (95% CI: 24-51%, p=0.003), reducing foraging efficiency by 29% (CI: 18-40%). Concurrent fox predation rates rose 2.3-fold in disturbed zones. Results demonstrate that recreational photography exacerbates predation risk through behavioral disruption, necessitating buffer zones during breeding.

We investigated Bar-tailed Godwit (Limosa lapponica) responses to altered storm regimes in managed wetlands of the Yellow Sea coast (Jiangsu Province, China) during 2018-2021. Using satellite telemetry (n=42 adults) and habitat modeling, we quantified storm-surge impacts on foraging habitat availability. Results showed a 32% reduction in preferred intertidal foraging areas following major storm events (95% CI: 28-36%), correlating with significant declines in pre-migration body condition (r = -0.71, p < 0.001). Our findings highlight the vulnerability of staging godwits to climate-driven hydrological extremes, urging adaptive management of tidal flat ecosystems.

This study examines the impact of recreational boating disturbance on American Coot (Fulica americana) behavior in freshwater wetlands. Through focal animal sampling at 12 sites across the Midwest, we quantified time-activity budgets before, during and after vessel approaches (n=156 events). Results indicate significant reduction in foraging time (p<0>01), increased vigilance (42% rise, p<0>05), and displacement from preferred habitats. Our findings underscore that even non-consumptive human activities can induce behavioral shifts with potential fitness consequences for this widely distributed rallid species.

We investigated anthropogenic bycatch mortality during migration in Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) populations wintering in Costa Rica (2008-2013). Using satellite telemetry (n = 38 birds), we documented incidental capture rates in aquaculture nets. Bycatch incidence was 2.6 times higher in juveniles than adults (95% CI: 1.2–4; p = 0.01). Our population viability model predicted a 19% decline over 20 years at current mortality levels, predominantly driven by juvenile losses. Results underscore the need for juvenile-targeted mitigation in freshwater aquaculture systems.

We investigated juvenile survival rates in Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon) populations along coastal river systems of the Pacific Northwest. Using mark-recapture models on 127 banded individuals over three breeding seasons, we assessed how anthropogenic disturbance (boat traffic, shoreline development), water quality degradation, and prey fish availability influenced first-year survival probability. Survival rates declined significantly with increased turbidity (β = -0·23, SE = 0·08), while proximity to marinas reduced survival by 34% compared to undeveloped reaches (χ² = 16·2·, p < 0·001). Conservation efforts should prioritize riparian buffer zones to mitigate these threats.

We investigated competitive interactions between Least Sandpiper (Calidris minutilla) and invasive European Green Crab (Carcinus maenas) in intertidal mudflats of Willapa Bay, Washington, USA (2018-2021). Using focal-animal sampling (n=42 sandpipers) and prey availability surveys, we documented significant reductions in foraging efficiency (mean intake rate: 0.8 vs. 1.3 prey/min; p=0.007) and habitat displacement (35% reduction in preferred foraging zones) when crabs exceeded 5/m². Population modeling indicated local declines >20% under sustained competition, highlighting the vulnerability of small-bodied shorebirds to invasive competitors.

We studied the food habits of Whiskered Auklets (Aethia pygmaea) at Buldir Island, western Aleutian Islands, Alaska, during the summer of 1976. At Buldir, these birds fed primarily in and near convergent tidal fronts in the passes between three islets just offshore; feeding occurred throughout the day. Whiskered Auklets ate at least 10 different species of zooplanktonic prey, of which the copepod Neocalanus plumchrus was the most important. Next in importance were chaetognaths (probably Sagitta elegans), the amphipod Parathemisto pacifica, megalopae of the crab Erimacrus isenbeckii, and an unidentified amphipod. Pteropods (probably Limacina helicina), larval cephalopods, and a larval fish occurred in trace amounts. During most of the summer, Whiskered Auklets were nearly monophagous on N. plumchrus; we do not consider a difference in prey during late incubation/early chick rearing to represent a biologically-significant trend. We collected Least (A. pusilla), Crested (A. cristatella), and Parakeet (Cyclorrhynchus psittacula) auklets during late chick rearing, to compare their food habits with those of Whiskered Auklets. At this time, both Least and Whiskered auklets were monophagous on smaller N. plumchrus, whereas Crested and Parakeet auklets mainly ate larger N. cristatus and P. pacifica; Parakeet Auklets ate the widest diversity of zooplankton. Selection of prey by the four auklet species appeared to occur in relation to size, with the smaller auklets eating smaller zooplankters.

We assessed juvenile survival rates in Great Blue Herons (Ardea herodias) across coastal estuaries using satellite telemetry (n=35 fledglings). First-year mortality exceeded 65%, primarily linked to wetland habitat fragmentation and bioaccumulation of industrial pollutants in prey. Heavy precipitation events during nesting reduced fledging success by 42% (p=0.007). Management strategies must address watershed contaminants and protect contiguous marsh corridors to sustain populations.

We investigated the impact of invasive apple snails (Pomacea spp.) on Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) foraging behavior in Louisiana coastal marshes. Using focal observations and GPS tracking, we documented significant shifts in egret foraging locations and reduced prey capture rates in snail-infested areas compared to control sites. Dietary analysis revealed snails constituted 38% of egret diets in invaded marshes, displacing native fish and crustacean prey. Our results demonstrate how invasive species can alter wading bird foraging ecology through both competitive exclusion and habitat modification.

We evaluated climate change impacts on Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) nesting ecology in Gulf Coast estuaries using longitudinal monitoring (2013-2022). Nest survival models incorporated tidal inundation frequency, water salinity, and extreme weather events. Results demonstrated a 27% decline in fledging success associated with sea-level rise (β = -0.43, p<0.001), with mangrove nest sites experiencing disproportionate flooding. Salinity intrusion further reduced prey availability, compounding reproductive effects. These findings highlight mangrove-dependent Ardeids as sentinels for coastal ecosystem vulnerability, necessitating adaptive management strategies for critical nesting habitats under climate scenarios.

We investigated the impact of anthropogenic noise pollution on migratory behavior of Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa islandica) staging in the Wadden Sea (53.5°N, 8.0°E). Using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults, 2019-2021), we quantified stopover duration and foraging efficiency near wind farms versus control sites. Godwits exposed to >65 dB noise exhibited 28% shorter stopovers (p=0.012) and 19% lower prey intake rates (CI: 15-23%). These behavioral changes may reduce pre-migration fattening, highlighting noise mitigation as critical for this declining subspecies.

We investigated the influence of coastal development on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) foraging behavior and nest-site selection in Chesapeake Bay tributaries (2018-2021). Using GPS telemetry (n=22 adults) and habitat suitability modeling, we demonstrated significant avoidance of high-density residential zones (p<0·001) and preferential use of undisturbed marsh edges. Nest productivity declined 18±5% near marinas versus remote areas. Community-level implications include cascading effects on fish assemblages where predator-prey dynamics are altered by raptor displacement.

This study investigates the impact of hydrological regime alterations on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) reproductive success in managed prairie pothole wetlands. Using nest monitoring and vegetation surveys across 12 sites, we found that delayed spring drawdowns significantly reduced nest survival rates (β = -0.##, p<0.##) by exposing eggs to increased predation risk. Our results highlight the need for adaptive water management strategies to conserve this secretive rallid species amid changing precipitation patterns.

Aerial roots from hemiepiphytic Heteropsis (Araceae) vines have long been used in Amazonia as a strong flexible material in construction and making handicrafts. Commercial demand for this product known in Brazil as “titica” has increased in recent decades for making wicker furniture. We conducted inventories, harvests and experimental root cutting in the Alto Rio Guamá Indigenous Reserve in the eastern Brazilian Amazon to investigate several aspects of titica ecology, root biology, and harvest impact to estimate root harvest potential in a range of intact and disturbed forest areas. The average density of host trees with titica roots in relatively undisturbed upland “terra firme” plots with light to moderate forest use was 371 trees/ha with 115 of these having commercially harvestable roots. These areas had an average of 0.9 commercially harvestable roots and 2.4 non-harvestable roots per host tree generating a titica root density of 1332 roots/ha with 26% of these being commercially harvestable. Titica plants did not show a positive preference for particular types of host trees, but the number of titica roots per host tree did increase with host tree size. The vines were virtually absent from forest areas subject to periodic flooding, a common palm tree found near small streams, and on pioneer tree species in patches of secondary forest recovering from a fire that occurred almost 20 years ago. Experimental cutting of mature titica roots showed that harvesting can have a severe impact on root survival. In the two treatments, where at least half of mature titica roots per host tree were cut 4m above the ground, an average of 63% cut roots died and only 16% showed some regrowth after 7 months. The roots that did start to grow back had an average of 1.7 new roots arising from them, but each cut root had only one commercial quality root to replace it. These commercial quality roots were growing at an average of 220cm per host tree per year. The high mortality and slow regrowth following root harvest indicate that many decades will be needed in between intensive titica harvests in one area. Options for managing titica harvests include reducing the percentage of roots removed per plant, setting up blocks of forest that would be harvested in succession, and in some cases integrating titica harvests into long-term timber cutting cycles.

We assessed the impact of accelerated sea-level rise on Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) population dynamics in Atlantic coastal marshes. Using Bayesian hierarchical models with 12 years of mark-recapture data across 7 sites, we found tidal inundation frequency negatively influenced adult survival (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.68 to -0.15) and nest success. Marsh fragmentation further reduced juvenile recruitment, projecting a 72% population decline under RCP 8.5 scenarios by 2050. These findings underscore urgent habitat management needs for this saltmarsh-obligate species.

Particulate matter and interfacial sediment from a seasonally anoxic coastal salt pond were analyzed for fatty acids and sterols to examine variations in organic sources, and compositional changes across the oxic-anoxic interface in the water column and at the sediment-water interface. Fatty acid distributions in suspended particles varied seasonally and as a function of depth. Fatty acids of algal origin (e.g. 16:3, 16:4, 18:3, 18:4) were abundant in particles in oxic surface waters, but these labile components were depleted in particles from the anoxic zone which instead were enriched in bacterial fatty acids (e.g. 16:1Δ 9, 18:1Δ 11, anteiso-C 15). Sterol distributionsvaried less than fatty acid distributions and particles throughout the water column reflected an upper water algal source with little in situ alteration. There was evidence for an in situ conversion of Δ 5-stenols to 5(α)H-stanols in suspended particles in the anoxic zone. Sinking particles and the interfacial sediment were compositionally similar to each other, but different from suspended particles. These data reflect differences in particle source, transport and transformation processes occuring in the water column.

This study examines the impact of recreational boating on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nesting success in Chesapeake Bay estuaries. Using nest monitoring and disturbance logging from 2018-2021, we quantified behavioral responses (nest attendance, provisioning rates) to vessel proximity. Results indicate significant reductions in feeding frequency (p<0.01) and increased nest abandonment at sites with >15 boats/hour within 100m. Management recommendations include establishing 200m seasonal buffer zones around active nests to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this apex piscivore.

We investigated thermal stress impacts on American Avocet (Recurvirostra americana) breeding success in the Great Salt Lake ecosystem, Utah (2018-2022). Using temperature loggers at 120 nests and daily survival modeling, we found a 1°C increase in maximum daily temperature reduced nest survival by 7.2% (95% CI: 4.1-10.3%; p=0.002). Chick growth rates declined significantly above 32°C (linear mixed model: β = -0.18 g/day/°C, SE=0.04, p<0.001). These results demonstrate acute vulnerability to climate warming, urging adaptive management of wetland habitats for this declining shorebird.

We investigated the impact of dredging noise on Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus) vocal behavior in coastal Louisiana, USA. From March-July 2020, we recorded 1,200 alarm calls at 12 nests near active dredging sites and 12 control sites using autonomous recorders. Alarm call rate increased by 42% (95% CI: 28-56%) and peak frequency shifted upward by 310 Hz (p=0.003) at dredge sites. Nest abandonment probability rose to 0.67 vs. 0.21 in controls (χ²=9.8, df=1, p=0.002). These bioacoustic shifts indicate chronic stress responses, suggesting acoustic masking may disrupt anti-predator communication during critical breeding periods.

Understanding demographic responses to anthropogenic stressors is critical for Clapper Rail (Rallus crepitans) conservation. Using multi-year mark-resight data (2018–2022) across six fragmented saltmarsh sites, we analyzed survival, recruitment, and population growth rates. Adult survival probability (φ = 0.72 ± 0.05) showed significant negative relationships with proximity to urban development and tidal restriction structures. Fecundity was less impacted. Sensitivity analyses revealed adult survival as the key driver of population viability, emphasizing threats from coastal squeeze and hydrological alterations in rapidly developing estuaries.

We assessed impacts of domestic dog (Canis lupus familiaris) disturbance on parental care in Kentish Plovers (Charadrius alexandrinus) at Ebro Delta, Spain (2021-2022 breeding seasons). Using GPS-tracked adults (n=36) and 280h of behavioral observations across 54 nests, we quantified parental attendance and foraging budgets in designated dog-access (n=28) and dog-restricted zones (n=26). Nests in dog-access areas experienced 27% lower parental attendance (χ²=8.41, p=0.004) and 32% longer foraging commutes (t=3.67, p<0.001), resulting in 21% lower nest success (95% CI: 14-29%). These disruptions significantly reduced chick-provisioning rates (r=-0.53, p=0.002). Findings underscore the critical need for enforced leash regulations in shorebird breeding habitats.

We assessed heavy metal exposure impacts on Short-billed Dowitcher (Limnodromus griseus) demography at Delaware Bay, USA (2018-2021). Blood samples (n=142 adults) quantified cadmium, lead, and mercury concentrations via ICP-MS. Individuals with elevated cadmium (>0.8 ppm) showed 32% lower annual survival (95% CI: 18-44%; p=0.003) based on Cormack-Jolly-Seber modeling. Mercury exposure correlated with reduced clutch sizes (β = -0.21, SE=0.09, p=0.02). Results indicate metal pollution as a critical threat requiring targeted wetland remediation.

We investigated the impacts of hurricane-induced disturbance on Semipalmated Plover (Charadrius semipalmatus) energy budgets during fall migration along the Atlantic Flyway. Using miniaturized accelerometers deployed on 32 individuals at Delaware Bay (2018-2020), we quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) before, during, and after Hurricane Dorian (2019). DEE increased by 42% ± 8% (mean ± SE) during storm passage (p = 0.003), with compensatory reductions in foraging efficiency persisting for 5.2 ± 1.1 days post-event. These findings highlight acute energetic costs of extreme weather events for migratory shorebirds and underscore the need for protected stopover habitats to buffer climate change impacts.

Abstract: We investigated the impacts of invasive Argentine ant (Linepithema humile) colonies on the nesting success of Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger). Using monitored nest sites along the Gulf Coast, we documented predation events and quantified microhabitat alterations. Results showed ant presence correlated with 38% lower hatching success (p<0 05), primarily through egg predation and nest abandonment. Management implications for ground-nesting coastal avifauna are discussed.

This study examines the impacts of coastal marsh degradation on Snowy Egret (Egretta thula), an ardeid wading bird. Using GPS telemetry and nest monitoring across 12 sites in Louisiana, USA, we documented a 22% decline in fledging success associated with Spartina alterniflora loss (R²=0 67, p<0 001). Habitat fragmentation reduced foraging efficiency, particularly affecting juvenile provisioning. Conservation strategies for non-charadriiform waterbirds must address watershed-scale sediment deficits driving marsh collapse.

This study examines the role of environmental contaminants in the reproductive impairment of Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri), a coastal-dependent larid facing habitat degradation. Through gas chromatography-mass spectrometry analysis of eggshell contaminants and multi-year monitoring of nest success in Gulf Coast colonies (n=15, 2018-2021), we documented significant negative correlations between polychlorinated biphenyl concentrations in maternal tissue and fledging rates (R²=0·67, p<0·001). Results indicate legacy pollutants remain primary drivers of demographic decline despite reduced contemporary emissions.

We investigated the impact of recreational boating activity on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nesting success in coastal Georgia, USA. Using motion-activated cameras at 32 nests across barrier islands, we quantified disturbance frequency and duration during incubation and chick-rearing periods (2018-2020). Nest abandonment probability increased significantly with daily boat approaches within 100 m (GLMM: β = 0.87, SE = 0.21, p < 0.001), particularly during early incubation. Productivity declined by 42% at high-disturbance sites compared to protected areas. Our findings highlight the need for buffer zones around osprey nests during critical breeding stages to mitigate anthropogenic impacts.

We investigated molt migration patterns in Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) populations along the Atlantic coast using GPS telemetry. Tracking data revealed bimodal migration routes differing from shorebird strategies, with prolonged stopovers in estuarine habitats vulnerable to microplastic pollution. Analysis of feather samples showed delayed molt phenology correlated with coastal development intensity, suggesting anthropogenic stressors disrupt physiological cycles in this coastal specialist.

Introducción
                  La neurocisticercosis (NCC) es una patología emergente en países desarrollados debido principalmente, al aumento de la inmigración desde áreas endémicas. El gran poliformismo de la NCC hace necesaria la individualización del tratamiento en cada caso. La toma de decisiones en paises no habituados a esta patología puede ser compleja.
               
                  Objetivos
                  Establecer unas pautas diagnósticas y terapéuticas en los diferentes tipos de NCC.
               
                  Material y métodos
                  Se ha realizado un análisis descriptivo y retrospectivo de seis casos de neurocisticercosis atendidos en el Servicio de Neurocirugía del Hospital Clínic de Barcelona desde 1992 al 2000 (ambos incluidos). Se realiza una revisión de la literatura sobre los métodos diagnósticos y terapéuticos actuales en las diferentes modalidades de NCC.
               
                  Discusión
                  El diagnóstico definitivo o probable de NCC se realiza en función de criterios clínicos, inmunológicos, radiológicos y epidemiológicos. En pacientes con enfermedad inactiva se recomienda únicamente tratamiento sintomático. No hay datos concluyentes sobre el beneficio del tratamiento con antiparasitarios en la enfermedad activa parenquimatosa, sin embargo, los pacientes con enfermedad activa extraparenquimatosa se pueden beneficiar del tratamiento antihelminítico asociado a corticoides durante los primeros días. El tratamiento quirúrgico está indicado en lesiones que provocan focalidad neurológica progresiva, hipertensión endocraneal o hidrocefalia.
               
                  Introduction
                  The incidence of neurocysticercosis (NCC) is increasing currently in developed countries due to the migration movements from endemic countries. Due to NCC polymorphism, treatment would be individualized in each case. Countries not used to this disease have to deal with.
               
                  Goals
                  To set up diagnostic and therapeutic guidelines in all sorts of NCC and choose the correct treatment would be challenging.
               
                  Patients and methods
                  To perform a descriptive and retrospective analysis of six cases of NCC seen in the Neurosurgery Department of the Hospital Clinic de Barcelona from 1992 to 2000 (both included). We have performed a revision of the literature about diagnostic and therapeutic methods.
               
                  Discussion
                  Definitive or probable diagnosis of NCC is based on clinical, imaging, immunological, and epidemiological criteria. In patients with inactive disease only symptomatic treatment is indicated. In active parenchymal forms there are not consensus if antiparasitic treatment is indicated. However, in extraparenchymal active disease aggressive treatment with antiparasitic agents and steroids is recommended. In cases of intracranial hypertension, neurological deficits or hydrocephalus surgery is the treatment of choice.

Primarily because of their high levels of microbiological activity, wetland soils play a key role in ameliorating nitrogen pollution and reducing nutrient loadings to coastal zones. Saltwater intrusion associated with climate change is expected to dramatically affect the biogeochemistry of these soils and induce changes in the composition of the soil microbial community that may alter their ability to process nitrogen. In this study, the abundance and community structure of microorganisms associated with two key nitrate removal pathways – denitrification and dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA) – were assessed for eight tidal wetlands along a naturally-occurring salinity gradient (0–2ppt) in the Chesapeake Bay watershed (USA). Molecular analyses targeted functional genes specific for each pathway (denitrification: nirS and nosZ; DNRA: nrfA). Shifts in abundance and community structure of both groups of nitrate reducers were strongly coupled to changes in salinity, and correlation analyses suggested that the effect of salinity on these organisms may have been mediated, at least in part, by changes in soil organic matter availability. Considering the growing body of evidence that microbial community composition may help regulate ecosystem process rates, an increased understanding of how salinity affects nitrogen cycling microbial communities may help us better predict how wetland soil function will be affected by global change and issues such as sea level rise.

This study examined parental care behaviors in Brant geese (Branta bernicla) within coastal estuarine habitats. We quantified nest attendance rates and brood defense intensity across 52 breeding pairs exposed to varying levels of recreational disturbance along the Eastern Seaboard. Using generalized linear mixed models, we identified significant reductions in incubation constancy (β = -0 38, SE=0 11, p<0 001) and aggressive responses to simulated predators following human recreational events. Our results demonstrate that anthropogenic disturbance significantly compromises parental investment in this declining waterfowl species.

We examined how coastal tourism disturbance affects maternal care in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima) across three Baltic Sea colonies. Using GPS-tracked females (n=42) and nest cameras, we measured incubation constancy and brood defense intensity. Frequent human presence (>5 events/day) significantly reduced nest attendance (β=-0.31, p=0.008) and increased egg predation risk (HR=2.7, CI:1.4-5.1). Findings highlight anthropogenic threats to waterfowl parental investment in rapidly developing coastal zones.

<jats:p>Sustainable groundnut production can be realised through development and adoption of high yielding cultivars possessing durable rust resistance. Integrating conventional breeding with genomic tools in identifying candidate rust resistance genes, and introgressing the genes into adapted elite germplasm, with the aid of molecular makers, could enhance breeding for rust resistance. This review highlights breeding approaches for groundnut rust resistance, with emphasis on integrating conventional breeding with marker-assisted selection. The life cycle, symptoms and epidemiology of the pathogen are also discussed to understand the host-pathogen interaction and guide groundnut rust resistance breeding</jats:p>

This study examines genetic diversity and population structure of Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) colonies along the Atlantic coast using microsatellite markers. We analyzed 120 individuals from six breeding sites experiencing habitat degradation. Results indicate moderate genetic differentiation (FST=0.08) and significant isolation-by-distance, suggesting limited dispersal capabilities. Bottleneck analysis revealed recent population declines in three colonies, correlating with wetland loss events. Findings highlight vulnerability to habitat fragmentation and emphasize the need for landscape-scale conservation strategies for this non-shorebird wading species.

We assessed juvenile Osprey survival along the Atlantic coast using satellite telemetry (n=35 fledglings). Annual survival probability was 0 38 (SE=0 11) during the first migration/post-fledging period Mortality drivers included severe weather events (42% of deaths), anthropogenic structures (collisions: 31%), and predation (19%). Coastal habitat degradation significantly reduced survival likelihood (β=-0.67, p<0 01). Results underscore vulnerability during early life stages amid changing environmental conditions.

Wilson's Plover (Charadrius wilsonia), nesting on southeastern Atlantic coast mudflats (31°12'N, 81°24'W), faces habitat loss from reclamation. We monitored 72 nests during 2021–2022 using camera traps and nest checks. Daily survival rate (DSR) declined significantly in drained areas (DSR=0·934 vs. 0·962 intact; β= -1·23, SE=0·31, p=0·001). Fledging success dropped 38% in reclaimed zones. Strategic buffer zones and hydrological restoration are critical for this declining species.

<jats:p> Cladonia arbuscula (Wallr.) Flotow sensu lato is a widespread species complex traditionally divided among several subspecies on the basis of thallus morphology and secondary chemistry. Here we examine the evolutionary relationships of four of these segregates, C. arbuscula subsp. beringiana Ahti, C. arbuscula subsp. squarrosa (Wallr.) Burgaz, C. mitis Sandst., and an unnamed subspecies (referred to as C. arbuscula subsp. squarrosa PD– strain) in an attempt to link them to specific genotypes. The internal transcribed spacer regions of the nuclear ribosomal DNA (ITS rDNA) and the β-tubulin genes were sequenced for phylogenetic and haplotype analyses. In addition, the ITS2 RNA region was folded and changes were applied to the evolutionary hypothesis. We conclude that morphological differentiation within C. arbuscula s.l. is largely independent of variation in ITS rDNA and β-tubulin sequences, notwithstanding the distinct albeit incomplete clade formed by C. mitis. Compensatory base changes in the ITS2 RNA secondary structure could not support reproductive isolation. It is recommended that C. mitis be recognized at the subspecific rank as C. arbuscula subsp. mitis , and that subsp. squarrosa be included in subsp. beringiana . The apparent lack of correlation in C. arbuscula between genetic variability in the mycobiont and observed morphological variation in the thallus is intriguing, and requires explanation. </jats:p>

We investigated mercury contamination in Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) populations across coastal Louisiana using stable isotope analysis (δ15N, δ13C) of feathers and blood. Samples from 35 individuals revealed elevated δ15N values correlating with mercury concentrations in liver tissue (r=0.72, p<0.001), indicating biomagnification through aquatic food webs. Habitat degradation metrics explained 41% of isotopic variation, demonstrating how wetland loss exacerbates contaminant exposure in this piscivorous wader. Our findings highlight vulnerability of non-shorebird waterbirds to pollution in altered estuaries.

We investigated climate change impacts on Great Egret (Ardea alba) nesting phenology in the Mississippi Delta using 25 years of colony monitoring data. Rising spring temperatures (β = 0·47 ± 0·08 days/°C; p < 0·01; n = 17 colonies) advanced egg-laying by 11·6 days since 1998. Reduced precipitation correlated with lower fledging success (r = 0·68; p < 0·001), suggesting hydrological changes may threaten wetland-dependent Ardeidae populations. This study demonstrates accelerating phenological shifts in non-Charadriiformes waterbirds.

This study evaluated the impacts of domestic dog (Canis familiaris) disturbance on Peruvian Thick-knee (Burhinus superciliaris) predator-prey dynamics within the Sechura Desert ecosystem, Peru (2021-2023). Using GPS telemetry (n=18 adults) and continuous focal observations (500 hr), we quantified foraging displacement responses and predation rates across disturbance gradients. High dog encounter rates (>1.2 encounters/hr) reduced foraging efficiency by 38% (95% CI: 29-47%; p<0.001) and increased nest abandonment by foxes (Lycalopex sechurae) 2.7-fold (OR=2.71, p=0.008). Results demonstrate that anthropogenic disturbance cascades through trophic levels, necessitating dog exclusion zones in critical shorebird habitats.

We assessed the impact of hydrological management on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) breeding success in 12 restored freshwater marshes (2018-2021). Using nest cameras and vegetation surveys (n=67 nests), we documented that artificial drawdowns exceeding 5 cm/week increased nest abandonment by 37% (p=0.008) due to premature exposure. Clutch survival correlated strongly with stable water levels (r=0.82) and dense cover of cattail (Typha spp.). These findings emphasize how water management for agriculture disrupts critical nesting habitat for this secretive rallid species.

We quantified energy expenditure in Surfbirds (Calidris virgata) during winter at Ocean Beach, California, USA, where beach nourishment projects alter intertidal habitat. Using accelerometry (n=22 birds) and prey sampling over two winters (2020-2022), we found foraging costs increased by 32% in nourished zones (95% CI: 18-46%, p=0.003) due to reduced prey density and increased sediment compaction. This elevated expenditure corresponded with a 19% decline in body condition (R²=0.41, p<0.001). Results indicate nourishment practices compromise energetic budgets, necessitating habitat management strategies that minimize sediment disruption for this declining shorebird.

This study quantifies morphological variation in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) across six Atlantic coastal marsh populations experiencing varying levels of human disturbance. We measured 215 adult specimens for bill length, tarsus length, and wing chord. Results indicate significant clinal variation in bill morphology correlated with salinity gradients and habitat fragmentation. Coastal development-driven marsh degradation was associated with reduced body size indices, suggesting adaptive responses to anthropogenic stressors distinct from predation pressures observed in Charadriiformes.
