Basic information on the distribution, spread and impacts of non-native species in the USA is not available to those who shape national environmental policy. Although the USA spends billions of dollars annually on introduced species research, monitoring and control efforts, only a limited number of government agencies or private institutions are able to provide definitive reports on more than a handful of these species at a national scale. Research on invasive species is only of marginal practical value if the information cannot be succinctly and effectively transmitted to those who determine the management policies, budgets and objectives. To remedy this situation, a national-scale approach for monitoring established non-native species has been developed under the auspices of the Heinz Center as part of ‘The State of the Nation’s Ecosystems’ project. This paper specifically describes the strategies for reporting on indicators for non-native vertebrate species developed through inputs by experts from academia, industry, environmental organisations and government.

We investigated the impact of invasive European green crabs (Carcinus maenas) on Herring Gull (Larus argentatus) foraging behavior in coastal Maine. Using GPS tracking and prey analysis, we documented significant dietary shifts and increased foraging effort in gulls exposed to crab-invaded habitats compared to control sites. Our results demonstrate how invasive species can indirectly alter avian predator-prey dynamics through competition for benthic invertebrates.

We investigated plastic ingestion rates and foraging site fidelity in Long-billed Curlews (Numenius americanus) wintering in Tomales Bay, California. Using GPS telemetry (n=22 birds tracked over 2 winters) and necropsy of salvaged carcasses (n=17), we documented plastic in 41% of gastrointestinal tracts (95% CI: 18-64%). Individuals exhibiting high foraging site fidelity to urbanized coastlines had 3.2 times higher plastic occurrence (OR=3.2, p=0.01) than those utilizing protected estuaries. Results indicate anthropogenic habitat selection as a key driver of plastic ingestion risk in this declining shorebird.

This study evaluates climate change impacts on Least Bittern (Ixobrychus exilis) nesting ecology in Mid-Atlantic coastal marshes. Using drone surveys and hydrological modeling (2015-2021), we quantified relationships between tidal inundation frequency and nest abandonment rates. Results demonstrate significant negative correlations between sea-level rise metrics and reproductive success (R²=0.78, p<0.01), with thermal stress further reducing chick survival. Projections indicate 67% habitat degradation by 2040 under RCP8.5, highlighting urgent conservation needs for marsh-obligate species.

We investigated microplastic ingestion effects on Mountain Plover (Charadrius montanus) movement ecology using GPS telemetry across Colorado shortgrass prairie (2019-2021). Of 32 adults tracked, individuals with detectable microplastics in fecal samples (n=14) exhibited 23% reduced daily displacement (mean ± SE: 1.2±0.3 km vs 1.5±0.2 km; p=0.02) and 19% lower nest attendance (GLMM, β=-0.31, CI: -0.55 to -0.07). Results suggest microplastic exposure may impair foraging efficiency in this declining grassland shorebird, warranting inclusion in habitat management frameworks.

This study investigated anthropogenic food subsidy utilization by Herring Gulls (Larus argentatus) foraging in urban refuse sites on the Baltic coast during 2018–2020. Using GPS trackers deployed on 25 breeding adults, we quantified landfill visitation frequency and correlated it with chick provisioning rates. Gulls consumed 87% less natural marine prey when foraging predominantly at landfills (R²=0·74, p<0·01), suggesting significant dietary shifts with potential fitness consequences.

This study examines Great Blue Heron (Ardea herodias) nesting success in managed freshwater wetlands of the Pacific Northwest. Using longitudinal nest monitoring (n=87 nests across 5 sites), we quantified impacts of hydrological regime alterations on chick survival rates. Results indicate that artificial water level fluctuations exceeding natural variability reduced fledging success by 32% (p<0.001) through increased predation and nest abandonment. Our findings highlight wetland management trade-offs between waterfowl habitat provision and maintaining stable conditions for wading bird reproduction.

We investigated the impact of recreational beach use on Piping Plover (Charadrius melodus) molt migration at Cape Henlopen, Delaware (USA) during 2018-2020. Using GPS telemetry (n=32 adults) and feather corticosterone analysis, we quantified disturbance frequency and physiological stress responses. Plovers exhibited 42% higher corticosterone levels (95% CI: 28-56%) and delayed molt initiation by 9.2 days (SE=1.8) in high-traffic zones (>50 visitors/day) compared to protected areas. These findings highlight the need for temporal beach closures during critical molt periods to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this threatened shorebird.

Conservation genetics of Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) populations in degraded freshwater marsh ecosystems revealed significant genetic structuring. Using microsatellite analysis of 12 loci across 6 breeding colonies (n=192), we documented reduced gene flow (Fst=0.14) and increased inbreeding coefficients (Fis=0.18) in hydrologically fragmented habitats. Mitochondrial DNA sequencing indicated historical connectivity loss correlated with ditching and drainage practices. Results emphasize the urgency of restoring wetland connectivity to maintain adaptive potential in isolated populations facing climate-induced habitat contraction.

Habitat selection by Ruddy Turnstones (Arenaria interpres morinella subspecies) within shell-rich intertidal zones of eastern Korea was quantified in relation to anthropogenic shell collection pressure. GPS trackers deployed on 42 adult individuals during 2016–2019 breeding seasons revealed avoidance of beaches with >2 shell collectors/km/day (β = -0.73; 95% CI: -0/91 to -0/55). Nests in such areas exhibited 18.7% lower hatching success (χ² = 5.32, df=1 p=0/021). These findings demonstrate that coastal shell harvesting necessitates spatial management practices to preserve critical feeding substrate.

This study examines juvenile survival rates of Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) populations along the Gulf Coast. Using a mark-recapture approach over three years (n=342 banded individuals), we quantified mortality drivers. Results indicate that entanglement in fishing gear accounts for 48% of juvenile mortality, exceeding mortality from avian predation (32%) and disease (12%). Coastal development reducing foraging habitat availability shows significant correlation with reduced survival (r=-0 71, p<0 01). Conservation strategies should prioritize bycatch mitigation and habitat protection initiatives.

This study examines Black Skimmer (Rynchops niger) stopover ecology along the Gulf Coast, focusing on habitat selection and anthropogenic threats. Using GPS tracking and habitat modeling, we identified critical estuarine foraging areas vulnerable to coastal development. Results show significant avoidance of high-traffic zones and preference for undisturbed sandbars. Population declines correlate with increased recreational disturbance and shoreline modification, highlighting conservation priorities for this non-shorebird species.

Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of American Coot (Fulica Americana) feathers revealed significant dietary shifts from agricultural wetlands to urban reservoirs during seasonal transitions. We sampled 84 individuals across the Pacific Flyway, finding higher δ¹³C values in wintering birds exploiting anthropogenic food sources, correlating with reduced body condition indices. Results demonstrate how hydrological alterations force facultative omnivores into suboptimal foraging habitats, with implications for coot population resilience under land-use change.

We investigated foraging habitat selection by Green Sandpipers (Tringa ochropus) in response to wetland drainage in the Biebrza Marshes, Poland (53°N, 22°E). Using GPS telemetry (n=12 birds tracked over 2 breeding seasons) and prey availability surveys, we quantified habitat use before and after drainage events. Post-drainage, individuals exhibited 42% reduced foraging time in affected zones (95% CI: -58% to -26%, p=0.003) and shifted to suboptimal habitats with 31% lower invertebrate biomass (p<0.001). Our results demonstrate acute sensitivity to hydrological alteration, highlighting the need for wetland conservation to maintain functional foraging landscapes for this declining shorebird species.

We investigated coastal foraging strategies of Brant (Branta bernicla) in the Hudson Bay region using stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N). Feather samples from molting adults indicated significant dietary shifts from eelgrass to marine macroalgae over two decades. This trophodynamic change correlated with coastal eutrophication (r=0.84, p<0·001) and concurrent loss of intertidal seagrass habitats.

We analyzed long-term (1987-2022) breeding data for Ospreys (Pandion haliaetus) in Chesapeake Bay to quantify demographic changes. Using multi-state mark-recapture models (n=1,748 banded individuals), we documented significant declines in adult survival rates (-1.7% annually; P<0 .01), particularly impacting prime-age breeders (5-12 yrs). Nesting success decreased by 4.3 percentage points per decade (P=0.03), primarily due to increased frequency of hypoxic events affecting prey delivery. Climate-driven expansion of Bald Eagle (Haliaeetus leucocephalus) territories intensified nest competition, reducing reproductive output.

<jats:p>Comparative cognitive and behavior research aims to investigate cognitive evolution by comparing performance in different species to understand how these abilities have evolved. Ideally, this requires large and diverse samples; however, these can be difficult to obtain by single labs or institutions, leading to potential reproducibility and generalization issues with small, less representative samples. To help mitigate these issues, we are establishing a multi-site collaborative Open Science approach called ManyBirds, with the aim of providing new insight into the evolution of avian cognition and behavior through large-scale comparative studies, following the lead of exemplary ManyPrimates, ManyBabies and ManyDogs projects. Here, we outline a) the replicability crisis and why we should study birds, including the origin of modern birds, avian brains and convergent evolution of cognition; b) the current state of the avian cognition field, including a ‘snapshot’ review; c) the ManyBirds project, with plans, infrastructure, limitations, implications and future directions. In sharing this process, we hope that this may be useful for other researchers in devising similar projects in other taxa, like non-avian reptiles or mammals, and to encourage further collaborations with ManyBirds and related ManyX projects. Ultimately, we hope to promote collaboration between ManyX projects to allow for wider investigation of the evolution of cognition across all animals, including potentially humans.</jats:p>

We examined Willet (Tringa semipalmata) habitat selection vulnerability to oil spills along the Louisiana Gulf Coast during 2019-2021 using GPS telemetry (n=38 birds). Kernel density analysis revealed disproportionate usage of saltmarsh edge habitats within documented oil spill trajectories (mean selection index 2.3 ± 0.4 SE vs 0.7 ± 0 2 for inland marshes; p=0.007). Projected mortality increased 27% under modelled spill scenarios. Conservation efforts must prioritize spill-resistant marsh restoration.

We investigated competitive interactions between American Avocets (Recurvirostra americana) and Black-necked Stilts (Himantopus mexicanus) in the Great Salt Lake wetlands, Utah, USA (2018-2020). Using focal animal sampling (n=42 avocets, 38 stilts) across 12 saline ponds, we quantified foraging niche overlap via prey size selection (Mann-Whitney U=312, p=0.02) and habitat partitioning. Avocets shifted to deeper water (>15 cm) when stilt density exceeded 0.8 birds/ha, reducing bill-sweeping efficiency by 22% (95% CI: 15-29%). Results indicate asymmetric competition favoring stilts, necessitating habitat mosaics to prevent avocet exclusion in shrinking saline wetlands.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p><jats:italic>Tenuisvalvae notata</jats:italic> (Mulsant) (Coccinellidae) is a predatory ladybird beetle native to South America. It specializes in mealybugs prey (Pseudococcidae), but relatively little is known about its ecology. In contrast, the ladybird beetle <jats:italic>Cryptolaemus montrouzieri</jats:italic> Mulsant (Coccinellidae) is indigenous to Australia and has been introduced to many countries worldwide including Brazil for biological control of mealybugs. The potential impacts of these introductions to native coccinellids have rarely been considered. The software CLIMEX estimated the climate suitability for both species as reflected in the Ecoclimatic Index (EI). Much of South America, Africa, and Australia can be considered climatically suitable for both species, but in most cases, the climate is considerably more favorable for <jats:italic>C. montrouzieri</jats:italic> than <jats:italic>T. notata</jats:italic>, especially in South America. The CLIMEX model also suggests seasonal differences in growth conditions (e.g. rainfall and temperature) that could affect the phenology of both species. These models suggest that few locations in South America would be expected to provide <jats:italic>T. notata</jats:italic> climatic refugia from <jats:italic>C. montrouzieri</jats:italic>. Although other ecological factors will also be important, such as prey availability, this analysis suggests a strong potential for displacement of a native coccinellid throughout most of its range as a consequence of the invasion by an alien competitor.</jats:p>

This study examines habitat selection patterns of Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) populations along the Maine coast during winter. Using GPS telemetry and resource selection functions, we quantified eider preferences for sheltered bays with eelgrass beds versus exposed rocky shores. Results indicate strong selection for shallow subtidal zones (<5m depth) with high benthic invertebrate biomass, particularly avoiding areas with high vessel traffic. Eider occupancy declined significantly in sites experiencing coastal development, suggesting sensitivity to anthropogenic disturbance. Management implications emphasize protecting inshore foraging habitats from dredging and recreational boating pressures.

This study examines the impacts of recreational boating on American Coot (Fulica americana) nesting success in freshwater marshes of the Upper Mississippi River. Using observational surveys and nest monitoring across 12 sites with varying disturbance levels, we documented significant negative correlations between boat traffic frequency and coot clutch survival rates (r = -0.78, p<0.01). Disturbance-induced nest abandonment was highest during peak incubation periods, suggesting management should prioritize temporal restrictions during critical breeding phases.

<jats:p>Medicinal plants (MPs) are important resources widely used in the treatment and prevention of diseases and have attracted much attention owing to their significant antiviral, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and other activities. However, soil degradation, caused by continuous cropping, excessive chemical fertilizers and pesticide residues and heavy metal contamination, seriously restricts the growth and quality formation of MPs. Microorganisms, as the major biota in soil, play a critical role in the restoration of the land ecosystem. Rhizosphere microecology directly or indirectly affects the growth and development, metabolic regulation and active ingredient accumulation of MPs. Microbial resources, with the advantages of economic efficiency, harmless to environment and non-toxic to organisms, have been recommended as a promising alternative to conventional fertilizers and pesticides. The introduction of beneficial microbes promotes the adaptability of MPs to adversity stress by enhancing soil fertility, inhibiting pathogens and inducing systemic resistance. On the other hand, it can improve the medicinal quality by removing soil pollutants, reducing the absorption and accumulation of harmful substances and regulating the synthesis of secondary metabolites. The ecological and economic benefits of the soil microbiome in agricultural practices are increasingly recognized, but the current understanding of the interaction between soil conditions, root exudates and microbial communities and the mechanism of rhizosphere microecology affecting the secondary metabolism of MPs is still quite limited. More research is needed to investigate the effects of the microbiome on the growth and quality of different medicinal species. Therefore, the present review summarizes the main soil issues in medicinal plant cultivation, the functions of microbes in soil remediation and plant growth promotion and the potential mechanism to further guide the use of microbial resources to promote the ecological cultivation and sustainable development of MPs.</jats:p>

This study employs stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) to investigate trophic position and habitat use of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations in Mid-Atlantic tidal marshes. We analyzed feather samples from 42 individuals across six wetland complexes experiencing varying degrees of anthropogenic degradation. Results indicate significant isotopic shifts toward marine-derived nutrients in fragmented habitats (p<0.01), suggesting altered foraging strategies due to freshwater wetland loss. Our findings demonstrate how coastal development disrupts trophic pathways for this secretive rallid species, with implications for marsh conservation planning.

This study examines parental care behaviors in Virginia Rails (Rallus limicola), focusing on sex-specific contributions to chick provisioning. Using radio telemetry and direct observation at 12 wetland sites, we quantified feeding rates and habitat use during the nestling period (May-July 2019). Males provisioned chicks at significantly higher rates than females (p=0.

We assessed invasive Pacific oyster (Crassostrea gigas) impacts on Pied Avocet (Recurvirostra avosetta) reproductive success under coastal development pressure in the Dutch Wadden Sea (2018-2021). Nest monitoring (n=142) and GPS-tagged foraging surveys revealed oyster density negatively predicted clutch survival (β=-0.67, 95% CI: -1.21 to -0.13; p=0.017), with 42% lower hatching rates in high-development zones. Shoreline hardening increased foraging trip duration by 38% (p=0.003). Results demonstrate synergistic threats requiring integrated invasive species management and setback buffers.

<jats:p><jats:bold>Abstract:</jats:bold> Remote camera traps are becoming an increasingly popular, affordable, and valuable tool for wildlife research. However, theft and vandalism of these camera systems can result in substantial financial loss and loss of valuable data. We developed an adjustable steel camera security box to protect our Cuddeback® (Non Typical, Inc., Park Falls, WI) digital scouting cameras. Our cameras were deployed for 160 days and experienced no theft or vandalism during that time. Our armored camera box successfully protected our equipment and data, can be sized to accommodate any brand of camera, and can be used in a variety of field situations.</jats:p>

We quantified the impact of recreational shell collection on juvenile Black-bellied Plover (Pluvialis squatarola) survival during wintering periods along Georgia's barrier islands (2018-2021). Using VHF telemetry (n=52 juveniles), we tracked daily survival across three shell-harvesting intensity zones. Juveniles in high-harvest areas exhibited significantly reduced survival probability (Φ=0.78, SE±0.04) compared to low-harvest zones (Φ=0.93, SE±0.02; HR=2.81, p=0.008, 95% CI: 1.31-6.04). Shell removal reduced critical invertebrate prey abundance by 62% (ANOVA F₂‚₉=18.3, p<0.001), forcing prolonged foraging in high-risk intertidal areas. These findings demonstrate that unregulated shell collection directly threatens juvenile plover populations, necessitating seasonal harvest bans in critical foraging habitats.

<jats:p>O objetivo deste trabalho foi descrever e ilustrar os caracteres morfológicos de fruto, semente e plântula de Annona crassiflora, A. squamosa e A. muricata. Foram avaliados, em 50 frutos de cada espécie, a forma, coloração, peso, diâmetros longitudinal e transversal, peso da polpa, peso da casca + receptáculo, peso das sementes e número de sementes por fruto. Também foram determinados diâmetros longitudinal e transversal, espessura e peso individual de 100 sementes de cada espécie. Para o estudo da morfologia de plântulas, a semeadura foi efetuada em substrato contendo terra e areia (3:1) em DIC, com quatro repetições de 25 sementes para cada espécie. Foram realizadas observações diárias sendo determinadas oito fases de desenvolvimento. Os frutos das três espécies são múltiplos formados por numerosos frutículos, concrescidos entre si, formando um sincarpo; as sementes são glabras de forma oblonga e testa dura. Na análise dos dados biométricos foi observada uma grande variabilidade interespecífica, sendo que em todas as espécies a polpa revelou-se o principal constituinte dos frutos. A. crassiflora e A. squamosa apresentaram germinação epígeo-fanerocotiledonar e A. muricata, hipógea criptocotiledonar. Em cada espécie, os aspectos morfológicos, nas distintas fases, apresentaram-se homogêneos e constantes podendo ser seguramente empregados em estudos taxonômicos e ecológicos. </jats:p>

We investigated the impact of recreational photography on Red Phalarope (Phalaropus fulicarius) breeding ecology under climate change stressors in the Canadian High Arctic (Nunavut, 78°N). Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=42) and nest monitoring (2018-2021), we quantified disturbance frequency and duration. Photography events increased nest abandonment by 27% (95% CI: 15-39%) during warm years (mean summer temp >5°C), exacerbating climate-driven phenological mismatches. Conservation requires seasonal no-access zones around hypersensitive breeding ponds.

American Avocet (Recurvirostra americana) foraging ecology was studied in relation to human disturbance and brine shrimp (Artemia franciscana) fluctuations at Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Utah (2019-2022). Using GPS telemetry (n=41 adults) and invertebrate sampling across disturbance gradients, we quantified prey availability and foraging efficiency. High-disturbance sites showed 32% lower brine shrimp density (95% CI: -27% to -37%) and 24% reduced avocet peck rates (p=0.008) compared to controls. This demonstrates how human activity exacerbates climate-driven food resource instability, necessitating disturbance buffers around critical hypersaline foraging habitats.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) during post-breeding dispersal along coastal Texas. Using GPS telemetry on 22 individuals, we determined occupancy probabilities for mangrove inlets vs. artificial seawalls relative to prey density, human disturbance, and water quality indices. Pelicans showed avoidance of developed shorelines (Coeff = -0.74±0.18 SE, p<0·001), preferentially utilizing undisturbed tidal channels despite lower prey biomass availability. Conservation implications emphasize protecting mangrove ecosystems from coastal armoring.

<jats:p>This research deals with an efficient and low cost methodology to obtain a metric and photorealstic survey of a complex architecture. Photomodeling is an already tested interactive approach to produce a detailed and quick 3D model reconstruction. Photomodeling goes along with the creation of a rough surface over which oriented images can be back-projected in real time. Lastly the model can be enhanced checking the coincidence between the surface and the projected texture. The challenge of this research is to combine the advantages of two technologies already set up and used in many projects: spherical photogrammetry (Fangi, 2007,2008,2009,2010) and structure for motion (Photosynth web service and Bundler + CMVS2 + PMVS2). The input images are taken from the same points of view to form the set of panoramic photos paying attention to use well-suited projections: equirectangular for spherical photogrammetry and rectilinear for Photosynth web service. The performance of the spherical photogrammetry is already known in terms of its metric accuracy and acquisition quickness but time is required in the restitution step because of the manual homologous point recognition from different panoramas. In Photosynth instead the restitution is quick and automated: the provided point clouds are useful benchmarks to start with the model reconstruction even if lacking in details and scale. The proposed workflow needs of ad-hoc tools to capture high resolution rectilinear panoramic images and visualize Photosynth point clouds and orientation camera parameters. All of them are developed in VVVV programming environment. 3DStudio Max environment is then chosen because of its performance in terms of interactive modeling, UV mapping parameters handling and real time visualization of projected texture on the model surface. Experimental results show how is possible to obtain a 3D photorealistic model using the scale of the spherical photogrammetry restitution to orient web provided point clouds. Moreover the proposed research highlights how is possible to speed up the model reconstruction without losing metric and photometric accuracy. In the same time, using the same panorama dataset, it picks out a useful chance to compare the orientations coming from the two mentioned technologies (Spherical Photogrammetry and Structure for Motion).</jats:p>

We investigated how altered precipitation regimes affect Spotted Sandpiper (Actitis macularius) breeding ecology in managed wetlands of the Prairie Pothole Region (North Dakota, USA). Using nest monitoring (n=127 nests) and hydrological modeling across 2018-2021, we found that increased spring precipitation delayed nest initiation by 5.2 days per 100mm rainfall anomaly (95% CI: 3.1-7.3). Nest survival probability declined from 0.42 to 0.28 under extreme wet scenarios in our simulations. These precipitation-mediated phenological shifts reduce reproductive output, highlighting the need for adaptive water-level management in climate-vulnerable shorebird habitats.

We investigated Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) breeding biology in the Chesapeake Bay estuary during 2018-2020. Using nest monitoring and GPS tracking, we assessed clutch size (mean=3.2±0.4 eggs), fledging success (68%), and foraging range (median=4.7 km). Key threats included habitat degradation from shoreline development (27% colony decline) and increased boat traffic disrupting parental provisioning. Results demonstrate vulnerability of wading birds to anthropogenic pressures despite wetland protections.

Abstract Hawkmoths (Lepidoptera, Sphingidae) comprise around 1500 species, most of which forage on nectar from flowers in their adult stage, usually while hovering in front of the flower. The majority of species have a nocturnal lifestyle and are important nocturnal pollinators, but some species have turned to a diurnal lifestyle. Hawkmoths use visual and olfactory cues including CO 2  and humidity to detect and recognise rewarding flowers; they find the nectary in the flowers by means of mechanoreceptors on the proboscis and vision, evaluate it with gustatory receptors on the proboscis, and control their hovering flight position using antennal mechanoreception and vision. Here, we review what is presently known about the sensory organs and sensory-guided behaviour that control feeding behaviour of this fascinating pollinator taxon. We also suggest that more experiments on hawkmoth behaviour in natural settings are needed to fully appreciate their sensory capabilities.

This study examines the impact of wetland degradation on Great Egret (Ardea alba) nesting success in the Mississippi River Delta. Using a combination of aerial surveys and nest monitoring over three breeding seasons (2019-2021), we documented significant declines in fledging rates correlated with marsh subsidence and invasive plant encroachment. Generalized linear mixed models revealed that nest abandonment increased by 37% in areas experiencing >15 cm/year land loss. Our findings highlight the vulnerability of colonial wading birds to coastal habitat fragmentation and underscore the need for targeted marsh restoration efforts.

We investigated how dredging operations affect migration ecology of Solitary Sandpiper (Tringa solitaria) using GPS telemetry in the Peace-Athabasca Delta, Canada (2019-2021). 20 adults received solar-powered transmitters (1.5g). Individuals exposed to active dredging (n=9) showed 43% reduced foraging time (95% CI: -68% to -18%, p=0·007) and prolonged stopover durations (mean +4·3 days vs. controls, p=0·028) during fall migration in 2020/2021 seasons. These results indicate that sediment removal severely disrupts energy accumulation, necessitating pre-dredging assessments and buffer zones around critical wetland habitats.

We investigated climate change impacts on Limosa limosa breeding success via trophic mismatches in the Friesland peatlands, Netherlands (2015–2020). Using weekly arthropod sampling (n=1,200 quadrats) and nest monitoring (n=87 pairs), we quantified phenological shifts. A 1°C spring warming advanced Tipulidae emergence by 4.2 days (95% CI: 2.8–5.6) but reduced godwit chick survival by 18% (β = -0.32, p=0.008) due to prey scarcity during peak demand. Adaptive water management is critical to buffer climate-driven resource asynchrony.

We investigated the effect of wetland loss on Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) survival rates in the Gulf Coast region using mark-recapture data (2018-2022). Coastal development reduced available habitat by 38%, correlating with declining juvenile recruitment (β = -0 72; p<0.001). Adults showed compensatory survival responses but population viability analysis projected a 32% decline under current trends.

We investigated trophic niche partitioning in Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations across freshwater wetlands using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N). Samples from breast feathers revealed significant isotopic differences between juveniles and adults, indicating ontogenetic dietary shifts. Habitat degradation from agricultural runoff correlated with reduced isotopic niche breadth, suggesting decreased foraging flexibility. This study demonstrates how isotopic signatures can track ecological impacts on cryptic marsh birds.

<jats:p>Facilities at AARC include an acoustic wind tunnel (AWT), a pressurized pulse tube, and a reverberant water tank. The AWT may also be used as an anechoic room. The AWT was designed primarily for the acoustic evaluation of submersible propulsors. It is large enough to use prototype hardware for an important class of such vehicles. A model afterbody with control surfaces and propulsor is submerged in an open jet surrounded by a large anechoic room. In addition to the low background noise levels and turbulence required for this duty, the AWT has a unique nose-sting model mounting arrangement that avoids the noise and flow disturbances of strut or wire supports. The pulse tube provides measurements of reflection and transmission properties of materials and coating systems samples at submergence pressures to 1000 psi and with controllable temperature. The acoustic water tank provides a highly reverberant facility useful for measurement of radiated power from submerged sources and has been used to measure radiation transfer gains by the application of reciprocity.</jats:p>

This study examines the impact of wetland degradation on genetic diversity in Great Egret (Ardea alba) populations across the Mississippi Flyway. Using microsatellite analysis of 200 individuals from 12 breeding colonies, we detected significant population structuring (FST = 0.083) and reduced heterozygosity in agriculturally fragmented habitats. Landscape genomic models revealed strong associations between allelic richness and marsh connectivity (R² = 0.67), highlighting how drainage practices erode adaptive potential. Our findings emphasize the need for wetland corridors to maintain gene flow in this non-migratory heron species facing climate-induced habitat contraction.

This study investigates the impact of declining sardine stocks on Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) foraging efficiency along the California Current. Using GPS tracking and dive loggers on 32 individuals, we quantified plunge-dive success rates relative to prey density surveys. Results demonstrated significant reductions in foraging yield (p<0.01) during low-sardine periods, with compensatory increases in foraging time elevating energy expenditure by 37%. Findings highlight how fisheries-induced prey depletion threatens pelican energetics despite adaptive behavioral responses. Conservation must address forage fish management to buffer cascading effects.

This study examines the impact of coastal marsh fragmentation on Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) wintering ecology across the Mississippi Flyway. Using GPS telemetry and habitat modeling, we quantified resource selection in 120 individuals across degraded estuarine landscapes. Results indicate 32% lower occupancy in fragmented zones, with salinity intrusion and anthropogenic disturbance reducing foraging efficiency. Community-level analysis revealed displacement by invasive aquatic vegetation. Conservation requires integrated watershed management to maintain brackish wetland mosaics.

This study examines parental care behaviors in Ring-billed Gulls (Larus delawarensis), a species exhibiting facultative colonial nesting. Through focal observations across 24 nests at an inland reservoir colony, we quantified provisioning rates and nest defense responses to simulated predator intrusions. Results indicate biparental investment with males provisioning at higher rates than females (t-test; p<0 .01), while both sexes showed equivalent aggression intensity against intruders. Brood size positively correlated with feeding frequency (r=0 .68), suggesting compensatory care strategies. These findings highlight plastic behavioral adaptations in a non-migratory population facing increased avian predation pressure due to wetland habitat fragmentation.

We investigated how coastal sediment disturbance affects foraging efficiency in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima). Using focal sampling across four tidal cycles in Nova Scotia, we quantified benthic prey availability via coring and recorded dive metrics. Eiders increased dive duration significantly (p<0·001) in disturbed sites with lower prey density but similar community composition. This suggests compensatory energy expenditure in degraded habitats may impact winter survival.

In the present work, bee foraging plants were determined by palynological analysis of colony stored samples (honey and pollen) of Apis dorsata collected from southern West Bengal, India. Then flowering phenology and pollen morphologies were described to evaluate the forage preference of the bee species. In addition, chemical cues were analysed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Foraging strategy of the bee species was profitable in that almost all the bee-visited plants were utilised for both nectar and pollen sources. The bee species became generalist visitor of several plants having diverse life form, flower characters and pollen morphologies. However, most of the bee-visited plants were of trees with synchronous type of flowering. Most plants had small-sized, yellow, cream and white coloured flowers and pollen was openly presented. We did not find any patterns in the morphological traits of bee collected pollen, though the pollen types were predominantly of medium sized with trizonocolporate apertural pattern and reticulate surface ornamentation. Floral volatile organic compounds (VOCs) of bee visited plants were also diversified. Compounds frequently found in the floral VOC bouquets were amphetamine-3-methyl; butane, 2-cyclopropyl; 2,3-butanediol; cyclohexan, 1-methyl-5-(1-methylethyl); d-limonene; methyl (2E)-2-methoxy-2-butenoate; phenol, 4-[2-(methylamino)ethyl]; phthalic acid, di(2-propylpentyl)ester; propanamide, N-(aminocarbonyl) and pyrrolo[1,2-a]pyrazine-1,4-dione, hexahydro-3-(2-methylpropyl). In conclusion, floral traits and chemical cues of plants influence the host selection specificity (to collect floral rewards) of the rock bees.

We investigated the impacts of ocean acidification on Wattled Jacana (Jacana jacana) foraging ecology using GPS telemetry in the Pantanal wetlands, Brazil (2019-2021). Twenty adults were tracked for 12 months; δ13C analysis revealed a 32% decline in aquatic invertebrate consumption in acidified habitats (pH < 7.2) versus controls (p = 0.008). Nest abandonment rates increased by 40% in affected areas. Results demonstrate acidification-induced trophic shifts threaten jacana reproductive success, necessitating wetland carbonate buffering conservation measures.

We investigated the impacts of beach nourishment on post-breeding molt migration of Piping Plovers (Charadrius melodus) along the US Atlantic Coast. Using GPS tags (n=38) deployed on adults from Massachusetts to Virginia during 2018-2021, we tracked movement patterns to molting sites. Plovers utilizing nourished beaches (n=12) exhibited delayed migration onset by 8.7±1.9 days (p=0.01) and used 37% fewer stopover sites compared to controls (n=26; p=0.03). Our results demonstrate that habitat alteration significantly disrupts pre-migration fueling, suggesting nourishment projects should incorporate temporal buffers around migration periods.

Abstract
            
              Iron in root plaque is usually thought to be Fe(III) because of rhizosphere oxidation. This study was conducted to examine Fe oxidation states on root surfaces of the common reed [
              Phragmites australis
              (Cav.) Trin. ex Steudel]. Using an EDTA‐BPDS method, Fe(II) and Fe(III) on the surfaces of roots sampled from various environments were stabilized, extracted and determined simultaneously. The proportion of extracted Fe(II) to total Fe ranged from 0.17 to 0.65 for the roots grown in constructed wetlands, fields, and hydroponic culture; and from 0.34 to 0.70 for different sections of wetland plant roots. The observed results suggested that Fe plaque is caused not only by rhizosphere oxidation, but also by Fe(II) compound formation on the root surfaces.

This study examines the impact of hydrological regime alterations on Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor) nesting success in managed wetlands of the southeastern US. Using a before-after-control-impact design across 12 sites, we monitored 127 nests over two breeding seasons. Results indicate that controlled drawdown timing significantly influences fledging rates (β=0.47, p<0.01), with premature water level reductions correlating with increased nest abandonment. Our findings underscore the importance of synchronizing wetland management practices with heron reproductive phenology to mitigate anthropogenic impacts on this species of conservation concern.

Stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of osprey (Pandion haliaetus) nestlings' blood and prey remains quantified marine vs. freshwater foraging plasticity near industrialized coasts. Higher trophic enrichment in δ¹⁵N correlated with prey from contaminated estuaries. Isotopic niches differed significantly between riverine and coastal colonies, indicating site-specific threats from bioaccumulative pollutants. Results reveal ospreys serve as sentinels for ecosystem health in non-estuarine habitats.

              2
              evolution measured by the inverted— and closed—box methods did not differ significantly (P>0.2). Respiration rates from bagged oak leaves were significantly correlated (P<0.01) with respiration rates from the floor in an oak stand, but not with rates in pine and maple stands.
