Rates of respiration from the floors of pine, oak, and maple stands were not significantly different (P>0.05).

This study investigates the breeding ecology of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola), a secretive marsh-nesting rail, in southern Ontario wetlands from 2018–2020. Using nest monitoring and radio-telemetry (n=32 pairs), we quantified reproductive success in relation to hydrological fluctuations and vegetative structure. Nest survival declined sharply during seasonal water drawdowns (β = -1.73, SE=0 31), with predation accounting for 78% of failures. Conservation requires maintaining stable water levels and dense emergent vegetation during April–July breeding periods.

We investigated parental care trade-offs in American Oystercatchers (Haematopus palliatus) exposed to agricultural pesticide runoff along Georgia's Altamaha River estuary (2018-2020). Using GPS-tracked foraging paths (n=22 breeding pairs) and plasma cholinesterase assays, we quantified time allocation during incubation. Adults from contaminated sites (mean cholinesterase inhibition: 42.7±5.8%) spent 31% less time incubating (p=0.008) and showed 2.3-fold higher nest abandonment rates versus controls. Reduced parental investment correlated with 18% lower fledging success (95% CI: -27% to -9%). Results demonstrate sublethal pesticide effects disrupt biparental care dynamics in coastal Charadriiformes, necessitating buffer zones around critical nesting habitats.

This study investigates climate change effects on the breeding phenology and reproductive success of the Common Eider (Somateria mollissima), a coastal duck species nesting in arctic ecosystems. We analyzed 25 years of nest monitoring data from Greenland and Iceland coastal colonies, correlating clutch initiation dates and hatching success with spring sea ice retreat and temperature anomalies. Results show significantly advanced breeding phenology (β = -0·76 days/year, P < 0·001) but reduced hatching rates associated with earlier ice melt (r = -0·83, P = 0·002), suggesting mismatch risks as climate warming accelerates.

The impact of photography disturbance on Mountain Plover (Charadrius montanus) breeding ecology was assessed in Wyoming's Thunder Basin grasslands (2019-2021). We monitored 87 nests using time-lapse cameras and GPS-loggers, quantifying photographer approach frequency and distance. Nests with >2 daily approaches within 50m experienced 32% lower hatching success (β = -0.41, 95% CI: -0.68 to -0.14, p = 0.003) and 4.2× higher abandonment risk (OR = 4.2, p < 0.001) versus controls. Results demonstrate acute sensitivity to photographic pressure, necessitating 100m seasonal buffer zones in management plans for this declining Charadriiform.

Climate-driven shifts in bivalve prey availability threaten American Oystercatcher (Haematopus palliatus) populations along the Mid-Atlantic Bight. We assessed genetic vulnerability in 126 individuals across 12 breeding colonies (VA to NY, 2019-2021) using reduced-representation genome sequencing (ddRAD). Populations experiencing >30% prey biomass decline exhibited 18% lower nucleotide diversity (π=0.0011 vs 0.0017, p=0.003) and elevated inbreeding coefficients (Fis=0.12 vs 0.04, p<0.01). Bayesian clustering revealed novel genetic structure (K=4) correlated with historical shellfish abundance gradients. Results indicate rapid genetic erosion from trophic mismatch, necessitating targeted habitat restoration to maintain adaptive potential.

We investigated the impact of wetland drainage on Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) foraging ecology using stable isotope analysis (δ¹³C, δ¹⁵N) of feather samples collected from 42 individuals across 7 coastal sites in southern California, USA (2018-2020). Results indicated significantly depleted δ¹³C values (-24.3‰ ± 0.7 vs. -21.1‰ ± 0.9; p=0.002) and reduced trophic position (δ¹⁵N: 8.2‰ ± 0.5 vs. 9.8‰ ± 0.6; p<0.001) in drained wetlands compared to intact habitats. These shifts reflect decreased estuarine prey consumption and reduced dietary quality, highlighting wetland drainage as a critical threat requiring targeted conservation interventions for this federally threatened shorebird.

We investigated Brant goose (Branta bernicla) winter habitat selection in coastal marshes across the Atlantic Flyway. Using GPS telemetry (n=48 individuals) and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs), we assessed resource selection functions relative to anthropogenic disturbance and Spartina alterniflora availability. Disturbance from recreational boating significantly reduced eelgrass utilization (β=−0.27,p<0 01). Conservation priorities should mitigate human recreational impacts on submerged aquatic vegetation.

<jats:p>One objective of establishing Yellowstone National Park was to minimize human influence on the biotic communities.  However, from the time of establishment (1872) through 1972, the policy was to suppress forest fires.  Since natural fires play an important role in many environments, their importance to the Yellowstone ecosystem is being assessed.  Little knowledge exists on avian succession immediately following a forest fire and several years postfire.</jats:p>

This study examines the impact of hydrological regime alterations on Black-crowned Night-Heron (Nycticorax nycticorax) nesting success in managed freshwater wetlands. Using nest monitoring and water level data from 2018-2022, we demonstrate that artificial drawdown timing significantly influences fledging rates (GLMM: β = 0.87, p<0.001). Early drawdowns reduced prey availability, causing 32% lower chick survival compared to natural hydroperiods. Results highlight the need for adaptive water management strategies prioritizing heron reproductive phenology in conservation planning.

This study examines nest site selection in Great Egrets (Ardea alba) within a southeastern US wetland complex. Using GPS telemetry and habitat modeling, we assessed how anthropogenic disturbances and hydrological changes influence colony establishment. Results reveal significant avoidance of areas with elevated human activity levels (>5 events/week) and preferential selection for stands >200m from roads. Rising water levels due to altered drainage patterns reduced suitable nesting habitat by 38% over three breeding seasons. Our findings emphasize vulnerability to habitat fragmentation and hydrological instability in managed wetlands, necessitating buffer zones around rookeries.

Our study evaluates how urban light pollution affects the nocturnal foraging efficiency of Sternula antillarum (Least Tern) along Mississippi River reservoirs. Using GPS tracking and fecal glucocorticoid analysis, we demonstrate that artificial lighting disrupts circadian rhythms, reducing chick provisioning rates by 37% and elevating corticosterone metabolites by 42% compared to dark-sky sites (p<0 001). This anthropogenic stressor may contribute to regional population declines in this insectivorous waterbird.

This study investigated the response of Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) populations to hydrological manipulation in managed coastal wetlands. Using mark-recapture techniques and vegetation surveys across 12 impoundments with varying water depth regimes over two annual cycles (2018–2020), we quantified how controlled drawdown timing influenced brood survival rates and invertebrate prey abundance. Results indicated earlier summer drawdowns reduced dipteran emergence by 42% (p<0·01), correlating with 31% lower duckling survival. Our findings underscore the critical importance of synchronizing wetland management schedules with waterfowl reproductive phenology.

{"abstract": "We investigated plastic ingestion in Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) relative to wetland management practices in Costa Rica's Palo Verde National Park (2018-2020). Necropsies (n=47) revealed 31.9\% individuals contained macroplastics (mean 3.2±1.8 particles/bird). Prevalence correlated inversely with hydrological manipulation frequency (β = -0·34, 95% CI -0.51 to -0·17; p = 0·002). Annual drawdown regimes reduced plastic accumulation but fragmented floating vegetation mats crucial for foraging. Conservation requires balancing water control with habitat integrity to mitigate this emerging threat."}

We investigated the impact of ocean acidification on migration ecology of Wandering Tattlers (Tringa incana) along the Pacific Flyway. Using miniaturized GPS loggers deployed on 32 individuals from Alaska breeding grounds (2019-2021), we tracked migration routes and stopover durations. Stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of feather samples revealed significant shifts in trophic position (Δδ15N = -0.8‰, p=0.01) at acidification-vulnerable coastal stopovers. Population modeling projected a 17% decline (95% CI: -24% to -9%) in migratory success by 2050 under RCP 8.5 scenarios, highlighting urgent conservation needs for intertidal habitats.

We investigated how human recreational disturbance exacerbates invasive European beachgrass (Ammophila arenaria) encroachment impacts on Black Turnstone (Arenaria melanocephala) breeding ecology in coastal Oregon, USA (2018-2021). Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=32) and nest monitoring (n=87 nests), we quantified displacement effects: turnstones avoided disturbed zones by 127±23m (mean±SE), reducing foraging time by 34% (p=0.008) in invaded habitats. Nest survival probability decreased by 0.18 (95% CI: 0.07-0.29) with combined disturbance and invasion. Conservation requires managing both stressors to prevent habitat degradation.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p> <jats:ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="#b75"><jats:bold>Valladares and Gianoli (2007)</jats:bold></jats:ext-link><jats:bold> tried to answer a key question, “how much ecology do we need to know to restore Mediterranean ecosystems?” by focusing on (1) plant–plant interactions; (2) environmental heterogeneity and the potential adaptation of transplanted plants; and (3) phenotypic plasticity of the planted species. We consider their choice of topics incomplete and potentially misleading because (1) it is clearly biased toward a narrow set of research topics (phenotypic plasticity, facilitation, and climate change); (2) it assumes that active restoration, and specifically revegetation, is needed; and (3) it conveys a false perception that other basic ecological aspects of Mediterranean ecosystems are sufficiently known. Instead, we review the current knowledge on seed dispersal, succession, and ecosystem functioning for Mediterranean ecosystems. We argue that decades of research on these topics have yielded few practical guidelines for restoration, something that needs to be urgently corrected. First, the current “establishment limitation paradigm” for plant recruitment does not acknowledge the role of dispersal limitation at large spatial scales. More attention should be paid to nucleation processes and directed seed dispersal mediated by animals. Second, studies of vegetation dynamics and succession in the Mediterranean have led to an overly simplistic view of successional dynamics. How fast and deterministic succession is remains mostly unexplored; long‐term monitoring of successional dynamics at different spatial scales is urgently needed. Third, information on the functional status of Mediterranean ecosystems is required to identify processes hindering natural recovery after disturbances and to set priorities on the areas and ecosystem components to be restored.</jats:bold> </jats:p>

This study examined molt migration ecology of Mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) in coastal Louisiana using GPS telemetry (n=48). We documented significant shifts from inland breeding areas to brackish marsh molting sites. Regression models revealed that marsh fragmentation (β = -0.72, p<0.01) and boat traffic disturbance (β = -0.54, p<0.05) negatively impacted feather regrowth rates. Conservation strategies must address estuarine habitat degradation to maintain critical molt staging areas for this declining waterfowl population.

Climate-induced storm intensification threatens shorebird foraging. We investigated storm impacts on Eurasian Oystercatcher (Haematopus ostralegus) foraging in the German Wadden Sea (2019-2022 winters). Using GPS-tracking (n=42) and focal observations, we quantified prey intake rates before/during/after storms. Foraging efficiency declined 28% during storms (p=0.003, CI:15-41%) due to reduced bivalve accessibility. Recovery required 3-5 days (LMM: p<0.001). Increased storminess necessitates adaptive management of intertidal habitats.

This study examines Snowy Egret (Egretta thula) population dynamics in the Gulf Coast region, focusing on anthropogenic threats. Using mark-recapture data from 2015-2020, we quantified annual survival rates and breeding success across 12 colonies. Key findings indicate significant declines in fledgling production (β = -0.32, p<0.01) correlated with coastal wetland degradation. Increased mercury contamination in prey items (mean ± SE: 0.87 ± 0.15 ppm) was associated with reduced hatching success. Our results highlight the vulnerability of Ardeidae species to habitat loss and bioaccumulation, necessitating targeted conservation measures beyond protected areas.

We investigated Brant (Branta bernicla) stopover ecology along the Mid-Atlantic coast using GPS telemetry and habitat surveys. From 2018-2020, we tracked 42 individuals to quantify site fidelity and resource selection in response to Spartina decline. Results show high fidelity to historically used marshes despite 60% habitat degradation. Birds compensated by increasing foraging time in remaining patches, leading to elevated stress hormone levels. This study highlights how coastal waterfowl persist through habitat loss but incur physiological costs during migration.

We investigated the impact of invasive European green crabs (Carcinus maenas) on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) foraging success in Chesapeake Bay estuaries. Using GPS telemetry and nest cameras, we monitored 22 breeding pairs from 2020-2022. Results showed a significant negative correlation (r = -0.72, p<0.001) between crab density and Osprey catch rates, with nestling provisioning rates declining by 32% in high-invasion sites. Our findings demonstrate how invasive prey species can disrupt trophic dynamics, potentially affecting raptor reproductive output in coastal ecosystems.

This study investigates the genetic structure and diversity of Common Eider (Somateria mollissima) populations along the northeastern Atlantic coast using microsatellite markers. We analyzed 200 individuals from 10 breeding colonies to assess the impact of habitat fragmentation and hunting pressure on gene flow. Results reveal significant population differentiation (FST = 0.12) and reduced heterozygosity in isolated subpopulations, indicating genetic erosion due to anthropogenic barriers to dispersal. Conservation strategies should prioritize maintaining connectivity corridors to mitigate inbreeding depression in this declining sea duck species.

We investigated morphological plasticity in Wilson's Snipe (Gallinago delicata) across a gradient of invasive reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea) encroachment in Wisconsin sedge meadows. From 2019-2021, we captured 127 adults at 12 sites, measuring bill length (mean ± SD: 66.3 ± 2.1 mm), tarsus length (34.8 ± 1.5 mm), and body mass (115.7 ± 8.3 g). Bill length increased significantly with invasive cover (R² = 0.37, p = 0.008), suggesting adaptive foraging responses. Our findings indicate that morphological shifts may buffer snipe populations against habitat degradation but highlight the need for invasive species control in critical wetland habitats.

We investigated the impact of coastal wetland degradation on the genetic structure of Pacific Brant (Branta bernicla nigricans). Using reduced-representation genome sequencing (ddRADseq) on 142 individuals across 8 Alaskan breeding colonies, we assessed population connectivity and effective population size (Ne). Anthropogenic habitat loss significantly reduced gene flow (FST = 0.15, p < 0 01), with distinct genetic clusters corresponding to fragmented estuarine habitats. These findings emphasize the role of eelgrass conservation in maintaining genetic diversity (mean He = 0.32) in this declining waterfowl species.

Bycatch mortality threatens the Double-striped Thick-knee (Burhinus bistriatus) in wetlands. We studied 42 radio-tagged individuals in Llanos de Moxos, Bolivia (2018–2020), using telemetry and daily surveys. Annual bycatch mortality was significantly higher in managed (19.2%; 95% CI: 13.4–25.0) than unmanaged sites (7.1%; 95% CI: 3.2–11.0; p=0.018). Wetland management must incorporate bycatch mitigation to conserve this species.

<jats:p>Dryland vegetation is inherently patchy. This patchiness goes on to impact ecology, hydrology, and biogeochemistry. Recently, researchers have proposed that dryland vegetation patch sizes follow a power law which is due to local plant facilitation. It is unknown what patch size distribution prevails when competition predominates over facilitation, or if such a pattern could be used to detect competition. We investigated this question in an alternative vegetation type, mosses and lichens of biological soil crusts, which exhibit a smaller scale patch‐interpatch configuration. This micro‐vegetation is characterized by competition for space. We proposed that multiplicative effects of genetics, environment and competition should result in a log‐normal patch size distribution. When testing the prevalence of log‐normal versus power law patch size distributions, we found that the log‐normal was the better distribution in 53% of cases and a reasonable fit in 83%. In contrast, the power law was better in 39% of cases, and in 8% of instances both distributions fit equally well. We further hypothesized that the log‐normal distribution parameters would be predictably influenced by competition strength. There was qualitative agreement between one of the distribution's parameters (μ) and a novel intransitive (lacking a ‘best’ competitor) competition index, suggesting that as intransitivity increases, patch sizes decrease. The correlation of μ with other competition indicators based on spatial segregation of species (the C‐score) depended on aridity. In less arid sites, μ was negatively correlated with the C‐score (suggesting smaller patches under stronger competition), while positive correlations (suggesting larger patches under stronger competition) were observed at more arid sites. We propose that this is due to an increasing prevalence of competition transitivity as aridity increases. These findings broaden the emerging theory surrounding dryland patch size distributions and, with refinement, may help us infer cryptic ecological processes from easily observed spatial patterns in the field.</jats:p>

We investigated the impact of recreational photography on American Avocet (Recurvirostra americana) breeding biology at Bear River Migratory Bird Refuge, Utah (2018-2020). Using nest cameras (n=42) and behavioral observations, we quantified disturbance frequency and nest success. Avocets exposed to >3 photographer approaches/day exhibited 32% lower hatching success (95% CI: -45% to -19%, p=0.007) and 2.3x higher nest abandonment rates compared to control sites. Our results demonstrate that unregulated photography constitutes a significant threat requiring buffer zones during incubation.

This study examines Northern Pintail (Anas acuta) habitat selection in managed coastal wetlands of California's Central Valley. Using GPS telemetry (n=32) and vegetation surveys, we assessed how water depth manipulation and invasive plant control influence pintail foraging site fidelity during winter. Results indicate pintails strongly prefer shallow (<15 cm) flooded areas with native sedge cover, avoiding monotypic stands of perennial pepperweed (Lepidium latifolium). Our findings demonstrate that targeted hydrological management can enhance habitat quality for declining dabbling duck populations amid agricultural encroachment.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Shear stress driven grain boundary (GB) migration was found to be a ubiquitous phenomenon in small grained polycrystalline materials. Here we show that the GB displacement shift complete (DSC) dislocation mechanism for GB shear coupled migration is still functioning even if the geometry orientation of the GBs deviates a few degrees from the appropriate coincidence site lattice (CSL) GBs. It means that any large angle GB can have a considerable chance to be such a “CSL-related GB” for which the shear coupled GB migration motion can happen by the GB DSC dislocation mechanism. We conclude that the CSL-DSC bi-crystallographic lattice structure in GB is the main reason that GB can migrate under shear stress.</jats:p>

<jats:p xml:lang="en">MedSens index provides the environmental status of subtidal rocky coastal habitats based on open data collected by trained volunteers using the Reef Check Mediterranean Underwater Coastal Environment Monitoring protocol. It is based on 25 species, incorporating their sensitivities to the EU Marine Strategy Framework Directive pressures and their distributions and abundances. MedSens was applied along the Tuscan Archipelago National Park Islands’ coasts, providing the mean sensitivity of the assemblages. It can help decision-makers in implementing marine biodiversity conservation measures.</jats:p>

Assessing anthropogenic disturbance impacts on Black-necked Stilt (Himantopus mexicanus) habitat selection in coastal wetlands is critical for conservation planning. We quantified photography pressure effects through behavioral observations (≥6m distance) in the Bolsa Chica Ecological Reserve, California (May-August 2020-2021). Human approach trials (n=124) showed a 68% reduction in foraging time (P<0·01; CI:-79·3% to -56·7%), while nest monitoring (n=37 pairs) revealed a 2·7× higher predation risk at high-disturbance sites. Conservation strategies must establish buffer zones around critical habitats to mitigate cumulative recreational impacts.

This study assesses human disturbance impacts on Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) colonies in Mississippi coastal wetlands. Through field observations and drone surveys during 2020-2022, we documented reduced chick survival rates near boat channels (β = -0⃰.29, p<0⃰.01) and increased nest abandonment with recreational shoreline access (OR = 4⃰.2). Management recommendations emphasize buffer zones.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:sec><jats:title>Aim</jats:title><jats:p>The biogeography of terrestrial organisms across the Florida Keys archipelago is poorly understood. We used population genetics and spatioecological modeling of the Amblypygi <jats:italic>Phrynus marginemaculatus</jats:italic> to understand the genetic structure and metapopulation dynamics of Keys populations that are otherwise isolated by human development and ocean.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Location</jats:title><jats:p>The Florida Keys archipelago and mainland Florida.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Methods</jats:title><jats:p>We sequenced a 1,238 bp fragment of mt<jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">DNA</jats:styled-content> for 103 individuals of <jats:italic>P. marginemaculatus</jats:italic> from 13 sites in the Florida Keys and South Florida, binned into four regions. We used population genetic analyses to understand the population structure of the species throughout its <jats:styled-content style="fixed-case">US</jats:styled-content> range. Furthermore, we used ecological modeling with climate, habitat, and human development data to develop habitat suitability estimates for the species.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Results</jats:title><jats:p>We found clear genetic structure between localities. The Lower Keys, in particular, support populations separate from those in other regions studied. Ecological modeling and genetic analyses showed the highest habitat suitability and genetic isolation in the Lower Keys, but urban development across the species range has resulted in the loss of most historical habitat.</jats:p></jats:sec><jats:sec><jats:title>Main conclusions</jats:title><jats:p>A mainland‐metapopulation model best fits <jats:italic>P. marginemaculatus</jats:italic> gene flow patterns in the Florida Keys and mainland. Ocean currents likely play a role in metapopulation dynamics and gene flow for terrestrial Keys species like <jats:italic>P. marginemaculatus</jats:italic>, and genetic patterns also matched patterns consistent with geologic history. Suitable habitat, however, is limited and under threat of human destruction. The few remaining pockets of the most suitable habitat tend to occur in parks and protected areas. We argue that conservation efforts for this species and others in the terrestrial Florida Keys would benefit from a deeper understanding of the population genetic structure and ecology of the archipelago.</jats:p></jats:sec>

We investigated nest site selection in Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) along coastal riverine systems in Maine, USA. Using logistic regression models, we assessed habitat variables influencing burrow establishment across 42 active and 58 inactive sites. Key predictors included bank height (β=0.87, p<0.001), soil composition (sand content: β=0.63, p=0.01), and distance to human disturbance (β=-1.22, p<0.001). Results indicate anthropogenic pressures significantly reduce suitable nesting habitat availability, with only 23% of surveyed banks meeting optimal criteria. Conservation strategies should prioritize riparian buffer zones to mitigate erosion and recreational impacts.

We quantified demographic consequences of heavy metal exposure in Spotted Sandpipers (Actitis macularius). From 2018-2021 at Detroit River International Wildlife Refuge (MI/ON), we monitored 47 breeding pairs, measuring cadmium (Cd) and lead (Pb) concentrations in blood (ICP-MS analysis). Integrated Population Models revealed elevated Cd levels (geometric mean ≥ 0.85 μg/g dw) reduced annual survival by 32% (β = -1·12, 95% CI: -1·98 - -0·26). Fledging success decreased by 24.3% per 1 μg/g Pb increment (GLMM: z = -2·89, p = 0·004). These findings highlight critical contamination thresholds requiring remediation in industrial riparian ecosystems.

We investigated phenological mismatch risk in Willet (Tringa semipalmata) breeding at Churchill, Manitoba (58°N, 94°W) during 2015-2020. Using temperature loggers and nest monitoring (n=127 nests), we quantified hatch date shifts relative to arthropod emergence. Hatch dates advanced by 0.8 days/decade (p=0.03), while prey emergence advanced by 1.2 days/decade (p<0.01), creating a mismatch gap. Nest survival declined with increasing mismatch (R²=0.47, p=0.002). Our results demonstrate climate-induced trophic asynchrony threatening subarctic shorebird productivity.

This study investigates juvenile survival rates in Great Egrets (Ardea alba) nesting in freshwater wetlands of the southeastern US. Using mark-recapture methods over three breeding seasons (2019-2021), we assessed impacts of hydrological variability and anthropogenic disturbance on fledgling recruitment. Results indicate significant negative effects of water level fluctuations (β = -0.37, p<0.01) and recreational boating activity (β = -0.29, p<0.05) on first-year survival. Management recommendations emphasize stabilizing wetland water regimes and establishing buffer zones to enhance recruitment in this declining wading bird population.

We investigated legacy contaminant accumulation in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) within an industrialized estuary. Tissue samples from 45 adults revealed high PCB concentrations (mean ± SE: 12.3 ± 1.8 μg/g wet weight). Generalized linear models demonstrated significant negative relationships between contaminant loads and eggshell thickness (β = -0.24, p < 0.001). Mercury burdens exceeded toxicity thresholds in 78% of sampled individuals, correlating with reduced fledgling survival rates (r = -0.68, p = 0.003). Results indicate persistent pollution impacts on piscivorous waterbirds despite regulatory controls.

We investigated juvenile survival of Common Ringed Plovers (Charadrius hiaticula) across predation gradients in Svalbard (78°N), where introduced Arctic foxes (Vulpes lagopus) significantly threaten ground-nesting birds (2018-2021). Using mark-recapture (n=143 fledglings with coded leg flags) and camera trapping at 32 nests, daily survival rate (DSR) modeling revealed a 68% reduction in fledgling survival where fox density exceeded 0·5/km² (β= -1.73, SE=0·8, p=0·001). Annual recruitment decreased from 0·23 to 0·07 individuals/km. We recommend targeted predator control and habitat restoration to sustain migratory populations under climate-driven predator range expansions.

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title><jats:p>Vine weevil, <jats:italic>Otiorhynchus sulcatus</jats:italic> F. (Coleoptera: Curculionidae), is widely considered to be one of the most economically important pests of soft-fruit and ornamental crops. The chemical ecology of vine weevil has been extensively studied in the pursuit of a semiochemical lure to improve monitoring tool sensitivity/reliability and develop novel control methods. Although vine weevil adults exhibit a strong tendency to aggregate, the mechanism underlying this behaviour has not, to date, been identified. It is notable, however, that previous studies have not considered the impact of feeding status on vine weevil aggregation behaviour. To investigate the importance of feeding status on aggregation behavior, this study recorded the responses of satiated and starved vine weevil adults to the odour of starved conspecifics. Satiated adults exhibited a preference for the odour of conspecifics while starved vine weevils exhibited no such preference. Therefore, this study provides evidence to support the hypothesis that feeding status is an important factor for vine weevil aggregation.</jats:p>

We quantified microplastic exposure effects on juvenile Green Sandpiper (Tringa ochropus) survival in the Odra River floodplains, Poland (2020-2022). Fecal samples (n=94 individuals) were analyzed for polymer composition via μFT-IR spectroscopy, while survival was monitored through radio-telemetry (mean tracking duration: 78±12 days). Juveniles with high microplastic burdens (>15 particles/g feces) showed 27% lower 90-day survival probability (HR=1.54; 95% CI: 1.21–1.96, p=0.002) compared to low-burden conspecifics, with polypropylene fragments being predominant (68%). Results demonstrate microplastic ingestion as a critical sublethal threat to early life-stage shorebirds, necessitating wetland pollution mitigation in key stopover habitats.

This study quantifies juvenile survival rates in Great Egret (Ardea alba) populations across managed wetlands in the southeastern US using radio-telemetry and mark-resight methodologies. We assessed how hydrological regimes altered by climate change and intensified agricultural runoff affect post-fledging mortality. Results indicate significantly reduced first-year survival (38% decline) associated with compromised prey availability and bioaccumulation of contaminants. Management interventions must address watershed-level pollution control to sustain recruitment in this wading bird species.

We investigated post-fledging dispersal patterns of Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) along the Gulf Coast using GPS telemetry. Twenty juvenile pelicans were tagged with solar-powered transmitters and tracked for 12 months. Results revealed extensive coastal movements exceeding 500 km, with individuals exhibiting high site fidelity to natal colonies during breeding seasons. Anthropogenic disturbances, particularly boat traffic near roosting sites, significantly reduced foraging efficiency. This study highlights the vulnerability of juvenile pelicans to coastal development pressures and informs conservation strategies for this protected species.

We investigated competitive interactions between invasive Common Carp (Cyprinus carpio) and native American Coots (Fulica americana) in freshwater wetlands. Using observational surveys and experimental exclosures, we quantified impacts on coot foraging efficiency and habitat use. Results indicate carp-induced turbidity reduces submerged macrophyte availability, forcing coots to shift diets toward less nutritious surface vegetation. This resource competition highlights carp invasion as an understudied threat to rallid waterbirds.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>The zebra mussel,<jats:italic>Dreissena polymorpha</jats:italic>, continues to spread from its native range in Eurasia to Europe and North America, causing billions of dollars in damage and dramatically altering invaded aquatic ecosystems. Despite these impacts, there are few genomic resources for<jats:italic>Dreissena</jats:italic>or related bivalves, with nearly 450 million years of divergence between zebra mussels and its closest sequenced relative. Although the<jats:italic>D. polymorpha</jats:italic>genome is highly repetitive, we have used a combination of long-read sequencing and Hi-C-based scaffolding to generate the highest quality molluscan assembly to date. Through comparative analysis and transcriptomics experiments we have gained insights into processes that likely control the invasive success of zebra mussels, including shell formation, synthesis of byssal threads, and thermal tolerance. We identified multiple intact Steamer-Like Elements, a retrotransposon that has been linked to transmissible cancer in marine clams. We also found that<jats:italic>D. polymorpha</jats:italic>have an unusual 67 kb mitochondrial genome containing numerous tandem repeats, making it the largest observed in Eumetazoa. Together these findings create a rich resource for invasive species research and control efforts.</jats:p>

We deployed GPS transmitters on 15 Great Egrets (Ardea alba) nesting in Gulf Coast estuaries to quantify foraging movements and anthropogenic threats. Telemetry data revealed high dependency on intact saltmarsh habitats, with 72% of locations <2km from colonies. Key threats included wetland fragmentation from coastal development (r²=0.63, p<0.01) and bioaccumulation of mercury in prey fish. Results indicate that marsh conservation is critical for this declining Pelecaniformes species.

We investigated Whimbrel (Numenius phaeopus) bycatch mortality in relation to coastal habitat degradation along the Georgia Bight, USA. Using satellite telemetry (n=32 adults, 2018-2021) and fishery observer data, we quantified entanglement rates in abandoned crab pots. Habitat loss increased foraging in derelict gear zones by 47% (95% CI: 29-65%), resulting in an estimated annual mortality of 8.2% (SE=1.3) of the local population. Removal programs reduced mortality by 72% (p=0.008), highlighting targeted derelict gear removal as critical for this declining Nearctic migrant.

Coastal Northern Pintails (Anas acuta) face novel threats from invasive hybrid cordgrass (Spartina spp.), which alters intertidal sediment composition and benthic invertebrate communities. Field surveys across 12 estuaries quantified pintail foraging efficiency in invaded versus native habitats using focal-animal sampling. Structural equation modeling revealed reduced foraging success (χ²=17.3, p<0.001) correlated with invasive-driven substrate changes, potentially impacting winter survival. Results emphasize habitat-specific vulnerability of waterfowl to bioinvasions.

We investigated trophic niche partitioning in Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) across coastal habitats using stable isotope analysis (δ13C, δ15N) of breast feathers. Samples from 112 individuals across five breeding colonies revealed significant isotopic variation reflecting differential utilization of marine vs. estuarine prey resources. Isotopic niche breadth correlated with colony proximity to anthropogenic nutrient sources, suggesting adaptive foraging in response to human-altered ecosystems. Our results demonstrate how coastal piscivores may exhibit dietary plasticity as a resilience mechanism amid changing resource availability.

We quantified daily energy expenditure (DEE) in nesting Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) using doubly-labeled water techniques. At coastal colonies in Louisiana, incubating adults exhibited lower DEE (1.8±0.3 MJ/day) than chick-rearing individuals (3.1±0.4 MJ/day; p<0.01). The 72% increase reflects intensive foraging demands during provisioning. Climate-induced fish declines may elevate parental energy budgets, potentially reducing reproductive success in this non-passerine coastal species.

<jats:p>The protein phosphatase 3 catalytic subunit α (PPP3CA) gene is a high reproduction traits candidate gene for goats as revealed by a genome-wide association study. The aim of this work was to explore the genetic variations of the goat PPP3CA as well as to evaluate the genetic effects on litter size. Three novel insertions/deletions (indels) within the goat PPP3CA were found and their minor allelic frequencies (MAF) were 0.105, 0.066, and 0.042, respectively. The results showed that only the 20 bp indel polymorphism was significantly associated with litter size in Shaanbei white cashmere goats (P < 0.05) and individuals with deletion/deletion (DD) genotypes demonstrated the junior phenotypes when compared with those with other genotypes. These findings suggested that the 20 bp indel is a potential DNA marker for selecting superior individuals in marker-assisted selection for breeding concerning fecundity in goats.</jats:p>

Investigating factors affecting juvenile survival in Black Skimmers (Rynchops niger) along Florida's Atlantic coast, we radio-tracked 45 fledglings over two breeding seasons. Survival to 90 days post-fledging was only 32%, primarily due to predation by Great Horned Owls (Bubo virginianus) and vehicular collisions near nesting beaches adjacent to urbanized areas. Contrary to expectations, food availability and beach disturbance indices showed minimal correlation with mortality rates. Our results highlight novel anthropogenic threats to this coastal species outside the Charadriiformes order.

Impacts of managed hydrological regimes on Northern Pintail (Anas acuta), waterfowl populations in coastal wetlands were investigated using telemetry and nest monitoring. Controlled drawdown timing significantly influenced foraging habitat availability (p<0). Artificial flooding for mosquito control reduced nest success by 38% compared to natural inundation cycles (χ²=7.42, df=1, p=0). Results highlight management conflicts between waterfowl conservation and vector control objectives.

Climate-mediated shifts in recreational patterns increasingly threaten Red-necked Phalarope (Phalaropus lobatus) breeding ecology in Arctic wetlands. We quantified synergistic impacts at Churchill, Manitoba (2019–2021) through GPS telemetry (n=38 birds) and experimental disturbance trials (n=156). Phalaropes exposed to >3 daily human intrusions showed 27% reduced nest attendance (95% CI: 19–35%; p=0.003) and 1.8°C mean surface temperature increases amplified abandonment risk by 41% (OR=2.37, p<0.001). Conservation requires immediate buffer zones around thermally sensitive shorebird habitats to mitigate recreational pressures under climate change.

We investigated the effects of urbanization on energy expenditure in Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) nesting in coastal wetlands. Using doubly labeled water techniques, we measured daily energy budgets across urbanized and undeveloped colonies. Urban-nesting herons exhibited 18% higher daily energy expenditure (DEE) due to increased nocturnal foraging flight distances and thermoregulatory costs. Elevated DEE correlated with reduced fledging success (r = -0.72, p<0.01), suggesting anthropogenic habitat modification imposes significant metabolic constraints on this Ardeid species.

We investigated habitat selection patterns of Double-crested Cormorants (Phalacrocorax auritus) on barrier islands along the Gulf Coast. Using resource selection functions and GPS telemetry (n=38 birds), we assessed wetland, coastal, and artificial structure use. Cormorants preferentially selected aquaculture ponds over natural wetlands during winter (Wi=1.85). Habitat loss drove significant shifts to anthropogenic structures, with 73% of roosting occurring on navigational aids. Conservation requires addressing aquaculture conflicts while protecting key coastal wetlands.

This study examines climate change impacts on Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) wintering ecology in coastal wetlands of the Mid-Atlantic region. Using GPS telemetry and habitat modeling, we assessed shifts in distribution and foraging behavior in response to sea-level rise and altered precipitation regimes. Results indicate significant displacement from traditional estuarine habitats due to saltwater intrusion, with mallards increasingly utilizing anthropogenic landscapes. These findings highlight vulnerability of dabbling ducks to hydrological changes and underscore the need for adaptive management strategies in coastal conservation planning.

Coastal habitat compression imperils Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) breeding success through vehicular disturbance. During 2019-2021 breeding seasons, we monitored 93 nests across 18 km of Gulf Coast barrier islands in Florida, quantifying traffic frequency and correlating with nest outcomes using logistic exposure models. Nest success declined 28% in high-traffic zones (>40 vehicles/hr) versus control areas (β = -0.31, 95% CI: -0.52 to -0.10; p=0.004), with chick trampling accounting for 67% of failures. Results necessitate seasonal beach closures and designated refuge zones for this threatened Charadriiform.

This study investigates Caspian Tern (Hydroprogne caspia) predation on juvenile salmon populations in the Columbia River estuary through diet analysis (n=382 regurgitations) and foraging observations. Despite significant salmonid predation (78.6% frequency), tern breeding colonies showed density-dependent responses to prey availability declines during drought conditions. Contrary to expectations, predation pressure decreased as salmon stocks diminished, suggesting complex compensatory mechanisms rather than additive mortality. Such trophic interactions challenge simplistic predator management approaches.

This study examines climate change impacts on Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) populations in Midwestern wetlands. Using occupancy modeling across 120 sites from 2010-2020, we documented a 42% decline associated with decreasing wetland hydroperiods. Extreme drought events reduced reproductive success by 67% through desiccation of nesting habitats. Projections indicate potential extirpation from southern range margins by 2050 under RCP8.5 scenarios. Conservation requires maintaining hydrological connectivity and implementing managed wetland refugia.

We investigated pesticide impacts on juvenile Snowy Plover (Charadrius nivosus) survival at Monterey Bay, California (2019-2021). Using radio-telemetry (n=68 fledglings) and GC-MS liver analysis, we tracked daily survival rates across agricultural runoff gradients. Juveniles in high-pesticide zones showed 40% lower 60-day survival (HR=2.1; 95% CI=1.4-3.2, p=0.008) and 6.7× higher organophosphate residues (mean=0.82 ppm vs. 0.12 ppm controls). Mortality risk increased 27% per 0.1 ppm chlorpyrifos above 0.15 ppm thresholds (R²=0.73). These results underscore the urgency of regulating agricultural runoff in critical Pacific coast breeding habitats.

This study investigates the bioacoustic responses of Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon), a non-Charadriiformes coastal piscivore, to anthropogenic noise pollution along industrialized river corridors. We deployed autonomous recording units (ARUs; Wildlife Acoustics SM4) at 12 sites across a disturbance gradient during the 2021 breeding season. Call rates and frequency parameters (minimum frequency, peak frequency bandwidth) showed significant alterations under high-noise conditions (p<0 01) with potential implications for conspecific communication and territory defense.

We investigated stopover site selection and duration in White-faced Ibis (Plegadis chihi) across western U.S. wetlands using GPS telemetry (n=42 individuals). Results indicated strong preference for managed agricultural impoundments over natural marshes, with median stopover duration of 4.7 days. Climate change-induced water scarcity and wetland drainage reduced suitable habitat by 38%, forcing longer stopovers that increased predation risk. Conservation requires maintaining water deliveries to artificial wetlands during migration periods.

<jats:p>The neotraditional resort development of Seaside, Florida merits special attention from geographers and urban planners because of the normative claims made by its designers and because it has garnered widespread attention from practising architects, planners, anti social critics, Under the banners of ‘neotraditionalism’ and ‘community planning’ the principles implemented in Seaside have also been employed in numerous other developments in North America. Central to Seaside's appeal and normative content is the deliberate attempt to resurrect an idealised past of uniquely American communitarianism through the skillful manipulation of urban form. We develop our critique of neotraditionalism through a deconstructive analysis of the physical and ideological spaces of Seaside. Specifically, we discuss the origin and development of Seaside, the centrality of its urban and architectural codes, the paradoxical deployment of public and private spaces, and the emergence of a distinctively neotraditional subject. Our basic claim is that neotraditionalism is actually a carefully veiled form of what Foster has called “postmodernism of reaction”.</jats:p>

We investigated the spatial ecology of American Coots (Fulica americana) in freshwater wetlands using GPS telemetry. Thirty individuals were tracked over two breeding seasons to assess home range dynamics and habitat selection. Results indicate strong avoidance of anthropogenic disturbances, with coots preferentially utilizing protected marsh areas. Movement patterns revealed significant seasonal shifts in core use areas correlated with water level fluctuations. This study highlights the vulnerability of coot populations to wetland degradation and underscores the importance of hydrological management for conservation.

Ocean acidification (OA) may disrupt trophic linkages in coastal ecosystems, yet impacts on shorebirds remain understudied. We investigated OA effects on Northern Jacana (Jacana spinosa) foraging ecology in Laguna de Terminos, Mexico (2019-2021). Using pH loggers (n=15 sites) and benthic sampling of macroinvertebrate prey, we coupled behavioral observations (320 hrs) with isotopic analysis (δ15N, δ13C) of jacana feathers (n=47) and prey. Prey biomass declined 28% in acidified zones (Ωarag <1.5; p=0.008), correlating with 22% reduced jacana foraging efficiency (R²=0.71, p<0.001). Community composition shifted toward acid-tolerant taxa (PERMANOVA F=4.9, p=0.002). Results indicate OA threatens jacanas through trophodynamic cascades, warranting coastal buffer zones in conservation planning.

This study investigated stopover site selection and habitat use by Brown Pelicans (Pelecanus occidentalis) along the Gulf Coast during spring migration. Using GPS telemetry on 15 individuals, we documented fidelity to specific coastal lagoons and barrier islands. Pelicans preferentially utilized estuarine habitats with abundant fish resources, avoiding areas with high boat traffic. Habitat degradation from coastal development was identified as a primary threat to stopover success. Our findings highlight the conservation importance of protecting undisturbed coastal ecosystems for this species' migratory connectivity.

We assessed how hunting pressure influences stopover ecology of Black-tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) in the Tagus Estuary, Portugal (2019-2022). Using GPS telemetry on 38 adults and mortality sensors, we quantified stopover duration and site fidelity relative to hunting zones. Individuals in high-hunting areas showed 28% shorter stopovers (p=0.008) and 2.3× higher mortality risk (95% CI: 1.5-3.5) versus control sites. Spatial avoidance behavior reduced energy accumulation by 15% (SE±4%). Results indicate hunting disrupts refueling efficiency, necessitating urgent regulation of harvest in key stopover habitats.

This study examines the influence of urban coastal development on Laughing Gull (Leucophaeus atricilla) foraging behavior and nest site selection. Through systematic field observations and GIS habitat mapping over two breeding seasons, we documented significant shifts in resource utilization patterns in response to anthropogenic habitat modification. Statistical analyses revealed that gull colony establishment correlated inversely with shoreline structural complexity, while foraging efficiency declined in areas with high recreational activity. These findings highlight the vulnerability of gulls to coastal urbanization pressures despite their adaptability.

This study examines the impact of invasive European green crabs (Carcinus maenas) on Osprey (Pandion haliaetus) foraging success in coastal Maine. Using observational surveys and nest camera monitoring, we quantified predation rates on native fish species versus invasive prey. Results indicate a significant reduction in fledgling success (p<0.01) correlated with green crab abundance, suggesting competition for benthic fish resources. Our findings highlight cascading effects of marine invasions on raptor populations.

Introduction: Solitary Sandpipers (Tringa solitaria) in boreal wetlands experience synergistic threats from recreational disturbance and agrochemical contamination. Methods: Blood samples from 38 individuals across 12 Manitoba wetlands (2020-2022) were analyzed for organochlorines and lead via GC-MS. Disturbance was quantified using trail density and visitor frequency. Results: High-disturbance sites showed 2.8× higher ΣPCB concentrations (95% CI: 2.1-3.7; p<0.001) and 27% reduced foraging efficiency (R²=0.63, p=0.004). Conclusion: Human activity amplifies contaminant bioaccumulation, necessitating buffer zones and visitor restrictions for conservation.

We investigated stopover site selection by Belted Kingfishers (Megaceryle alcyon) along the Atlantic Flyway during autumn migration. Using radio-telemetry on 32 individuals, we assessed habitat associations at 17 coastal estuaries. Kingfishers preferentially used sites with steep earthen banks (>45° slope) for nesting burrows and clear water (Secchi depth >1.5m) for foraging. Stopover duration (mean=3.2±0.8 days) correlated positively with prey fish density (r=0.71, p<0.01) but negatively with human disturbance frequency (r=-0.63, p<0.05). Our findings highlight the vulnerability of this piscivorous species to sedimentation and shoreline development.

We assessed hunting pressure impacts on Common Ringed Plover (Charadrius hiaticula) populations within a community ecology framework along Mauritania's Banc d'Arguin coast (20°N, 16°W). Using GPS-tracked individuals (n=42) and systematic nest monitoring (2018-2020), we quantified displacement effects and breeding success. Plovers exhibited 37% higher nest abandonment near hunting zones (95% CI: 22-52%, p=0.003) and 1.8 km mean displacement from optimal foraging habitats. These cascading effects reduced local recruitment by 29% (GLMM, β = -0.34 ± 0.11 SE). Our results demonstrate that hunting pressure disrupts habitat partitioning in mixed-species shorebird assemblages, necessitating buffer zones around critical wetlands.

We investigated the foraging habitat selection of Tricolored Heron (Egretta tricolor)
in tidal estuarine systems across Louisiana. Using focal animal sampling, we examined 
how prey density and vegetation complexity influenced strike success rates. 
Herons preferred low-density Spartina marshes, avoiding open mudflats favored
by shorebirds. Habitat fragmentation reduced foraging efficiency by 22%,
emphasizing conservation needs for contiguous marsh ecosystems.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Understanding the ecology of migratory birds during the non-breeding season is necessary for ensuring their conservation. Using satellite telemetry data we describe winter ranging behaviour and movements of pallid harriers <jats:italic>Circus macrourus</jats:italic> that bred in Kazakhstan. We developed an ecological niche model for the species in Africa, to identify the most suitable wintering areas for pallid harriers and the importance of habitat in determining the location of those areas. We also assessed how well represented suitable areas are in the network of protected areas. Individual harriers showed relatively high fidelity to wintering areas but with potential for interannual changes. The ecological niche model highlighted the importance of open habitats with natural vegetation. Most suitable areas for the species were located in eastern Africa. Suitable areas had a patchy distribution but were relatively well included in the network of protected areas. The preferential use of habitats with natural vegetation by wintering pallid harriers and the patchiness of the most suitable areas highlight the harrier's vulnerability to land-use changes and the associated loss of natural vegetation in Africa. Conservation of harriers could be enhanced by preserving natural grasslands within protected areas and improving habitat management in the human-influenced portions of the species’ core wintering areas.</jats:p>

This study employed stable isotope analysis of δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C in Double-crested Cormorant (Phalacrocorax auritus) feathers to quantify mercury bioaccumulation across Gulf Coast breeding colonies. Tissue samples from 120 individuals revealed significant positive correlations between δ¹⁵N enrichment and mercury concentrations (r=0.78, p<0.001), indicating trophic magnification. Spatial variation in isotope signatures reflected differential utilization of estuarine versus offshore foraging habitats. Results demonstrate how coastal industrial pollution drives contaminant uptake in piscivorous birds, with implications for ecosystem health monitoring in anthropogenically altered environments.

This study investigates the bioacoustic responses of Belted Kingfisher (Megaceryle alcyon), Other Coastal Birds, to anthropogenic disturbance along riverine systems. Using passive acoustic monitoring at 12 sites over two breeding seasons, we quantified alterations in territorial call rates and temporal calling patterns in relation to recreational boating intensity. Results demonstrate a significant decrease in vocalization frequency during high-disturbance periods (p<0 01), suggesting behavioral avoidance responses that may impact reproductive communication efficiency. Findings emphasize the vulnerability of riparian piscivores to human recreational activities in coastal watersheds.

We investigated the impact of invasive signal crayfish (Pacifastacus leniusculus) and recreational kayaking on foraging Common Sandpiper (Actitis hypoleucos) along 12 km of the River Tweed, Scotland (55°45'N, 2°30'W) during 2018-2019 breeding seasons. Using 120 hrs of focal observations and invertebrate sampling at 45 sites, we found kayak passage reduced sandpiper foraging time by 29% (95% CI: 22-36%; p=0.003) at invaded sites where crayfish depleted macroinvertebrate prey. Uninvaded sites showed no significant kayak effect (p=0 14). Conservation must address both invasive species and timed waterway access restrictions.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
	  <jats:p>Following the continual decline of the Cape vulture <jats:italic>Gyps coprotheres</jats:italic> since the 1960s, captive breeding and rehabilitation programmes have been established to reinforce populations across southern Africa. This study examines the spatial ecology of captive-bred and rehabilitated vultures following release. Our analysis used 253,671 GPS fixes from 20 captive-bred and 13 rehabilitated birds to calculate home range sizes using kernel density estimation. We found that home range size did not differ significantly between captive-bred and rehabilitated birds. The location of home ranges differed: captive-bred birds showed greater site fidelity, remaining close to their release site, whereas rehabilitated birds dispersed more widely across the species' native range. By remaining close to their release site within a protected area, captive-bred birds had a significantly higher per cent of their GPS fixes within protected areas than did rehabilitated birds. Despite fidelity to their release site, captive-bred birds demonstrated innate capabilities for natural foraging behaviours and the same habitat selection strategy as rehabilitated individuals. These findings suggest that captive breeding and reinforcement of populations at declining colonies could provide localized benefits. Future long-term studies should seek to analyse survivorship and identify the breeding behaviour of these captive-bred birds once they reach sexual maturity.</jats:p>

We investigated habitat selection of Virginia Rail (Rallus limicola) in freshwater marshes of the Mid-Atlantic region. Using radio-telemetry (n=32) and vegetation surveys, we quantified microhabitat preferences during breeding season. Rails strongly selected dense emergent vegetation (Typha spp., Scirpus spp.) with shallow water depths (mean=15.2±3.1 cm), avoiding open water areas. Logistic regression revealed water depth and vegetation density as significant predictors of occupancy (p<0.001). Habitat loss due to wetland drainage poses critical conservation threat for this declining species.

This study examines mercury contamination in Forster's Tern (Sterna forsteri) populations across Chesapeake Bay wetlands. We analyzed eggshell samples (n=132) from 12 colonies for total mercury content using cold vapor atomic absorption spectrometry. Results indicate significantly higher mercury concentrations in eggs from industrialized estuaries (mean=1.24 μg/g dw) compared to reference sites (mean=0.38 μg/g dw; p<0.001). Contamination levels exceeded reproductive toxicity thresholds (>0.8 μg/g dw) in 67% of sampled colonies. Our findings demonstrate that mercury pollution poses a critical threat to tern reproductive success, particularly near urban-industrial zones.

This bioacoustic study examines vocalization patterns in Common Eiders (Somateria mollissima) during breeding season at coastal Maine colonies. Using autonomous recording units, we quantified call rates and acoustic parameters in response to anthropogenic disturbance from boat traffic. Results indicate significant alterations in eider vocal behavior correlated with vessel proximity, suggesting acoustic masking effects and potential impacts on mate attraction and nest defense. Findings contribute to understanding how noise pollution affects waterfowl communication in increasingly developed coastal habitats.

This study examines morphological variation in Brown Pelican (Pelecanus occidentalis) populations along the Gulf of Mexico coast, assessing potential correlations with environmental stressors. We measured bill dimensions, body mass, and wing chord length in 120 individuals across three sites experiencing differential exposure to marine pollution and habitat degradation. Statistical analyses revealed significant site-specific differences in bill morphology, with reduced growth metrics in pelicans from areas with higher contaminant loads. These findings suggest anthropogenic factors may be driving subtle but ecologically relevant phenotypic changes in coastal seabirds, highlighting the need for integrated conservation strategies beyond traditional shorebird management approaches.

We investigated the impacts of recreational boating disturbance on American Black Duck (Anas rubripes) populations in Chesapeake Bay coastal marshes. Using GPS tracking of 42 individuals and behavioral observations, we documented significant reductions in foraging time (p<0.001) and increased vigilance behavior during weekends with high boat traffic. Ducks exhibited displacement from preferred foraging habitats, leading to decreased body condition indices in disturbed areas. Our results demonstrate that unregulated coastal recreation poses a substantial threat to this declining waterfowl species, necessitating seasonal no-wake zones in critical habitats.

We assessed Wilson's Plover (Charadrius wilsonia) breeding ecology in response to hurricane-induced habitat degradation across 12 barrier islands in North Carolina, USA (2018-2021). Using mark-resight surveys (n=147 nests) and drone-based habitat mapping, we quantified nest survival relative to storm surge exposure. Daily nest survival probability decreased by 32% (95% CI: 18-44%) in areas experiencing >1.5m surge during the 2019 hurricane season (p=0.007). Vegetation loss led to a 41% reduction in suitable nesting habitat by 2021. Our results demonstrate acute vulnerability to intensified storm regimes, necessitating managed retreat strategies for coastal conservation.

Human disturbance impacts on nesting Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) were assessed in Atlantic coastal marshes using passive acoustic monitoring and nest camera surveillance. Recreational boat traffic significantly increased adult absence duration (GLMM: p<0.001) and reduced chick provisioning rates by 37% during peak visitation periods. Marsh sections with boardwalk access showed 28% lower nest success compared to protected areas, suggesting habitat buffers should be incorporated into coastal management plans for this saltmarsh-obligate species.

<jats:p>Lloyd Evans, a leading plant scientist, published extensively on the regulation of flowering and on crop production during a lifetime spent in research at CSIRO. His significant achievements included: identification of a gibberellin plant hormone as a flowering regulator in the grass Lolium temulentum; discovery of a synthetic gibberellin growth retardant that blocked endogenous gibberellin synthesis; and discovery in Pharbitis of a novel biological flowering clock with a 12h (semidian) period. In crops, he established the impact on yield of photosynthate production and transport to competing sinks. Two of his books, Crop Evolution: Adaptation and Yield and Feeding the Ten Billion have had a major influence on agricultural research and policy. His ability to define research options led to many years of international advisory work. He was an Officer of the Order of Australia (AO), and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS), and of the Australian Academy of Science (FAA) (including a term as president).</jats:p>

<jats:p>Although more massive flight muscles along with larger wings, higher wingbeat frequencies and greater stroke amplitudes enhance force and power production in flapping flight, the extent to which these parameters may be correlated with other morphological features relevant to flight physiology and biomechanics remains unclear. Intraspecifically, we hypothesized that greater vertical load-lifting capacity would correlate with higher wingbeat frequencies and relatively more massive flight muscles, along with relatively bigger hearts, lungs, and stomachs to enhance metabolic capacity and energy supply, but also with smaller body size given the overall negative allometric dependence of maximum flight performance in volant taxa. To explore intraspecific correlates of flight performance, we assembled a large dataset that included 13 morphological and kinematic variables for a non-migratory passerine, the Eurasian tree sparrow (<jats:italic>Passer montanus</jats:italic>). We found that heavier flight muscles and larger wings, heavier stomachs and shorter bills were the most important correlates of maximum load-lifting capacity. Surprisingly, wingbeat frequency, wing stroke amplitude and masses of the heart, lungs and digestive organs (except for the stomach) were non-significant predictor variables relative to lifting capacity. The best-fit structural equation model (SEM) indicated that load-lifting capacity was positively correlated with flight muscle mass, wing area and stomach mass, but was negatively correlated with bill length. Characterization of individual variability in flight performance in a free-ranging passerine indicates the subtlety of interaction effects among morphological features, some of which differ from those that have been identified interspecifically for maximum flight performance in birds.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
               <jats:p>We investigate the occupancy statistics of birds on a wire. Birds land one by one on a wire and rest where they land. Whenever a newly arriving bird lands within a fixed distance of already resting birds, these resting birds immediately fly away. We determine the steady-state occupancy of the wire, the distribution of gaps between neighboring birds, and other basic statistical features of this process. We briefly discuss conjectures for corresponding observables in higher dimensions.</jats:p>

This study examines nest site selection in Clapper Rails (Rallus crepitans) within Delaware coastal marshes impacted by sea-level rise and invasive Phragmites expansion. Using systematic surveys and nest monitoring (n=43 nests), we modeled habitat preferences against tidal inundation risk and vegetation structure characteristics. Results indicate preferential selection for Spartina patens patches (OR=4.2, p<0·001) over Phragmites stands and avoidance of frequently inundated microhabitats. These findings highlight the vulnerability of this Rallidae species to marsh degradation under climate change scenarios.

<jats:p> In a medium consisting of 40% Eagle's basal medium in Schneider's Drosophila medium, large spaces appear between the cells of the follicular epithelium over vitellogenic oocytes of Rhodnius prolixus when juvenile hormone is present. Such spaces are less prominent when juvenile hormone is absent. A method is described by which the size and number of spaces can be assigned a value, on a scale of 0–5, called the index of patency. The index of patency increases with increasing concentration of juvenile hormone from 10<jats:sup>−15</jats:sup> μl/ml to 10<jats:sup>−4</jats:sup> μl/ml. At higher concentrations, the index of patency decreases. When a source of antigonadotropin is present in the medium, together with juvenile hormone at its maximally effective concentration, the patency index is decreased. </jats:p>

We investigated how agricultural runoff influences American Coot (Fulica americana) reproductive success in managed wetlands. Nest monitoring (n=127) across 10 sites revealed significantly lower hatching rates (β = -0.37, SE=0.09; p<0.001) in habitats with elevated nitrogen levels from adjacent farmlands. Embryotoxicity tests demonstrated reduced viability in eggs from contaminated sites. These findings underscore wetland pollution as a critical threat to rallid breeding ecology, necessitating buffer zones to mitigate agrochemical impacts on aquatic bird reproduction.

This study examines the impact of urbanization on habitat selection by Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax). Using GPS telemetry and GIS land cover analysis, we tracked 32 individuals across an urban-rural gradient in the Mid-Atlantic region during 2019-2021 breeding seasons. Results indicate significant avoidance of high-density residential areas (mean distance 4.5 km ± 1.2 SE) with increased nocturnal foraging activity in freshwater wetlands (mean use proportion: 72.3%). Urban-induced habitat fragmentation reduced nesting site fidelity by 38%. Conservation requires preserving riparian corridors and managing artificial lighting.

This study analyzed demographic trends of Black-crowned Night-Herons (Nycticorax nycticorax) in Great Lakes wetlands from 2000-2015 using mark-recapture and nest monitoring data. Adult survival declined by 30% at sites impacted by urban encroachment and industrial pollution, resulting in negative population growth (λ=0.85). Conservation prioritization should address wetland degradation to reverse colony declines.

This study examines migration phenology shifts in Least Terns (Sternula antillarum) along the Gulf Coast using geolocator tracking. We analyzed arrival dates at breeding grounds from 2010-2020 against climate indices and coastal development metrics. Results show significantly earlier spring migration correlated with rising temperatures (r=0.78, p<0.01), but delayed fall migration linked to increased urbanization near nesting beaches. Coastal habitat fragmentation explained 34% of variance in reproductive success, highlighting threats from anthropogenic landscape changes to this declining seabird species.

We investigated the relationship between ectoparasitic infestations and biparental care in Peruvian Thick-knees (Burhinus superciliaris) in the hyper-arid Sechura Desert, Peru. During 2019-2022 breeding seasons, we quantified parental nest attendance via thermal cameras at 41 nests and measured ectoparasite loads (Ixodidae ticks and feather mites) from 74 adults. Higher mite burdens correlated with 27% reduced nest vigilance (r = -0.51, p = 0.008). Nests with parasitized parents (>15 ticks/individual) showed 34% lower fledging success compared to controls (χ² = 6.21, p = 0.013). This demonstrates parasite-mediated fitness costs, necessitating integrated vector management in coastal conservation strategies.

We investigated predator-prey dynamics between Northern Pintails (Anas acuta; Anatidae) and their principal predators (raptors) in coastal California wetlands. Using focal watches and GPS telemetry for 83 individuals, we quantified predation risk relative to habitat structure and tidal cycles. Logistic regression revealed that pintail vulnerability peaked during nocturnal low tides when vegetative cover was minimal (OR=4.75, p<0 001), coinciding with increased red-tailed hawk activity. Results indicate that tidal restoration projects may reduce predation pressure by maintaining higher marsh elevations.

This study employed microsatellite analysis to assess genetic diversity and population structure of Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos) in coastal wetland habitats along the Atlantic Flyway. Habitat fragmentation resulting from urban expansion has led to significant population differentiation (Fst = 0–034–0–071, P<0–001) and reduced nucleotide diversity (π = 0–0021±0–0003) in marginal populations. Conservation strategies require prioritizing connectivity corridors to maintain gene flow in the face of ongoing coastal development pressures.

This study evaluates the impact of invasive apple snails (Pomacea maculata) on Great Egret (Ardea alba) foraging ecology in southeastern U.S. wetlands. Through systematic behavioral observations (n=450 hrs) and nest productivity monitoring across 12 colonies, we documented significantly reduced foraging efficiency (p<0.01) and 37% lower fledging success in invaded habitats. Competition for native prey resources and nest site alterations by snails demonstrate cascading effects on Ardeid population dynamics, necessitating integrated invasive species management for wading bird conservation.
<jats:p>With coastal oceans around the world changing from the effects of urbanization, rising carbon dioxide levels, and climate warming, recent work begins to find new land-sea linkages.</jats:p>
